News.title: Putin’s madcap MPs BAN chicken Kyiv from menu… and then serve exact same dish under petty rebrand
News.content:
FOWL PLAY Putin’s madcap MPs BAN chicken Kyiv from menu… and then serve exact same dish under petty rebrand







Next

PUTIN’S madcap government has banned Chicken Kyiv from the menu – and then serves the same dish under a different name.

The canteen at the State Duma, Russia’s parliament in Moscow, has stopped serving Chicken Kyiv, instead renaming the dish “cutlet with butter.”



The dish has been removed from the menu for MPs in their canteen, according to Alexander Yunashev, a Russian journalist.

The canteen is available to elected MPs, many of whom allegedly entered office following “rigged” elections to secure a majority for pro-Putin, pro-war politicians.



A Ukrainian report mocked the Russian parliament for its “sanctions against a cutlet.”

An image shared by Yunashev shows the cutlet costs £2.42.



In contrast, the Moscow-based restaurant chain Brusnika continues to sell “Chicken Kyiv,” charging £3.90.

The bizarre change is not the first time the popular dish has been renamed in Russian state institutions.

The New York Times reported that the Russian Foreign Ministry’s canteen listed a meal called “Chicken Crimea,” long before the Ukraine war escalated.

Following the invasion of Ukraine, several Russian cafes and restaurants quietly scrubbed “Chicken Kyiv” from their menus and renamed the dish.



The madcap move comes more than four-and-a-half years into the violent war.

Russia has also rebranded companies or changed the names of certain locations that the country deems related to Ukraine or the West.

Following Russia’s exit from global networks in 2022, new domestic owners bought the abandoned assets and renamed them.



Starbucks became Stars Coffee, Pizza Hut became Pizza N, and McDonald’s became “Vkusno & tochka,” or Tasty and That’s It.

Several financial institutions also rebranded their former Russian operations to local independent names with Deloitte becoming Business Solutions and Technologies (BST) and PwC changed to Technologies of Trust.

After an arduous battle for Bakhmut, Russian authorities declared the city would be known by its Soviet-era name, Artemovsk.

Putin recently vowed he will be “victorious” in his bloody war against Ukraine after he called up thousands more troops.

Since Russia invaded in February 2022, the Russian President’s military machine has caused much violence and death in Ukraine.

News.title: Horror moment huge ball of fireworks explodes at festival leaving 13 injured & panicked festival-goers fleeing for cover
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horror moment a huge ball of fireworks explodes at a festival and injures 13 – including children.

Screaming families ran for cover as the terrifying blasts ripped through a packed square in San Jeronimo Cuatro Vientos, Mexico.



Shocking footage shows a burning red fireball spinning across a stage, showering sparks, before spiralling out of control.

Cheerful horn and drum music plays while the fizzling fireworks explode beneath strings of shiny bunting.



Suddenly a terrifying boom shatters the party atmosphere and the live band abruptly cuts out as the camera jolts to the floor.

Out-of-control pyrotechnics fire into the crowd and appear to explode close to the person filming as the screen lights up with a white-hot blast.

Children can be heard screaming as adults shout instructions and flee from the horrifying blasts.

The terrifying spectacle unfolded on Sunday night during a festival held in honour of the community’s patron saint.

Emergency services scrambled to the scene of the horror to find at least 13 people injured, including children.

Victims suffered first and second degree burns, bruising and suspected fractures with some reported to be in serious condition.



Those with more severe burns were rushed to the Regional High Specialty Hospital of Ixtapaluca.

Early reports said the explosion happened during the burning of a traditional “torito”, a bull-shaped frame loaded with fireworks that is carried or moved among crowds during celebrations.

A stray firework or spark may have ignited a large stash of pyrotechnics and triggered an explosion, according to investigators who are looking into the theory.



The Attorney General’s Office of the State of Mexico has launched a probe into the incident.

Local authorities are also checking whether organisers had the required permits from Mexico’s Defence Ministry and Civil Protection authorities for the fireworks display.

Earlier this month in Mexico a huge firework blast killed ten people and injured 64.

The religious celebration in Nuestra Señora de la Luz church, Temascalcingo ended in tragedy after a botched spectacle caused a wall to collapse and crush festival-goers.

Horrifying explosions rocked the square in front of the church during the burning of the traditional bull.



Just days later, a second botched display sent fireworks shooting into a packed square and injuring four people.

Fiery explosions ricocheted through the city centre of Palenque during festivities for Mexican Independence Day.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shocking footage shows family members grabbing their kids and fleeing for their lives as sparks fly all around them.

Showers of sparks and whizzing rockets splattered the dark skies.

News.title: Paedo ex-world snooker champ Graeme Dott ‘targeted in prison’ as jail bosses move perv for his own safety
News.content:
Next

PAEDO ex-world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been targeted in jail by other lags over his twisted crimes.

Dott, 49, was caged for seven years today after being convicted of historical sex attacks on two children.



The beast, of Larkhall in Lanarkshire, targeted the boy and girl from the ages of eight and nine.

Dott, who was found guilty last month following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow, exposed himself to the primary school-age boy and girl, touched them inappropriately and kissed them.



The girl was abused between 1993 and 1996, and the boy between 2006 – the year Dott was world champ – and 2010.

His lawyer today revealed jail chiefs have had to move the paedo snooker star after he was threatened by other lags.



Defence advocate Euan Dow said Dott’s public profile and the nature of the offences meant he had “already been the target of threats” in custody which meant he had been moved in the prison.

He added Dott was “separated from his wife”. He added: “However, she remains supportive of him.”



And he said they have two children and he “continues to enjoy the support of his family and friends”.

He told the court that Dott had a successful snooker career spanning 25 years, but has “long standing mental health issues”.

He said Dott “continues to deny responsibility for the offences”.

But he recognises a custodial sentence is inevitable, he added.

Mr Dow said Dott – who he said has two minor road traffic convictions – was interviewed in 2001 in connection with his crimes but was not formally charged.



He added: “He accepts that both personal and professional reputations have been destroyed.”

At the High Court in Edinburgh today Lord Harrower said his “behaviour towards both children involved a gross breach of trust”.

He added: “You robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood.”

He was placed on the sex offenders register indefinitely.

Jurors heard the female victim, now in her 40s, said Dott abused her repeatedly. He began by “caressing” her bottom during a piggy-back and went on to expose himself and touch her with parts of his body.

The male victim, now in his late 20s, said much of the abuse happened in a shower, where Dott would enter partly or fully undressed and touch him “in inappropriate places”.



He tried to buy their silence with gifts or money. Claims against him were made in 2001 by his female victim, but a breakthrough did not come until 2024 when the second person came forward.

Father-of-two Dott, from Larkhall, Lanarkshire, denied all the allegations during a week-long trial branding them “nonsense and lies”.

Lord Harrower said: “So far as culpability is concerned, each child was vulnerable for reasons that went beyond simply their age. Your behaviour towards them bore the classic hallmarks of grooming.

“You rewarded them with treats, or warned them that they wouldn’t be believed if they told anyone. You disguised your abuse as part of a game or personal care.”

He said that during the offences against the female “you yourself were still a child”. But the judge said that by the time he started abusing his male victim Dott was a married man” in his thirties, with a family of his own. He added: “Your behaviour towards both children involved a gross violation of trust.



“As for harm, you robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood. I am grateful to each of them for providing me with personal statements, in which they describe their struggles to make sense of their lives amid the overwhelming emotions of fear, shame and anger, as well as the continuing impact into adulthood that your actions have had on their mental well-being.”

He said Dott’s only previous convictions were for relatively minor road traffic offences, and said a social worker who provided a report for the hearing assessed Dott “as presenting with a below average risk of sexual re-offending”.

But he added: “You continue to maintain your innocence, which is of course your right. However, it also means that I am unable to take account of any remorse on your part, or any insight into the harm you inflicted.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The sentence was backdated to last month when Dott was convicted.

The disgraced player, who was wearing a suit, turned to people gathered in the court and “I’ll see you later” as he was led away in cuffs.

News.title: Five years since Wayne Couzens was sentenced our girls STILL aren’t safe as monsters dodge jail & sex crimes rise
News.content:
Next

WHEN Libby Squire was raped and murdered by a stranger on a night out, her mum was enraged to find out her daughter’s attacker had struck before.

Pawel Relowicz, 26, had already been convicted for a string of sexually motivated offences including voyeurism.



Now, ahead of the fifth anniversary of Wayne Couzens being sentenced for Sarah Everard’s murder on 30th September, The Sun can reveal how career criminals are routinely spared jail for sex crimes.

Sarah was heading home in Brixton, London, when she encountered Couzens who is said to have handcuffed her before driving out to Kent where he raped and strangled her, before burning her body.



Victims and experts warn that perverts are getting away with sick behaviour – while Libby’s mum Lisa Squire warns that unless courts don’t get to grip with lesser sex offences, more women could be killed just like her daughter.

Shocking figures uncovered by The Sun show that ONE career criminal is spared jail every day after committing a sex crime.

Over a third of beasts with ten or more prior convictions or cautions dodged jail when they struck again last year, a Sun investigation has found.

“It doesn’t surprise me at all that the courts aren’t taking these ‘softer’ offences seriously,” Lisa said.



“The police are taking crimes against women and girls much more seriously, but the judiciary isn’t taking the same approach.

“We need to get magistrates and judges to actually realise that these offences are really dangerous red flags, and they will escalate in most cases.

“If you can punish those properly at the very beginning and get that perpetrator some help, then hopefully we can stop some rape and murders further down the line.”

Of 1,094 sex beasts sentenced in 2025 who had double or even triple digits of previous convictions and/or cautions 393 walked free from court with non-custodial terms.



Instead of being banged up, hundreds of perverts were handed soft punishments like community service or a fine.

The horrifying sum includes 11 of England and Wales’ most prolific offenders – who have more than 75 previous convictions to their name.

The statistics reveal a steady and alarming increase in leniency over recent years.

In 2021, just 28 per cent of these heavily convicted and cautioned criminals were spared jail after committing a sex crime.



That figure jumped to 30.9 per cent in 2024. Now, the latest figures show it has surged again, with 35.9 per cent dodging prison in 2025.

Libby was attacked and murdered on 1st February 2019 after being attacked by Relowicz who was said to have been ‘prowling’ the streets looking for a victim.

Two years prior, the butcher, now 31, had put his head through an open window to watch a couple having sex. He went on to burgle two houses, leaving a used condom in one and stole sex toys.

Lisa has been campaigning for better education in schools around sexual offences with her charity It Does Matter, and hopes that women and girls will be safer by 2031.

“The government pledged to halve violence against women and girls in ten years but so far it’s not happened,” she said.



“I want to see harsher sentences for these crimes, and I’m hopeful that the specialised rape courts will help reduce waiting time for victims.

“We’ve still got a huge mountain to climb, but I’m hopeful that things will get better.”

Like Relowicz, Couzens is believed to have been displaying behaviours linked to sexual offences. In 2015 a man – believed to have been Couzens – was reported in Kent for being naked waist-down in a car.

'Unspeakable savagery' Jodie Edith hoped her sister’s nightmare at the hands of an abusive partner would be over when Laura Mortimore announced she was leaving him. But days later the 31-year-old and her daughter Ella Dalby, 11, were murdered by Christopher Boon in an attack a judge called “unspeakable savagery” in 2018. Ella had rushed into the house after seeing Boon attacking her mother, which family believe was in an attempt to save them both. He had previously been convicted of domestic violence in 2010 after assaulting a previous partner and her mother. Jodie told The Sun: “We had no idea of his previous conviction, and if we had been aware there would have been opportunities to step in. “If there was a national register, then a service could have stepped in. We know that concerns were raised at school because Ella’s behaviour had changed, but nothing came of that.” A report in 2022 found that opportunities had been missed to prosecute Boon after cops visited the house on boxing day in 2014. Laura told officers that she had been assaulted but didn’t want to press charges, and Ella made comments supporting what had happened. Gloucestershire Police admitted they may have had enough evidence to pursue a prosecution. “We have to live with the fact that we had no idea about how violent he was,” Jodie said. “There is always previous behaviour in a case like Laura’s. There is always escalation and a register would allow people to access that information quickly. “I also want to see more education in schools so children know who they can talk to if they’re seeing stuff at home. “Things are getting better with specialised courts for rape victims, but there is still a long way to go.” Boon was jailed for life and has to serve a minmum of 29 years in prison.

It was also alleged that he was referred to as ‘the rapist’ by his colleagues at the Nuclear Constabulary.

He was handed a whole life order for the killing which shocked the nation and led to widespread vigils and calls for changes to reduce violence against women and girls.



However, their fight continues.

Lenient sentences imposed by soft-touch judges mean communities up and down the country are unknowingly sharing their streets with repeat offenders.

Although 701 serial offenders were jailed for their crimes last year, critics said releasing one in three back onto the streets was a massive public safety risk.

Former Met detective Peter Bleksley said: “These judges facilitate these offences and create further victims of crime.

“Serial offenders will do one thing – commit more crime, and cause more mayhem.



“Any experienced police officer will tell you there is escalation in offending if it is not nipped in the bud.

“A shoplifter will become a burglar, a flasher will become a rapist if they are not stopped, punished, and shown the error of their ways.

“If we freed up capacity in prisons by deporting foreign criminals, then we could lock up our own wrong’uns.

“Politicians need to fund more prison places and rehabilitation programmes.”



Carole Gould, whose daughter Ellie, 17, was murdered by her former boyfriend Thomas Griffiths after calling off their relationship, wants to see laws changed to stop offenders getting a more lenient sentence for using a weapon from inside the home.

Under current laws, if a killer uses a weapon in their victim’s home they get a maximum of 15 years in jail. Weapons wielded outside attract tougher sentences of 25 years because they are considered premeditated.

Ellie was murdered at her home in Calne, Wilts, in May 2019 after ending her relationship with fellow six former Griffiths.

He repeatedly stabbed Ellie before washing the knife to get rid of his DNA and sticking it back into her neck to make it look like suicide. He also told pals scratches on his face, caused by Ellie as she fought to live, were self- harm marks due to stress.



Despite the callous cover-up, Griffiths, who pleaded guilty to murder, was told he would be eligible to apply for parole after 12 and a half years of a life sentence.

Carole, 50, said: “It’s as if my child’s life is worth less because she was killed inside the home where she felt safe.

“The law makes no sense at all. He even tried to cover up what he’d done and tried to stage a suicide. This wasn’t a crime in which he suddenly lost control in some way and then showed sorrow.

“A criminologist described Griffiths as deeply unknowable because you don’t know what’s going on in his head and you never will. He will be 30 when he’s freed and can start dating again.



“In my opinion, he’ll carry on being a danger to women.

“There’s no robust probation service and no domestic abuse register to protect victims.”



Similarly, Gail Smith’s daughter was murdered by a man with multiple convictions including hitting a man with his car.

Kevin Mannion stabbed Elinor O’Brien, 22, in the groin following an argument, and she died three days later in hospital in 2022. He had stabbed her in the breast a few days earlier during another argument.

“As a society we’re very complacent about men killing women and I don’t think that’s changed in recent years,” Gail said.

“We just accept that some men just get violent and kill their partner. That shouldn’t be acceptable.

“Mannion was a very violent man and had several convictions. I don’t think there is enough funding that goes into tracking people like him.



“I’d like to see probation services and prisons properly funded so men with a pattern of violent behaviour can be monitored when released from prison.

“I’d also like to see longer sentences for perpetrators. Ellie’s killer got 23 and a half years, but he’ll still be a danger to women when he comes out.

“He’ll be able to form relationships and put those women at risk. It does worry me.”

'More needs to be done' By Yasmin Harisha STANDING in the darkness, with flashing blue lights of emergency vehicles, Nour Norris watched in complete horror as paramedics frantically tried to save her 22-year-old niece, and 49-year-old sister. “I saw the ambulance, I headed towards it and they were trying to bring Raneem back to life,” Nour recalls. “I think she was just taking her last breath. I saw that, that was really, really upsetting.” It is the first time Nour has revealed the harrowing detail of being at the crime scene just minutes after her niece, Raneem Oudeh, and her sister, Khaola Saleem, 49, were brutally stabbed to death outside Khaola’s home in Solihull in August 2018. Raneem’s ex-husband, Janbaz Tarin, 21, launched the frenzied knife attack after stalking the women to a Shisha bar earlier that evening. In the two hours leading up to her death, a terrified Raneem called West Midlands Police five times begging for help. They told her to go home. But when she reached the front lawn of her home, Tarin jumped out of the bushes with a 12-inch blade. When Khaola stepped in to protect her daughter, he knifed her too. Nour, who had seen them alive just two and a half hours earlier, arrived on the scene after receiving a frantic call from her family. Witnessing the aftermath of the slaughter forged a determination in Nour that has never wavered. “I made them a promise from that night to campaign and that it will never end until I bring justice to them and to all domestic violent victims,” she explains. Prior to the murders, Raneem had contacted the West Midlands Police 13 times regarding stalking and threats to her life, including calling 999 four times on the night she was killed. An inquest later ruled that systemic police failures and a dismissive attitude toward domestic abuse had “materially contributed” to their deaths. Tarin was sentenced to a minimum of 38 years in prison. Nour says: “I knew that there were failings, but was shocked at just how many failures that they made with Raneem. This means that there is more out there that needs to be done.” Now, alongside domestic abuse survivor and WalkSafe app founder Emma Kay, Nour is calling out the government for an “epidemic” of abuse, warning they are nowhere near on course to meet targets to halve violence against women and girls. Speaking exclusively alongside Emma – who is launching her new podcast Survivor Stories on Thursday (16/9) with Nour as her flagship first guest – the pair warn that the government’s upcoming early prison release scheme will actively put women and domestic abuse victims in danger. Nour says the government is taking “catastrophic” steps backward. “Not just for victims, for the public because these people are dangerous to the public,” Nour says of the early release scheme. “So if they don’t harm their ex, they’ll be harming someone else. And the statistics tell you very well that people who’ve done a crime as such, will always come out and do another crime to someone else or to the same people. “We’re trying to protect people but the government is allowing perpetrators to be out of prison, into the public and that’s so heartbreaking. It feels like we walk one step forward but four steps back. “It gives the wrong message to perpetrators, that we’re still dismissive.” Nour worked directly with the Labour Party prior to their election, securing a pledge to introduce “Raneem’s Law” – a measure establishing specialist domestic abuse call-handlers in 999 control rooms. When asked if police attitudes have improved, Nour remains clear that society is still battling a dismissive mindset. “We still have a long way to go. Things need to be in place, ready for anyone because we deserve to live. Everyone has a right to live. That’s why I call it a secure life because we all have a right to live. “It’s not just the police matter, this is everyone’s matter because we’re all responsible for it, you know, in our workplace and in our daily life and with our loved ones and in our social services. “There’s women getting killed every three days in the United Kingdom and that’s just the basic statistics. This is everybody’s matter.” Demanding swift action from ministers, Nour says: “They need to be quicker. When they take a decision like releasing early prisoners, think about it really carefully. It’s quite disappointing for us as campaigners who lost our loved ones. “It’s a national crisis. We still have a long way to go with domestic abuse. This fight will continue for years and years, but we’re not going to stop just because the government’s failing again. We are going to keep pushing for change.”

Our investigation found that of the 393 adult serial offenders who were spared jail, we can reveal that 60 were left to go free to roam the streets in London alone.

A further 26 dodged prison in West Yorkshire, while 19 walked free from courtrooms in Manchester.



Some 137 of these hardened criminals were handed community orders, involving unpaid work in the community, attending rehabilitation sessions, and adhering to a curfew.

Another 119 walked free from the dock with a suspended sentence, meaning they did not spend any time in custody post-sentence.

Perhaps most shockingly, 23 of these prolific offenders bought their freedom by paying a fine.

Those spared jail include serial offenders who hoarded child abuse images.

The Ministry of Justice said: “Sentencing decisions are made by independent judges, but our message is clear – repeat offenders must face tough consequences that cut crime and protect the public.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Prison will always remain the place for dangerous offenders and through our action to fix the broken justice system we inherited.

“We’re strengthening community sentences to deliver punishment that works to cut crime.”

News.title: Nine in 10 Gen Zs have friends they now communicate with exclusively through memes, poll finds
News.content:
PICTURE THIS Nine in 10 Gen Zs have friends they now communicate with exclusively through memes, poll finds







Next

NEARLY nine in 10 Gen Zs have friends they now communicate with exclusively through online memes – and rarely or never see them in real life.

A poll of 1,000 Gen Z found those who send memes typically fire off 572 to friends, and receive 661 each year.



With 74 per cent claiming this form of online talk including funny videos, gifs and images has brought friendships together.

This is because they make everyone laugh (58 per cent), they are relatable (44 per cent) and they can tap into a niche, shared sense of humour (40 per cent).



And for those who say memes have brought them closer, 36 per cent claim they are good at conveying specific emotions – including, happiness, excitement and amusement.

The research was commissioned by National Express, which is working with communications expert Amira Mansour to reveal how communication styles have changed over the years, and the importance of maintaining in-person connections.



Amira said: “Memes have become such a natural part of how Gen Z communicate because sometimes sending one is just a way of saying, ‘I saw this and thought of you’ or ‘you’ll understand this because you get me’, without needing to start an entire conversation.

“Shared humour also creates its own language between friends and sometimes a meme can express an emotion or experience that feels harder to put into words.



“What I find interesting about the research is that despite Gen Z growing up with more ways to communicate digitally than any generation before them, they still place higher value on being together in person.

“That tells us digital communication isn’t necessarily replacing human connection; it can help us maintain it in the moments when we can’t physically be together.

“There are parts of communication that a screen simply can’t replicate. When we’re face-to-face, we’re responding to tone of voice, facial expressions, body language, energy and all the smaller cues we pick up from another person, without even thinking about it.”

The research went on to find a quarter think memes are some of the most expressive ways of communicating.

But face to face conversations were voted the most meaningful form (52 per cent), followed by video calls (32 per cent) and phone calls (29 per cent).



And 46 per cent say they laugh the most with their friends in person, even though 73 per cent think digital communication has had a positive impact on their friendships.

Furthermore, 77 per cent claim sending and receiving memes is great, but nothing beats meeting friends in person.

And 66 per cent believe they need to see each other at least once a month to maintain a strong friendship.

But lack of free time (38 per cent), living too far apart (36 per cent), and limited transport options (15 per cent) can make things difficult.

And 68 per cent believe residing in different towns and cities can make it hard to keep friendships, according to the stats by OnePoll.



Take the quiz here.

Rocio Escondrillas, commercial director at National Express, which is running a competition on its Instagram and TikTok encouraging students to turn their memes into miles, said: “Memes have become a huge part of how Gen Z keeps in touch, and it’s great to see how they can help maintain friendships when you’re miles apart.

“But as the research shows, there’s nothing quite like spending quality time together in real life.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We know students are often juggling busy lives and tight budgets, so getting together with friends and family isn’t always easy.

“With millions of young people travelling on our services each year, we understand how important it is to have access to affordable and reliable travel, our nationwide network helps you get to where you need to be so you can stay connected with the people who matter, wherever they live.”

News.title: Woman ‘grabbed from behind and raped in garden by man, 21, who told cops he was “out and about to play sex games”‘
News.content:
'VILE ATTACK' Woman ‘grabbed from behind and raped in garden by man, 21, who told cops he was “out and about to play sex games”‘







Next

A WOMAN was allegedly grabbed from behind and raped in a garden by a man who told police he was “out and about to play games”.

Natti Abebe, 21, denies intentional strangulation and assault by penetration of a woman in the early hours of March 27 2026.

The victim, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was allegedly “grabbed from behind” and carried to a “nearby garden”, jurors at Cambridge Crown Court were told on Monday.

Abebe, who was accompanied in the dock by an Amharic interpreter, told police that “he was out and about to play games and confirmed those games included sex”, the court heard.





The victim was walking home from her sister’s house, Sarah Porter, prosecuting, said.

She continued: “She was in the Eastfield Road area and she came upon her assailant which the crown says was this defendant, Mr Abebe.”

Ms Porter added: “They then go their separate ways and the next thing she realises is she’s being grabbed from behind, thrown into a nearby garden.”

A resident inside the house attached to the garden described being “awoken by the screaming and shouting” and seeing a man on top of the victim, the court heard.

CCTV footage seen by jurors on Monday showed an alleged interaction between Abebe and the woman on the street at around 4.30am.

The victim is later captured returning to the street looking visibly distressed about 15 minutes later.

She gave evidence on Monday afternoon, and told the court that it was her and the defendant on the footage.

Asked by Abebe’s barrister, Minal Rajshakha, how much she had to drink that night, she replied: “What because if I was drunk then he had the right to rape me?



“If I was drunk does that make it OK?”

The woman told the court that she was not drunk, and had only half a can of cider that night.

Abebe, of no fixed abode, is remanded in custody, and denies all charges.

News.title: Huge emergency response after car smashes through barrier into river – as public urged to stay away & search ongoing
News.content:
RIVER HUNT Huge emergency response after car smashes through barrier into river – as public urged to stay away & search ongoing







Next

A HUGE emergency response has been launched after a car appeared to smash through a barrier and into a river as the public are urged to stay away.

Emergency services remain at the banks of the River Wear in Sunderland after the vehicle reportedly entered the water at around 1.30pm today.



Police, the fire service and ambulances have attended a cordoned off a car park, where the vehicle is understood to have entered the water.

It is not yet known if anyone was inside the car at the time, but locals fear up to four people could be trapped.



A 31-year-old nearby resident, who did not wish to be named, said: “There were loads of ambulances here, we had helicopters here at one point.

“This is the first time I’ve ever seen anything like this around here.



“I’ve lived here for three years, this is sad to see. Some families may get some awful, awful news today.”

He said his neighbour called emergency services after witnessing the incident from his window.

The coastguard and RNLI have been seen using poles to probe the water, alongside their helicopter which has been deployed in the search.

Dozens of panicked onlookers have gathered on either side of the river and are watching the response unfold.



A Northumbria Police spokesperson previously said: “Shortly before 1.30pm today (Tuesday), we received a report of a car entering the River Wear near Monkwearmouth Bridge in Sunderland.

“Emergency services are currently at the scene.

“We would ask members of the public to avoid the area.”

A North East Ambulance Service spokesperson said: “We received a call to 999 at 1.23pm today (Tuesday 29 September 2026) to reports of an incident involving a car entering the River Wear near Wearmouth Bridge in Sunderland.

“We sent to the scene an emergency ambulance, a clinical team leader, three officers, air ambulance and the full Hazardous Area Response Team (HART). We are working closely with the coastguard and the police. We remain on scene at this time.”

News.title: Watch: How did Burnham's speech go down in the conference hall?
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said the government will end the pensions "triple lock" in an emotional speech at his first Labour conference as prime minister.

Reflecting on the recent death of his father, Burnham set how he was determined to honour his memory by creating a new national care service funded by savings from pensions from 2030.

He also announced a plan to end the ban on water companies being owned publicly and a proposal to change the UK's electoral system.

The BBC's Jack Fenwick explains how the big announcements were received by Labour MPs and members in Liverpool.

More on this story.

News.title: Rayner announces crackdown on 'cowboy' leasehold property agents
News.content:
Leaseholders will be given extra protections from "cowboy" property agents and hidden fees, Angela Rayner has announced.

The housing secretary told Labour's annual conference the government would legislate for a new independent regulator and launch a consultation to cap "rip off" administrative fees.

The changes would cover the estimated five million leaseholders in England and Wales who can be forced to pay a landlord for simple changes to their home, despite having bought it.

Rayner told party activists she had heard of leaseholders being charged Â£250 for permission to own a pet and Â£400 to change their front door.

She said people in these situations were "powerless against the vested interests that only take, while giving nothing back in return".

The government is already legislating, external to ban new leasehold flats, described in Labour's 2024 election manifesto as a "feudal" system where people own the right to occupy a property via a lease for a limited number of years from a freeholder, or landlord, who owns the land.

Through the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, ministers want a commonhold system where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Now, Rayner is taking aim at the web of management companies that operate between leaseholders and their effective landlords.

She said the sector had many decent businesses which were "undermined by far too many cowboys, crooks and con artists".

People excited at buying their own homes are "tricked" into using in-house services, meaning that "with no transparency or accountability, vultures can take advantage", Rayner added.

"We will legislate for an independent regulation to rein these cowboys in," she said, announcing legislation for an independent watchdog of property agents.

This includes estate agents, managing agents and estate managers.

News.title: Daniel Sandford on what's next in the RAF Fairford investigation
News.content:
Five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire, have been bailed.

The men, all UK nationals in their 20s, were initially detained on suspicion of terror offences near the base, which is used by the US military.

Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that the incident "clearly involves the hand of a foreign actor".

BBC correspondent Daniel Sandford explains where the investigation goes from here. What angles are the police exploring and what evidence will they be collecting?

More on this story

News.title: Body of newborn baby found on shoreline in Wales as police search for mother
News.content:
The force has not revealed any information about the baby's gender or age.

Giraud said they "have real concerns for the health of the mother".

"We recognise that she is likely to be extremely vulnerable. She may be fearful of seeking the support she needs through fear of identifying herself.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe, and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, to please get in touch with us. You can speak to a healthcare professional, approach a police officer or attend a police station.

"If you are watching or listening to this appeal, please know that we want to hear from you. Please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you."

Det Sgt Kelly Wynne said they were concerned the mother "may not be in a position to reach out for support", and appealed to the baby's father and the mother's family, friends, neighbours or colleagues who may have information.

"If you have any information regarding a woman or girl you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us.

"We appreciate coming forward is difficult, but inaction is not an option."

A post-mortem examination is due to take place on Wednesday afternoon.

The force said people living in Bangor may see an increased police presence over the next few days while the investigation continues.

It urged anyone with information to contact them on 101, quoting Operation Melex.

It added a Major Incident Public Portal, external (MIPP) had been created where anyone with information that could help the forces enquiries can directly contact police.

News.title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel.

Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared via videolink at Portsmouth Crown Court accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at the boat with a knife.

The 37-year-old, whose address was withheld by the court at a previous hearing, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He has been remanded in custody, with a provisional trial date set for 1 March.

The defendant, wearing a grey t-shirt and holding a copy of the Bible, did not enter a plea during the hearing but previously pleaded not guilty to both charges at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Friday.

News.title: Watch: US journalist Evan Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents
News.content:
US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia.

In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him.

He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange.

He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Nowak killer given leave to appeal against sentence
News.content:
The man who murdered student Henry Nowak is being allowed to appeal against the length of his sentence.

Vickrum Digwa stabbed 18-year-old Henry Nowak to death in Southampton in December 2025. In June, he was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years.

He has now been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.

The court will also decide on a referral by the Attorney General's office, which argued the sentence was too lenient.

Digwa has also applied to appeal against his conviction for murder, which will be decided separately.

The 23-year-old was also sentenced for possessing a knife in public, despite claiming in court that the 21cm (8in) blade was being carried as part of his Sikh faith.

News.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
News.content:
Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.

It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.

Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.

Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns".

Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder affecting the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.

He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by Guinness World Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".

Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.

Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind".

"He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said.

Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer, and so far it has raised almost Â£26,000.

He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.

Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts.

The paper also reported concerns about Sir Ranulph have been raised with the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG), the government agency which helps people to stay in control of decisions about their health and finances.

In a statement to the BBC, an OPG spokesperson said: "We have a strict duty of confidentiality to all individuals who have made a lasting power of attorney, and it would be deeply inappropriate to comment on a specific case.

"We take all safeguarding concerns seriously and investigate thoroughly where there is the evidence and legal basis to do so."

News.title: RAF Fairford incident involves 'foreign actor', says Rubio
News.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor".

In an interview with Fox News on Monday, Rubio said "I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally".

He did not provide evidence or further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

A major incident was declared at the weekend after "suspicious vehicles" were seen near the RAF base in Gloucestershire, which has been used by US forces to carry out strikes against Iran.

Dozens of homes were evacuated after the three vehicles were reported to police in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Five men, who are all UK nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of terror offences, and later released on bail.

On Monday Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), said officers are considering all angles, including that "this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state".

In his comments to Fox News, Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation." He added: "There's a lot more news that'll come out on this in the days to come, but there's only so much I can say right now at this point about it."

The Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for what the government calls defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

According to CTP, the five men - aged between 23 and 25 and from London - remain under investigation, and their release is "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others".

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott jailed for seven years for child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years after being convicted of child sexual abuse.

Judge Lord Harrower said Dott robbed his victims of "a significant part of their childhood" and said his behaviour bore the hallmarks of grooming.

Dott had denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010 but was found guilty following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow.

The 49-year-old Scot, who won the world snooker title in 2006, showed no emotion as he was sentenced, only nodding to someone in the public gallery as he was led away.

News.title: Amputee, nine, tells Catherine of Three Peaks success
News.content:
The youngster from Holywell, Flintshire, was born without a fibula in his left leg and his foot was removed at 15 months.

Despite this, at four he became the youngest amputee to scale Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, Wales' highest peak.

Albie-Junior and his father have since embarked on several climbing challenges together raising thousands for their local football club in the process.

In August, he finished the Three Peaks Challenge in 22 hours and 30 minutes alongside his dad, powered by ham and cheese sandwiches, sour sweets and four months' training.

This included conquering Ben Nevis in Scotland and Scafell Pike in England as well as Yr Wyddfa.

Daniel described the moment they received a phone call inviting them to Windsor Castle as "unbelievable".

Once they arrived, Daniel said he stayed in the background, letting Albie-Junior enjoy the experience as "it was his thing".

"For him it was just like a chat to a lady, you know, just the innocence of it," he said.

"It's like a mother talking to a son."

He said the conversation stood out to him because of how "pleasant" it was and said Catherine made him like they were "both equals".

In a post on X, the princess said: "Listening to their experiences of the challenge and their reasons for taking it on was a powerful reminder that recovery is rarely a journey we make alone, and of the importance of the people who walk alongside us along the way."

News.title: Lives 'will be lost' unless UK does more to combat wildfires, committee chairwoman says
News.content:
Lives "will be lost" unless more is done to combat the increasing risk of wildfires, the chairwoman of the UK's Climate Change Committee (CCC) has said after a record number of blazes this summer.

Baroness Brown told BBC File on 4 Investigates "not enough action" had been taken in light of predictions the UK is facing longer, drier summers because of global warming.

Earlier this year, one man died in a wildfire in Gloucestershire, while 19 homes were destroyed in Stourbridge, near Birmingham, and villagers were evacuated in the Cairngorms.

The government said it was investing nearly Â£100m to improve national resilience capabilities, which includes piloting specially trained firefighting teams.

News.title: 'Ship buster' missiles sink old US warship in live fire training off Scotland
News.content:
A decommissioned American warship has been sunk off Scotland's west coast during a training exercise involving both US forces and the Royal Navy.

USS Klakring was hit by missiles and a torpedo before sinking in the North Atlantic about 170 miles (274km) off the Outer Hebrides last Monday.

The US Navy said the ship went a through "rigorous" cleaning process first, and personnel checked for the presence of whales and dolphins before the live-firing exercise started.

Other warships, including an aircraft carrier in 2006, have been deliberately sunk at sea by the US as part of training and to create artificial reefs for marine life.

News.title: Met Police officer charged after BBC Charing Cross investigation
News.content:
A Metropolitan Police officer has become the first person to be charged as a result of a BBC Panorama investigation into alleged misconduct at Charing Cross police station in London.

Sgt Sadiq Al-Hasani, 37, has been charged with perverting the course of justice.

He will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

In a statement, the Met Police said the charge related to an allegation Sgt Al-Hasani, who was attached to Central West Command Unit, "deliberately sought to discourage another officer from making a statement to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC)".

The IOPC had begun an investigation following the broadcast on 1 October 2025 of BBC Panorama â Undercover in the Police.

As part of the programme, a BBC journalist went undercover working in the custody suite, secretly filming a number of officers making racist comments and bragging about violence used against suspects.

Al-Hasani was charged on 13 August in relation to an incident on 2 October 2025.

In a statement, the IOPC said Sgt Al-Hasani allegedly approached a junior officer, who was a potential key witness in the wider Charing Cross investigation, with the intention to obstruct or interfere with the probe.

He remains suspended from duty, the Met said.

The IOPC began its investigation after a mandatory conduct referral from the Met on 3 October.

As part of this, the IOPC reviewed footage gathered as part of the programme which was not broadcast.

Its investigation finished in June, at which point it decided to refer a file of evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service.

According to the IOPC, 15 officers have been found to have committed gross misconduct. All except one of the 15, a former PC, have been barred from policing.

Investigations continue into the conduct of a further 14 officers or police staff.

News.title: Ex-England captain Dallaglio to sell World Cup winner's medal
News.content:
Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt.

The 54-year-old has put a number of items from his illustrious career up for auction including medals, trophies and caps.

The World Cup medal is expected to raise between Â£50,000 and Â£80,000 while in total the collection has an estimated value of Â£180,000.

Dallaglio was one of the stars of the England side that won the World Cup in dramatic fashion against Australia 23 years ago.

Other items up for sale include a British and Irish Lions cap, his 1993 World Cup Sevens winner's medal and a 2003 Six Nations Championship winner's medal.

During an appearance on The High Performance podcast, external earlier this month, Dallaglio spoke about his bankrupcy.

He said: "As a result of getting divorced, I was made bankrupt.

"I had some financial problems - I could've done things a lot better."

He also said he sought therapy after his divorce and bankruptcy left him wallowing in "self-pity".

The auction at Budd's, external in Northamptonshire takes place on 13 October.

News.title: Drumcree stalemate continues as Orange Order and protesters meet NI secretary
News.content:
Protesters remain on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown and Orangemen at Drumcree church as the parade dispute continues.

The main parties involved in the dispute in Northern Ireland are still in a stalemate, following a day of political talks and heated exchanges at Stormont.

Members of the Orange Order are still waiting to begin a parade, which was due to take place on Sunday, and walk down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road.

The road was blocked by protesters and the parade did not go ahead.

Both the Orange Order and members of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition are meeting the NI Secretary Sir Chris Byrant at Hillsborough Castle again on Tuesday afternoon.

About 30 to 50 protesters have been sitting roadside on a grass verge throughout most of Tuesday, but traffic has flowed freely.

A gazebo has been set up, with tea, coffee and snacks available and many of the residents and supporters have deck chairs.

Meanwhile, a small group of about 10 people gathered at Drumcree church on Tuesday morning.

Orange Order Deputy District Master Alistair Power said he had told police they were ready to march down the Garvaghy Road whenever it was safe to do so.

Power said the "position of the district remains the same" and that the Parade Commission's determination is still "a live document", to bring the parade "down its traditional route of via the Garvaghy Road to complete its parade in Carleton Street".

A low-key police presence remains in place 100m from the church, with just one Land Rover there

Police said a "significant public safety operation" remains in place on the Garvaghy Road.

"We will continue to explore and keep under review a range of tactical options to safely bring this matter to a conclusion and keep the peace," Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said.

Holiday shoppers will break records this year - but there’s more to it than presents.

Consumers are expected to spend an unprecedented $275.1 billion online from November 1 to December 31, with many stocking up on discounted essentials along with gifts, according to a study published Tuesday by analytics and software firm Adobe.

“While consumers have historically embraced holiday deals to buy gifts or adopt the latest gadgets, many are taking advantage of discounts to stock up on essentials,” Adobe noted.

Month-on-month sales during Cyber Week (November 26-30) are expected to jump 210 percent for clothing basics and 150 percent for personal hygiene products, the study said.

The best deals on gifts depend on the day, Adobe noted. Cyber Monday is best for electronics while Black Friday is projected to be the top day for TVs, toys, apparel, appliances and furniture.

Shoppers are approaching this year’s holiday season looking for discounts on essentials as they struggle to make ends meet. November will offer the best deals on necessities, according to Adobe ( Getty Images )

Early November will offer the biggest discounts on essentials - up to 21 percent, Adobe projected.

Multiple holiday shopping projections echo what many experts already know about consumers - inflation and tariffs are forcing household spending cuts.

Consumers are projected to spend a $708 on gifts this year, down $106 from 2024 and $13 from 2025, according to a September analysis from accounting firm PwC.

Some 69 percent of shoppers are worried about tariffs raising prices on holiday purchases, leading a third of them plan to shop earlier so they can avoid increases, consultancy Sprout Social found in a September analysis.

Inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve’s target rate. The Fed’s recent decision to raise its interest rate means borrowing will likely become more expensive.

Those concerns are warranted - federal data estimates that tariffs will cost households around $2,500 this year.

President Donald Trump’s tariffs on multiple foreign countries likely won’t end soon.

Strained relations between the U.S. and Canada seem set to worsen after Washington decided early Tuesday to prohibit roughly $1 billion in Canadian goods, targeting dairy items, motorcycles, and alcohol.

Amid the tariff chaos and other cost concerns, consumers are more likely to turn to AI to find lower prices this year, Adobe’s study said. Consumers will visit retail sites via AI prompts 130 percent more this season than they did in 2025, the study said.

Spotify has gone down in a major outage.

Users reported problems listening to music, instead seeing an error messaging indicating that “something went wrong”.

But the problem appears to be limited to only some users, and some parts of the app. Some found that playing music seemed to work, for instance, but searching for other songs or artists showed nothing or an error message.

Others found that the errors only appeared to occur on the mobile version of the app, while it loaded as normal on the desktop. Users may therefore be able to work around the problems by trying different parts of the app, or using it on a different device.

The problems began just before 3pm UK time, or 10am in New York, according to tracking website Down Detector.

”We’re aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!” the company said on its official page on X, formerly Twitter. It did not give any information about the problem, or when it might be fixed.

Unlike many other large tech platforms, the company does not operate an official status page on its own website.

Spotify says that it has around 800 million users, with 300 million of them paying for a monthly subscription. It is available in 184 different countries.

Singer-songwriter Frank Turner has announced that he intends to take a break from live performances for the foreseeable future, after he concludes the 10th edition of his Lost Evenings festival next year.

Turner, 44, made the announcement on his social media this week, writing: “My dear friends, as a skinny half-arsed English country singer once said, the only thing certain is that everything changes.

“After 28 years on the road, 10 albums and well over 3,000 shows, it’s time for a change. As announced yesterday, next year’s Lost Evenings will take place in London, at OVO Arena Wembley. It will be the biggest, best and final edition of the festival.”

Turner then revealed: “The four shows there will be my last for the foreseeable future.”

The “Get Better” star said there were a number of reasons behind his decision, not least the fact that he has been on the road for most of his life.

“I want to try new things,” he said. “I want to recharge, spend more time with my friends and family, and explore other ways of life. I’m excited to pursue other ideas and projects.”

Turner pointed out that the realities of touring today had also played a part in his decision: “The economics of touring have gotten harder, the music industry has been swallowed by social media in a way that doesn’t really interest me, and as I get older my physical and mental health could do with some care.”

Still, Turner said he was “excited for the future” and wanted to leave the stage “with my head high”.

His final shows next year would be “a pinnacle”, he said, and a “chance for all of us to celebrate the last 20 years and bid them the farewell they deserve”.

Turner thanked his band, the Sleeping Souls, as well as his record label, touring crew and “everyone who worked on my music with me over the years”.

“But mostly I’m grateful to you; the people who made it possible, by giving me your time and attention,” he concluded. “There are many friends I’ve made, many faces I know, but truly, to every single person who ever cared – thank you.”

open image in gallery Frank Turner has been performing live for almost three decades ( ANP/AFP/Getty )

Turner has released 10 solo albums, as well as two albums with his post-hardcore band Million Dead, and various other projects.

His 2013 album Tape Deck Heart is widely regarded as his commercial breakthrough, while he achieved his first ever Number One album on the UK charts in 2022 with FTHC.

He separated from his wife Jessica Guise in 2024, the year he released his most recent album, Undefeated. In a public shared statement, Guise said she had “no choice but to accept” their marriage was over after “things [came] to light about Frank’s actions on his US tour” in June that year.

In a later statement posted to his Instagram in October last year, Turner said he wanted to address “gossip, misrepresentation and untruths” about his personal life.

“I wasn’t looking, but I met my soulmate; the most wonderful person I’ve ever known,” he wrote. “I made a connection that is unlike anything I ever experienced. I found a joy, acceptance and love that still has me pinching myself. I found peace beyond my understanding, one that I sincerely wish for everyone.”

The 10th edition Turner’s Lost Evenings festival takes place from 4 – 7 November 2027 at Wembley Arena in London, with Turner & the Sleeping Souls headlining and further artists performing across two stages.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged Tuesday to give Britain “a new social contract for the 21st century," reform the country's electoral system and reset its relationship with its European neighbors. But he acknowledged that economic constraints make delivering his sweeping plans a big political risk.

“Small things will not get us through what are difficult times,” Burnham said in a tough-love speech to the center-left Labour Party’s annual conference.

He set out a crowd-pleasing vision of more social housing, better education and more affordable care for the elderly. But he warned that money would have to come from welfare and pension spending to deliver the changes.

Anticipating opposition to his plans, Burnham said: “I have given you what you often say is missing from politics: honesty, ideas and a clear direction for the country we all love.”

Bold plans bring high costs

Some of Burnham’s announcements in the hour-long speech will spark big political fights. Burnham said he would stake his political legacy on establishing a “national care service” to fix what he called a “ broken” social care system. He said that like the much-loved but overstretched National Health Service it would be free to use and paid for through taxation.

Burnham held back tears as he spoke about his experiences of the care system with his father, Roy, who died earlier this month.

To help fund the care service, Burnham said he would water down the long-unassailable pensions triple lock, an expensive policy that guarantees pensions rise each year by the annual increase in consumer price inflation, average wage growth, or 2.5%, whichever is higher.

“I accept I may pay a political price,” he said. “But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.”

Burnham vowed to “move beyond a decade of drift and division” and end the economic and political turmoil that have made him the U.K.’s seventh prime minister since the country voted in 2016 to leave the European Union.

In a major move on that front, he said Labour would contest the next election on changing Britain’s winner-takes all electoral system to a form of proportional representation.

He also promised a rethink of Britain’s relationship with the EU, saying “Brexit has done more harm than good” and the U.K. needs “clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in.”

Also on Burnham’s ambitious agenda: ending street homelessness, cutting youth unemployment and exerting more control over Britain’s privatized utilities.

At the same time, he said the government would “stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down.”

“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford,” Burnham said.

Burnham has buoyed his party

Burnham’s relaxed, social-media friendly confidence has been a tonic to his party as Labour held its conference under the slogan “Hope again.” As the sun glinted on the River Mersey beside the conference center in Liverpool, the mood was a world away from last year’s downbeat gathering, when delegates despaired about then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s dire approval ratings and the seemingly unstoppable rise of the anti-immigration opposition party Reform UK.

But as delegates gathered, terror arrests near a U.S.-run air base in England brought home the daunting global situation and unexpected challenges facing the neophyte prime minister, just two months into the job.

Five men were arrested Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses outside the RAF Fairford base in western England. They were released on bail Monday as police probe lines of inquiry including a link to a hostile state. That meant Burnham and his Cabinet were peppered during the conference with questions about security lapses and potential state threats from Iran or Russia.

Burnham and others also acknowledged the gloomy economic backdrop against which Treasury chief John Healey will deliver the government’s budget on Oct. 28.

The U.S.-Iran war continues to choke shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices soaring and pushing up inflation and the cost of government borrowing. The price of diesel in Britain hit a record high of just under 2 pounds a liter on Monday, according to figures compiled by the Royal Automobile Club.

The next general election does not have to be called until 2029, but Labour’s revival has sparked talk of a snap election.

Burnham insists he won’t go to voters early, and John Curtice, professor of politics at the University of Strathclyde, said that’s a wise decision.

Curtice said Burnham had given Labour “a halo effect from a popular leader.”

“But the challenge for this party now is to change that halo effect from the leader to the party,” Curtice said. “This party needs to make much more progress before it can contemplate the prospect of an election.”

Donald Trump rolled out a new chatbot aimed at helping Americans interact with federal agencies and streamlining the processes associated with them on Tuesday.

The president spoke Tuesday morning at an event hosted by Tony Robbins as the service — America.gov — launched to the public.

“It’s going to save you tremendous time,” the president promised.

The tool can be used to direct Americans to services across the federal government in a manner similar to other existing AI chatbots, like the Gemini service integrated into Google’s search function. In a video presentation from Robbins and chief design officer Joe Gebbia, the designers teased greater functionalities in the future that did not appear to be available yet, like passport renewal and updating/obtaining other official documents through a one-click system.

“America plans to let you renew a passport right here in 2027. See what's coming,” the chatbot tells users today, with a link to a promotional video showing those features.

“Instead of forcing citizens to search through the endless maze of tens of thousands of terrible government websites and rules...you’ll now have one front door for every single question. Everything will be answered easily and quickly,” Trump promised, vowing that the site would save average Americans “hundreds” of hours per year filling out government paperwork, accessing benefits and searching for information.

open image in gallery Donald Trump speaks at an event rolling out an AI chatbot tool for assisting with federal agency websites ( AP )

“Anyone who has used Grok, or Gemini, or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov. Not complicated,” Trump said. The technology is reportedly built using Gemini and Grok code.

“Whether you’re a Scout leader who wants to reserve a campsite at a national park, a senior citizen trying to choose a Medicare plan, or an American veteran trying to get the benefits that you’ve earned, you so justly deserve, America.gov will be there to help,” said the president.

The announcement comes as Trump met Monday evening with Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic who has warned that his industry’s growth needs government supervision and guardrails to avoid courting disaster. The president is due to meet with Amodei and other officials from Anthropic again on Tuesday.

Americans’ views on artificial intelligence are also changing at a rapid pace, with opposition to the growth of data center projects becoming a bipartisan issue in communitites around the country. Both Democratic and Republican governors and other candidates have signaled support for pauses, bans or temporary moratoriums of various kinds as the expansion of data centers as well as the overall role of AI in society continues at a fever pitch.

A CNN/SRSS poll conducted this month laid out Americans’ fears in stark view. As many as 9 in 10 Americans now fear that aritificial intelligence could surpass human control and intelligence, and view the technology with skepticism and disdain by similarly wide margins. Nearly half of those surveyed thought that AI would likely negatively impact their own personal economic outcomes in the future. Less than 20 percent said the opposite.

open image in gallery Donald Trump congratulates members of the National Design Studio at the launch of America.gov ( Reuters )

Seven in ten Americans also say that the federal government is not doing enough to regulate the technology, a prospect that the president has seemingly dismissed out of hand as he remains one of the loudest cheerleaders for AI in Washington. At the event on Tuesday, the president repeated his quip that he wants to change the name of artificial intelligence to “super intelligence”, before joking that the was going to begin referring to the “fake news” media as the “artificial news”.

The rollout and transfer of responsibilities from federal workers and agency websites to an AI agent raises both possibilities for streamlining government access as well as serious concerns about privacy, security, and economic ripple effects. Both Grok and Google’s Gemini service, which the America.gov service are built on, carry disclaimers that information provided by AI agents may be incomplete, unreliable, or flat-out untrue. While the rollout of America.gov doesn’t yet mean that any individual agencies will undergo major changes, its launch follows the second Trump administration’s efforts to radically transform many federal agencies under both the cost-cutting and efficiency pledges of Elon Musk’s shuttered DOGE initiative as well as the efforts of Russell Vought at the Office of Management and Budget to further diminish government spending.

Trump administration officials could seek to further offload the work of federal agencies to the America.gov system in the future as many figures within the administration continue to push for agencies to be slimmed down and federal positions to be eliminated.

A Pennsylvania developer is offering every eligible household in a small township $10,000 if a massive data center project moves forward – but many residents still aren’t sold.

NorthPoint Development wants to build a 1,300-acre data center campus in Hazle Township, near the Pocono foothills, with as many as 15 data center buildings and other infrastructure, the Wall Street Journal reports.

The company outlined the offer in letters sent to residents in June, setting aside about $45 million for roughly 4,500 households. Residents could spend the money however they choose, but only if the project reaches the required stage. NorthPoint expects the first data center to receive its certificate of occupancy in late 2027, triggering the payments, according to the WSJ.

But the prospect of a $10,000 check has done little to quiet concerns in the township, which has about 10,460 residents. People living near the site have raised questions about construction, noise and potential impacts on property values.

Jeff Fasnacht, a retired teacher who lives nearby, told the WSJ the payment would not make up for the potential loss in his home’s value.

NorthPoint Development is offering residents of Hazel, Pennsylvania, $10,000 if a massive data center project moves forward in the small town, but so far, many residents aren't buying it ( Project Hazelnut )

“$10,000 doesn’t match how much it’s going to tank my property value,” Fasnacht said.

Retired homeowner Ed Negra said the offer could backfire by encouraging residents to scrutinize the project's potential drawbacks.

“I think it works the opposite way, because most people have the opinion that, ‘Hey, are they trying to bribe us here?’” he said.

NorthPoint chief marketing officer Brent Miles said the payments were created after a public meeting last year, when residents pressed the company on what they would personally gain from the project.

“I think we’ve got something here that’s on the cutting edge, really in direct response to ‘what’s in it for me?’” Miles told the WSJ.

The company also plans to provide another $120 million over 15 years for community needs, including funding for the local police department, according to the WSJ.

Some residents said the money is worth considering. Charlie Leshko, a retired maintenance and janitorial worker who lives in a senior residence, said the payment could help him buy a car or put a down payment on a home.

“$10,000 don’t come along every day,” he said. “I always wanted to have my own house.”

Retired foundry worker Carl Majusiak initially considered the offer but ultimately decided it was not enough to justify the development.

“At first it seems like ‘well, OK, maybe I’ll think about it,” he said, before concluding, “we don’t need that around here.”

The Independent has contacted NorthPoint Development for comment.

The debate in Pennsylvania comes amid a nationwide backlash against data centers entering local communities. The facilities provide the computing power needed to run artificial intelligence but also require huge amounts of electricity, land and other resources.

Public anxiety over AI itself has also intensified. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that people developing advanced AI systems “earnestly believe” the technology could kill all humans by the end of the decade. Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger has similarly warned that he believes there is a greater than 10 percent chance advanced AI could cause human extinction within the next decade.

The warnings come as President Donald Trump – a frequent AI user – continues to push for U.S. leadership in AI. Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson were meeting Tuesday with executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Nvidia to discuss AI, regulation and safety.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani debuted a sweeping plan Tuesday to combat antisemitism and hate crimes against Jewish people in New York City, moving to assuage lingering concerns from critics who see his steadfast denunciations of Israel as antisemitic.

The strategy includes increased security funding for synagogues, an increased focus on folding Jewish history into public school education, and a pledge to highlight important Jewish cultural and religious sites in the mayor's day-to-day governance of the city.

Mamdani said the overarching goal of the initiative was to “confront the scourge of antisemitism now and in the future," noting that Jewish people make up only 12% of the city's population but are the victims of around half the city's reported hate crimes.

“This is not only unacceptable, it's something we all have an obligation to change. And City Hall will lead the way,” he said in a video.

Mamdani, a Democrat and the city's first Muslim mayor, has long been a vocal supporter of Palestinian civil rights and has accused the Israeli government of committing a genocide in Gaza. He has said his criticism of Israel does not amount to antisemitism, though his opponents have argued his heated rhetoric around the conflict has made Jewish people feel unsafe in the city.

The plan announced Tuesday amounts to the mayor's most forceful attempt to address concerns from the Jewish community over antisemitism, with Mamdani promising to "build a city where Jewish New Yorkers are not only safe but celebrated.”

City Hall will increase grant funding to to community organizations that focus on hate crime prevention and survivor support. It will also work with public schools to address complaints of discrimination and launch public awareness campaigns on the city's human rights law and how to report suspected discrimination.

Mamdani faced a barrage of criticism during his campaign last year after he declined to disavow the phrase “globalize the intifada,” a slogan some see as a call to violence against Israeli civilians, though he did not use the phrase and later said he would discourage others from saying it.

He has also faced questions over a decision in June to skip an annual parade honoring Israel, which has long been a must-attend event for politicians in the city.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dedicated a portion of an address at the United Nations last week to assailing Mamdani, accusing him of spreading lies about Israel and calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York.”

Mamdani has repeatedly called for Netanyahu to be arrested under a warrant from the International Criminal Court alleging war crimes in Gaza, where more than 73,000 people have been killed since the prime minister launched a punishing war in retaliation for the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.
