“I welcome the constructive intent reflected in each of your letters. We may differ on the best route forward, but I have no doubt that each of us wants what is best for Fifa, its member associations and football.”

Sports.title: Sam Gough’s journey from being ‘a hazard’ at PE to becoming Para Lionesses captain
Sports.content:
Helga has spotted a pigeon just outside the changing rooms at Poltonhall Sports Complex in Bonnyrigg and it suddenly becomes clear from her ears, tongue and tail that she would very much like to chase it. But not today. She is a good girl, she resists the exciting temptation, and stays true to her task. Helga, a three-year-old black labrador, is a guide dog, partnered with the England women’s blind football captain, Sam Gough, and the duo have important work to do.

Gough is preparing for the 2026 IBSA Women’s Blind Football European Championship, which gets under way in Istanbul on Saturday, full of confidence in her everyday life since partnering with Helga last year, a moment she says has been liberating.

“It was as if I was a bird trapped in a cage and finally was able to fly and spread my wings,” Gough, 23, says of Helga, as she sits down for an exclusive interview with Moving the Goalposts, two days after claiming second place in the Home International Rowing Beach Sprints in her other international sporting career, rowing for Scotland. “As I train full-time in two sports, my training load is a lot and I used to have to rely on my parents to drive me up and down the country. Helga’s changed that because I can get to camps by myself.

“Helga came into my life at the right time when I really needed her most. I remember finding out about her, sitting in the nail salon getting my nails done and I got a phone call. I just remember crying, I was so emotional. You wait for so long for this life-changing moment.

“Growing up, I was always setting myself goals, [such as] ‘what age will I be able to go independently to the shops and get milk?’ And I gave myself until 18 to do it. When I got to 18, I wasn’t able to. Then when I got Helga, one of the first things I did was go down to the local shops and get a pint of milk. ‘Finally’, I was able to do something so simple, and it really just sunk in how valuable it is, having a guide dog in my life.”

View image in fullscreen Sam Gough walking with Helga, who ‘came into my life at the right time when I really needed her most’. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

Gough, who is based in Edinburgh, has a condition called cerebral vision impairment, caused by damage to the connecting pathways between her eyes and her brain when she was born. Her sight gradually declined through her childhood and she now competes as a para athlete in the B1 blind classification; Helga is a regular in the dugout as she trains. A Scot, she is allowed to compete for England purely because Scotland does not have a women’s blind football team. Nor do Wales, so the English team currently include players from across Britain.

England’s captain since 2022, Gough is one of the best strikers in the world. Blind football is a five-a-side game, with all four outfield players wearing eye masks and spectators having to remain silent during play. Players must shout “voy” before tackling and metal plates inside the ball create a rattling sound to help players locate it. That makes the ball heavy – “when you’re striking a ball, your big toe can get quite sore. My toenail is no longer existent because you’re hitting off a metal plate all the time!” Gough says, before explaining: “Balance is very, very, very important. You’re playing a game just through hearing and battling so your stability has to be really, really strong to your core.”

England’s team, known as the Para Lionesses, will be joined in Turkey at the upcoming European Championship by teams from Austria and Poland, as well as the host nation and a neutral para team. In the inaugural women’s edition of the championship, which was held in Pescara on Italy’s Adriatic coast four years ago, England were the runners-up, to Germany. Gough’s team also finished second at the 2025 World Championship in India, losing to Argentina in the final after victories over Japan, Poland and India. This bid for a European title comes a year ahead of the next World Championship, in October 2027, in São Paulo, Brazil.

Gough says travelling to Turkey this week for the Euros is “nerve-racking” but adds: “Our performance at the World Champs in India just really gave us the confidence we needed. There are a couple of teams that are strong and we’re just going to go into each game really having confidence in our ability as a squad and supporting each other for it.”

Gough had always had a passion for football as a child but initially found herself taken out of PE lessons and bullied at school, recalling: “I really wanted to be involved but, as I lost more and more of my vision, I was told I wasn’t going to be able to participate in sport. I was actually removed from PE due to being a ‘hazard’. I thought that that dream would never really come to fruition, until I went to the Royal National College for the Blind in Hereford. There, I tried blind football for the first time and realised the football door would open for me.

“As I’ve grown up I’ve been able to realise that actually things weren’t acceptable and that was an exclusion in sport, where younger Sam was told that she couldn’t take part. It’s why I’m such a big advocate now for sport to be inclusive and young people to have the opportunity. Young Sam went through a lot of bullying as well, so it kind of toughened me up a little bit but also was one of the worst experiences of my life.”

In June this year Gough received an MBE in the king’s birthday honours list, for her services to sport and the visually impaired community. She has taught blind football to schoolchildren and also to the Brazilian football icons Kaká and Cafu, as well as giving demonstrations to some of Sarina Wiegman’s Lionesses.

Sports.title: Aston Villa sack manager Natalia Arroyo with club second-bottom of WSL
Sports.content:
Aston Villa have sacked Natalia Arroyo as their women’s manager, with the side winless and second-bottom of the Women’s Super League.

Arroyo was let go on Monday night, after Villa endured a 4-0 defeat at Tottenham on Sunday. It was a second loss in their opening four games of the season, with a 4-1 defeat by Manchester City sandwiched between 1-1 draws with Chelsea and Brighton, with performances largely poor.

Arroyo was appointed in January 2025, signing a three-and-a-half-year contract with the club. The former Barcelona and Espanyol player, who spent time as a journalist before focusing on her coaching career, joined Villa following four impressive years in charge at Real Sociedad where she guided the club to a second-place finish in the 2021-22 season and a Copa de la Reina final in her final campaign.

The 40-year-old replaced Shaun Goater, who took temporary charge following Robert de Pauw’s departure amid allegations over remarks he had made to players. Villa had only two wins from their first 12 WSL games when Arroyo took charge. Five consecutive league defeats followed as the team adapted to the new manager and they won their remaining five games to finish sixth.

Villa finished ninth in Arroyo’s first full campaign, with 20 points from 22 games, but a poor run of form and four successive defeats blighted the end of the season. “Everyone at Aston Villa would like to thank Natalia for her efforts and wish her all the best in her future endeavours,” the club said in a statement.

Villa have confirmed that Brian Sørensen, the women’s technical adviser, will take temporary charge of the team, including for their Subway Players Cup tie against Newcastle on Wednesday. Sørensen joined Villa as technical adviser in March, following his exit from Everton in February after four years with the Merseyside club.

Sports.title: Australia go down fighting to Brazil in fiery 4-2 friendly defeat
Sports.content:
SUNCORP STADIUM, Brisbane – His first touch taking the ball goalward, Vanderson felt the pressure from Australian defenders closing in and laced a shot goalward, burying it in the top corner of Patrick Beach’s net and putting Brazil ahead. All of 132 seconds had transpired at Lang Park, and, after being forced to salvage a 1-1 draw with effectively the last touch of the game four days prior, it not only represented a perfect start for the Seleção, but also felt like it was sending a message. We’re Brazil, you’re Australia, and we’re going to put you in your place. And 90 minutes later, a level of pride had been restored when it finished 4-2 to the South Americans.

As that effort from the Monaco defender nestled in the back of the net, memories of Nestory Irankunda’s free-kick blast at Queensland Country Bank Stadium were already fading. And as Raphinha twice thundered efforts into the body of Beach a minute later, it started to feel almost like it was 2017 again, when Diego Souza scored after just 11 seconds at the MCG to set up a comprehensive 4-0 win or 2013, when Jô scored after seven minutes in Brasília to set up a 6-0 win.

The Socceroos looked shellshocked. After being savaged back home for being held to a draw against a perceived lesser footballing nation, the tourists had come out of their corner and socked them straight in the mouth.

Yet the collapse that so easily could have occurred didn’t. And after taking stock and getting their foot on the ball, the hosts began to work their way back into the contest. More than that, they began to show some of the same attacking intent and bravery in possession as they had flashed in Townsville four days ago. There were some nervy exchanges as they attempted this – a 19th-minute turnover almost giving Vinícius Júnior scope to shoot, only to be closed down at the last – but they didn’t simply bunker down and try to survive to halftime. They were trying to play their way out of trouble.

“We’ve played a lot of big nations over the last few years – top opposition, top players – and we were always competitive in these games,” said Jackson Irvine. “But I think we showed tonight we can be competitive in a different kind of way. And I think that’s really exciting to see; that we’ve added that to our game.

View image in fullscreen Alessandro Circati of Australia celebrates scoring his team’s first goal. Photograph: Chris Hyde/Getty Images

“We still run and defend and have that part of our game, which is a non-negotiable. It has to be there. But the ability [and] desire to run, to get on the ball, to break pressure, to get yourself free. Fantastic. A lot a lot to be pleased with. Obviously disappointing that we couldn’t [win].”

In the greater context of this side’s progression, with an Asian Cup looming in January, the result almost felt immaterial as the darting runs and slick pieces of interplay were demonstrated. It was near unrecognisable from the side that couldn’t find a way to break down Egypt just three months ago at the World Cup; the evolution that had been demanded from Tony Popovic playing out before our eyes.

“They played differently [to the World Cup] today,” Brazil boss Carlo Ancelotti said. “Honestly, I have to say, they press really well with high intensity. They are really well organised, and they surprise us in this sense. Considering the first game and this game… they put much more pressure in front, and we had more building up from the back. It’s a really good team, in my opinion, a really good team.

“Maybe you don’t have the quality that we have, but they are really powerful players, well organised, strong in the duels. A really good national team.

View image in fullscreen Connor Metcalfe of the Socceroos is mobbed by teammates after his goal. Photograph: Darren England/AAP

Then in the 28th minute, it was 1-1: a Connor Metcalfe corner found its way through a mass of bodies – taking a touch off Gabriel, allowing VAR intervention to overrule the subsequent offside flag – and all the way to Alessandro Circati to flick home at the back post. Then, in the 33rd minute, the Socceroos were ahead, Metcalfe receiving a lay-off from Circati and thundering a pearl of a strike beyond debutant keeper Otávio.

Forget the pyro and light show that preceded kickoff, the real fireworks were on the pitch, with more action delivered on the stroke of halftime: Harry Souttar – who didn’t have his best game – brought down Danilo and conceded a VAR-adjudged penalty converted by Raphinha, and Irankunda blasted over the bar just minutes later instead of making it 3-2.

The Japanese referee, Yusuke Araki, was far busier than he probably expected for a friendly, as further fireworks broke out as the second half progressed, this time between the two teams. A 64th-minute clash between Souttar and halftime substitute Endrick sparked an all-in by the touchline that at one point saw the young Brazilian go to ground and almost clean up Socceroo assistant Paul Okon Sr.

But that proved something of a turning point. After coming on for Raphinha, Endrick ultimately proved the spark that turned the game. He provided the cutback that allowed Bruno Guimarães to make it 3-2 minutes after the fracas. Brought down by a faint touch by Irankunda in the 79th minute, Vinícius then sealed the game from the spot.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel resists change against Czechia despite England defensive errors
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel will resist making drastic changes to his defence despite England going six games without a clean sheet before facing Czechia in the Nations League on Tuesday.

Although Tuchel acknowledged that his side were a “danger to ourselves” when they lost 3-2 against Spain last Saturday, the head coach stood by Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly after their errors against the world champions.

The message was one of continuity as England arrived in Prague for their second game in Nations League Group A3. Tuchel has injury concerns over O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa but is likely to keep the changes to a minimum at the back. James Trafford will continue in goal and Tuchel believes the defeat against Spain was down to individual mistakes rather than structural issues with England’s defending.

“I didn’t see a pattern,” the German said. “It was individual mistakes. I didn’t see a pattern in defending. I think we defended very well in a block when we were organised, but we had just big individual mistakes. But I could not see any defensive pattern that would concern me.

“From a purely defensive approach I felt that we defended much more disciplined, cohesive and organised than in some matches in the World Cup. That was a step in the right direction. We constantly pushed out from our middle block, we tried to go into the opponent’s half and pushed out of the deep block. We didn’t suffer too for long periods of time in defending. We never lost our structure.

“I will not change now because someone made an individual mistake, and they’ve been good for us through all the other matches.”

Two of Spain’s goals came from Guéhi and O’Reilly losing the ball in dangerous positions. “We need to improve these things but when we had the ball we were the biggest danger to ourselves around the box because we just had too many individual mistakes,” Tuchel said. “Purely in defending, I have no concerns.”

Lewis Hall is in line to replace O’Reilly at left-back against Czechia and Trevoh Chalobah will hope to get the nod over Jarrad Branthwaite as Guéhi’s partner in the middle if Konsa is out. England want to reach next year’s finals and losing to Spain means they cannot experiment too much against Czechia, who were beaten by Croatia in their opening game.

The big question is whether Trent Alexander-Arnold replaces Jarell Quansah at right-back and wins his first cap since June 2025. Alexander-Arnold, who did not go to the World Cup, was an unused substitute against Spain.

“He had a very good training week and an excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” Tuchel said. “Today was a good training session. Everything is fine. He’s ready to go.”

Tuchel has explained that starting Trafford in England’s first two Nations League games is to see whether the Leeds goalkeeper can compete at this level. Jordan Pickford, who has been the No 1 since 2018, will return for the trip to Croatia on Saturday and the home game against Czechia next Tuesday.

“We use the Nations League to see where we are with the other goalkeepers,” Tuchel said. “There was no reason from performances to open up this position for competition.

“I think it’s necessary with every other player that we are aware of ‘what if’. If a player that starts a season well, like Traff at Leeds, [he] has the chance to prove it and to play in our style. We just need to see it at some point. We use this competition to actually give him the chance to push on.”

Sports.title: Every saint has a past: how man at heart of City’s first scandal became a United hero | Sean Ingle
Sports.content:
When the Manchester City decision finally dropped, the Guardian’s verdict was damning. “FOOTBALL SENSATION – MANCHESTER CITY’S GRAVE OFFENCES – HEAVY PUNISHMENTS”, the headline read. “It is now proved that the club had for years systematically broken the rules of the Football Association by very unscrupulous means.”

But these words weren’t written last Friday. Instead they were penned more than 120 years ago, at the culmination of English football’s first big illicit payments scandal.

Back then City were a club rapidly on the up, with money and attitude to burn – which might sound familiar. Yet having won the FA Cup in 1904, everything began to unravel.

It started on the final day of the 1905 season, when City were on the verge of winning the title only to lose against Aston Villa in a match that involved punches and literal mud-slinging. Far more seriously, City’s star player, Billy Meredith, was also heard offering a £10 bribe to the Villa captain, Alec Leake, to throw the game.

Some say it was not serious. To this day no one knows the mysterious spectator who reported it. But it created a butterfly effect that led to Meredith being suspended for a season, and ramifications that lasted for decades.

Soon after, when Meredith was seen still hanging around City despite his ban, the FA launched a fresh investigation into the club’s finances. It found that not only was City’s gate money being funnelled into the private accounts of club directors, it was being used to give off-the-books payments to players.

Meredith, for instance, was on £6 a week when the maximum wage was £4. And he was far from the only one being given a little extra on the side. It led to the FA banning 17 players from playing for City again, while two of the club’s directors were banned for life.

View image in fullscreen After the 1906 scandal, Manchester City’s star forward joined Manchester United – what price Erling Haaland following in Billy Meredith’s footsteps? Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme. So is what happened to City all those years ago relevant to modern times? Yes, absolutely.

First off, the 1906 case proves that strong punishments work. While City were hardly the only club to be making similar illicit payments, the FA’s sanctions led to the club slipping down the table, being relegated three years later, and not winning the title until 1937.

That City team also offered an early example of one of football’s immutable laws of gravity. The faster a club rises, the more its foundations may be shaky or unsustainable, and the more it is likely to plummet back to earth.

The other interesting thing in all this? While City had the book thrown at them, Meredith enjoyed a redemption arc that continues to this day.

It helped that some felt he had been unfairly targeted for trying to set up a players’ union and campaigning for the abolition of the maximum wage. The wiry winger could certainly play too, which certainly didn’t hurt either.

Indeed no less a judge than David Lacey, the Guardian’s legendary football correspondent, described Meredith as ranking “with that of Stanley Matthews in the history of the British game”.

And when Manchester United fans voted Eric Cantona as their greatest ever player in 2001, Lacey suggested that a couple of decades earlier they would have gone for George Best, and before that Meredith himself.

The fact that Meredith, who turned out for City from 1894 to 1905 and again from 1921 to 1924, is also in United’s hall of fame marks him out as a unique and substantial force.

View image in fullscreen Meredith (front row, centre, with moustache and no hat) was a key part of the team that won Manchester United their first league title in 1908. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Intriguingly, those switches across Manchester don’t appear to have attracted much condemnation. Indeed, when Meredith played in the Manchester derby in 1910, the Guardian’s man on the ground was left unimpressed by the lack of fire and venom.

“Both sides tried hard, no doubt; there was no shirking to speak of,” he wrote. “But the game differed in no way that one could see from a hundred other games in which local rivalry has had no place whatsoever. The teams might have represented Penzance and Berwick-on-Tweed respectively for all the evidence the play gave to the contrary.”

In echoes of more modern times, the Guardian’s man also questioned whether modern players cared enough about the shirt on their backs.

“Is it reasonable to expect local or even club fervour in professional football as it exists today?” he wrote after United had won 2-1. “Can local patriotism thrive under a red jersey this year, a blue one the next, and perhaps a white one after that? It does not seem likely.”

Incredibly, Meredith kept playing until he was 49, helped, as the Guardian noted in his obituary, by being a details man whose “mind persistently dwelt on the problems of the game”.

Meredith, who was affectionately known as “old skin” and played with a toothpick in his mouth to help him concentrate, eventually called it a day four months before his 50th birthday when he took over a pub.

Not that it was a quiet retirement. During the Manchester blitz, for instance, a bomb exploded at the back of the pub and a shower of Welsh international caps scattered across the local neighbourhood. It took some time to collect them all given he played 51 times for his country.

Meredith was certainly a smart cookie too. When he was asked about the secret of City’s success, he openly admitted it was because the “club put aside the rule that no player should receive more than £4 a week”.

“Clubs are not punished for breaking the law – they are punished for being found out,” he also admitted. Which applies as much to 2026 as it did all more than a century ago.

Sports.title: Saracens bizarrely change chief Brendan Venter's job title to 'head of rugby culture and WINE consultant'... as club exploit media loophole after racking up a £5,000 fine
Sports.content:
Saracens have changed boss Brendan Venter’s job title to ‘head of rugby culture and wine consultant’ in a bid to ensure the eccentric South African can avoid undertaking media duties.

In January, the Londoners confirmed Venter was returning for a second stint at the club to replace Mark McCall – who had been in charge for 15 years – as director of rugby.

PREM Rugby rules state that the person who occupies that role – or relevant position as the head of the rugby operation – of each of its 10 teams must attend a weekly media conference and undertake pre and post-match duties with television and written journalists.

Saracens received a £5,000 fine from the PREM because Venter did not attend the league’s official pre-season media day at Twickenham earlier this month.

Further financial punishments followed after Venter was not seen both before and after Saracens’ impressive league-opening win at Leicester.

Head coach Joe Shaw spoke to media instead and is set to continue to do so moving forwards.

Saracens have changed Brendan Venter’s job title to ‘head of rugby culture and wine consultant’ in a bid to ensure he can avoid undertaking media duties

Saracens are understood to be disputing the fines handed out to them after arguing that Venter’s official position has now changed and asking for permission for Shaw to be the one who undertakes press commitments.

That is despite the fact it is Venter who is quite clearly the man in charge. He celebrated his team’s victory at Leicester enthusiastically.

Further, Daily Mail Sport understands that Venter has already mapped out Saracens’ team selection for the coming weeks, making a mockery of his new title.

During his first spell at Saracens, Venter was fined on several occasions for comments made to the media.

In 2010, after his team were beaten by French side Racing Metro in a European clash, the now 56-year-old gave an infamous, cringeworthy interview to Sky Sports that lasted just 57 seconds.

He is keen to avoid a repeat of that scenario but the wine expert’s new official position may yet only serve to cause Saracens further trouble.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White

It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am show Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: 'Fergie asked me to inject it': Wayne Rooney reveals extreme lengths he went to for Man United after playing Champions League match despite arriving at Old Trafford on CRUTCHES
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney has given an insight into the extreme lengths he went to for Man United, often playing through the pain barrier. The club legend, now 40, was known for his mental and physical toughness and has lifted the lid on how Sir Alex Ferguson expected him to take pain-killing injections to play through nasty injuries. Speaking on the Stick to United podcast, Rooney explained: 'I remember playing against Bayern Munich (2010) where I turned up on crutches in my car, the team had come on the bus. 'I went into the dressing room to wish the players good luck and ended up starting the game.' Co-host Mark Goldbridge then asked how that extraordinary turn of events came to pass. Rooney added: 'Because Fergie asked me to inject it to play. I injected it, I had to come off at half time. Took my boot off at half time and my ankle had gone up like that.' The former striker was asked about United's current injury issues and Bruno Fernandes' persistent minor issue. Wayne Rooney, pictured after the Bayern Munich game in 2010, injected his ankle to play through the pain barrier for Man United He went on: 'He strikes me as someone who wants to play every game, I was exactly the same. I don't have any issue with him wanting to play for Portugal. 'If it was an issue where there was no way he could then play for Man United for the next few weeks that would be different but it looks like an injury he's trying to manage. I'll be honest, 90 percent of the time in the Premier League you're managing an injury, you're playing with something that's uncomfortable. 'I think it's refreshing that players want to play more and I don't think we should be judging players because they want to play, it's a good thing. With the Nations League now there's games players can miss anyway.' United are suffering with a number of injury concerns, with Benjamin Sesko suffering with a shin problem, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford not fit enough for international duty and Fernandes nursing his knock. It is a concern for Michael Carrick, who has overseen a poor start to the campaign, with two draws, two defeats and a solitary victory. Rooney was also asked about Man City being found guilty of the vast majority of their charges and whether he would accept a retrospective Premier League title win. 'I have heard Rio has come out saying about getting another Premier League medal... I wouldn't really feel comfortable accepting another Premier League medal, if I'm being honest,' he said. 'I don't think we deserve it, we didn't do enough that season to win the league. I think we were six or seven points clear with four or five games to go and we threw it away.' 'I've seen everything that has come out over the past few days and listening to people and I was putting myself in a Man City player's shoes... they're players, they're doing everything they can to try and win the Premier League title and in their mind they have done it, if those players have no understanding of what is going on above them, if that happened to me... I would be absolutely devastated. 'It might happen, they might take them [medals] away, but I wouldn't want it [a medal] because I don't think as a team we deserved it that year because obviously we didn't finish first.'

Sports.title: Ex-world snooker champion Graeme Dott is jailed for seven years after he sexually abused young boy and girl
Sports.content:
Disgraced former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years for sexually abusing two children.

The 49-year-old subjected a girl and a boy, both of primary school age, to 'lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour' by touching and kissing them inappropriately.

The abuse, which took place in the Glasgow region, occurred between 1993 and 1996 involving the girl, and from 2006 to 2010 involving the boy.

Dott inappropriately touched the girl, instructed her to remove her clothes and exposed himself.

He separately abused a boy by making sexual remarks, molesting him and entering a bathroom where he watched him shower.

Both charges, which Dott had denied, stated the incidents occurred on 'various occasions'.

He was found guilty of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour and has now been sentenced at the High Court in Edinburgh - with judge Lord Harrower telling Dott he had 'robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood'.

Imposing a backdated sentence of seven years, he said Dott’s behaviour had involved a 'gross violation of trust'.

Lord Harrower remanded Dott in custody and his name was added to the sex offenders register indefinitely.

Disgraced former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years for sexually abusing two children

Graeme Dott is seen here playing a shot at a quarter-final match at Wembley Arena in London in January 2011

Dott, 49, was put in handcuffs as he was jailed for seven years at Edinburgh's High Court

Dott was told by a judge his behaviour had involved a 'gross violation of trust'

The disgraced ex-snooker player is pictured outside Glasgow's High Court in August this year

Sentencing Dott, Lord Harrower said his actions bore 'the hallmarks of grooming'.

Referring to the girl as Jane and the boy as Kevin, both pseudonyms, the judge said: 'In both cases the abuse included penetrative sexual activity and in the case of Jane behaviour that would now be classed as rape.'

He said that both children were vulnerable and told Dott: 'Your behaviour bore the hallmarks of grooming.'

Lord Harrower said that while the offending against Jane happened while Dott was still a child aged about 16 or 17 himself, the offences against Kevin took place while Dott was an adult.

He said: 'You robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood.'

The court heard that Dott continues to maintain his innocence.

During the trial, jurors heard from one of Dott's victims, a woman now in her 40s, who told the court the Scottish former professional snooker player had sexually abused her on multiple separate occasions while she was a child.

She said the abuse had started with Dott 'caressing' her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggy back.

The woman also described an occasion when she said Dott suggested playing a 'guessing game' where she had to guess what he was doing.

She told the court she lay down and he exposed himself to her and then began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis.

The woman told the court that Dott told her not to tell anyone he was sexually abusing her.

The second victim, a man who is now in his late 20s, said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts.

He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed.

'He would come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,' the man said.

'While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.'

He said looking back at it now, Dott was 'clearly getting sexual gratification from it', and he was 'pleasuring himself' while the abuse was taking place.

The victim said that because of his age at the time, he 'did not know what was going on', and it was only later he realised the interaction 'wasn't right'.

The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips, and 'push himself up against me'.

The trial heard Dott would buy him items such as Thai chilli crisps and Irn-Bru - which the victim said he can no longer eat to this day.

Dott also once gave the victim a £50 note then accused him of stealing it when his parents found out about the money.

The man told jurors the lead-up to being given the cash was 'sexually motivated' and that it was a 'reward strategy' for what had gone on.

Dott was also repeatedly inappropriate with him in a room while he played online poker games.

Other incidents occurred in a car after he parked up in an area 'out of the public eye', with the abuse taking place approximately five times.

Asked about any further recollections, the witness stated anything related to Dove soap gives him PTSD 'flashbacks' as Dott used it for a skin condition.

Dott faced a fresh investigation in 2024. He was later suspended by snooker's governing body prior to the case first calling at the high court last year.

He testified himself at the trial and denied all accusations. Dott described the then girl's claims as 'disgusting' and also insisted he had never been alone with the boy.

He said: 'I have never acted inappropriately with anyone.'

Giving evidence, Dott had said there was 'absolutely no way' he sexually abused two children – branding the allegations 'nonsense' and 'lies'.

He had been on bail for the trial at the High Court in Glasgow, but was remanded in custody by Lord Harrower.

Under cross-examination by prosecutor Lindsey Dalziel, Dott denied being attracted to the girl when she was young, calling the idea 'disgusting'.

When Ms Dalziel put it to Dott that he touched the first victim and told her what to do, he denied the allegation and called it 'lies'.

Speaking about the second victim, Dott said he was 'never in my company' and denied all allegations of abuse.

In her closing speech, Ms Dalziel called on the jury to find Dott guilty of both charges.

She said: 'The Crown's case is that Graeme Dott subjected vulnerable children to the worst kind of abuse with a course of conduct which relied on opportunity, for his own gratification.'

Dott's lawyer Euan Dow had invited jurors to clear his client of both charges.

But Dott was found guilty following the trial that began on August 18.

Dott, who had been living in Glasgow's Dennistoun district, held his head in hands as the verdicts were delivered, but showed no emotion as he was led handcuffed to a cell.

Kirsty Aitken, NSPCC assistant director for Scotland, said after the verdict: 'Graeme Dott sexually abused two young children between 1993 and 2010.

'His victims, who were primary school aged at the time, have lived for many years with the impact of this abuse, knowing that Dott had not been held accountable and was able to continue with his snooker career.

'Child sexual abuse can have a devastating and long-lasting impact on a person's life, and these victims have shown immense courage in coming forward and helping to bring Dott to justice.

'We hope this verdict supports their recovery, and it is vital they can access the help they need to move forward with their lives.

'No matter who the perpetrator is, or how many years have passed, it is never too late for those who have experienced abuse to speak out and seek support.'

The Scottish former professional snooker player won his first world title and first ranking title at the 2006 World Championship.

In 2008 he was said to have begun experiencing 'clinical depression' which affected his performance, amid a string of defeats.

Dott was suspended from competing in April 2025 after he was charged with sexual abuse and he has since been removed from World Snooker's Hall Of Fame.

Sports.title: Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly dropped by Lionesses: Sarina Wiegman leaves out two of her most trusted players for World Cup qualifiers - and tells them their 'levels' have dropped
Sports.content:
Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly dropped by Lionesses: Sarina Wiegman leaves out two of her most trusted players for World Cup qualifiers - and tells them their 'levels' have dropped

Sarina Wiegman has said that Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly weren't showing 'the levels' after dropping them from her Lionesses squad for their upcoming World Cup qualifier matches.

Both Toone and Kelly have been among Wiegman's most trusted players since the Dutch coach took charge in 2020, making their omission a surprise to many Lionesses supporters.

Kelly has started just one of Arsenal's four opening league games this season and has been dropped by Wiegman before, in February 2025, after lack of game time at her former side Manchester City.

Toone meanwhile has had a difficult start to her season under new Manchester United manager Eva Olid, and was dropped for their match against Arsenal two weeks ago - although returned to the starting XI for their subsequent game against West Ham.

Wiegman said: 'The main reason is that I think the levels weren't what I expect from them on the pitch. I've had a conversation with them. There's big competition going on too.'

On whether she felt Toone had been affected by United's difficult start to the season, where they lost their first two games against London City Lionesses and Chelsea before recording a draw at Arsenal and a win against West Ham: 'I don't know. Could be but I think there's some clubs that had a great start of the season, but I also look at how you execute your own football actions.

Chloe Kelly and Ella Toone have been dropped from the Lionesses squad for their upcoming World Cup qualifiers matches

Sarina Wiegman has said that Toone and Kelly weren't showing 'the levels' she expected

'At times it's complicated, but we have to focus on what I can control.'

There had been reports stating that Kelly had been struggling with a hamstring injury this season, although Wiegman said: 'It's just what I saw on the pitch. We kept it to football.'

Chelsea forward Aggie Beever-Jones has also been omitted by Wiegman in a statement of intent from the Dutch coach ahead of this month's two-legged World Cup semi-final qualifier against Greece.

There has also been a first call-up for Chelsea's Lexi Potter, who has impressed this season alongside Keira Walsh in the heart of the Blues' midfield.

She has started three of Chelsea's four WSL matches and was particularly impressive in their 1-0 defeat of Arsenal at the weekend.

The uncapped Erica Meg Parkinson, 18, has also been recalled after impressing at NWSL side North Carolina Courage since moving in July.

Sports.title: Arsenal legend Patrick Vieira reveals he held secret talks with Sir Alex Ferguson over stunning move to Man United - with Old Trafford boss pitching midfield vision with arch rival Roy Keane
Sports.content:
Patrick Vieira has revealed he held secret talks with Sir Alex Ferguson over a move to Manchester United, who planned to pair the Frenchman with his rival Roy Keane in the heart of their midfield. Vieira played for Arsenal between 1996 and 2005, a period defined by the intense rivalry between the two clubs. The Frenchman frequently clashed with United captain Keane, most notably when the pair had a heated exchange in the tunnel before a match at Highbury in February 2005. Speaking to Sky Sports, Vieira has admitted he could have been playing for the Red Devils after having a meeting with Ferguson. 'I had the opportunity to move to Real Madrid a couple of times and I even had an opportunity to move to Manchester United,' Vieira said. 'I had a meeting with Sir Alex Ferguson. Full respect, I couldn't say no to meeting him because he was an important figure in the Premier League. Patrick Vieira admitted to having a secret meeting with Sir Alex Ferguson over a potential move to Man United from Arsenal Vieira explained that Ferguson had wanted to pair him with his great rival Roy Keane in the heart of Man United's midfield 'We met and we talked and he explained to me his vision that he had for Manchester United and the team that he wanted to build. 'He wanted to play me with Roy Keane, (Ryan) Giggs on the left-hand side, David Beckham on the right-hand side and (Paul) Scholes to play behind (Ruud) Van Nistelrooy, so it wasn't a bad team. 'But I couldn't leave Arsenal, I was too happy there and we were on the way of building something quite really special for the club and that's the way it was. 'When you do well, of course there's teams who are interested and then you have to make a decision. 'But the decision for me was to stay at Arsenal because I felt the love from the club, from the players and from the fans. Everything was there for me to grow up as a player and to achieve what I wanted to.' While Vieira did not disclose when the meeting with Ferguson took place, Man United were linked with a move for the then-Arsenal captain in the summer of 2003. It was reported at the time that Ferguson had ordered the Red Devils' hierarchy to explore his potential signing, with Vieira only having one year remaining on his contract. Arsenal vice-chairman David Dein told the BBC at the time that 'Patrick Vieira is not for sale. Keane and Vieria had several notable clashes with captaining their teams during the peak of Man United and Arsenal's rivalry 'We have not had any inquiry from Manchester United for Patrick and even in the event of one he is not for sale.' Vieira would ultimately captain Arsenal to the Premier League title the following season as part of the 'Invincibles' team, with the Gunners crowned champions without losing a game. It was the third league title Vieira won with the Gunners, before he later left in 2005 for Juventus. Vieira later spent time at Inter Milan, before finishing his playing career at Manchester City. The Arsenal legend had previously admitted Ferguson's interest had been a 'compliment' when appearing on the documentary 'Keane and Vieira: Best of Enemies' back in 2013. Vieira and Keane, who missed when attempting to punch each other in a match in February 1999, had their most famous clash in their last meeting in 2005. Vieira had admitted in the documentary that he had caused the tunnel bust up at Highbury after warning Gary Neville he would come after him if he touched Robert Pires. ‘I started it. I was cool, I was really calm, I was smiling at him – and then he [Keane] lost it,' Vieira said. Vieira has previously admitted to causing the famous tunnel row between the pair back in 2005 'When we played at Old Trafford his [Gary Neville’s] tackling was flying in on Robert Pires and he was doing it on purpose, and I said “listen, we are not at Old Trafford here, this is Highbury”. ‘So I said to him “if you touch Robert, I will come after you”.’ Keane responded saying: ‘What really annoyed me that night was that you were picking on Gary, you were almost picking on the weakest link, so that’s what got my back up. 'There were two or three of you ganging up on Gary, simple as that.’ Vieira and Keane have since worked together as pundits both on ITV's coverage of major tournaments, as well as on Sky Sports.

Sports.title: Revealed: Fearful Argentina youngsters are reluctant to move to the Premier League with World Cup villains hit by fan abuse following semi-final exploits against England
Sports.content:
Revealed: Fearful Argentina youngsters are reluctant to move to the Premier League with World Cup villains hit by fan abuse following semi-final exploits against England

Argentina's top youngsters are having doubts about moving to the Premier League after seeing their World Cup stars targeted by fans.

The top flight is feeling the aftershocks of Argentina’s controversial victory over England in the World Cup semi-final, with Enzo Fernandez, Lisandro Martinez and Valentin Barco among the players to cop abuse from rival supporters during the opening weeks of the campaign.

Premier League clubs scout extensively in South America and try to find the best players before they move to other European clubs, where their value will increase quickly.

Tomas Aranda, Leonel Flores and Tobias Andrada are just three of the outstanding young talents in the Argentine top flight who are on the radar of Premier League clubs.

Yet Daily Mail Sport has spoken to recruitment experts in Argentina who believe their top prospects may be advised to move to Spain, Portugal or Italy while the atmosphere in England remains hostile.

Enzo Fernandez provocatively celebrated scoring for Argentina against England at the World Cup and has been targeted by fans back in the Premier League

While senior internationals like Fernandez and Martinez can handle the heat, it would be a significant extra challenge for inexperienced players already adapting to a new league, culture and lifestyle.

Fernandez, then with Chelsea but now with Manchester City, scored the equaliser in the semi-final and then infuriated England supporters with a provocative celebration.

Despite being an unused substitute, Barco celebrated Argentina’s goals wildly and Jude Bellingham slapped him on the back of the head after the final whistle.

Meanwhile Martinez displayed a banner bearing the words ‘Las Malvinas son Argentinas’ (The Falklands are Argentina’s), for which FIFA fined the Argentine FA £237,000.

Sports.title: 'We have lived through a period of deceit': Mauricio Pochettino says no punishment can repair the damage of Man City's rule breaking
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino has claimed Man City being found guilty of the vast majority of charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules would confirm a 'period of deceit' and believes 'no punishment' could repair the damage caused. City have been found guilty of all substantive charges brought by the Premier League, over a time period in which they lifted three titles as part of an eight-trophy haul. The findings of the tribunal, which concluded in December 2024, are still to be made public. The breaches of Premier League financial regulations span between 2009 and 2018. Pochettino managed Southampton from 2013 to 2014, before a five-year spell in charge of Tottenham from 2014 to 2019. 'We have lived through a period where sporting justice did not exist,' Pochettino said, in Spanish, when asked about the verdict in the Man City case. Former Tottenham boss Mauricio Pochettino, left, has claimed Man City being found guilty breaches of Premier League financial rules would confirm a 'period of deceit' Man City were crowned champions twice during Pochettino's time in charge of Tottenham 'It's very difficult when out of 115 charges you are found guilty of 114 to know what the punishment should be to make it fair. 'Because there are other clubs like Nottingham Forest or Everton that broke rules and received different sanctions, whether point deductions or fines. 'It's a very difficult situation that causes astonishment given the magnitude of the verdict. And it's also fair to ask where the controls were for the rules to be broken like that. That's what catches my attention the most.' Tottenham missed out on Champions League qualification after finishing fifth in Pochettino's first season in charge, with Man City finishing as league runners-up. Man City were crowned champions in both 2018 and 2019, as Pochettino's side finished third and fourth in the league. Pochettino highlighted that his Tottenham side had operated under financial constraints during his final years at the club. Tottenham famously became the first Premier League side not to sign a player in both the summer and winter transfer windows during the 2018-19 season. The period coincided with the construction of the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Pochettino also referenced his recent comments that Tottenham should be awarded the 2017 Premier League title. Pochettino stated 'We have lived through a period where sporting justice did not exist' and that 'no punishment' handed to Manchester City would be able to repair the damage caused Pochettino recently claimed Tottenham should have been awarded the 2017 Premier League title after Chelsea admitted to breaking rules by making secret payments to secure transfers Chelsea pipped Spurs to the Premier League title under Antonio Conte in 2017, finishing the season on 93 points – seven clear of Tottenham's 86 – but have since admitted to breaking the rules by making more than £47million in secret payments to unregistered agents and third parties to facilitate transfers. 'That was a big disadvantage because we were fighting among the best teams and reaching a Champions League final [in 2019],' Pochettino said. 'Why were those controls so strict with us and not as much with others? That's why I say everything is very strange, and the problem is that everything gets clouded. 'If it's true that they broke 114 rules, we have lived through a period of deceit. 'No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done, and the Premier League's controls are severely damaged. 'It's a very sad situation because what was already achieved and celebrated maybe wasn't real, and what wasn't so good could have been better. 'We have lived through a period where sporting justice did not exist. If the charges are proven, it's very difficult to repair what happened. I hope that at least it serves to ensure equality exists in the future. 'I said at the time regarding Chelsea's situation when we fought for the title with them while I was at Tottenham, that they were better because they got more points, but by breaking rules. How do you repair that?' In total, Tottenham missed out on lucrative Champions League qualification four times during the years covered by Man City's charges. Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano (left) has warned their fight against the Premier League will take ‘a lot more time’ to conclude Tottenham finished fifth in 2010-11, 2012-13 and 2014-15, while they finished fourth in 2011-12 but missed out on qualification because Chelsea won the competition despite finishing sixth. Spurs are among four clubs – along with Arsenal, Liverpool and Man United – who served legal notices last year reserving their right to take action should City be found guilty. They will argue, should the verdict stand, that City's misdemeanours cost them titles, trophies, European qualification and, above all when it comes to these things, money. Representatives have already begun putting together a case on how much they feel they have a claim for, pointing out that they have lost potential income on the back of City’s cheating. Despite news of the independent commission siding with the Premier League, Man City chief executive Ferran Soriano has warned their fight will still take ‘a lot more time’ to conclude. Soriano was at a private meeting with the executive board of European Football Clubs’ body along with other bosses of top clubs and, according to sources, was quick to address the elephant in the room. ‘It’s taken eight years to get here,’ Soriano told the assembled club chiefs, ‘and it’s going to take a lot more time’. City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a statement on Saturday: ‘The process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.’ An appeal from City’s expensively assembled legal team is viewed as an inevitability. They have 14 days to lodge such a request which would be heard by a separate panel. A wide range of punishments, including expulsion, are available under Premier League rules. The original panel would take arguments from both sides before deciding on a penalty it feels befits the crime.

Sports.title: Training duo given 12-month disqualification after dead horse tested positive for ADHD drug
Sports.content:
Training duo given 12-month disqualification after dead horse tested positive for ADHD drug

The husband and wife team of Grant and Alana Williams, who have dominated racing in Western Australia, pleaded guilty to the charge but blamed contamination

View 2 Images Grant and Alana Williams: Western Australia's leading trainers (Image: X)

The husband and wife team who run one of Australia’s most formidable racing operations have been disqualified for 12 months.

‌



Grant and Alana Williams have dominated racing in Perth, Western Australia, where they are reigning champion trainers. They have sent out 924 winners, including 12 at Group 1 level.

‌



They were temporarily suspended in January after one of their runners tested positive for an ADHD drug after breaking down and dying after a race. Stewards opened an inquiry after a prohibited substance was found in a sample taken from nine-time winner Starry Heights who died after being pulled up in a Listed race at Kalgoorlie in October last year.

‌



OLI BELL: Exciting times ahead for leading jumps yard diversifying towards the Flat READ MORE :

The suspension was lifted after 29 days after a stay was granted, but on Tuesday, Racing Western Australia announced the outcome of the stewards’ inquiry.

The couple had pleaded guilty to presenting Starry Heights to take part in a race where “the Prohibited List A substance ritalinic acid was detected in a post-mortem sample taken after it had competed in and been eased out of the race”.

In deciding the penalty, the stewards took into account that the substance is banned at all times in racing.

‌



The panel added: “Although submissions were made with respect to the detection of the substance being due to contamination, the Stewards were not satisfied that there was sufficient basis upon which to accept those submissions.

View 2 Images Grant and Alana Williams: blamed the finding on contamination (Image: X)

“Consequently, the inquiry was unable to establish an accepted explanation for the detection of the substance.”

‌



According to Racenet , the Williams’s plan to appeal against the severity of a sentence, which will expire on August 29 next year.

In a message to owners they said they were “devastated by the decision".

"We believe the penalty imposed is grossly excessive and disproportionate and does not properly reflect the circumstances surrounding this matter," they said.

Article continues below

"We have instructed our legal counsel to immediately take the necessary steps to appeal this decision. We will also be seeking a stay of this disqualification pending the determination of that appeal."

Sports.title: La Liga chief demands 'severe' Man City punishment in clear message to Premier League
Sports.content:
La Liga chief demands 'severe' Man City punishment in clear message to Premier League

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled against them by the Premier League in February 2023 and their punishment is yet to be decided

View 2 Images Javier Tebas has discussed Manchester City's charges (Image: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press via Getty Images)

Manchester City must face a "severe punishment" for breaching spending rules - according to La Liga president Javier Tebas. City have been left in crisis after it emerged the club has been found guilty of the majority of the charges brought against them by the Premier League.

‌



City are expected to launch an appeal, with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak remaining confident the club will prove its innocence. But Tebas has called for City to face the strongest possible sanctions available to the Premier League - if they have breached financial rules.

‌



The most severe punishment available to the Premier League is expulsion, an outcome that would require the support of at least 15 of the competition's 20 clubs at a general meeting. Tebas, a campaigner against 'financial doping' in European football, believes any sanction should make an example of City.

‌



He said: "I don't know the exact rules, but I believe it should be the strictest punishment in the Premier League regulations regarding this matter. It should be a punishment intended to set an example.

"This isn't a matter of a father and his children - it is a punishment to ensure rules are followed. And violating the rules for over 10 years - no matter how minor the infractions - is a very serious matter.

"Therefore it has to be a severe punishment for the non-compliance. Not just to set an example, but because the rules were broken."

The Premier League are yet to publicly confirm the verdict but have declined to comment on the reports. On Saturday, Al Mubarak wrote a letter to supporters to reaffirm the club's stance.

‌



"Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues," the City chairman said.

Sports.title: Triple relegation, £40m fine: Football's biggest punishments as Man City face nervous wait
Sports.content:
We waited three-and-a-half years, and now we wait again.

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League back in February 2023. The club continue to deny any financial wrongdoing and insist that they'll clear their name.

But the conversation has quickly shifted to the potential punishment. Could City be relegated and their owners forced to leave? How about a rolling points deduction and a transfer ban? Or might they get away with just a fine?

Mirror Football looks back at some of the biggest punishments for breaching financial rules in football history.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN CITY FB PAGE! Follow our Manchester City Mirror Football Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Swindon Town - 1990

If you thought that last season's Championship play-off final was controversial, get a load of 1990's. Ten days after Swindon Town beat Sunderland 1-0 at Wembley to secure promotion to the old First Division, the club were found guilty of making illegal payments to players.

Not only were Swindon stripped of promotion and replaced in the top flight by Sunderland, Ossie Ardiles' side were sent down to the third tier. Tranmere Rovers were due to replace them in what's now known as the Championship, but following an appeal, Swindon's punishment was reduced to a one-division relegation.

‌



How should Manchester City be punished? Have your say in the comments section.

View 7 Images Swindon Town's play-off final victory was chalked off (Image: Professional Sport/Popperfoto via Getty Images/Getty Images)

Tottenham Hotspur - 1994

Ever feel like you've suffered the consequences of what someone else did? Well, in 1994, Tottenham were fined £600,000, thrown out of the FA Cup and docked 12 points after being found guilty of making illegal payments to players under their previous ownership.

With Alan Sugar now running the club, Spurs informed the FA themselves but were still dealt rough justice. Upon appeal, however, Tottenham saw both their cup ban and points deduction overturned, although the fine was raised to £1.5million.

‌



View 7 Images Alan Sugar's Tottenham paid the price of previous wrongdoings (Image: Graham Chadwick /Allsport)

Luton Town - 2008

To this day, Luton Town's 30-point deduction remains the largest in English football history. Having initially been docked 10 points ahead of the 2008-09 season and fined £50,000, it was soon found that the Hatters had broke the EFL's rules by leaving administration without having made a Company Voluntary Arrangement with its creditors.

The Football League offered Luton the chance to continue playing in League Two on the condition that they were deducted a further 20 points. They appealed, of course, but it was thrown out and Mick Harford's men were relegated to non-league for the first time in their history, finishing rock bottom of the table.

View 7 Images Luton Town were relegated to non-league following the 30-point deduction (Image: Clive Rose/Getty Images)

‌



Rangers - 2012

Go on social media and you'll find plenty of memes about Manchester City playing in the fourth division. But for Scottish giants Rangers, it was reality.

In July 2012, Rangers were denied entry into the Scottish Premier League due to the club's liquidation. A vote subsequently took place between the chairmen of Scottish Football League clubs to determine where Rangers would land.

Twenty-five of the 30 clubs decided that it would be the fourth tier, sparking what could've been years in the wilderness at Ibrox. Fortunately for Rangers, who also received a 12-month transfer ban, they won back-to-back promotions before returning to the top flight in 2016.

View 7 Images Ally McCoist led Rangers to their first two promotions (Image: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images)

‌



Queens Park Rangers - 2018

From big spenders in the Premier League to fighting for survival in the Championship, the first half of the 2010s for Queens Park Rangers was tumultuous to say the least. Their problems off the pitch were exacerbated by issues in the boardroom, too.

QPR were ordered to pay a world-record £40m fine in 2017 after the club lost its a three-year battle after being found guilty of breaching Financial Fair Play rules during the 2013-14 season when they were promoted back to the Premier League. The Rs would, though, reach a settlement with the EFL the following year, agreeing to pay £42m.

The settlement was made up of a £17m fine, the EFL's legal costs worth £3m and an agreement from club shareholders to write off £22m of outstanding loans. QPR, who'd argued that the existing FFP rules were unlawful, were also placed under a brief transfer embargo.

View 7 Images Queens Park Rangers ended up paying £42million (Image: Clive Rose/Getty Images)

‌



Man City - 2020

Manchester City have been here before. In February 2020, the reigning Premier League champions were slapped with a two-year ban from UEFA club competitions over 'serious breaches' of FFP regulations between 2012 and 2016.

But five months later, the Court of Arbitration for Sport announced that City had been cleared of 'disguising equity funds as sponsorship contributions'. Their fine was also reduced from €30m (£26.9m at the time) to €10m (£9m).

That season, City came closer than ever to winning the Champions League before losing 1-0 in the final to Chelsea. Two years later, Pep Guardiola's team would finally get their hands on it.

‌



Juventus - 2023

As if the ignominy of only being able to qualify for the Conference League wasn't enough, Juventus didn't even get to play in the competition during the 2023-24 season. The punishment came after the CFCB First Chamber (an independent judicial body responsible club finances) concluded that the Serie A heavyweights had breached the UEFA's regulatory framework and went against a settlement agreement which had been signed in August 2022.

Fiorentina, who'd finished eighth the season prior, replaced Juventus in the Conference League and went on to reach the final. UEFA also ordered Juventus to cough up a fine worth £17.14m, although they'd only have to pay half of that amount if their financial records for the next three years complied with regulations.

View 7 Images Juventus were banned from Europe for one season (Image: Stefano Guidi/Getty Images)

UEFA's verdict compounded a woeful few years for the Bianconceri. Former president Andrea Agnelli, as well as other members of the board, had resigned after Juventus were found guilty of false accounting.

‌



It also saw Juventus deducted 15 points. Even those who'd already left the Allianz Stadium were punished, with Tottenham managing director of football Fabio Paratici given a 30-month worldwide ban by FIFA.

Sports.title: Maurcio Pochettino hits out at Premier League with clear verdict on Man City charges
Sports.content:
Maurcio Pochettino hits out at Premier League with clear verdict on Man City charges

Mauricio Pochettino has issued a clear verdict on Manchester City's alleged financial breaches with the ex-Tottenham head coach also hitting out at the Premier League

View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino has given his verdict on Man City's charges (Image: The Overlap)

Former Tottenham boss Mauricio Pochettino has admitted that "no punishment will repair the damage" that has been caused by Manchester City's alleged 114 financial breaches - as he asked why the Premier League didn't act sooner.

‌



The 54-year-old, who is now in charge of the Unites States national team, was in charge of Spurs during the period which City have been found in breach of Premier League regulations. The club are planning to appeal the outcome and continue to deny any wrongdoing.

‌



When asked for his thoughts on the guilty verdict, Pochettino delivered a clear response and also took aim at the Premier League.

‌



"It’s very difficult when out of 115 charges you are found guilty of 114 to know what the punishment should be to make it fair,’ Pochettino told a press conference. "Because there are other clubs like Nottingham Forest or Everton that broke rules and received different sanctions, whether point deductions or fines. It’s a very difficult situation that causes astonishment given the magnitude of the verdict."

Asking how the governing bodies allowed such serious breaches over a sustained period of times, Pochettino said: "And it’s also fair to ask where the controls were for the rules to be broken like that. That’s what catches my attention the most.

"It’s a very sad situation because what was already achieved and celebrated maybe wasn’t real, and what wasn’t so good could have been better.

‌



"We have lived through a period where sporting justice did not exist. If the charges are proven, it’s very difficult to repair what happened. I hope that at least it serves to ensure equality exists in the future.’

"That was a big disadvantage because we were fighting among the best teams and reaching a Champions League final. Why were those controls so strict with us and not as much with others?

"That’s why I say everything is very strange, and the problem is that everything gets clouded. If it’s true that they broke 114 rules, we have lived through a period of deceit. No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done, and the Premier League’s controls are severely damaged.

‌



View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino faced off against Pep Guardiola on several occasions

In Spanish, he also told the Guardian: “Where were the controls? That’s what gets my attention. Where were the controls? If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham – I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months.

"I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer]. They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that’s why I say: it’s all very strange.

‌



"Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn’t come for a lot of years] – what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points?

"It’s really hard and it is a huge sadness. At the end of the day we get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn’t that real, what seemed good maybe wasn’t so good, what didn’t look good maybe was good but couldn’t be good because of what happened."

Pochettino's thoughts are perhaps not that surprising given he believes that Tottenham should have a Premier League title due to Chelsea's violations that they admitted to upon the arrival of the new ownership.

Article continues below

The Argentine was linked with a return to north London but signed a new contract overseas following the arrival of Roberto De Zerbi, who kept Spurs in the Premier League last season.
