Sports.title: Former world heavyweight champion boxer, 53, loses sad comeback against club fighter after 12 years retired
Sports.content:
Hasim Rahman shocked the boxing world when he knocked out Lennox Lewis to become heavyweight champion in 2001.

But 25 years later, he was fighting in front of just a handful of people in Lowell, Indiana and losing a split decision to a club fighter on Thursday night.

Rahman made a sad return to the ring 12 years after his last fight at VFW Post 6841, fighting against 4-4 opponent Phillip Triantafillo for the Indiana State heavyweight belt.

And he lost a six-round unanimous decision, with two judges' scorecards scoring the bout 59-55 and the other 58-56. The loss drops his record to 50-10-2 in a fight that was a far cry from his glory days as the king of boxing's biggest division.

Rahman has been threatening a comeback for years, finally announcing in May he would return to the ring and claiming he had ambitions of becoming boxing's oldest heavyweight champion.

That record is held by George Foreman, who regained the heavyweight championship at 45, eight years younger than Rahman.

Hasim Rahman lost a unanimous decision as he made a sad comeback to boxing at the age of 53

Rahman was once the IBC and WBC heavyweight boxing champion back in 2001

His low-key loss against Triantafillo drew criticism from those within the boxing community.

Legendary promoter Lou DiBella wrote on X: 'In the early hours of this morning, in Lowell, Indiana, 53 yr. old former heavyweight champion Hasim Rahman lost a six round sanctioned #boxing match to a 3-4 guy... a SANCTIONED fight.

'Every day, in many ways, across borders, from billionaire and corporate supported events to unsafe silliness in tiny venues, boxing is showing you what it is in 2026. You can have it!'.

Boxing writer Dan Rafael wrote: 'Just watched some sad s***: Utterly washed former heavyweight champion Hasim Rahman, age 53, ending a 13-year retirement & losing a slow motion 6-rounder to 40-year-old novice Phillip Triantafillo (now 5-4) in what looked like a community center gym in front of maybe a dozen people. #Boxing is unforgiving.'

Baltimore, Maryland native Rahman last fought professionally in June 2014, losing a three-round decision in Auckland, New Zealand against Anthony Nansen.

Two years earlier, he had been knocked out in the second round by Alexander Povetkin in a fight that marked the end of his career at the top level.

Rahman produced one of the sport's great upsets when he beat Lewis in April 2001 in South Africa, knocking him out in the fifth round before losing a rematch later that year.

He went on to fight the likes of Evander Holyfield, James Toney and Wladimir Klitchsko in his long career which has now featured another chapter long past his 50th birthday.

Rahman was beaten by his 4-4 opponent in a six-round contest in front of barely any people

Rahman shocked the boxing world when he knocked out Lennox Lewis in South Africa in 2001

Another former world heavyweight champion, Mike Tyson, made headlines for his return to the ring in 2024 aged 58 against Jake Paul.

He recently insisted he would 'never' return again, saying: 'That’s why I did the last fight. So I never have to do it again.'

Tyson earned a reported $20 million payday for that return to the ring, which ended with a sad unanimous decision loss, but he later wrote: 'This is one of those situations when you lost but still won.

'I’m grateful for last night. No regrets to get in ring one last time. I almost died in June. Had 8 blood transfusions. Lost half my blood and 25lbs in hospital and had to fight to get healthy to fight so I won.

'To have my children see me stand toe to toe and finish 8 rounds with a talented fighter half my age in front of a packed Dallas Cowboy stadium is an experience that no man has the right to ask for. Thank you.'

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua's long-awaited fight with Tyson Fury has finally been confirmed for December 11 at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium – and it will save Joshua around £7.5million in tax. It is understood each man will pocket around £75m for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil after Joshua’s team, led by Eddie Hearn, succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York. Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff. The ring walk is expected to take place around 2am to suit a US-based audience, in line with the demands of Netflix, which will broadcast the heavyweight showdown. Although the delivery of the fight in Wales will be positioned as a victory for British fight fans, pragmatism around tax was also a key consideration in Hearn’s argument against Madison Square Garden in New York. As Daily Mail Sport revealed earlier this month, the two fighters would have been taxed around 30 per cent of their purses in America, compared to 20 per cent in the UK, with Joshua particularly unhappy about the prospect of an extra £7.5m being added to his bill. The two-time world champion instead demanded that his contract be honoured, which stipulated a British-based fight. Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh said: 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. 'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.' Netflix today confirmed the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 a month in the UK. Bookmaker Betfair make Fury the early favourite to win, pricing him at 8/15. Joshua is priced at 13/8. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been announced for Friday, December 11 The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation', alongside an emoji of the British flag. His promoter Eddie Hearn, who fought relentlessly to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.' Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua. The pair had originally been pencilled in to fight on November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil. Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home, and fought hard to make that happen. Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away. Now those fears, after ten years of frustration, have been put to bed. The fight will take place in Cardiff, with the later-than-usual start time expected to mean ring walks at around 2am UK time as organisers attempt to satisfy the American audience watching on Netflix. Wembley had been the preferred venue for the showdown, but the major stumbling block was securing the necessary late-night permit. With Netflix and Turki Alalshikh keen for the event to cater to viewers in the United States, organisers required a start time significantly later than would normally be permitted at Wembley. Cardiff, however, was able to secure the required permit - clearing the final obstacle to bringing the fight back to Britain. Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

Your browser does not support iframes.

The scale of the occasion is already being felt in the Welsh capital, with hotels in Cardiff now understood to be sold out as supporters scramble to secure accommodation for one of the biggest fights in British boxing. For Joshua, the move represents the culmination of a push to ensure the fight was staged in the UK. The former two-times world champion and Hearn had been clear that, after years of watching British heavyweight stars travel overseas for major fights, Joshua-Fury belonged in front of their home crowd. Fury was willing to compromise on the location if necessary, however, with his priority being to finally get the fight over the line. The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects. Joshua won Olympic gold at London 2012 before turning professional, while Fury had already made his professional debut in 2008 and was building an unbeaten record of his own. For years, the prospect of the two eventually sharing a ring became one of British boxing's great hypothetical match-ups. Fury's stunning victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015 elevated him to the summit of the heavyweight division, while Joshua was rapidly closing in on world-title status himself. FURY VS JOSHUA - BIG FIGHT ODDS Fury to win - 8/15 Draw - 16/1 Joshua to win- 13/8 Victory method: Tyson Fury by Points or Decision - 16/5 Fury by TKO/KO/DQ - 13/10 Anthony Joshua by Dec/Tech Dec - 15/2 Joshua TKO/KO/DQ - 13/5 Fight to go the distance: Yes - 13/8 No - 4/9 Odds courtesy of Betfair Joshua claimed the IBF heavyweight title by stopping Charles Martin in 2016 before adding the WBA and IBO belts to his collection. By 2017, Joshua-Fury had evolved from a fantasy fight into a genuine target. But the negotiations repeatedly broke down. The closest it came to fruition was in 2021, when the two camps appeared to be on the brink of agreeing a two-fight deal. The proposed showdown was publicly discussed and appeared to be edging towards reality, only for Fury to become contractually obligated to face Deontay Wilder after an arbitration ruling. That fight ultimately took place, with Fury beating Wilder for a third time, while Joshua embarked on his own defining chapter against Oleksandr Usyk. Joshua lost his WBA, IBF and WBO titles to Usyk in 2021 before suffering a second defeat to the Ukrainian in their 2022 rematch. Once again, Joshua-Fury seemed to drift further away. Then came another tantalising opportunity. Negotiations accelerated in late 2022, with both camps discussing a potential December showdown, but the fight again failed to materialise. Fury moved on to other opponents while Joshua began rebuilding his career following the two defeats by Usyk. The emergence of Alalshikh and the rapid expansion of Saudi Arabia's influence over boxing created a fresh route to making the fight. And this time, the years of disappointment are finally over. The contracts have been signed. Joshua-Fury is no longer a fight being negotiated, teased or promised. It will take place in Cardiff on December 11.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's torture training! Boxer uses ancient Cossack warriors' stretching machine to prepare himself to fight Tyson Fury in a painful-looking workout routine
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has been summoning the strength of an ancient warrior as he prepares for his long-awaited bout with Tyson Fury on a stretching machine.

Boxing's biggest battle of the year is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in early December, after a venue war that saw it move from Madison Square Garden in New York.

Despite the superfight being shrouded in uncertainty for much of the year, both Joshua and Fury have been knuckling down in the gym in preparation for their showdown.

Away from the usual training drills associated with boxing, it appears that Joshua is trying something new in order to get the best out of himself when he faces the Gypsy King.

The two-time heavyweight world champion has posted a video to Instagram of him using a Pravilo machine, a stretching machine used by warriors in medieval times.

The machine is a training and conditioning device that originates from Slavic and Russian traditions. It is best-known for being used by historical Cossack warriors for over 1,000 years.

Anthony Josshua has posted a video of him using the ancient warrior Pravilo machine

And if the video posted by Joshua is anything to go by, it can be somewhat of a torturous bit of equipment, based on how it stretches out each limb of the human body.

The 36-year-old can be seen being pulled into a starfish position by the modern version of the machine, which he keeps in his new training gym in Dubai.

Earlier this year, Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic due to the conflict in the Middle East.

The post on Instagram – which is captioned 'When the instructor says, relax and breathe' – also shows the 251.0lb (113.9kg) frame of Joshua being easily rotated 180 degrees, displaying the strength of his core.

Joshua will be returning to the Welsh capital where he has won twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in 2017 and 2018 respectively.

Wembley had looked an ideal venue for the fight, but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in December

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

The streaming giant Netflix has yet to sign off on Cardiff, but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last week reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Sports.title: Why Conor Benn's 85-second humiliation against Ryan Garcia was the inevitable consequence of his fast-tracked career - and how the Brit became a sacrificial pawn in boxing's power struggle, writes JEFF POWELL
Sports.content:
The Wizard Of Oz is now a spectacular fantasy production encompassing the inside of the giant globe called The Sphere which looms large over the Las Vegas Strip.

Where the yellow brick road leads for Conor Benn after his one round, one minute and 25 seconds destruction by the fastest gun in Sin City is a question to which nobody had the answer as he was being ferried to hospital for precautionary checks. And may not have for some time to come.

There is no clear pathway back to the heights to which he was thrust all too prematurely and without justification this Saturday night.

Benn had no place being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia, who is emerging as the golden goose saviour of American and Mexican boxing. Nor had he done anything like enough in his patchwork career thus far to qualify for the honour of topping the bill at an arena as grand as the T-Mobile in as hallowed a home of boxing as Las Vegas.

This was a match made far away from fight heaven, deep in the casino vaults. Benn Jr leaves here millions of dollars the richer but with not so much as a scintilla of evidence that he will ever be able to mix it with the royalty of the ring, in which King Ry sits upon the throne. He has the payoff but not the legacy he craved.

For the second time in as many months English sport comes home from America with its tail between its legs. Only this clinical beat-down of an inferior boxer was aeons more humiliating than the retreat of our footballers from the World Cup. His defeat more comprehensive than that by Argentina.

Conor Benn was beaten inside two rounds by Ryan Garcia in their welterweight championship fight

Benn's humiliating defeat came after he thrust all too prematurely and without justification into the title fight

Benn had no place in being in the same ring as world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia

Little did Benn know, in his delusion of self grandeur, that in return for securing his family’s financial future he was used as a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between the houses of Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White on their doorstep.

Garcia, younger of the two by a year but a decade wiser, knew. He tried to cushion Benn’s fall from grace by calling him a ‘good dude who I hope can come back from this.’

But as a man who likes to tell it as it is he felt compelled to add: ‘ I knew exactly how the fight would go. Rushing in against me from the start is not a good idea. Not the way to go. You need patience in this game.’

When it was pointed out to him that Benn has not stopped an opponent for more than four years he added: ‘I must be honest. I did not feel any power in his punches.’

Not that there were many of them. Benn’s charge from the first bell was suicidal against the best, fastest and hardest counter puncher in the world. He ran headlong into a hail of Garcia’s trademark left hooks. To note that he lost the first round is as understated as saying that Goliath had a bad day at the office against David. And when in the second Garcia brought into play the right hand which is now almost as deadly as the left Benn was gone in 85 seconds.

Gone crawling on the canvas and still so unsteady when reeled to his feet that the referee let him continue only so far as the next battering.

Garcia observed: ‘It could have been stopped after the first knock down. I looked into his eyes down there and they were glazed over. He was already gone.’

He echoed the pre-fight fears of many of us that Benn could be in critical jeopardy if this went on too long, saying: ‘It would not have been good for Conor if this lasted any further.’

Benn appears to have been a sacrificial pawn in the power struggle for control of big-time boxing between Queensberry and Matchroom against the arrival of UFC promoter Dana White

Has he lived to fight another day? Dana White sounded less than totally convinced: ‘I’ve told Conor to go on holiday with his family and call me when he’s ready to come back. Then we can try to find the right fight for him.’

That would not be at welter after his ‘hellish’ struggle to cut his poundage. But if he can be hammered into oblivion by a 147-pounder what will become of him if he goes back up two divisions to middleweight?

No such doubts hang over Garcia. Having been saluted to the reverberating rafters of the T-Mobile by his half-brother Mexicans in the delirium of their Independence weekend celebrations, this Californian will resume his American love affair in more world title fights against the likes of Devin Haney and Teofimo Lopez.

He, not Conor Benn in his wildest dreams, is the face and the future of boxing over here.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia destroys Conor Benn with brutal second-round TKO to retain WBC welterweight title in Las Vegas showdown
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas on Saturday night, retaining his WBC welterweight title in the process.

Benn ran blindly to the slaughter - in a fight which was always a lunge too far - and was left groveling on hands and knees at the feet of the new face of American and Mexican boxing.

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the upstart son of Nigel the great.

Benn’s predictable sally forth from the first bell was as pointless, desperate and doomed to disaster as The Charge of the Light Brigade.

He was stopped in his tracks by the barrage of left hooks which have taken Garcia to the welterweight championship of the world, over which he will reign for as long as he likes.

The first round was but a prelude to the carnage to come in the 85 seconds which the first round lasted. A punishment doubled by the dynamite which also explodes from Garcia's right fist.

Ryan Garcia sealed a stunning second-round TKO win over Conor Benn in Las Vegas

Garcia took just four minutes and 25 seconds to devastate and humiliate the British star

The 28-year-old retained his WBC welterweight title after the devastating display in Sin City

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by a two-fisted assault to which he had no answer. When he staggered drunkenly to his feet referee Thomas Taylor looked long and hard into his glazed eyes before letting him carry on.

The kill was mercifully swift. A combination of lefts and rights which the third man in the ring could no longer ignore.

This is a warning which his handlers must not forget. This was fight too much, too soon. As Garcia had warned he done nothing to deserve the tilt at the WBC belt his father had worn with such pride.

Nor his elevation the top of a bill in the T-Mobile arena nor in this Mecca of boxing Whether he will ever be ready to mix with the company of prize-ring loyalty is doubtful.

He was not only outclassed, out-sped an out-thought but was treated to punching of almighty power with which his dad could not gift him.

The last 24 hours before the first bell had been consumed by doom-casts about Benn’s drastic weight draining to reach the welter limit of 147 lbs.

Followed by extraordinary claims that he had put on more than two stones following Friday’s weigh-in which, if authentic, would have catapulted him into the ring three divisions even heavier than the super-middleweights.

The truth would out as his robe slipped off. But if he had gorged himself between stepping on the scales and the first bell that might done him much good. Such drastic shifts in poundage are as debilitating as dehydration.

If this was another of the mind games played by Benn and Garcia throughout the wind up and build up it seemed doubtful that any of that would have a material effect on the fight itself. Would anyone in this hardest of all games risk being beaten by indigestion.

Conor was reduced to crawling on the canvas by an assault to which he had no answer

The referee swiftly waved off the bout after a barrage of punches from the American star

The substantive issue was Garcia’s boxing class and knock out power versus Benn’s frenzy and punch resistance.

For the high-paying fans – Benn’s long-haulers from the old country and Garcia’s Gen Z armies of groups from his two nations of identification the US and Mexico – what mattered most was that both delivered the barn-burner of a fight they promised.

Quite beautifully those three congregations fell silent together in commemoration of one boxer who never gave in, never gave up, never delivered a disappointing fight, never offended anyone, never betrayed a friend.

The giant screens in the 02 went into black and white mode for a nostalgic picture of Ricky Hatton who died too young as the previous British fighter to top the bill in what was until recently the fight capital of the world. Over to you Master Benn.

Garcia came to the ring to the strains of a patriotic Mexican song, wrapped in that country’s flag and to rapturous acclaim from the baying Amex majority in the house.

Unabashed and as expected Benn went instantly on the offensive only to be met by barrage of Garcia’s trademark left hooks.

Less than three minutes later it was all over.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia was banned for racial slurs, hit with a $1m doping fine and U-turned on his support for Donald Trump... but America's controversial rock-and-roll boxer is out to save his sport by beating Britain's Conor Benn
Sports.content:
Ryan Garcia was banned for racial slurs, hit with a $1m doping fine and U-turned on his support for Donald Trump... but America's controversial rock-and-roll boxer is out to save his sport by beating Britain's Conor Benn

A dazzling talent just reaching his prime will enter the T-Mobile Arena here this Saturday night with the hopes of a fighting nation resting on his shoulders.

Conor Benn, not so much. British boxing is enjoying a boom, not least with its dominance in the marquee heavyweight division.

The young man the son of Nigel is challenging for the world welterweight crown carries the burden of restoring America to its historic pre-eminence in the prize-ring.

Not just by adding to an unusually low head count of their champions but by resuscitating the excitement, the stardust, the impudence, the controversy, the brilliance and the fascination of the public over here with the hardest game of all.

Ryan Garcia is the only poster boy left to them following the retirement of Floyd Mayweather. Vitally, he has all it takes to bring a new generation of fans clamouring to his fights.

At 28 he has the matinee idol looks of a young Elvis Presley which brings the girls squealing into the crowds. A rock and roll bad-boy reputation which chimes with the lads. Showmanship within the ring and charisma outside the ropes.

Ryan Garcia will take on Conor Benn on Saturday night with the American carrying the hopes of a fighting nation on his shoulders

Garcia has reconciled with Andrea Celina Velarde (left), the beautiful mother of two of his three children (above)

Benn has arrived in Las Vegas with the aim of taking the WBC welterweight belt from Garcia

Glamorous blondes vie for his favours. Even though he is resisting those temptations now he has scrapped divorce proceedings and reconciled with Andrea Celina Velarde, the beautiful mother of two of his three children.

And, boy, can he box. The speed of hand and foot. The knock-out punching power. The taunting evasion. And, yes, the conceit which on occasion gets him into trouble.

The two defeats scarring his 28-fight record – against two of America’s other world champions Gervonta Davis and Rolly Romero – came when he was at his most arrogant and complacent.

The no-decision verdict which negated his stand-out victory over Devin Haney was imposed for failing a post-fight drug test for performance-enhancing Ostarine.

Like Benn he protested his innocence: ‘I’ve never knowingly taken drugs.’ His relatives revealed he had been struggling with his mental health and against alcohol. But unlike Conor he preferred taking his punishment – a $1million fine and a 12-month ban – rather than financing a protracted court case which would also have kept him under lengthy suspension.

Not that King Ry - he wears a gold crown for his ring entrances - is prone to compromising his regally unvarnished opinions. Garcia was a vociferous backer of Donald Trump in his first presidential election campaign. But given his Mexican roots he criticised Trump’s second-term deportation policy. Finally he renounced his support, denouncing the Trump administration’s handling of the Epstein Files.

A devout Christian, he called rapper Eminem a satanist and posted on Twitter: ’I don’t support the LGBTQ+. F*** you guys. Rot in hell.’

He called for a boycott of the Olympics for ‘disrespecting Jesus Christ' with the section of the opening ceremony of France 2024 in which drag queens imitating Greek gods were widely supposed to be parodying the Last Supper.

Garcia scrapped divorce proceedings with influencer Andrea in August 2025

Garcia turned down WBC offers to help with his mental health difficulties but progress has been deemed to be made, leading to him fighting and beating Mario Barris in February

The rock-and-roller came out in him when he was arrested for causing $150,000- worth of damage while trashing a room and a corridor at the ritzy Waldorf Astoria hotel in Beverly Hills. That risked a short prison term, which has not been applied.

Another suspension was imposed. This one from competing in fights sanctioned by the WBC for racist slurs live on the internet against the black community and muslims. President Mauricio Sulaiman reported that Garcia had turned down a number of offers from the WBC to help Garcia with his mental health difficulties.

Sulaiman relented last November, saying he recognised the progress made in that regard by the fighter’s large family.

Promptly, this February, Garcia defeated the highly rated Mario Barrios to claim the WBC welterweight belt, inflicting a first round knockdown on his way to a unanimous decision.

The braggadocio bubbles to the surface before fights. As soon as this weekend’s bout was announced he told Benn to his face: ‘You box like amateur trash. You're just a flashy trash can. I’m going to throw you out with trash.’

All the ingredients are there for the making of a turbulent, troubled super-star son of this angry and violent 21st century. All wrapped up in the rare skills and brave heart of a potentially great fighter.

Some indication of whether all that will be enough for him to kindle another golden age in US boxing may be seen in how he deals with Benn. The huge scale of that task is evident in this, my overwhelmingly American list of the 20 greatest boxers of all time, with Lennox Lewis the Brit who came closest to inclusion...

Sports.title: Aston Martin retains Alonso and Stroll for F1 2027
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso has finally confirmed that he will continue with Aston Martin into the 2027 Formula 1 campaign, ending all speculation surrounding his future.

For months the 45-year-old had been answering questions about whether or not he will stick with F1, given his then Aston Martin contract expired at the end of the current 2026 campaign.

The double champion claimed it depended on which direction the regulations would take, as he strongly dislikes the new-for-2026 ruleset that has more emphasis on electric power.

But Alonso not publicly committing was partly an effort to increase pressure on F1, particularly as he’d held meetings with Stefano Domenicali and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

So now has come the news that the F1 paddock expected: Alonso has signed a new deal with Aston Martin, which he joined in a shock move from Alpine for the 2023 season.

"I'm very happy to sign a new contract with Aston Martin," said the 32-time race winner. "I took my time to make this decision, but racing is my life, my passion, and I know I still have the speed and determination to compete at the highest level.

"I'm committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed. I truly believe in what we are building: we have strong leadership, incredible people, partners and facilities.

"I look forward to making more memories on the racetrack in front of the passionate fans. Their energy creates an atmosphere that inspires me and is what makes our sport special."

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

The Spaniard has endured a real up-and-down journey with the Silverstone outfit, having made a blistering start with six podiums in his opening eight grands prix before two more that year.

But since then it has been mainly lows, as Aston Martin was outdeveloped by its rivals before making a horrendous start to the 2026 regulations, partly due to its uncompetitive Honda engine.

Aston Martin sits 10th in the standings with just three points - all scored by Alonso - after 15 rounds and is only ahead of newcomer Cadillac.

The Silverstone squad has also announced the extension of Lance Stroll's contract, so he is set for his ninth season at Team Silverstone after joining from Williams.

"I'm very happy to continue with Aston Martin for the long term," said Stroll. "I've been on this journey since the beginning and I believe we have the resources and the people to become a winning team.

"There is so much hard work going on at Silverstone with real progress being made, and the determination I see in every department is a huge motivation for me.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin, Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I know we are heading in the right direction, and my commitment is stronger than ever to help us achieve our goals."

Team owner Lawrence Stroll added: "Lance and Fernando have been a crucial part of our journey and we are very pleased to confirm that they will continue with us into the next chapter for the team.

"Having two drivers with their level of experience, commitment and knowledge provides tremendous value to the whole organisation.

"We are here to win, and whilst our short-term focus remains on improving performance, I believe we have the world-class talent we need to achieve our long-term objectives."

Sports.title: Azerbaijan GP was a step forward for upgraded Williams - but real test is still to come
Sports.content:
If there is a definition of a mixed bag, that's what the Baku weekend was to Williams. It progressed to Q3 for the first time in 2026, but didn't start there due to a grid penalty for Carlos Sainz. It scored points for the first time since Monaco, with some fortune, but also saw Alex Albon crash out.

Azerbaijan was a key weekend circled in red on Williams' calendar as it finally upgraded an FW48 starved of significant improvements for months. The Grove team wheeled out an all-new chassis, which was finally on the required weight, as well as a new floor and other aerodynamic parts.

The car's long run pace in FP2 looked encouraging, unlocking a long-shut door to the midfield ballpark that includes the likes of Haas, Racing Bulls and Audi.

In qualifying, Sainz claimed ninth but a grid penalty dumped him back to 14th behind Albon. From the belly of the pack it was looking like a long-awaited chance to score points went begging until Franco Colapinto took out Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris at a restart.

"It's been a mammoth effort to bring the update that we have here this weekend and it's nice to walk away with a point," said team principal James Vowles. "You can see we didn't have the pace on that first stint, and we need to dig and understand that because that was a critical part of the race where we weren't able to make progress."

The point for 10th was a reward for all the hard work in the factory, but did the Williams B-spec really deliver as much as hoped? "I think it's exactly the step we expected," Albon insisted. "Maybe we didn't expect Q3, to be fair to you. But yes, it put us in a midfield fight."



Sainz added: "Our initial feel is that the car feels just a bit quicker. But we were so far away that even though we've been bringing such a big upgrade, it still feels like we are playing a lot of catch-up. So as promised, no big massive surprises in terms of pace, a healthy step forward."

James Vowles, Williams Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

An additional factor is that Baku was a real Williams track, which can't be said from Malaysia's Sepang and the Singapore street circuit which will put a much bigger emphasis on downforce. So, coming away with a point and a DNF feels like at least half of a missed opportunity if it means Williams will regress again over the remainder of the triple header.



"This track, even without the upgrade, it would have favoured us," Albon said. "Malaysia will be telling to see where we are on a much more downforce-focused circuit. We've also got now a few days to actually understand the package.

"If you look at the big picture, we'll make the car go faster in terms of optimising it. But we'll be slower relative to the rest of the field, because that track will not suit us. Expect us to fall back in Malaysia, and then maybe in Singapore we can come somewhere in between."



As far as Albon's crash is concerned, which brought out the safety car on lap 31, he took responsibility for outbraking himself but felt it also further exposed of a key Williams weakness which has carried over across regulations.

"It was odd," he explained. "I braked a little bit later, but not much later. Then we had a big wind gust. I thought I would run a little bit wide, but I never thought I would hit the wall.

"I'm sure I have to hold my hand up in that situation, but at the same time we've had these issues before. We know our car likes to lift the front wheel and we three-wheel. We know when we brake a little bit late, we can expose ourselves to that three-wheeling. And sometimes when it does that, the penalty for front locking is huge on our car. It happens.

"For sure, with the wind gust and braking late at the same time, it just tips it over the edge. It wasn't a huge amount; it was a few metres, but that's too much."

Alexander Albon, Williams Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Williams fans may have expected more from such a long-awaited upgrade on a circuit that historically suited the team. But 2026 is already a lost season for Williams, at least on the track as it languished in ninth in the standings.

Perhaps it is more constructive to view the process of redesigning its chassis while adding aero performance as a stress test for the team. And a round of evidence gathering for Vowles that the Grove-based squad is now more capable of bringing through new parts than it was 12 months ago, and a way to course correct as the 2027 car project gathers steam.

With the latest chassis expected carry over into the 2027 campaign, that's already one big-ticket item out of the way.



"I'm confident you're going to see us stepping forward now that that big rule change is behind us," Vowles told Sky. "There's an aero change for next year, there's a power unit change for next year. But it's smaller in size so we can absorb it.

"But it's going to take a little bit of time to catch up on the mess that's happened this winter. My real learning from it is we need a lot more investment to bring us just the ability to keep up with those in front. And the cost cap restrains us from doing that.



"[The upgrade] is directionally right. I think more importantly, it's the foundation we wanted to set ourselves for next year. We recognise this year's a little bit behind us, unfortunately, but there's a lot to do in going into 2027."

Sports.title: Herta still aiming for F1 by 2028
Sports.content:
“It would be foolish to sit here and think that I will be on the pace right away, that I will be on the pace and ready to win in my first race. I may be older, but speed-wise, these guys are just as fast as anybody out there.”

This was how Colton Herta viewed his gamble of a Formula 2 switch from IndyCar as he pursued his Formula 1 dream, and he has so far been proven right – actually more than he initially imagined.

Cadillac’s protege was well aware that F2 was a tricky championship for rookies, especially when bypassing F3 and having to master the Pirelli tyres from the get-go, but he certainly didn’t expect to struggle to the extent that he has.

The Hitech driver lies 19th in the drivers’ standings, with 26 points to his name and fifth place in the Barcelona sprint race as his best result – from third on the reversed grid. He is at a loss to explain such a lack of performance.

Asked by Autosport in an exclusive interview what exactly has been tough for him to get his head around, Herta responded: “Nothing in particular, it's just been the whole thing. Unfortunately, there hasn't been a whole bunch of positives at any point. For whatever reason, there's been zero pace, and nothing has really changed.

“It's unclear why we can't put a weekend together from start to finish and it be completely strong. I think it's just a head-scratcher to be qualified three seconds off here [in Baku]. It just makes zero sense to me.”

Colton Herta, Hitech Photo by: Getty Images

Pressed on whether he struggled to get used to the car or to the tyres, Herta clarified: “Initially, no. Through the winter testing, we were fairly strong. All the private testing that I’d done, I was strong, but for some reason on race weekends, it just hasn't ever translated.”

The American’s analysis is accurate. He was joint 11th-fastest in pre-season testing at Barcelona, 0.574s down on pacesetter Rafael Camara – also a rookie as the reigning F3 champion. That performance clearly was encouraging.

But it didn’t last. Herta qualified 14th on average in the first five rounds, with a 0.848s deficit to the top, and his form gradually worsened, as he averaged 18th across the next eight qualifying sessions. Over the latter period, the mean gap was 1.088s – discounting the latest Baku event, where his deficit inexplicably ballooned to 2.484s in Q1 and 3.091s in Q2.

Crashes also have been more and more frequent, with no fewer than three across the recent Monza and Madrid rounds.

“It's frustrating, but all we can do is just keep trying,” Herta added. “I guess, unsure if that's the last one [of the season, with Qatar and Abu Dhabi at threat due to the Iran war] or if we have more, but we'll keep working like we have two more races to do. I'll try to get the most out of it.”

It’s fair to say this season hasn’t exactly been amazing for Herta’s F1 prospects, especially given Cadillac F1 CEO Dan Towriss expected a top-10 finish in the championship, which is all but mathematically out of reach.

Cadillac had been clear that its test and development driver had a real chance of an F1 seat in a not-too-distant future if he did well enough in F2, but Herta said he hadn’t had feedback from the team about his performance in the feeder series.

Colton Herta, Hitech Photo by: Getty Images

The former IndyCar frontrunner added that he was currently in talks with the F1 outfit regarding his 2027 plans and clarified, amid conflicting media reports, that he wasn’t ruling out a second season in F2 – though this clearly isn’t his priority.

“I said ‘I don't have an interest’,” Herta pointed out. “This year, I think if there was clear progression and whatnot, it would be more interesting to return, but there's zero progression.

“I've been doing a lot more with the F1 team now as far as sim stuff. I just did a TPC [Testing of Previous Cars] day on Monday, which was very strong. On the F1 sim and the TPC stuff, the pace has been really strong, but for whatever reason, it's just not translating to F2.”

Yet, asked if he was still firmly on Cadillac’s books for 2027, Herta replied: “I don't have anything for next year at the moment, but we're discussing, getting through that as far as what the opportunities are for me within the team.”

And when we inquired whether the 2024 IndyCar runner-up would consider a return to the series, Herta made it clear where his priority lay: “It all depends on what next year looks like. My focus is still on getting to F1, and I still think I have a chance of that in these next two years. But I don't know exactly, I have to sit back and see what the plan is for Cadillac for me.

“And once I know that, then I can make more decisions on maybe if I'm in Formula 1, if I'm not. What does that look like in terms of, is it a reserve role? Is it still a test role? If that's the case, what other series can I race in during that to stay busy?

“So, there's a lot of just, like, nothing to say at the moment, unfortunately, until I have more solidified plans for next year – then I can build everything out around that.”

Sports.title: What made Red Bull so fast in the Azerbaijan GP after Verstappen’s qualifying issue
Sports.content:
Red Bull might consider the FIA’s assessment that it has the strongest power unit as a blessing and a curse, but at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix it was key to its first double Formula 1 podium.

After fixing Max Verstappen’s ill-behaving internal combustion engine after qualifying, an issue that triggered his painful Q3 which left him eighth on the grid, both he and team-mate Isack Hadjar were able to demonstrate Red Bull’s prowess in Baku to surge up to second and third respectively.

It marked Red Bull’s first double podium in almost two-and-a-half years and left the team accepting a victory would have been more likely without Verstappen’s qualifying woes.

But where did this turn of pace come from having been considered to have the fourth-fastest car on the grid for long periods of this season?

Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies detailed a couple of factors, starting with its Red Bull-Ford power unit: “We have a fantastic PU, we have a fairly narrow band to use it at best. And it takes a lot of energy from everyone back in Milton Keynes and on the race track to try to keep us on the narrow window of performance. So that's what we do every day, there was nothing different this weekend.

“Every track comes with this challenge on how you do that and you hear it with our radio communications, with our drivers. So getting the right energy management, getting the right deployment and getting the right power is certainly something that keeps us busy.”

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

As is well documented, Red Bull has the most powerful internal combustion engine on the grid, and getting it into the “fairly narrow band” along with optimising electrical deployment meant it had plenty of punch on Baku’s straights. Red Bull’s sister squad, Racing Bulls, which runs the same engines, topped the speed trap in the race with Liam Lawson clocking 349.4km/h, while both Verstappen and Hadjar sat into the top 10 for highest speeds.

It was a tool that gave both drivers the ability to carve through the frontrunners and Mekies acknowledged had it not been for Verstappen’s engine problem in qualifying, an even better result was possible.

“We had two different issues in terms of power units,” he said. “It has cost us a lot yesterday [in qualifying]. But that's what it is, that's part of the game.

“I think in fairness Max was very strong from Friday onwards and probably would have been fighting for that first row or more yesterday without the issues we had with the PU. So of course, fixing that today [in the race] with the new engine has allowed us to go back to the competitive level that we were hoping to have.”

Verstappen felt Baku was Red Bull’s best – and potentially last – chance of a first win in 2026 with dominant squad Mercedes set to deliver a major upgrade package next weekend at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

Mekies echoed the common theme of upgrades having a major influence on the performance order in F1 this season and, despite his team admitting it will not deliver another major update package this year, he remains optimistic it will still have opportunities to avoid a first win-less F1 season for the team since 2015.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

“We have seen this year the pecking order has been alternating based on the timing of the upgrades,” he said. “I think what is however important is that in the fairly long timeframe between Australia and here, where we didn't have a big package coming, we have nonetheless managed to close that gap.

“If you look at Madrid, we were a tenth-and-a-half from pole in Madrid, I think we were two tenths from pole in Monza. So we have managed to close that gap with everyone in the team, chassis side, PU side, extracting from the actual car specifications. And then yes, the upgrades today probably gave us another edge and has eaten up that last tenth.

“We need to see how it's lasting on other tracks and then how we will react to the other competitors.”

Sports.title: Norris apologises to Colapinto over F1 race ban comments
Sports.content:
Reigning world champion Lando Norris has apologised to Franco Colapinto for demanding a race ban for the Alpine driver after the collision at Formula 1’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Colapinto caused a pile-up at the lap 36 restart by locking up into Turn 1 of the slippery Baku street circuit, which eliminated himself, team-mate Pierre Gasly and McLaren’s Norris.

Norris was left furious by the accident, feeling Colapinto's careless driving should be punished harshly by F1's race stewards.

"I've not seen it. I just got taken out. I think the FIA should be stricter and start handing out bans for this kind of stuff," Norris vented.

"It's careless from people. It costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin now. People should just get banned, because that's not driving that deserves to be in Formula 1."

When asked if there were mitigating circumstances for what happened on the slippery Baku circuit, Norris added: "In Formula 1, I think you expect drivers to anticipate things.

“Grip is going to be low. Tyre temps are low, they weren't even that low. In Formula 1, we want to be against the best drivers in the world, and when stuff like this happens, it's because [they] shouldn't be there.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine, Lando Norris, McLaren, Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

"I've not seen it, but if you cause a crash in a restart like this, you should have at least a one-race ban."

With the benefit of two days to reflect on the incident, Norris has now rowed back those comments and says he has privately apologised to Colapinto, having sparked further online abuse that has overshadowed the Argentinian's F1 career.

"Tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race," Norris posted on social media.

"After the race, I sent Franco a message apologising for the comments I made that I simply should not have said.

“I know better and emotions were running high but that is not an excuse, it was wrong of me. I've made mistakes of my own over the years and I know this is very much a part of racing and fighting on the limit.

"Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend."

Colapinto took responsibility for his "big mistake", which also angered Alpine chief Flavio Briatore as it cost the team a double points finish.

Sports.title: Why McLaren was so much slower than Mercedes on Baku's straights
Sports.content:
For all the talk of rivals catching Mercedes, which has held fire on its more significant upgrades until next weekend's Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the Brackley team has been able to weather the storm by excelling on some of the most power sensitive circuits like Monza and Baku, vindicating its patience.

But while Mercedes' dominant power unit package helps explain its gap to Ferrari and Red Bull, George Russell's scarcely believable eight-tenth gap to McLaren's Oscar Piastri was less straightforward to digest. Lando Norris fared even worse, 1.1s behind in Baku qualifying.

Read Also: Formula 1 Why Mercedes is still quicker than McLaren

Compared to Piastri, Russell made the difference by having better energy deployment through sector two, before motoring away on Baku's ultra-long straight, where his top speed was up to 10km/h higher than the Australian. In the race, Russell also enjoyed a leisurely cruise until a double safety car made things interesting for him at the end, setting up a grandstand finish with Max Verstappen.

When gaps between two otherwise closely matched teams sharing the same power unit are so vast, there are usually several compounding factors at play, and that's also what appeared to be the case in Azerbaijan.

To begin with, Baku isn't McLaren's happiest of hunting grounds. The MCL40 has continued a trend from its predecessors in that it's not the most competitive in low-speed corners, which the 6km Baku circuit almost exclusively features. McLaren's high-downforce prowess, which yielded wins in Hungary and Zandvoort and should have led to another victory for Norris in Madrid, counted for little.

McLaren's other aerodynamic weakness, a relative lack of efficiency on the straights, was also exposed despite the team bringing a suite of upgrades to generate more efficient downforce in all corner types. "The upgrades worked well throughout the weekend, we added some lap time to the car," said team boss Andrea Stella. "Somehow, we didn't see the effect of the upgrades because our car in general does not perform very well in these kinds of corners, so we would have needed a much bigger set to make a difference in Baku."

Without wanting to overlook Russell's return to form either, that again doesn't explain a gap of eight tenths. While McLaren feels its understanding of its Mercedes power unit, and its collaboration with Mercedes HPP, has improved compared to the start of the year, Stella acknowledged the team hadn't optimised its power unit as well for the race as it did in qualifying "and we paid a price in the race".

GPS traces provided by GP-Tempo show McLaren's shorter gearing compared to Mercedes. Comparing their fastest qualifying laps, Piastri (orange trace) was shifting up noticeably earlier than Russell (teal) Photo by: GP-Tempo.com

One baked in factor contributing to a top-speed deficit is the gear ratios it picked at the start of the year. The MCL40 is geared shorter than the Mercedes, costing it some top end speed on the likes of Monza and Baku.

"If we had to do it again, I think we would re-ratio to be closer to where Mercedes are," McLaren's technical director Neil Houldey said earlier this summer. "There are some performance opportunities that we can take because the ratios are shorter. We end up shifting less into lower gears around corners, potentially on restarts, things like that.

"But then when you're looking at the high-speed side, I think you'd probably take what the other teams have got. So it's a couple of compromises in either direction. It's a small lap time, but all these small little lap times add up to be some decent lap time performance."

McLaren elected not to use its one joker to make a mid-season gearing adjustment, opting to spend resources elsewhere instead.

"It is very apparent that it is not a single factor," said Stella. "Certainly, we've always talked quite openly and transparently that we need to improve the aerodynamic drag of the car. But at the same time there's a few factors which refer to our ratios, for instance we need to look whether we are on the right ratios to compete in circuits in which you have this sort of top speeds.

"And at the same time when we look at the data and we compare with MGP, we see that our power unit was not optimised. I think while for qualifying we managed to exploit pretty much the most that was available in the power unit, there's a few items that we were not able to optimise, and we paid a price in the race."

Lando Norris was collateral damage in Franco Colapinto's Turn 1 clash with Pierre Gasly Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

As to why Norris, who had been hitting his best form yet over the summer, had such a difficult weekend compared to an improving Piastri, it turns out the world champion had his own specific gremlins to deal with. The team found a power deficit in qualifying, believed to be linked to a fuel injection issue, that returned in the grand prix, while Norris didn't have his cleanest race and struggled for pace on the medium tyres.

"We occasionally saw the same problem during the race, but not as systematic as in qualifying," Stella explained. "Definitely there's a significant opportunity on the topic of fuel injection that we see occasionally also on Oscar's car during the race.

"In addition to that, Lando was overtaken by Verstappen, who was a quicker car. Lando was struggling a bit with the medium tyres. But credit to Oscar, Oscar managed to keep Verstappen behind. On Lando's side, we were struggling a little bit with power unit deployment.

"And also, Lando was having some inconsistencies in his driving, when he was overtaken by Hamilton, he had a lock-up and he had a few mistakes that meant that cars behind were within range. And when they are within range, then we struggle to defend, which goes back to the point on top speed."

Norris was furious after being a collateral victim of Alpine's Franco Colapinto spearing into his team-mate Pierre Gasly. But the Briton contributed to his own downfall by going off at Turn 1 right before the safety car, which cost him three positions and dumped him into the danger zone on the subsequent restart.

"I would say that for Lando this was one of the most difficult events in general that he has experienced in 2026," Stella concluded. "It's something that we need to take away, looking at whatever can be improved. But I would say most of the opportunities lie on the team side and on the car side, because we need to be able to offer our drivers a car that is more and just more consistent in terms of predictability."

Oscar Piastri suffered a monumental lock-up trying to hold off Isack Hadjar Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

With Piastri also locking up at Turn 1 later on, costing him a potential podium as he dropped down to 13th at the finish, the bitter end result of a series of minor problems, execution errors and shortcomings is a point-less weekend for the Woking squad.

"We had issues and some mistakes, but at the same time I think we paid for some fundamental limitations of our package in this kind of circuit," Stella's concluded.

"We were not fast enough in the corners, but at the same time and mainly we were not fast enough in the straights. This continuously exposed our drivers to being attacked and having to spend their race watching the mirrors rather than thinking about how they can progress in the race."

Sports.title: Alpine condemns abuse again following Colapinto's Azerbaijan GP crash
Sports.content:
The Alpine Formula 1 team has again spoken out against social media abuse following Franco Colapinto’s shunt in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Argentinian fans’ behaviour has been scrutinised lately following waves of hateful comments. Those were aimed at FIA stewards and the Alpine squad when Colapinto was handed a drive-through penalty for overtaking under a double yellow flag in Zandvoort.

Pierre Gasly was at the receiving end of abuse too after the Frenchman briefly refused to let his Alpine team-mate through in Madrid. Gasly revealed the threats targeted his family too; Colapinto meekly labelled the behaviour as “not nice to see” while insisting it was ‘not just his fans’.

This weekend in Baku, Colapinto lost control and caused a pile-up at a safety car restart, taking both Gasly and Lando Norris out of the race. The reigning champion was particularly upset and, before being able to view the footage himself, suggested whoever caused the crash should get “at least a one-race ban”.

While Norris did not even refer to Colapinto by name, this did trigger abuse on social media yet again – mainly aimed at the Briton, but Gasly and others weren’t spared.

“Mistakes happen when racing at the limit and no matter the result or outcome, nobody should be subject to hateful or abusive comments,” Alpine insisted in a statement on Sunday.

The team made a point of not antagonising its own driver’s fanbase: “Condemning abuse on social media is not aimed at any one fan base or the supporters of one team or driver, this is universal and should be called out and recognised to all fans of the sport.

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“As we have said in previous instances, we strongly condemn the reaction of some fans online and stand in solidarity with Formula One, the FIA, and other teams in wanting to stamp it out. It has become a regular occurrence in recent races and cannot be condoned.”

The latest abuse has occurred shortly after Alpine F1 boss Flavio Briatore reportedly threatened Argentinian media not to let them speak to Colapinto again if the hatred kept being spewed, damaging the outfit’s reputation.

Alpine’s statement in full

“As a team, we feel it’s necessary to speak out once more about the hate and abuse online following the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Not only aimed at one of our own drivers, but also members of the Formula One community, including media, and to our racing counterparts who we respect, admire, and revel competing against in the pinnacle of motorsport. Mistakes happen when racing at the limit and no matter the result or outcome, nobody should be subject to hateful or abusive comments.

“Condemning abuse on social media is not aimed at any one fan base or the supporters of one team or driver, this is universal and should be called out and recognised to all fans of the sport. As we have said in previous instances, we strongly condemn the reaction of some fans online and stand in solidarity with Formula One, the FIA, and other teams in wanting to stamp it out. It has become a regular occurrence in recent races and cannot be condoned.

“We know as a proud participant and stakeholder in the sport, we hold a responsibility to speak out and also help support in finding a solution. We will continue to work closely with the championship promoter and rights-holder, and the governing body to discuss ways in which to tackle online abuse and encourage healthy sporting rivalry, which Formula One is renowned for and what makes it so special.”

Sports.title: The detail that impressed Red Bull the most about Hadjar's F1 return
Sports.content:
After his wrist injury, Isack Hadjar certainly did not return behind the wheel of the Red Bull Racing RB22 at the easiest track on the Formula 1 calendar. The Baku City Circuit not only carries a considerable risk of crashes, but also features several very technical sections around the city's old town.

It requires confidence, but Hadjar had plenty of it despite missing three race weekends – having already made clear after practice that his wrist would not be a limiting factor.

Hadjar qualified fourth on the shores of the Caspian Sea and then produced a faultless race to claim his second podium of the season and his third F1 podium overall. His race weekend in Baku impressed Red Bull, Mekies acknowledged when addressing the written media post-race.

"I think it was outstanding what Isack has produced this weekend, really outstanding," Red Bull's team principal said. "At first, the most important thing is that straight away he felt good in the car, no pain. It means that every time we met together in the last few weeks and we said we will wait for Isack to come back at 100% because that's the priority, well, that's what happened.

"He was in the car, he didn't have any pain. Nonetheless, even without pain, this is not an easy track to come back to because there is no margin for error."

Hadjar himself was well aware of the latter and therefore built up his weekend steadily at one of the most treacherous street circuits.

"He has been building up his rhythm, session after session, very calmly, and with a lot of positive energy," Mekies added. "Already yesterday, to stick the car in P4 was a very, very strong result. I think today, the sort of race pace that he has shown on the medium and on the soft, is something we had not seen before.

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

"So on the weekend of his return, he has raised the bar again. We say to each other very often that we have seen him adding something to the business every time he was going out on track in the first part of the season, and he is continuing to do that."

Red Bull impressed by Hadjar's mature radio communication

Aside from his outright pace, there is another aspect that impressed Mekies: the way Hadjar conducted himself during the first stint. Red Bull asked the young Frenchman to give up his position to Verstappen, but even when the four-time world champion struggled with Pirelli's medium tyre, Hadjar remained calm.

"And on top of that, allow me to say that he also raced extremely cleverly with Max, very disciplined with his tyres," Mekies said. "It allowed us to have very, very strong teamwork between the two of them and between the pitwall. That has ultimately produced the best result possible."

It underlines that Hadjar is also making progress in that respect. In the junior categories and during the first year of his F1 career, Hadjar could often come across as hot-headed over the team radio, but Saturday in Baku was the exact opposite.

Of course, after several laps Hadjar asked whether he was free to attack – to which the team responded that he had to keep it clean – but the radio communication that preceded it was telling. When asked how much quicker Hadjar could go in clean air, the man behind the wheel replied: "Two or three tenths, but I’m honestly happy to be here."

In other words, Hadjar did not need the position back, thereby maximising the race time of both drivers and, with it, Red Bull’s chances. When Autosport asked Mekies about this specific moment, it was clear that this is what impressed the team principal most of all.

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I think you are pinpointing exactly on the right details that make you understand a lot more about the right pictures," Mekies said.

"It shows you how cleverly the kid is racing, and how much of brain capacity he is developing while in the car, and also how much emotional control he is managing to have.

"Those are as many indicators of the steps he has made in all these areas, on top of producing more speed. So it's exactly that trajectory that has been impressing us every day since he has joined the team, and probably last year as well.

"And also for that, we want to give him the best possible environment to continue to develop because that step was truly impressive."

Providing that best possible environment includes the contract extension for 2027 and the timing of it. Mekies acknowledges that Red Bull deliberately did so to take all the pressure off Hadjar’s shoulders, and as he walks away at the end of the media session, Mekies laughs: "I think Isack repaid our faith today!"

Sports.title: Alonso signs new contract to race for Aston Martin in 2027 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso has ended speculation over his future by signing a new contract to race in Formula 1 again next year.

Formula 1’s most experienced driver of all time will remain at Aston Martin for a fifth season.

The 45-year-old said he is “very happy” with his decision. His future in the sport had been in doubt due to his strong criticism of Formula 1’s new technical regulations and Aston Martin’s failure to provide a competitive car this year.

“I took my time to make this decision,” said Alonso, “but racing is my life, my passion, and I know I still have the speed and determination to compete at the highest level.

“I’m committed for the long term with this team and to helping us succeed. I truly believe in what we are building: we have strong leadership, incredible people, partners and facilities. I look forward to making more memories on the race track in front of the passionate fans. Their energy creates an atmosphere that inspires me and is what makes our sport special.”

Aston Martin also confirmed Alonso’s team mate Lance Stroll, son of team owner Lawrence Stroll, will drive for them again next year.

Sports.title: On This Day: Mansell and Senna thrill in first Spanish Grand Prix at Catalunya | Brief
Sports.content:
On this day in 1991 Nigel Mansell won the Spanish Grand Prix, held at the Circuit de Catalunya for the first time, after memorably going wheel-to-wheel with Ayrton Senna on a damp track.

Senna finished fifth after a spin, which kept Mansell’s fading title hopes alive. The pair headed into the final two rounds separated by 16 points, with 10 available for a win.

Behind Mansell, Alain Prost finished second and stood on the podium for the final time as a Ferrari driver. Their team mates followed them him, Riccardo Patrese ahead of Jean Alesi.

Michael Schumacher scored the final point in sixth place, sustaining his run of points finishes in all of his first three starts for Benetton, following his defection from Jordan.

Verstappen passed Hadjar at the beginning of lap seven. Red Bull told Hadjar not to put up a fight against his team mate: his race engineer Richard Wood pointed out “race time is priority here”:

Sports.title: Norris apologised to Colapinto for saying he “shouldn’t be in Formula 1” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris has revealed he apologised to Franco Colapinto for the comments he made about him following the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The reigning world champion slated the Alpine driver for triggering a three-car collision which eliminated the pair and Colapinto’s team mate Pierre Gasly

Following the crash Norris said he “just got taken out” and “some drivers […] shouldn’t be in Formula 1 to be honest.” He also called for Colapinto to face a race ban for triggering the collision.

However in a social media post two days later Norris said he has cleared the air with Colapinto.

“[A] tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race,” he said.

“After the race, I sent Franco a message apologising for the comments I made that I simply should not have said. I know better and emotions were running high but that is not an excuse, it was wrong of me. I’ve made mistakes of my own over the years and I know this is very much a part of racing and fighting on the limit.

“Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend.”

Yesterday Alpine issued a statement criticising abusive social media comments aimed at multiple people following the crash.

Since 1958 a world constructors’ championship title has also been awarded. The most successful F1 drivers in history are seven-times world champions Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher. In 2021 the former became the first and so far only driver to date to win 100 grands prix. While Schumacher retired from F1 at the end of 2012, Hamilton continues to race. His rival world champions in the series are Max Verstappen and Fernando Alonso. There are 10 teams active in the championship, each of which field cars for two drivers. Each team is required to design and build the majority of its cars but may source some parts including engines, gearboxes and certain other components. Sports.title: Alpine condemn online abuse again: “It has become a regular occurrence” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Alpine has issued another condemnation of social media abuse following the reaction to the crash triggered by Franco Colapinto yesterday.

Further abusive comments targeted various people involved in yesterday’s crash. Lando Norris , who sharply criticised Colapinto’s driving, was among those who received abusive messages.

“As a team, we feel it’s necessary to speak out once more about the hate and abuse online following the Azerbaijan Grand Prix,” said Alpine in a statement. “Not only aimed at one of our own drivers, but also members of the Formula One community, including media, and to our racing counterparts who we respect, admire, and revel competing against in the pinnacle of motorsport. Mistakes happen when racing at the limit and no matter the result or outcome, nobody should be subject to hateful or abusive comments.

“Condemning abuse on social media is not aimed at any one fan base or the supporters of one team or driver, this is universal and should be called out and recognised to all fans of the sport. As we have said in previous instances, we strongly condemn the reaction of some fans online and stand in solidarity with Formula One, the FIA, and other teams in wanting to stamp it out. It has become a regular occurrence in recent races and cannot be condoned.

“We know as a proud participant and stakeholder in the sport, we hold a responsibility to speak out and also help support in finding a solution. We will continue to work closely with the championship promoter and rights-holder, and the governing body to discuss ways in which to tackle online abuse and encourage healthy sporting rivalry, which Formula One is renowned for and what makes it so special.”

Alpine’s statement comes just three days after the FIA condemned the abuse aimed at Alpine’s other driver, Pierre Gasly, who was attacked by supporters of Colapinto for briefly delaying his team mate during the Spanish Grand Prix.

The FIA also defended its stewards last month following further abuse by supporters of Colapinto over the two penalties he received in the Dutch Grand Prix.
