World.title: Liberia: Opposition Puts Issues First in Bid to Break Its Losing Habit; Can Five Parties Do What the CPP Couldn’t?
World.content:
MONROVIA – For most of the last two decades, Liberia’s opposition has had a habit of losing to itself. Parties meet, pledge unity, sign documents, then split over who leads before the ruling party breaks a sweat. So when George Manneh Weah and four other political leaders (Alexander Cummings, Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, Simeon Freeman and Jonathan Mason) put their names to an eight-page communiqué on Sunday, the question was not whether they could agree on grievances. That part is easy. The question is whether they have found a way to stay together long enough to matter in 2029.

By Rodney D. Sieh

What the Communiqué Actually Is



Read closely, the document is two things at once. The first is a charge sheet: Foya and the Guinea border, the US$10 million Foya project, the US$8 million SIB transfer, the drug busts, the Supreme Court, the Cybercrime Act, evictions, the EU ambassador, the US deportee deal. It is the most comprehensive attack on the Boakai-Koung government to come from the opposition since the 2023 transition.

The second is a governance arrangement, and that is the more interesting part. The parties have not merged, have not named a leader, and have not touched the 2029 ticket. Instead, they have created a Joint Technical Committee, two members per party, to write policy positions and build county-level outreach. They say outright that they will not try “to manufacture opposition political unity by declaration.”

That line is aimed squarely at the ghost of the Collaborating Political Parties.

What Is Different This Time

The CPP brought together the ANC, Liberty Party, Unity Party and All Liberian Party with a framework that demanded a single standard bearer. It won the 2020 Montserrado senatorial seat, then tore itself apart over the framework document and the question of who would carry the flag. By 2023, its members were running against each other and Boakai rebuilt the Unity Party on his own terms. The lesson most opposition figures drew is that the ticket question, asked too early, destroys everything else.

This arrangement is built differently in at least four ways.

It has an anchor. The CPP was a gathering of roughly equal, mid-sized parties with no dominant base. This effort is organized around a former president who lost the 2023 runoff by about 20,000 votes and can still fill the road from RIA to Monrovia. That changes the arithmetic. The smaller parties bring policy credibility, regional contacts and technocratic names; the CDC brings the votes.

It puts the ticket last. By design, the parties have agreed on issues before structure, and structure before candidates. Cummings has spoken openly about drawing lessons from the CPP collapse, and the sequencing reflects that.

It is spreading ownership. The first roundtable was at Weah’s Jamaica Resort; the second was hosted by Freeman at the Sinkor Palace. Small as it sounds, rotating the host chips away at the charge, made loudly by Musa Bility before the first meeting, that this is a CDC project with a pre-appointed leadership.

It is issue-driven, not personality-driven. The communiqué reads like an opposition policy platform in draft. If the technical committee produces real positions on the economy, the courts, the NEC and the drug war, the group will have something the CPP never had: a reason to exist beyond beating the incumbent.

The Fault Lines

None of that guarantees survival, and the cracks are already visible.

The Citizens Movement for Change walked out three days before the signing, saying it would not endorse the draft and wanted cooperation tied to a clearly defined national reform agenda, including changes to the system of government. Bility’s objection, that hosting a meeting does not confer leadership over the opposition, has not gone away. It has simply left the room with him, and it may return from the others once the ticket question comes due.

Then there is the CDC’s own record. A communiqué that indicts selective justice, opaque procurement and pressure on the courts invites the obvious reply: what about 2018 to 2024? The Unity Party will point to missing money, the sanctions on CDC-era officials and the way the Weah government treated critics. The opposition’s claims will be judged partly on whether its lead party can answer that history.

The absences also matter. The Liberty Party is not at the table. The National Patriotic Party is divided, with its executive suspending partisans who endorsed the roundtable while its political leader, former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, faces drug-related charges she denies. Senator Samuel Kogar attended the first round but is not a signatory.

And the hardest question has only been postponed. Weah remains constitutionally eligible for another term. Cummings has run twice and is unlikely to stand aside quietly. Kemayah signs as his party’s “Standard Bearer.” A structure that defers the ticket can hold only if it also agrees, sooner rather than later, on how the ticket will be chosen: a primary, a polling formula, a negotiated power-sharing deal. Without that, 2029 becomes 2023 again.

Can It Become a Viable Opposition?

It can, if it does three things over the next 18 months.

First, turn the charge sheet into policy. Liberians have heard grievances before. What they have rarely heard from an opposition is a costed answer to squatter settlements, health worker pay or border diplomacy. The technical committee is the vehicle for that, and its output will show whether this is a movement or a press release.

Second, go where the votes were decided. The 2023 runoff was lost in the northwest and the southeast swing counties, not in Montserrado. County-level structures, which the communiqué promises, matter more than Monrovia roundtables.

Third, settle the selection rule early, even if the name comes late. The CPP died over process, not personalities. A signed, public mechanism for choosing a standard bearer would be the clearest signal that this effort has learned something.

What the Unity Party Should Do

The ruling party’s first instinct has been dismissal. Secretary General Amos Tweh, launching the Boakai 2029 Reelection Movement, said the opposition gathering posed no serious threat. That may be good for morale at party headquarters, but it is weak strategy. The communiqué is not really asking voters to love Weah; it is asking them to doubt the government. Dismissing the messenger does nothing about the message.

The more durable response is to take the sharpest charges off the table:

• Publish the Foya file. Funding sources, contracts and the MRU question. A US$10 million project in the President’s hometown will be a campaign issue for three years unless it is fully explained now.

• Let the drug investigation breathe. The opposition’s proposal for a commission including the Bar, the Press Union, churches and mosques is not radical. Accepting some version of it would take the “selective justice” line away from the opposition.

• Stop fighting the courts and the critics. Compliance with Supreme Court opinions and restraint in using the Cybercrime Act cost the government little and deny the opposition its “police state” narrative.

• Explain the deportee arrangement and the EU rift. Both are foreign-policy stories that are becoming domestic ones.

• Show delivery. The communiqué itself concedes the US$1 billion revenue milestone. The Unity Party’s best argument is to make that number visible in salaries, clinics and resettlement for displaced families.

There is also an internal question the UP will eventually have to face. President Boakai would be 84 in 2029. A reelection movement launched this early suggests the party intends to run him again, but voters will ask about continuity, and an opposition built around renewal will make the most of it.

The Bottom Line

Sunday’s communiqué does not mean Liberia’s opposition is united. It means five parties have agreed on what they are against and have built a slower, looser structure designed to survive the fights that killed the CPP. That is a genuine change in approach. Whether it becomes a change in outcome depends on two things no document can settle: whether the lead party can carry its own past, and whether the leaders can agree on a way to choose one of themselves before 2029 chooses for them.

For the Unity Party, the warning is simpler. The margin in 2023 was barely 20,000 votes. An opposition that stops beating itself does not need to win many hearts to reverse that.

World.title: Liberia: ‘Jaw Dropping’ El Niño” Could Test Liberia’s Weak Weather Warning System and Put Thousands of Lives at Risk, Experts Warn
World.content:
The sea continues to wash away at homes in the West Point township, in Monrovia. Credit: Allison Hunter for New Narratives

Summary

Scientists warn that a historically severe El Niño – a climate pattern that disrupts weather around the world – could bring erratic rainfall, and severe flooding, extreme heat, fishing and agricultural disruption to Liberia in coming months.

Experts say the government needs to invest in preparedness strategies now to protect people from to extreme heat and weather in coming months with extreme heat alone predicted to kill 450,000 people globally by February.

Liberia lacks adequate weather stations and relies heavily on global models, limiting its ability to issue accurate, community-specific warnings and meaning millions of Liberians will be left vulnerable.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

The sea off Liberia turns a deceptive shade of calm every year around this time as the rains give way to the dry season – warm, glassy, inviting.



But Nathaniel Blama, Liberia’s former chief environmental regulator, has learned to read that as a warning rather than an invitation.

“When you see the water very warm during that period, it’s time to be afraid because having storm surge, the movement of the current is completely different than normal,” he said. “A lot of people, children, go on the beach. They don’t come back.” Houses and livelihoods are also swept away.

But this year is shaping up to be much worse. New data by climate researchers shows the world is experiencing an exceptionally powerful weather pattern called El Niño—likely the strongest in at least 1,000 years—layered on top of human-caused climate change from burning fossil fuels. This combination means 2027 is expected to be the hottest year ever recorded by scientists.

The climate crisis is already making extreme weather more intense and deadly. Rising heat is now killing one person every minute globally. The El Niño will make this worse, intensifying heatwaves, droughts, and floods across the planet, including Africa. Newly released data from the U.S. based Climate Impact Lab estimates that more than 450,000 people are projected to die globally from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño by February, more than 30,000 in Nigeria alone.

“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” Prof. Friederike Otto of Imperial College London told The Guardian .

In West Africa, where millions rely on rain-fed agriculture, those shifts can be especially damaging. For Liberia, changes in the timing and intensity of rainfall could threaten crops, worsen flooding and increase pressure on already vulnerable communities.

“Farmers could face unreliable rainfall, while hotter, drier conditions threaten crops, water supplies, hydropower and increase the risk of bushfires in places like Wologizi and Foya,” said Isaac Nyaneyon Kannah Teah, a Liberian climate expert.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that occurs when waters in the Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, disrupting weather patterns across the world. It can shift rainfall, intensify heat and bring drought to some regions while causing heavy rains and flooding in others.

Some experts are calling this a “monster” weather event. Temperatures in the Pacific at the heart of El Niño reached a record 3.05C in September. Forecasts project the warming could peak at about 4 C in November and December. A rise above 2C is classified as a very strong, or “super,” El Niño.

Teah said the full impact of the developing El Niño on the country’s current rainy season, ending this month, remains uncertain, but changes in weather conditions in coming months appear certain.

“El Niño may contribute to a hotter and drier January-to-March dry season, placing pressure on water supplies, agriculture, forests and electricity generation,” Teah said. It could also make the beginning of the farming season less predictable, including false rainfall starts followed by prolonged dry spells that damage newly planted crops.

Farmer Oretha Weatoe of James Town, River Cess, looks on as her crops struggle to grow. Photo Eric Opa Doue/New Narratives.

Nearly seven out of 10 Liberians depend on farming for what they eat, so disrupted rainfall could threaten both food and income. Four in every five Liberians is already facing food insecurity. Just 1.6 percent is irrigated, leaving farmers heavily dependent on the rains.

At Liberia’s Meteorological Service, forecasters are already watching the signal build, but they are severely limited by a lack of sophisticated equipment. “We are not even having a marine weather station to give us the actual sea surface temperature,” said Albert Momolu Sherman, director of Liberia’s Meteorological Service, which operates under the Ministry of Transport. “We normally rely on global models.”

Those global models are consistent enough to worry him. He described how an intensifying El Niño fools farmers into planting too early.

“Farmers think that, ‘Okay, the rainy season has started,’ not knowing that this is just a false start,” Sherman said. Then, once the West African monsoon reasserts itself, the rain that finally does come arrives harder and more suddenly than usual, raising the risk of seedlings being waterlogged and communities swamped by flash flooding in a country whose drainage systems were never built for it.

Unlike other countries in the region, the Liberian government does not have a mechanism for warning Liberians about coming heatwaves and heavy rains. The Meteorological Service publishes a ten-day agricultural bulletin meant to guide farmers’ planting decisions. But reaching the people who need it most – in communities without reliable radio, internet or electricity – depends on partnerships with the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, the National Disaster Management Agency and the Red Cross that have yet to fully materialize.

It should not have been like this. International donors made a fund of $10 million available to establish a warning system six years ago. FrontPage Africa/New Narratives documented the suspected corruption and lack of capacity under the Weah administration that led to four-year delays in the project. The Boakai administration reports that it has got the project moving but it has also faced delays.

Teah said it is still too early to determine its effect on Liberia’s entire 2027 season but even if the farmers are spared, they’ll be hit by impacts elsewhere. Because Liberians depend on imports for 80 percent of their food , they could also face higher food prices as El Nino reduces agricultural production in countries from which we import rice and other foods.

Excessive heat will add another dimension. In addition to impacting farming, heat makes it harder for people to work—farmers, fishermen, and construction workers will tire faster in extreme temperatures, earning less money to buy food. Water sources dry up or become contaminated, spreading waterborne diseases that weaken children’s bodies and make malnutrition even more deadly.

A satellite weather-monitoring system used to forecast weather at Roberts International Airport. Photo credit: Liberia Meteorological Service.

For the millions of Liberians who are already food insecure, already eating less nutritious food because they cannot afford better, an intense heat wave could push families from precarious to catastrophic: crops will fail, prices will spike, work will become impossible, and children will face acute hunger. The rural communities hit hardest by heat—with no air conditioning, limited access to clean water, and no cushion of savings—will be the most vulnerable.

The knock-on effects reach further than the farm gate. St. Paul River which supplies the Mount Coffee Hydropower plant near Monrovia can run low as evaporation increases, threatening the electricity supply. It has already reduced electricity generation in recent years as dry-season water levels in the river fell, contributing to widespread power cuts across Liberia. This coming dry season could be worse.

Fishermen monitor the weather as their canoes sit offshore at West Point. Photo by Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon.

Offshore, artisanal fishers face a quieter but no less consequential disruption: warming waters altering fish stocks and pushing dangerous sea conditions closer to shore, threatening both catches and the fishers themselves.

Rising heat brings its own toll for humans: heat stress and other health complications for a population with limited access to cooling or medical care. It will be dangerous for the elderly, infants and those weakened by illness.

Experts said the government has a role to play in helping communities prepare for possible weather-related challenges.

“Closely monitor forecasts from the Liberia Meteorological Service and strengthen preparedness for heat, water shortages, bushfires, agricultural losses and possible flooding,” says Sherman.

The government can also put in measures to save lives including including cooling centers where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers.

President Joseph Boakai will be immersed in discussion of climate change and the super El Nino during his time at this month’s UN General Assembly. The issue has been a central topic of the meeting with world leaders approving a new declaration to tackle sea level rise with 770 million people live in coastal areas affected by sea level rise. 230,000 Liberians will lose their homes by the end of the century, according to UN models.

Experts said they hope the president comes home from the assembly with a renewed vigor and new ideas to protect Liberians in coming months.

This story was produced in collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: “The People Did a Fantastic Job” — Mary Broh Defends Defendants in Saudi Rice Trial
World.content:
Monrovia-Former General Services Agency Director General Mary T. Broh, delivered one of the defense’s strongest accounts Monday, September 28, in Liberia’s ongoing Saudi-donated rice trial, telling Criminal Court “C” that the government officials involved in handling the controversial donation “did a fantastic job” and questioning how they could be accused of stealing rice that, according to her testimony, was subsequently distributed to communities and government institutions.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Broh, appearing as a Subpoenaed witness on Monday, September 28, maintained that the movement of the Saudi-donated rice to the GSA was carried out through an inter-agency arrangement involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the National Disaster Management Agency, NDMA, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the GSA.



Her testimony provided a detailed account of how the GSA came to warehouse thousands of bags of the donation and sought to distance the accused officials from any suggestion that the movement of the rice was undertaken for personal benefit.

And as she walked out of the courtroom after her testimony, Broh was reportedly heard making an even more direct statement about the accused, “The people are innocent, the people didn’t do anything.”

The remark was made outside the witness stand and was therefore not evidence given under oath. But it underscored the position Broh had advanced during her testimony, that the officials involved were performing government duties and that the movement of the rice should not automatically be interpreted as theft.

“The People Did a Fantastic Job,”

Broh’s most striking testimony came when she addressed the allegation that the Saudi rice had been stolen or improperly diverted.

She questioned what happened to the rice that was actually distributed to communities and government institutions.

According to her testimony, “the people did a fantastic job.”

Broh challenged the suggestion that the movement of rice from one government institution to another, or its distribution to institutions and communities, in itself established that the officials had stolen the donation.

Her testimony presented a different picture from the prosecution’s case, one in which govand ernment officials were attempting to move, warehouse and distribute a large humanitarian donation through several state institutions.

She raised a concern, in substance, whether the officials had stolen the rice, what became of the rice that ultimately reached communities and institutions.

That question is central to the defense’s effort to distinguish between accounting discrepancies, administrative decisions and proof of criminal appropriation.

‘The People Are Innocent’

Broh’s statement after leaving the courtroom added an unusually personal dimension to her testimony.

As she reportedly walked away from the proceedings, she was heard saying, “The people are innocent, the people didn’t do anything.”

The statement appeared to refer to the officials whose handling of the Saudi rice has become the subject of criminal proceedings.

Broh did not make that statement while testifying under oath, and it therefore carries a different evidentiary status from her testimony before the judge and jury.

But it closely reflected the position she presented while on the witness stand, that the officials were acting pursuant to government instructions and an inter-agency mandate.

‘When He Called, We Must Work for Him’

Broh told the court that she became involved after receiving a call from then Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah.

“When I got the call from Ambassador Kemayah, he said he needed my assistance in term of warehousing the Saudi Donated rice at the GSA,” Broh testified.

She maintained, that Kemayah was a government colleague and that when he called for assistance, she agreed.

A meeting was subsequently held at the GSA involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Internal Affairs, NDMA and GSA.

According to Broh, Kemayah chaired the meeting, but she emphasized that the resulting mandate came from the meeting involving the institutions and not from Kemayah acting alone.

That distinction is important to the defense because the prosecution has alleged that Kemayah and former Deputy Foreign Minister Thelma D. Sawyer became improperly involved in the handling and distribution of rice that had been donated for disaster victims.

Broh’s account, however, was that the process involved several government agencies.

25,000 Bags Came

Through GSA

Broh confirmed that 11,200 bags of the Saudi-donated rice were stored at GSA.

She further testified that 13,895 additional bags were moved from NDMA to GSA.

According to her account, the rice came into GSA custody through two deliveries, with the total quantity estimated at approximately 25,195 bags.

Broh also challenged the use of figures contained in the indictment when compared with the actual movement records.

She told the court that the indictment cited one quantity, but that the gate passes showed a higher figure.

For that reason, she suggested that the quantities should have been calculated from the gate passes and other actual movement records.

Distribution Was Never Halted

Broh further testified that she did not know of any decision halting the distribution of the Saudi rice.

“The general distribution was never halted under GSA,” she told the court.

She acknowledged that portions of the rice were distributed to institutions including the Liberia National Police, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of National Defense, although the original donation was intended for disaster-affected persons.

But Broh offered an explanation for such institutional distributions.

She said that when she received a mandate to move rice to another location or institution, she could not simply reject the instruction when government officials had provided reasons for doing so.

She pointed particularly to prisons, saying a shortage of food in correctional facilities could create serious problems and even lead to scuffles.

In her view, preventing such a situation could itself be considered a disaster-related concern.

‘We Were Following Instructions’

Broh also told the court that she was never provided a concept note explaining the broader project.

Instead, she said, she was following instructions arising from the inter-agency meeting.

She said Kemayah did not tell her why he wanted the rice moved from NDMA.

His instruction, according to Broh, was that the rice should be moved as soon as possible.

She said GSA had the capacity to warehouse and implement the relevant part of the op eration.

Broh further explained, that Madan Thelma Duncan Sawyer became involved in a particular aspect of the implementation but was not involved in every stage of the process.

No Knowledge, ,of Sale

Broh den,i,ed having knowledge of the donated rice.

She also said she was unaware of any investigative committee allegedly established by Kemayah to examine the rice issue.

Madam Broh at the same time m, maintained that the meeting she attended concerned the movement of rice from NDMA to GSA.

Her testimony therefore sought to draw a line between the administrative movement of the rice and the allegations of subsequent misuse or sale.

Bonner Testimony Adds to Defense Challenge

Broh’s testimony followed that of defense witness Kpakolo Bonner, who testified last week about the distribution of rice to Norvling Town Community in Paynesville.

Bonner, a resident of the community and an employee of the Forestry Development Authority, testified that rice distributed to the community was intended for people affected by flooding.

He said the rice was distributed openly to affected residents, including people whose homes had been destroyed or damaged by floodwaters.

Bonner said he signed for rice as acting youth chairman and participated in verification and distribution.

However, when shown a waybill in court, he disputed the signature appearing on the document, saying it was not his.

His testimony has given the defense another basis for questioning whether every discrepancy in the documentary record can automatically be attributed to the defendants.

A Case Turning on Where the Rice Went

The prosecution has presented evidence alleging that substantial quantities of the Saudi donation were improperly handled or diverted.

The defense, however, has increasingly focused on the question of where the rice actually went and whether the documentary evidence can establish criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt.

Broh’s testimony was particularly significant because she occupied a senior position at the GSA, one of the institutions that physically handled a substantial quantity of the rice.

Rather than denying that the rice was moved, she acknowledged the transfers and distributions but described them as actions taken within an inter-agency framework.

Her testimony therefore gives the defense an argument that the existence of transfers, gate passes or institutional distributions should not by itself establish criminal intent.

The Saudi Donation

The Saudi government donated 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice to Liberia as humanitarian assistance.

The prosecution has alleged that thousands of bags were subsequently misapplied, diverted or stolen.

The defendants have denied the allegations and have maintained that the rice was handled as part of government efforts to respond to vulnerable and disaster-affected populations.

As the defense case continues, Broh’s testimony places emphasis on the distinction between the movement of the rice and the alleged criminal taking of the rice.

And her two statements, one from the witness stand that “the people did a fantastic job” and the other reportedly made as she left the courtroom that “the people are innocent, the people didn’t do anything”, have become the clearest expression yet of her view of the officials whose actions are now being examined by the court.

World.title: Liberia: Bon Jallah Seeks Acquittal As DNA Evidence Links Him to Four Exhibits, Defense Points to Crime-Scene Dispute
World.content:
Prosecution Given Until Tuesday to Resist Motion as Criminal Court “E” Suspends Trial; Rwandan Forensic Expert Says DNA Match Cannot Establish When or How Biological Material Was Deposited

MONROVIA — Lawyers representing Peter Bon Jallah have asked Criminal Court “E” to acquit their client, arguing that inconsistencies surrounding the alleged crime scenes and the circumstances of DNA evidence presented at trial raise reasonable doubt.

By Willie N. Tokpah



The motion was filed Monday, September 28, during the 42nd day of jury sitting at the Temple of Justice, following testimony from a Rwandan forensic expert that Bon Jallah’s DNA profile matched biological material found on four exhibits.

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr. gave the prosecution until noon Tuesday, September 29, to file a written resistance and suspended the trial pending a ruling on the motion.

The defense does not dispute the DNA match. Instead, it challenges what the scientific evidence establishes about the alleged offenses.

DNA Match Does Not Establish When or How Material Was Deposited

Pascal Bavugirije, Acting Division Manager of the Biology Division at Rwanda’s Forensic Institute, testified that DNA profiles obtained from a white T-shirt, black T-shirt, shorts and boxer matched Bon Jallah’s reference DNA profile.

A forensic report dated January 22 concluded that Bon Jallah could not be excluded as a contributor to the DNA profiles obtained from the four exhibits.

However, Bavugirije told the court that the laboratory could not determine when the biological material was deposited, how it was deposited, or the circumstances under which it came to be present on the clothing.

The laboratory’s role, he explained, was to examine materials submitted by Liberian investigators and compare the resulting DNA profiles with reference samples. It was not tasked with reconstructing the alleged events.

The forensic evidence also included a mixed DNA profile obtained from tissue or toilet paper reportedly collected from a crime scene. According to the report, that profile did not match the reference samples of either Bon Jallah or the alleged victim.

Bavugirije said the unidentified profile could potentially be compared with samples from other individuals if such persons were identified and reference samples obtained.

Defense Challenges Camp Johnson Road Crime Scene

The defense has also challenged the prosecution’s evidence concerning the alleged Camp Johnson Road location.

Two locations had been scheduled for a judicial inspection on September 24: a residence associated with Bon Jallah and the Camp Johnson Road location where the alleged victim testified that one of the incidents occurred.

The Camp Johnson Road site was not visited.

The defense cited testimony from Linsay Gould, identified during the trial as chief investigator of the Women and Children Protection Services, that investigators took the alleged victim to Camp Johnson Road on two occasions but that she was unable to identify the precise location.

Defense lawyers argue that the inability to identify the alleged crime scene undermines that portion of the testimony and contributes to reasonable doubt.

Dispute Over Inspection of Bon Jallah’s Residence

The inspection of Bon Jallah’s residence in the Airfield-Matadi area also became part of the defense’s argument.

According to the court record, representatives of both sides and their lawyers visited the residence on September 24. One room was opened while another remained closed after the family identified one room as the master bedroom and declined to open the other.

Defense counsel Cllr. Wilfred Sayeh argued that testimony before the court had identified the master bedroom as one of the locations where an alleged incident occurred, while the defense maintains that the inspection did not resolve discrepancies concerning the residence.

The defense has further pointed to an alleged difference between the police charge sheet and the alleged victim’s testimony regarding which room was involved.

The prosecution is expected to address those issues in its resistance.

Defense Invokes Criminal Procedure Law

In seeking an acquittal before Bon Jallah presents a defense, lawyers relied principally on Sections 2.1 and 20.10 of Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law.

Section 2.1 provides for the presumption of innocence and requires acquittal where reasonable doubt remains as to whether guilt has been established.

Section 20.10 provides for judgment of acquittal where the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction.

Defense lawyers argued that the prosecution’s evidence has exposed inconsistencies sufficient to justify ending the case at this stage.

Prosecutors requested additional time to respond, saying the defense had raised several issues requiring a detailed answer. Judge Wesseh granted the request but ordered the written resistance filed by noon Tuesday.

Court to Decide Whether Case Continues

The filing of the motion does not constitute a ruling that the prosecution’s evidence is insufficient. The court must now determine whether the evidence presented by the Republic is legally sufficient for the trial to continue.

If the motion is denied, Bon Jallah will retain his right to present evidence in his defense.

If the motion is granted, he would receive a judgment of acquittal. Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law provides the Republic a right to appeal an order granting a motion for judgment of acquittal.

For now, the immediate issue before Judge Wesseh is whether the prosecution’s evidence—including the DNA match on four exhibits and testimony surrounding the alleged crime scenes—is sufficient to allow the case to proceed.

The court’s ruling following Tuesday’s resistance will determine the next stage of the proceedings.

World.title: Liberia: Whein Town Residents Demand Landfill Closure, Cite Rising Health and Water Risks
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE — Residents of Whein Town are demanding the closure of the Whein Town Landfill, accusing authorities of continuing to use a site they say has exceeded its intended lifespan and is exposing surrounding communities to growing health and environmental risks.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Residents interviewed by FrontPage Africa cited increasing mosquito and fly infestations, foul-smelling water they fear may be contaminated, and the presence of rodents and snakes around homes.



They also complained that sections of the wall surrounding the landfill have collapsed, allegedly creating additional entry points for rodents and snakes into nearby residential areas.

‘We Want the Dumpsite Closed’

Samuel Kofi Jones III, Secretary General of the Whein Town Community Leadership, told FrontPage Africa that residents have raised concerns about the landfill for years and have previously protested activities they considered harmful to the community.

Jones recalled an incident around 2012 or 2013 when authorities allegedly brought seized drugs to the area and burned them near the landfill, saying fumes spread into the community.

The incident, he said, prompted residents to protest and demand greater community oversight of activities at the facility.

According to Jones, a community monitoring team was subsequently established, initially comprising eight residents who worked in shifts, including overnight, to monitor activities at the landfill.

He said the team was later reduced to four members because of financial constraints, while stipends have not been paid consistently.

Jones said two batches of community monitors have completed their assignments, while the latest group has worked for about two months awaiting payment.

But for Jones, monitoring is no longer enough.

“If you ask me what I want them to do, I would tell you to close the dumpsite,” he said, stressing that residents do not want the landfill to continue operating in the community.

He said residents remain open to discussions with the government but believe authorities have failed to follow through on commitments made to the community.

The Whein Town Landfill was established in 2011 as a temporary five-year emergency waste disposal site under the Emergency Monrovia Urban Sanitation (EMUS) Project, managed by the Monrovia City Corporation.

The facility was intended as an interim sanitary landfill to improve solid-waste collection and disposal in Monrovia and Paynesville.

Fifteen years later, however, it remains operational. Residents say the facility has far exceeded its intended lifespan and is now operating in a heavily degraded condition.

Mosquitoes, Flies and Water Concerns

Leon Miaway said mosquitoes have become particularly problematic in the community, especially during the evening.

He said residents often struggle to remain outdoors after 5 or 6 p.m. because of the mosquito population and rely on mosquito nets at night.

Miaway also cited an increase in flies, particularly during the rainy season, saying residents have difficulty eating outdoors without flies coming into contact with their food.

He expressed concern about water sources around the community, particularly following changes to the area where waste is being dumped.

According to Miaway, the new dumping area lacks adequate measures to contain liquid leaking from waste, which he believes has contributed to the pollution of water sources.

He said some residents now have to purchase water for drinking and cooking, adding to household expenses.

“Before you prepare any good food now, it means you have to spend more, even to buy water,” Miaway said.

Miaway also said malaria is common in the community and that children face additional risks when walking barefoot around areas affected by stagnant water.

He said residents have not seen government or humanitarian organizations regularly collecting household data or distributing mosquito nets and other supplies.

“It has been a long while, like, over two, three years now,” he said.

Residents Fear Retaliation

Miaway said residents have held meetings to discuss ways to push for the landfill’s closure but have been reluctant to organize direct confrontations with authorities.

He recalled previous protests in which residents blocked roads and some participants were arrested.

“We don’t want similar things to happen,” he said, adding that residents prefer their community leadership to advocate on their behalf.

Miaway also disputed claims that residents routinely use the landfill for open defecation, saying people living around the facility have access to their own latrines.

He questioned the enforcement of reported safety requirements requiring people entering the landfill to wear protective equipment.

Miaway said residents and some people working at the site can enter without masks or other protective gear.

‘They Are Still Dumping Every Day’

Princess Dennis, another resident, said families living near the landfill are increasingly concerned about illnesses they associate with conditions around the facility.

She cited malaria and other infections among illnesses residents experience and said children are particularly vulnerable.

Dennis said mosquito nets had previously been distributed in the community but did not reach all residents.

She alleged that during some distributions, the exercise stopped around the telecommunications junction, leaving residents in other parts of the community without nets.

But like other residents interviewed, Dennis said the primary demand is not for mosquito nets or other supplies but for the landfill to be closed or relocated.

“I’m upset about the dumpsite here,” she said, appealing to authorities to stop dumping waste at the site.

Dennis said waste continues to be dumped every day despite residents’ concerns.

She also operates a business along the road near the landfill and said the large number of flies affects her customers and forces her to cover her goods.

Water and Cost of Living

Dennis said access to safe water is another major concern.

She said some residents sometimes consume water they consider unsafe because they cannot afford alternatives.

“When we don’t get money, we can drink the water,” she said.

She appealed to the government and other organizations to improve access to safe water.

Amos Moore, called said residents of Whein Town feel betrayed by the Government. Moore said the government has failed to live up to its promise of closing the landfill since its five-year lifespan expired. “We are being used as sacrificial lambs,” he said. It is a shame that the government will unleash such suffering on a large group of its people.”

MCC: ‘Immediate, Aggressive Action’ Underway

In a statement, the Monrovia City Corporation said it is taking “immediate, aggressive action” to address technical challenges at Whein Town, acknowledging that the landfill “has outlived its usefulness” and that the rainy season has compounded the situation.

“The MCC considers the health concerns of the residents as a top priority; as such, we are constantly fumigating the facility and providing routine health care interventions to the residents,” the statement said.

The corporation added that mosquito nets have been distributed and that between March and April 2026, it conducted a free medical outreach for residents.

Addressing claims that garbage is being dumped directly on the ground, the MCC said it remains committed to responsible waste disposal and “would do nothing to endanger the health of the people of Whein Town.”

On the landfill’s future, the MCC said it is at an advanced stage of concluding a public-private partnership framework with a private-sector company for the joint management of the sanitary landfill.

A Community Seeking an End to Dumping

The residents’ accounts depict a community caught between immediate concerns over sanitation, water access and public health and a longer-standing demand for an end to landfill operations in the area.

While the MCC says it is taking measures to mitigate the facility’s challenges and is pursuing a new management arrangement, residents insist that temporary interventions are not enough.

For them, the central demand remains unchanged: close or relocate the landfill and end the dumping that they say has made life increasingly difficult in Whein Town.

Jaheim Tumu contributed to this story.

World.title: Liberia: ULAA Demands Seat at the Table, Warns Boakai Government Against Sidelining Independent Diaspora Voices
World.content:
Diaspora group says Liberians abroad must be valued for more than remittances

Monrovia – The Union of Liberian Associations in the Americas (ULAA) has called on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. and his government to back their stated commitment to the diaspora with genuine inclusion, warning that new government-created diaspora initiatives must not bypass or replace independent institutions Liberians abroad have built over decades.

In an open statement issued in New York on September 17, 2026, as President Boakai and his delegation arrived for the 81st United Nations General Assembly, ULAA said the government’s diaspora outreach falls short if it treats Liberians abroad mainly as a source of money and skills while shutting out their critical voices.



“The Government speaks of ‘Mobilizing the Global Liberian Diaspora for National Transformation,'” the statement said. “But the diaspora cannot be valued primarily for its remittances, investments, professional expertise and development contributions while independent diaspora institutions and critical voices are given inadequate space in discussions about the direction of the Republic.”

‘ULAA remains relevant’

Under the banner “ULAA Remains Relevant,” the organization reminded the government that it has served as an organized and independent voice for Liberians in the Americas for more than half a century.

“New government-created diaspora initiatives should complement—not bypass, marginalize or replace—the independent institutions Liberians abroad have built and sustained,” the statement said.

The statement did not name any specific government initiative, but it comes amid the Boakai administration’s push to formalize diaspora engagement.

Beyond economics

ULAA argued that national development cannot be reduced to economics and must address what it called the difficult issues affecting Liberia’s stability and democratic future. It listed border and national security, illicit drugs and trafficking, justice and due process, and “concerns and allegations regarding selective prosecution and political persecution.” It also cited political polarization, governance, accountability, economic opportunity, youth development and national reconciliation.

“These are Liberian issues—and Liberians must have the freedom and space to speak about them,” the group declared.

Call for formal mechanism

The organization called for a “formal and sustained Government–ULAA consultative mechanism,” along with a broader framework that welcomes independent Liberian voices at home and across the global diaspora.

ULAA also drew a contrast between the President’s appearance on the world stage and his administration’s engagement at home. It said that as President Boakai addresses the international community at the UN, his government should show the same commitment to dialogue by listening to the diverse voices of the Liberian people.

“ULAA must have a seat at the table—but the table must be large enough for every Liberian voice,” the statement said. “National development cannot be the conversation of a selected few. It requires inclusion, accountability, open dialogue and the meaningful participation of the Liberian people.”

The statement closed with the slogan “One Liberia. Many Voices. A Shared Future.” It was signed by the ULAA National President, identified in the document as Hon. Mohammad MSG1 Keita.

World.title: Archbishop Banda Faces Second Night in Chimbokaila as Lawyers Race to Meet Bail Terms
World.content:
Lusaka Archbishop Dr Alick Banda remains in custody as his lawyers work to meet the bail conditions set by Resident Magistrate Mwandu Nakazwe. A legal team led by State Counsel John Sangwa has been at the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court since morning, joined by Vicar General Andrew Simpasa and other senior Catholic clergy. Their aim is to secure the Archbishop’s release before the end of the day and spare him a second night at Lusaka Central Correctional Facility, commonly known as Chimbokaila. By 14:50, his sureties were still being interviewed by court officials as part of the bail process.

The 62-year-old cleric was granted K80,000 bail in his own recognisance on Monday, with three working sureties each bound in the sum of K50,000. The court also ordered him to surrender his travel documents pending trial. Despite the ruling, he spent Monday night at Chimbokaila because the bail formalities were not completed in time. Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri indicated that the Archbishop remained detained because the conditions may have been met late in the day.

Dr Banda was arrested by the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) on Monday after questioning at the Commission’s offices in Lusaka. He was charged with possession of property reasonably suspected to have been unlawfully obtained, contrary to Section 319 of the Penal Code. The particulars allege that between 22 April 2021 and 27 December 2023, he had in his possession a blue Toyota Hilux, registration number ALF 7734, reasonably suspected to have been unlawfully obtained from the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA). When the charge was read in court, the Archbishop pleaded not guilty. He remains presumed innocent until the court rules otherwise.

The vehicle is one of about 22 ZRA motor vehicles that the DEC says were improperly disposed of. Ownership of the Hilux was reportedly transferred into Dr Banda’s name in April 2021, and the DEC seized the vehicle in December 2023. The Commission announced in September 2024 that the Hilux had been forfeited after a six-month period to contest the seizure lapsed. The DEC’s Anti-Money Laundering Investigations Unit first summoned the Archbishop on 31 December 2025, and a warn and caution statement was recorded on 5 January 2026.

The wider investigation has already produced convictions. In October 2025, a court sentenced former ZRA Commissioner General Kingsley Chanda to six years and former Director of Administration Callistus Kaoma to nine years for failing to follow proper procedures in disposing of the vehicles. Both men were granted bail pending appeal. The Archbishop’s name surfaced during that trial when former ZRA Board Secretary Suzyo Ngandu testified that three vehicles which had not been advertised for sale were given away. According to her testimony, one went to Archbishop Banda and two to the Heart of Mercy charity.

The paper trail behind the Hilux has also been disputed. Mulopa Kaunda, the ZRA employee whose name appeared in the purported transaction, publicly denied ever buying the vehicle from ZRA or selling it to the Archbishop. He said documents and receipts had been generated in his name without his involvement. His account has not been tested in court, and the earlier proceedings concerned other accused persons rather than the Archbishop himself.

The Archbishop began Monday at a solidarity Mass surrounded by members of the faithful before presenting himself to the DEC. The Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops (ZCCB) has since come out firmly in his support. ZCCB President and Archbishop of Kasama, Most Reverend Ignatius Chama, said the Catholic Church stands in solidarity with Archbishop Banda as he goes through the process. In a statement, he urged all concerned to ensure that fairness and due process are upheld without prejudice or intimidation. He added that the Church remains confident in Archbishop Banda’s pastoral ministry and his contribution to both the Church and the nation.

Archbishop Chama called on the Catholic faithful and people of goodwill to keep praying for calm, peace and unity as the case unfolds. The bishops have framed their position around fair treatment rather than the merits of the charge, placing the Church’s weight behind the process instead of against it. Other voices have also urged calm and asked the public to let the legal process run without inflammatory statements. That tone matters in a case that touches both the law and the faith of millions of Zambians.

The case has drawn national attention because of Dr Banda’s standing as Metropolitan Archbishop of Lusaka and one of the most senior figures in the Catholic Church in Zambia. It now moves to trial, where the prosecution will have to prove its case against a defence led by one of the country’s most prominent constitutional lawyers. For now, the immediate question is whether the bail process concludes before the court closes for the day.

World.title: Stolen cattle traced to Luanshya farm
World.content:
Police in Luanshya have traced two cattle whose carcasses were recovered in Kitwe to Chichetekelo Children’s Orphanage Farm in Kamishishi.

Copperbelt Division Commissioner of Police Rae Hamoonga told the media that investigations established that the cattle, valued at K25, 000 in total, were stolen from the farm.

Mr Hamoonga said suspect Tilimbali Nyirenda, 36, led police officers to the farm on Monday morning.

At the farm, Gideon Siakamwi told police that he discovered a brown cow and a black cow missing at about 05:00 hours on Sunday.

Mr Siakamwi later identified the recovered carcasses as those of the missing animals.

Mr Nyirenda has since been jointly charged with other persons yet to be identified with theft of stock and is expected to appear in court soon.

The four pieces of carcass recovered in Kitwe have since been released to the owner through a court process.

A red Toyota Sienta, registration number BCG 6947 ZM, remains at Luanshya Central Police Station as an exhibit.

Earlier, police appealed to farmers in Luanshya District who had lost cattle to report to the police to help establish ownership of the recovered carcasses.

The appeal followed the recovery of carcasses believed to be from two stolen cattle at a house in Garnetone, Kitwe, where one suspect was arrested.

The animals were later traced to Luanshya and the matter was handed over to Luanshya police for further investigations.

World.title: Nalumango calls on youths to create jobs
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has urged young Zambians to move from seeking employment to creating jobs by investing in green businesses, innovation, value addition and technology.

Ms Nalumango says young people must be at the centre of the Grow Zambia Agenda by leading production, building businesses and developing technologies that can generate employment.

She was speaking in Lusaka today when she officially opened the two-day 2026 Youth Connekt National Summit being held under the theme: “Green Hustle: Cultivating Wealth, Creating Jobs.”

The Vice President said Zambia needs to move from farming to agribusiness, production to value addition and raw commodities to finished products, in order to create greater economic opportunities for young people.

She noted that youths can establish businesses in areas such as agricultural technology, mechanisation, irrigation, processing, packaging, transport, logistics, renewable energy and digital services.

Ms Nalumango also called for increased investment in technical and vocational training, digital and technological skills, entrepreneurship, financial literacy, green skills, apprenticeships and continuous skills development.

She explained that climate change, while presenting challenges to the economy, also provides opportunities for young people to develop businesses around solar-powered irrigation, water harvesting, renewable energy, recycling, waste management and climate-smart agriculture.

Ms Nalumango disclosed that the government will continue strengthening young people’s access to skills and entrepreneurship training, finance, productive assets, land, technology, irrigation, infrastructure, mentorship, markets and value-addition opportunities.

She further said Youth Resource Centres are also being developed into practical hubs for skills development, innovation, entrepreneurship and market access.

Ms Nalumango pointed out that the success of young people will contribute to the growth of Zambia and called for the Grow Zambia Agenda to also become a Grow Youth Agenda.

Speaking at the same event, Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts Permanent Secretary Kangwa Chileshe urged young people to harness their skills and creativity to establish enterprises and create sustainable employment, particularly in emerging green sectors.

Mr Chileshe said agriculture and agro-processing, renewable energy, digital enterprise, creative industries and sport, provide avenues for young people to participate in economic activity.

He said partnerships between governments, the private sector, development partners and civil society are critical to helping young people acquire skills, access finance, enter markets and grow their businesses.

Mr Chileshe said the government alone cannot address all the challenges facing young people and called for stronger collaboration among stakeholders.

And Youth representative, Mwewa Mulonga has called for increased support and partnerships to enable young people to participate more actively in national development.

Ms Mulonga said young people have the potential to contribute to Zambia’s development through innovation, agriculture, technology and other sectors if provided with platforms and opportunities to showcase their capabilities.

She has since called on development partners and other stakeholders to support more young people to participate in such programmes and summits.

Ms Mulonga said young people should take advantage of platforms created for them and use their skills and capabilities to contribute to national development.

Meanwhile, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Deputy Resident Representative Laurent Rudasingwa said increased investment in skills, technology, entrepreneurship and access to finance is critical to enabling young people to create sustainable businesses and jobs.

Mr Rudasingwa noted that young people have a central role to play in driving inclusive economic growth as Zambia implements the Ninth National Development Plan and pursues the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He, however, noted that many young people continue to face challenges in accessing finance, markets, technology, skills development, mentorship and productive opportunities.

Mr Rudasingwa advised that addressing these constraints requires strong partnerships and deliberate investments that place young people at the centre of development efforts.

He said UNDP is supporting youth-focused programmes in job creation, economic diversification, human capital development, climate resilience, digital transformation and private sector development.

He further said the organisation is also supporting young entrepreneurs and innovators through mentorship, enterprise development, skills training, financial literacy and market linkages.

Mr Rudasingwa also urged young people to continuously develop their skills, embrace innovation, seek partnerships and pursue opportunities with confidence.

World.title: Stakeholders Validate El Niño Response Strategy
World.content:
More than 50 stakeholders are meeting in Lusaka to validate the 2027–2031 El Niño Preparedness and Response Strategy.

The two-day multi-sectoral validation workshop is aimed at strengthening Zambia’s preparedness and response to the potential impacts of El Niño.

Speaking at the meeting, Civil Society Organisations National Coordinator on El Niño Preparedness Abel Musumali said the strategy seeks to strengthen early warning systems and improve access to climate information.

Mr. Musumali said the framework will also enhance the capacity of smallholder farmers, camp officers and agricultural extension officers to better understand and respond to the multi-sectoral impacts of El Niño.

He added that the workshop is expected to identify evidence-based adaptation and resilience measures that can be implemented at community level.

Meanwhile, Action Against Hunger Country Director Mary Kozi said the strategy aligns with the organisation’s work in seven provinces, where it is supporting smallholder farmers and communities to strengthen resilience against climate-related shocks.

World.title: Zambia Needs 8,000MW of Power to Produce 3 Million Tonnes of Copper
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema says Zambia will need about 8,000 megawatts of electricity to reach its goal of producing three million tonnes of copper a year. He told the UAE-Zambia Business Forum in Abu Dhabi that the power gap is a major investment opportunity for the United Arab Emirates and other investors. The 8,000MW figure covers copper production alone. It does not include the electricity needed to run the wider economy.

The President said energy sector reforms have opened the market to independent power producers, electricity traders and private investment in transmission and distribution. He pointed to long-term power purchase agreements of 20 to 25 years as a draw for investors seeking predictable returns. UAE Undersecretary for Foreign Trade Fahad Siddiq Al Gergawi said his country sees room to deepen cooperation with Zambia. He named agriculture, energy, healthcare, digital technology and mineral value addition as priority areas.

Zambia Development Agency Director General Albert Halwampa said Zambia issued investment licences for projects worth more than US$100 billion between 2021 and 2026. That figure exceeds the US$70 billion in licences issued over the previous 18 years combined. Mr Halwampa credited the surge to rising investor confidence in the country. He cited political stability, policy reforms and the Public-Private Dialogue Forum as key drivers of a more predictable business environment.

Industrial Development Corporation Chief Executive Officer Cornwell Muleya said the Corporation has identified 15 investment opportunities across five sectors, including mining, energy, manufacturing and agribusiness. He said the projects are aligned with the Grow Zambia Agenda. They aim to diversify the economy, create jobs and increase value addition at home. The pipeline gives investors ready-made entry points into Zambia’s growth plans.

World.title: HH Seals US$2.14 Billion in Pledges as Abu Dhabi Opens Its Doors to Zambia
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has witnessed the signing of memoranda of understanding worth US$2.14 billion at the Zambia-UAE Business Forum in Abu Dhabi, the first foreign trip of his renewed mandate. The two-day working visit, running from 29 to 30 September, is at the invitation of UAE President and Ruler of Abu Dhabi Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The agreements span several sectors. The President said Zambia now looks forward to a Comprehensive Partnership Agreement that will lift trade between the two countries. It is a strong opening to a second term that has put economic diplomacy at the centre of foreign policy.

“The UAE has harnessed its natural resources to develop its economy and raise the living standards of its people. As a country richly endowed with natural resources, we have much to learn from the UAE,” the President said.

The visit is a working visit rather than a full State visit, and it has been described that way from the start. It is, however, a packed and purposeful programme. It includes an official bilateral meeting between the two Heads of State, the business and investment forum, direct talks with Emirati business leaders and a meeting with Zambians living in the UAE. It is a working visit in the truest sense of the word.

At the forum, President Hichilema gave investors a clear number to work with. He said Zambia’s target of three million tonnes of copper a year will require about 8,000 megawatts of electricity, and that this is for copper alone, before the needs of the wider economy. He pointed to energy reforms that now open the door to independent power producers, electricity traders and private investment in transmission and distribution. He also offered long-term power purchase agreements of 20 to 25 years as a stable market for patient capital. The UAE’s Undersecretary for Foreign Trade, Fahad Siddiq Al Gergawi, said his country sees clear room to deepen cooperation with Zambia in agriculture, energy, healthcare and the digital economy.

The partnership already carries weight. Emirati-backed International Resources Holding has invested more than US$1.1 billion in Mopani Copper Mines, now a pillar of the copper drive. Zambia opened its embassy in Abu Dhabi in 2023, and the UAE posted its first resident ambassador to Lusaka this month. Sheikh Mohamed was also among the leaders who congratulated President Hichilema on his re-election in August.

Claims circulating on social media and in some local outlets have questioned the timing of the trip, suggesting the UAE was in a period of national mourning. The facts are more specific. A 10-day mourning period was declared in the Emirate of Dubai following the death of Sheikh Ahmed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the youngest brother of Dubai’s Ruler, and it applies to Dubai. The President’s engagements are in Abu Dhabi, the federal capital and a separate emirate, where the business forum went ahead with senior UAE officials in attendance.

The visit also comes as questions are asked about trade figures between the two countries. UAE records show far higher imports from Zambia than Zambia records as exports to the UAE, and gold accounts for most of the difference. Trade analysts note that such gaps often arise from how countries record the origin and destination of goods, and that they are not in themselves proof of wrongdoing. Government is already acting on the gold question, with ZCCM-IH moving to bring small-scale gold into formal channels and a cut to the 16 per cent VAT on gold transactions under consideration. A closer trade relationship with the UAE puts Zambia in a stronger position to reconcile those records and capture more value from its own gold.

The memoranda signed in Abu Dhabi are the first step. Their true worth will show as pledges turn into power plants, processing lines and jobs on Zambian soil, and the Comprehensive Partnership Agreement will give that work a firmer footing. For now, the message from Abu Dhabi is one of confidence in Zambia’s direction.

“Zambia remains open and ready for business and investment,” President Hichilema said.

World.title: Man shot dead in Nakonde
World.content:
A 43-year-old man of Kazembe Village in Nakonde District, Muchinga Province, has been shot dead by unknown people.

Muchinga Province Police Commanding Officer Lubinda Mayamba identified the deceased as Weston Siame.

Mr Mayamba, who confirmed the incident to the media, said the shooting occurred on Sunday, September 27, 2026, at around 19:00 hours.

He said Mr Siame, who was in a polygamous marriage, was shot while walking from his second wife’s house to his first wife’s house in the same village.

“The deceased married two wives and had eight children. On the material day, he left the second wife’s house to spend a night at the first wife’s house and was shot a few metres away along the footpath,” Mr Mayamba said.

He said the second wife heard a gunshot and rushed to investigate, only to find her husband lying lifeless about 50 metres from her house.

Mr Mayamba said the matter was reported to police, who visited the scene, located about 48 kilometres from Nakonde Central Business District, and found the body lying on its side on a narrow footpath.

He said a physical inspection revealed a gunshot wound on the left side of the chest, with a homemade firearm suspected to have been used in the shooting.

Mr Mayamba said preliminary investigations indicate that the deceased had previously been accused of practising witchcraft and that some villagers had engaged a witch finder who allegedly found him guilty.

He said the body has since been deposited at Nakonde Urban Clinic Mortuary awaiting a post-mortem examination to establish the exact cause of death.

Mr Mayamba said the motive for the murder remains unknown and that police have opened a docket and instituted investigations to apprehend the suspected perpetrator.

World.title: NRPUP Insists Ezra Tembo, Not Kampyongo, Is Leader Of The Opposition
World.content:
The National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) said its president, Dag Hammarskjöld MP Ezra Tembo, is its settled choice for Leader of the Opposition in Parliament. The party rejected claims that Shiwang’andu MP Stephen Kampyongo had been selected for the post. This decision reflects a strong commitment to leadership in zambia.

Party secretary-general Nonde Mubanga said in a statement that a binding decision in Mr Tembo’s favour was taken earlier this month at a properly convened meeting of 34 NRPUP parliamentarians. Luanshya MP Golden Mulenga proposed Mr Tembo, and the motion was seconded by Nyimba North MP Paul Lungu and Chembe MP Kasongo Chomba. This decision is vital for the political landscape in zambia.

The dispute turns on a second, later meeting, which Mr Mubanga said had no power to reverse what the full caucus had agreed. He said that meeting “cannot unilaterally overturn a prior collective decision made by the 34 MPs”. He urged the public, the media and the office of the Speaker to disregard what he called a misleading report now circulating. The future of opposition leadership in zambia is at stake.

The party’s position, he said, stands firm, and the nomination letter recognising Mr Tembo as Leader of the Opposition has already been submitted to the National Assembly of Zambia. Efforts to get a comment from Mr Kampyongo were unsuccessful.

The row has broken out in the first days of the new Parliament. Members of the 14th National Assembly are in induction, and presiding officers are due to be elected on Friday. Opening that induction, Speaker Nelly Mutti urged MPs to enter Parliament with a sense of duty, to disagree without becoming enemies and to hold each other accountable.

The Speaker said the strength of the House would be judged not by the absence of differences, but by its ability to resolve them. She asked veteran parliamentarians not to intimidate new members but to guide them through respectable conduct, and reminded all MPs that the credibility of the House depends on their character, judgment and conduct.

The timetable leaves the opposition little room for a long quarrel. President Hakainde Hichilema will officially open the first session of the 14th National Assembly on October 9. He is expected to outline the Government’s policy direction and priorities for 2026/2027.

Clerk of the National Assembly Loveness Mayaka said the ceremonial opening will take place at Parliament Buildings, and MPs will then consider the pronouncements in the President’s address. NRPUP’s nomination letter naming Mr Tembo is with the National Assembly, and Mr Kampyongo has not responded to requests for comment.
