World.title: News organizations ask court to bar White House enforcement of access ban
World.content:
News organizations ask court to bar White House enforcement of access ban

toggle caption Rod Lamkey/AP

Three news outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banished from White House grounds this month asked a federal court to block the ban until the case is resolved, saying the administration has "persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban" despite a judge's restraining order — including selectively barring CNN from White House pool duties.

"The White House's words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity," lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico wrote in a filing late Monday.

"Because the ban is an unlawful assault on the most fundamental First Amendment freedoms and will inflict irreparable harm on Plaintiffs and the public if not restrained, this Court should preliminarily enjoin its enforcement pending the resolution of this case," the filing said.

Sponsor Message

It was the latest development in the back-and-forth saga of the Trump administration and the news media during the second term of his presidency. It has been a contentious relationship that has raised multiple First Amendment questions, produced sanctions and restrictions on White House and Pentagon reporters and led to several lawsuits that are winding their ways through the federal court system.

A two-week temporary restraining order on Trump's ban of the three organizations, issued by U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly last week, restored the outlets' White House access, but expires Oct. 8. The preliminary injunction requested in Monday's filing would extend the White House access until the case is finally resolved.

In a statement emailed to The Associated Press immediately after the filing, the lead attorney for the three news outlets called the ban "a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process."

"The president and his administration have continued to make clear that this ban has only one purpose: to punish reporting he doesn't like," said the lawyer, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr.

"That's retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, pure and simple," Boutrous said. "With the district court's temporary restraining order expiring this week, it is critical to ensure that the White House continues to be prevented from implementing this unconstitutional ban on the free press."

Sponsor Message

The White House still says access is a privilege, not a right

The filing came a day after the Trump administration made clear it was not backing down from its contention that the sudden ban, which began Sept. 19, was justified.

"When it comes to the White House, it is the people's house," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on ABC on Sunday, invoking an argument the administration has made since the beginning. "It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there."

Monday's 42-page filing reiterated many of the arguments that the news outlets made in their original lawsuit against Trump and the White House, filed two days after the reporters were banned.

It also added mention of the White House broadcast pool rotation, which has become a battleground in the last few days in the standoff between Trump and the media.

The White House, it said, "has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on Sept. 26 — to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public."

When the ban was implemented, CNN was removed from its duties as part of the broadcast pool, which consists of the five main networks: CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. In solidarity, the other networks decided to suspend the pool until CNN was allowed back in.

On Friday, CNN was allowed to cover the president with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the National Archives. But in a new setback Saturday, the White House banned the network from Air Force One, preventing it from covering Trump's trip to a college football game in Tennessee. The rest of the pool declined to provide a replacement, in solidarity with CNN.

Blanche defended that decision, too. "The president has every right to decide who gets to fly on his plane," he said in the Sunday interview. He added that Trump was "sick and tired of certain media outlets just refusing to report accurate news." He added that news coverage he described as "misinformation" amounted to a national security issue.

Sponsor Message

"That is what is a national security problem, when you have complete misinformation coming out of the White House," he said.

Kelly threw cold water on that argument in his ruling last week granting the temporary restraining order against the White House ban. "The court is skeptical … that defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation" for removal of access, Kelly wrote.

His ruling did not directly address the TV pool rotation. In the new filing, the plaintiffs describe the important function the pool provides and makes the case that it's an important part of the regular access to the president, and his activities, that the media has traditionally had — and must be restored.

It singles out the Air Force One case. "CNN received no official communication from the White House explaining its exclusion," the filing says. "Because CNN was excluded and no replacement designated, no primary television network pooler accompanied the President on the trip."

Pool access issue has presented networks with tough choices

For now, networks in the pool have decided to address the ongoing standoff on a case-by-case basis, according to a person familiar with the pool's operation, speaking on condition of anonymity to give details of ongoing discussions.

On Sunday, Fox covered a pool event; on Monday, NBC was covering the president in the Oval Office. CNN is not in the rotation until Thursday. If the network is again barred from a pool event, the networks will decide together, presumably based on the newsworthiness of the situation, whether to provide a replacement or to refrain from coverage as they did previously.

The issues at stake are difficult. On the one hand, the networks want to take a stand on behalf of press freedom and against efforts to intimidate coverage. On the other, media outlets have an obvious purpose of providing news to their audiences.

Sponsor Message

"There are not a lot of good options," said David A. Schulz, director of the Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School.

Should the White House continue to bar CNN, Schulz said, networks may choose "to exert their market power and say, 'We're not going to play ball with you.'"

The question, Schulz added, is: "Who's going to back down first?"

The networks "may well feel like they're between a rock and a hard place," noted RonNell Andersen Jones, a law professor at the University of Utah.

"Capitulation might be perceived as abandonment of core components of press freedom," Andersen Jones said. "But the practicalities of lengthy White House news blackouts are also complicated, and refusing to cover major news at the highest levels of government might itself feel like a failure to serve the goals of democracy."

World.title: OpenAI delays latest model over security concerns, as industry faces pressure
World.content:
OpenAI delays latest model over security concerns, as industry faces pressure

toggle caption Michael Dwyer/AP

OpenAI said Monday it was delaying the release of a new artificial intelligence model out of security concerns voiced by its researchers, the latest in the company's effort to decelerate the pace of the technology's advance.

OpenAI's decision to hold back the model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up. The announcement comes a day before AI executives are set to huddle with President Donald Trump in Washington as technology companies face new pressure to be accountable for how their models can be abused.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report the delay of OpenAI's model release.

Sponsor Message

In a statement from OpenAI's head of safety systems Saachi Jain, the version "didn't quite meet the bar." It had become more persistent in completing tasks, but OpenAI needed to balance that capability against unauthorized behavior.

Jain insisted the company was committed to ensuring the model was safe whether in the company's testing or is in the hands of users. "We have an extremely high bar in terms of safety and alignment," she said.

OpenAI paused training of its most advanced models last week, saying training would resume "only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards."

That was after it disclosed instances in which AI agents exceeded their instructions, including by accessing government websites without authorization.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has joined other industry leaders in calling for a slowdown, warning that companies do not yet have adequate safeguards to control the most capable systems. Altman was scheduled to deliver the keynote address for OpenAI's annual conference for software developers on Tuesday in San Francisco. OpenAI President Greg Brockman is expected to attend the White House's event Tuesday.

World.title: U.S. bans on Canadian booze hit producers on one of trade war's thorniest fronts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.S. ban on select Canadian goods takes effect Tuesday, hitting alcohol producers particularly hard. The move shuts many Canadian spirits, beer and cider products out of their biggest export market as the trade war escalates.

Distiller James Lester has grown used to the on-again, off-again chaos of the trade war, but he's now grappling with a new kind of treatment — being shut out of the U.S. market altogether.

"It's a little sad, to be honest," said Lester, founder and operator of B.C.-based distillery Sons of Vancouver.

As of Tuesday at 12:01 a.m. ET, U.S. bans are in effect on some Canadian alcohol products, dairy byproducts, motorcycles and molasses, shutting certain producers out of the U.S. market entirely.

Sons of Vancouver usually ships a few pallets of wheated rye to the U.S. each year — less than 10 per cent of their business overall. But the change is a disappointment for Lester, as he'd been working hard to forge relationships south of the border and expand the business there.

"We still have a little bit available online in the U.S., but that'll be the last of it for who knows how long."

It leaves Lester with few options for his American consumers, since they wouldn't be able to take it back to the States with them even if they came to Canada to buy a bottle.

The import ban heightens the trade war on one of its thorniest fronts — alcohol, which has become a hot-button issue for politicians on both sides of the border throughout the tariff battle.

James Lester founded Sons of Vancouver distillery in 2015. He's grown used to the chaos of the trade war but is disappointed by the U.S. move to ban some Canadian exports entirely from crossing the border, given the hard work he's put into trying to expand into that market. (Andrew Lee/CBC)

Small makers could be hurt most

With import bans stopping the flow of some alcohol products in their tracks, there are lots of individual business owners who stand to be hurt by the ban, according to international trade lawyer with KPMG Law, Robert Glasgow, even if the macro impact isn't massive.

Spirits producers could be hit particularly hard because Canada sends more liquor to the U.S. than it does beer or wine. The U.S. imported $673 million US worth of spirits from Canada in 2025 , compared to $62.1 million US worth of wine and just $19.2 million US worth of beer that same year, according to trade data from the U.S. Census Bureau.

Spirits Canada, the national trade association for the spirits industry, says about 93 per cent of spirits sent outside of Canada are destined for the States — making the loss of the "very important" U.S. market concerning, according to the group's president, Cal Bricker .

But the ban won't apply to barrels of certain kinds of liquor over a certain volume, and tariffs were removed from bulk shipments of certain whiskies and liqueurs when the heightened trade measures were announced earlier this month.

That move will spare big, multinational spirits companies that have bottling and mixing facilities on both sides of the border from some of the impact of the ban, according to Glasgow — leaving smaller players feeling the brunt.

"There's going to be a number of breweries, distilleries and vineyards — largely the smaller, more independent shops that are more dependent on U.S. trade and U.S. markets — that this could have some significant impacts for," Glasgow said.

But others in the wine-making business have said the 50 per cent tariff rate effectively excluded Canadian products already, and industry groups are calling for more government support to help Canadian vineyards.

WATCH | U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says: U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol would bite deep, Spirits Canada says | Duration closed caption 3:06 About half of the $2 billion in spirits produced in Canada every year is sold to the U.S., says Cal Bricker, president and CEO of Spirits Canada. 'We sell more Crown Royal in Texas than we do in all of Canada.'

Why booze?

Alcohol has been a focal point in the trade battle since the start, when most Canadian premiers pulled U.S.-made bottles from the shelves of provincially run liquor stores in March 2025 in response to the U.S. imposing tariffs on Canada.

The move drew criticism from political leaders in certain regions of the U.S. where certain types of spirits are made — like Kentucky, where Gov. Andy Beshear appealed to leaders in this country to rethink the move, as it threatened bourbon makers in his state.

The White House also cited Canada's "discrimination" against American alcohol , as well as dairy and autos, when announcing new 50 per cent tariffs in July, which hit Canadian booze among other products, including everything from milk to paper products to synthetic wigs.

Despite booze making up a relatively tiny portion of Canada-U.S. trade, Concordia University economics professor Moshe Lander says it's become a thorny issue in the trade war in part because it's so personal.

"We identify ourselves at least in part by the stuff that we drink," Lander said.

Brands like Foster's in Australia or Guinness in Ireland are more than just drinks, they're part of a country's identity, says Lander. He adds the same is true for Kentucky bourbon and California wine, making them politically effective targets.

WATCH | Why booze has become a pawn in the trade war: Why booze is at the centre of Canada-U.S. trade talks | About That | Duration closed caption 10:05 Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. have hit a breaking point over alcohol, with Prime Minister Mark Carney urging premiers to put American liquor back on shelves. Andrew Chang explains how alcohol became a top bargaining chip, how provincial liquor boards complicate trade and what's driving the current tariff standoff. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters and Getty Images)

And despite having a taste for their favourite brand of wine or bourbon, it's relatively easy for consumers to substitute with a local bottle and still have a good night out, KPMG's Glasgow says, making it a smart product for policy makers to target.

"That's a type of retaliation that hits … the country that you're retaliating against harder than it hurts your own markets," Glasgow said.

A year and a half-long hangover

Joan Kautz, head of global sales and marketing for Californian winemaker Ironstone Vineyards, says she understands the strong message sent by taking U.S. alcohol off shelves in Canada.

"I don't like it, but I understand it," Kautz said.

The fight over alcohol has meant wines from the 2,500-hectare vineyard in Lodi, Calif., haven't been available in Canada for a year and a half.

Kautz says they're still selling some products to Alberta, where private-run liquor stores aren't restricting U.S. booze, but it's a fraction of the business Ironstone used to send north of the border.

'Canada is a very important market to us in all aspects,' said Joan Kautz with Ironstone Vineyard. About 35 per cent of U.S. wine exports go to Canada, worth more than $1 billion US annually. (Ironstone Vineyard)

Historically, she says 20 per cent of the winery's export business went to Canada, making it their most important market outside of the U.S.

"Obviously, it hits financially," Kautz said. "We've been building the market for 30 years and it all went away overnight."

Her family's business exports to dozens of countries, and has been able to focus on other markets as Canadian demand dried up. But for other wineries, the impacts have been greater — some have reportedly filed for bankruptcy or decided to close and sell their vineyards in recent months.

Across booze categories, exports from the U.S. to Canada for 2025 dropped after bottles were pulled from shelves, with spirits sales falling by 70 per cent and wine exports dropping 87 per cent, according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the U.S.

As a result of the economic impact, the council has called on U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to resolve the feud over over alcohol, so long-time trading partners can raise a glass together again.

Kautz is still hopeful that will happen eventually. She expects Canadian consumers' memories won't be too short, and they'll still have a taste for California wine when they can eventually get their hands on a bottle.

"There'll be a group that's probably slower to the table," Kautz said. "But you have to be hopeful."

World.title: Grave of boy who vanished at residential school found decades later, First Nation looks for others like him
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Johnny Kiyawasew was 11 years old when he died in a small town hospital in northern Alberta in 1943, a world away from his Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation family.

Forced to enroll at Catholic-run St. Francis Xavier Residential School in Calais, Alta., Johnny never returned home, and it was decades before his brothers and sisters learned what happened to him.

"My parents, like my dad, was never told about nothing. They wrote a death certificate without his knowledge or nothing," said Robert Kiyawasew, Johnny's younger brother.

"It's not right… the church should have told my dad that he had passed away."

After years of unanswered questions, Robert Kiyawasew said his older sister Roseann, with the help of a private investigator, found Johnny's gravesite in 2013.

"That caretaker said, 'I know exactly where he's buried and I'll show you where,'" said Robert Kiyawasew.

According to provincial records, Johnny died of pulmonary tuberculosis in a hospital in High Prairie, where he is buried, over 75 kilometres away from the residential school.

Now, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation and the University of Alberta say they're undergoing extensive research to uncover the stories of children like Johnny, including many of his relatives, who went to residential school but never made it home.

'It is heartbreaking'

Sheldon Sunshine, chief of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, said research shows many children enrolled at St. Francis Xavier died from tuberculosis and malnutrition.

"It's not data, it's people," said Sunshine.

"When you see the names and, you know, it's saddening, what our people went through, having perished because of the results of the living conditions in that school. It is heartbreaking."

Johnny Kiyawasew's grave is in High Prairie, Alta., where he died in a hospital. 'I visit every time I have a chance now. To see that lonely little grave, out there all alone,' says Robert Kiyawasew. (Submitted by Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation)

Robert Kiyawasew said he's thankful his sister was able to track down Johnny's grave before she died.

"I visit every time I have a chance now," said Robert Kiyawasew.

"To see that lonely little grave, out there all alone."

WATCH | Searching for Johnny Kiyawasew: Sturgeon Lake family's search for a brother lost at residential school | Duration closed caption 3:03 Robert Kiyawasew explains his family's long search for his brother Johnny, who was forced to attend the St. Francis Xavier residential school near Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation.

A day school survivor himself, Robert Kiyawasew said he experienced harms similar to his siblings who attended St. Francis Xavier, and was punished for speaking his language.

"To treat us Natives like we don't exist… no," said Robert Kiyawasew.

"We belong in our culture. Our heritage is our right to be like that."

According to the Sturgeon Lake residential school narrative at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (NCTR), a summary of the school's history prepared by the Government of Canada as part of its response to litigation, at least five children died at the school in 1943.

It quotes a 1943 document saying the school "is falling to ruin and has become a source of danger for the health of Indian children as well as a fire hazard," adding some student deaths "last winter" had been said to be due to "the lack of comfort" resulting from poor heating.

Difficulty obtaining records

Raymond Frogner, senior director of research and head of archives at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, said residential school records were disorganized, inconsistent and unreliable.

"It was managed by church groups, which are private, provincial governments, federal governments, and all of these organizations never talked to each other," said Frogner.

"It's like putting a jigsaw puzzle back together when the pieces are missing."

St. Francis Xavier residential school grounds at Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, year unknown. (Submitted by Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation)

Frogner said many church records are not available, have incorrect or different dates from provincial or federal documents, and when they are tracked down they are often withheld.

Sunshine said several times Sturgeon Lake researchers have been told by church officials they will only release the documents of a student to someone with family ties.

"How do you have family ties when a lot of them are passing away?" said Sunshine.

"That really shuts the door on finding that information…. It's going to limit us to finding all of our children."

Sunshine said the First Nation will continue to work to piece together the stories of children who were enrolled at St. Francis Xavier and never came home.

"If we don't know where these children are, how can we find closure for some of our families?" said Sunshine.

"Talking about intergenerational trauma? That's part of it."

World.title: LNG Canada to move forward with Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LNG Canada says its multibillion-dollar Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C., is going forward, in a move that could double exports of liquefied natural gas from the northern coastal facility to overseas markets.

In a statement Tuesday, LNG Canada CEO Chris Cooper said the project will create thousands of jobs and further strengthen Canada's role as a trusted energy partner.

"LNG Canada Phase 2 is another nation-building investment that demonstrates Canada can build big things when governments, First Nations partners, local communities, skilled trades, contractors and investors work together with shared purpose," Cooper said.

LNG Canada is a joint venture company made up of Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation and Korea Gas Corp.

Its Kitimat plant shipped its first cargo load of LNG destined for Asian markets last year.

WATCH | Expanding LNG Canada plant is a major priority, Carney says: Why Canada’s LNG export expansion is far from a sure thing | Duration closed caption 7:47

Prime Minister Mark Carney will be highlighting the decision, which his office calls a "historic investment in Canada's energy industry" while making an appearance in Vancouver later Tuesday.

His public itinerary says the news will be shared at 11 a.m. PT, followed by a 1:20 p.m. PT briefing on "new measures to protect Canada's oceans."

The Canadian government says the expansion would make the Kitimat plant the second-largest in the world, worth billions to the national economy.

But while the LNG industry has strong political support from the federal government, as well as the campaigning B.C. NDP and Conservative Party of B.C., critics worry its rapid expansion will further contribute to Canada's rising greenhouse gas emissions at a time of climate crisis.

What is LNG?

LNG is made from natural gas, a fossil fuel often extracted in northeast B.C. and Alberta through a practice called hydraulic fracturing or fracking.

It involves drilling down into the ground and injecting a mixture of water, sand and chemicals into the ground to force the release of the oil and gas.

WATCH | Some Kitimat locals concerned about LNG flaring: Locals express safety concerns over flaring gas at Kitimat’s LNG export terminal | Duration closed caption 2:19



The gas is then shipped via pipeline to terminals, which cool it to about –160 C, at which point it can be shipped overseas for use as a fuel.

The expansion project is expected to roughly double the production of liquefied natural gas from 14 million to 28 million tonnes annually, LNG Canada said.

It also said it is working with Coastal GasLink to expand the capacity of the existing 670-kilometre pipeline through the construction of five new compressor stations across northern B.C., including territory that was blocked by Wet'suwet'en hereditary chiefs and their supporters opposed to the line's construction, which led to nation-wide protests and arrests.

WATCH | RCMP make arrests over Coastal GasLink pipeline: RCMP arrests protesters at Wet'suwet'en blockade | Duration 1:44



LNG is often referred to as "clean" because burning it for fuel causes fewer emissions than coal or oil — but that claim is disputed by some analysts because of the energy and destruction it takes to produce.

One of the known impacts of fracking is an increase in earthquakes , which have been felt with increasing frequency in B.C.'s Peace River region in recent years.

Critics also point out ramping up LNG production would sharply increase the amount of emissions from natural gas production in British Columbia.

WATCH | Is LNG an example of greenwashing? Canada’s clean LNG pitch — and why not everyone is buying it | Duration closed caption 7:37



Environmentalists argue that reducing emissions carries more urgency in the wake of a federal report warning Canadians to prepare for a future that's 5 C hotter — which will lead to the disappearance of glaciers in western Canada and longer, more intense summer droughts, among other impacts.

Political priority

Still, the project has been identified as one of national importance under Carney, and has support from both the B.C. NDP and B.C. Conservative Party — who have each pledged to ramp up LNG production should they form government following the Oct. 24 election.

On the campaign trail Monday, B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson announced his plan to make B.C. an "energy superpower," promising to cut red tape in order to triple LNG production by 2035.

WATCH | Haisla Nation Chief Councillor Maureen Nyce on LNG: What impact will LNG Canada’s Phase 2 project have on local First Nations communities? | Duration closed caption 5:37



In response, the B.C. NDP argued the plan wasn't ambitious enough, and said it already has plans to have B.C. outpace Doerkson's projections.

The B.C. Greens, meanwhile, have called for a moratorium on LNG expansion, citing environmental risks and concerns about Indigenous rights, further saying that fast-tracking projects is eroding oversight and accountability.

World.title: Berlin Marathon winner limped to finish line after rupturing Achilles tendon chasing world mark
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Berlin Marathon winner Tigst Assefa "completely destroyed" her right Achilles tendon trying to regain her world record.

Assefa was on well on course to beat Ruth Chepng'etich's world record with two kilometres remaining in Sunday's race when she suddenly began limping with what appeared to be cramps. She grimaced and kept running in visible pain before ultimately finishing 68 seconds behind Chepng'etich's mark of two hours nine minutes 56 seconds from Chicago in 2024.

It transpired she Assefa suffered a "complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon," her representative Gianni Demadonna told The Associated Press on Tuesday.

Demadonna said the Ethiopian runner had been in pain from the 31st kilometre but decided to continue running before the injury struck at the 40K mark.

"She was no longer able to run, because when she was going to put her foot on the ground she had no power," Demadonna said of the issue at the 40 km mark. "She completely destroyed the tendon at the end, because running without the tendon — I mean the last 500 metres maybe she ran without the tendon, you know, only with the heel, so that was a disaster because maybe [if] she had stopped, [it] was not so bad, but she ran two kilometres with the problem."

The 29-year-old Assefa still ran the third fastest time ever in 2:11:04. It's her third victory in Berlin after 2022 and 2023, but she had been pushing for another world record after her record time of 2:11:53 in 2023.

Chepng'etich lowered that mark by nearly two minutes the following year but was banned for three years in 2025 after admitting a doping violation. The Kenyan runner's record still stands.

Assefa was on course to smash Chepng'etich's record on Sunday.

"She was on to run 2:09:30, 2:09:40, so that was the goal, and she still had eight minutes [to run] the last 2.2 kilometers. That is amazing," Demadonna said.

Assefa collapsed after crossing the line and was attended to by a medic as well as compatriot and marathon great Haile Gebrselassie, among others. She skipped the post-race formalities and was flown to Munich before undergoing what Demadonna called "very complex surgery" on her ankle on Monday at a hospital in Murnau, a town near the Austrian border southwest of Munich.

Demadonna, who was on his way back home to Italy after leaving Assefa in the hospital, said she will see another doctor in Munich on Thursday to see how the surgery went and to start her rehabilitation. He said she will need to use crutches for around six weeks by which time she will have started exercises for movement of the tendon.

"After starting walking and bicycle, maybe [she can] start running in three months, so I think seven months to compete in another marathon, maybe London Marathon 2027 at the end of April, but difficult to say now," Demadonna said. "We have to stay patient and see what the doctor will say."

He added that Assefa "is very sad, but what can we do? She knows that it's a long way to recover but the doctor said, ‘Don't worry, you can recover.' So we will see."

World.title: 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide is caused by infections, study suggests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For many people, sun exposure, smoking and family history are the first thoughts that come to mind regarding cancer risk factors. While infections are rarely high on the list, new research shows one in eight cancers worldwide are actually caused by them.

These viruses, bacteria and other microbes are the focus of a new paper published Monday in The Lancet Oncology that linked an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 — 12 per cent of all new cases — to these infectious agents.

A team of researchers at The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), an arm of the World Health Organization, conducted the study. They found the largest number of cancer cases attributed to infections globally were caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which can increase the risk of stomach cancer and accounted for 760,000 cases, predominantly in eastern Asia.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) followed close behind. HPV, which causes 100 per cent of cervical cancer cases and also anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and some head and neck cancers, accounted for nearly 750,000 new cases globally, with high rates in sub-Saharan Africa. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) were also linked to a significant number of liver cancer cases.

For the first time, researchers linked even more cancers to infections, expanding their list to include 16 additional ones.

Gary Clifford, a cancer epidemiologist and study co-author based in Lyon, France, said the science has advanced significantly.

"There's been new infectious agents identified in this time as being cancer-causing, and even the infectious agents that we knew about in the past, the evidence has increased about the number of different cancers that they can cause," he said.

Some of those new infectious agents included HIV and its link to cervical cancer, and a very rare virus called Merkel cell polyomavirus that can lead to an aggressive form of skin cancer.

To come up with numbers, researchers first examined which infections cause cancer, then calculated what fraction of these cancers can be linked to specific infections and applied those calculations to global databases of new cancer cases.

Another significant shift is the recognition of the role of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV was linked to about 260,000 cases globally in 2024, and can lead to nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers and Hodgkin's lymphoma.

"That's quite a big burden of cancer caused by Epstein-Barr virus that was not counted in the past, but is now recognized," Clifford said.

Epstein-Barr virus is also a key risk factor in developing multiple sclerosis , and unlike some of the other infections that have vaccines or antibiotic treatments, there are no available tools to fight against it.

"The fact that we're seeing Epstein-Barr has caused all these chronic diseases — it's increasingly becoming a target that people need to focus on for prevention," he said.

The global report highlights vast regional differences, mostly driven by historical disparities, researchers said. High-income countries that established cancer screening and vaccination programs over the last few decades are doing much better compared to lower- and medium-resourced countries where access to prevention and treatment is limited.

"We really still have a lot of work to do implementing things that we know work and we've known for a long time but haven't really made it into all populations in the world," Clifford said.

In North America, the burden of cancer-causing infections is much lower, but H. pylori and HPV are the most common sources.

Infections causing cancer in Canada

In Canada, according to a 2019 study , the rate of cancers attributable to infections was estimated to be at four per cent. Karena Volesky, an epidemiologist in Montreal, led the Canadian research team while at McGill University.

"It tells us how important each of the 12 infections are," Volesky said of the new global numbers.

While there is a lower prevalence of these forms of infections in Canada, her study estimated these infections lead to more than 7,000 cancer diagnoses each year.

WATCH | HPV vaccination urged: Doctors urge Canadians to get HPV vaccine to prevent cervical cancer | Duration closed caption 2:06 Doctors say Canada is facing a silent health crisis of HPV-related cervical cancer that could be prevented if more people got vaccinated against human papillomavirus, the virus that can cause the disease.

"HPV is certainly an infection that we're keeping an eye on in Canada," said Elizabeth Holmes, the director of health policy at the Canadian Cancer Society.

Holmes said cervical cancer rates had been steadily declining in Canada due to robust childhood vaccination programs, but plateaued last year.

"That's certainly a concern — that we might not meet our goal of elimination of cervical cancer by 2040 unless those rates start to decline again," she said.

Human papillomavirus is transmitted through sexual contact, but the HPV vaccine protects against the most common forms of infection that can cause cancer.

Canada's cervical cancer elimination plan aims to increase vaccination rates to 90 per cent, increase screening rates to 90 per cent and ensure timely followup care after screening.

"Right now, only about five provinces are above 80 per cent, and I think at least one is as low as 66 per cent," Holmes said.

An at-home self-testing HPV kits in Vancouver, British Columbia in January 2024. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The stomach bacteria that can lead to cancer

The infection leading to the most cancer cases is Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium first discovered in the early 1980s that mainly leads to gastric cancers. While the research found the highest burden in eastern Asia in countries like Japan, South Korea and China, it's a problem here, too.

"It's a horrible disease to die from," said Dr. Paul Moayyedi, a leading researcher and gastroenterologist at McMaster University. About 2,000 Canadians die every year from stomach cancer.

Moayyedi wants to see a universal screening program for the bacterium, which can be detected through a blood or breath test, stool sample or endoscopy and treated with a combination of antibiotics over a two-week period.

A microscopic image showing leukemia cells in blue that contain Epstein-Barr virus using a fluorescent stain that causes affected cells to glow green under ultraviolet light. (Paul M. Feorino/CDC)

Helicobacter pylori is associated with crowded living conditions and poor sanitation in childhood. While most people with it can live a long life without any issues, if left untreated, it can cause ulcers and stomach cancer for some.

Moayyedi said stomach cancers may not be seen as high priority compared to other types of cancers, but believes screening programs for those at high risk, such as people with a family history of stomach cancers or First Nations communities, would save lives.

"In consultation with the elders of local communities it would be important to at least offer those groups screening if they would want it," he said.

World.title: Inside 'Hood 420:' Bishnoi-linked gang tied to threats against B.C. radio station
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Documents obtained by CBC News have identified a suspect in a brazen shooting and extortion campaign which took place one year ago against an outspoken Surrey, B.C., radio station.

In addition to the attack on Radio Swift 1200 AM last September, Ravinder Singh is suspected of playing an organizing role related to extortion cases in Ontario that have resulted in more than 100 charges against 17 men earlier this year.

According to Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) records, obtained through an Access to Information request, the 25-year-old belongs to Hood 420.

Hood 420 is a gang authorities claim is either directly linked to Lawrence Bishnoi, or using his name to carry out threats in multiple provinces.

The IRB issued a deportation order for organized criminality against Ravinder Singh in July after he was implicated in shootings across Canada — including one on Sept. 29, 2025, at Radio Swift 1200 AM.

A transcript of the hearing says Ravinder Singh's phone contained a note matching the threat sent to Swift 1200 AM's owner in the names of Bishnoi and gang leader Goldy Dhillon "demanding five (5) million dollars and threatening harm if demands are not met."

Documents raise questions about inmate escape

Ravinder Singh's detention and admissibility hearings provide new insight into major extortion investigations in Ontario, Alberta and B.C. — most notably a mass crackdown by Peel Regional Police last May on a group facing 106 charges connected to 24 incidents.

While police had previously linked those extortions to a group called For Brothers, the IRB documents claim Singh "was part of the Bishnoi Gang or a closely tied subgroup under the name Hood 420 and that he and a number of other individuals were involved in criminal activity."

Jagdeep Singh escaped custody after contracted guards for the CBSA took him to hospital. He allegedly complained that he was suffering subtance abuse withdrawal symptoms. (RCMP)

The documents also raise questions about the November 2025 escape of Ravinder Singh's alleged accomplice in another set of extortions — Jagdeep Singh, a 24-year-old still wanted on a Canada wide-warrant in connection with multiple shootings in Surrey and northern Alberta.

The Canada Border Services Agency previously said only that Jagdeep Singh escaped from Rockyview Hospital in Calgary while undergoing medical assessment.

But the transcripts of Ravinder Singh's hearing suggest Jagdeep Singh complained of drug withdrawal to give the slip to the contracted guards charged with keeping him in custody while at hospital.

The escape was mentioned during Ravinder Singh's admissibility hearing because — despite having previously told the CBSA he had no drug issues — Ravinder Singh also started displaying substance withdrawal symptoms when he was arrested.

He told CBSA officers he "uses black tar heroin or opium daily."

A lawyer for the Ministry of Public Safety told the IRB Ravinder Singh "was transported to the hospital and it should also be noted that this is the exact same scenario that resulted in the escape of his friend Mr. Jagdeep Singh from CBSA custody."

According to the documents, Ravinder Singh was treated with suboxone and ultimately released back into immigration custody, where he was referred for ongoing medical treatment.

In a statement, the CBSA told CBC News the agency is "conducting a full review" of Jagdeep Singh's escape.

"It is standard practice for the CBSA to use contracted guards to maintain custody and control of detained individuals 24 hours per day, seven days per week. The guards keep individuals safe and secure through regular observation, monitoring, engagement, and intervention," the CBSA statement said.

"Guards are also responsible for transporting individuals, including their luggage and personal effects, to and from various locations as required. All other aspects of detention operations are handled by CBSA officials."

'Get rid of them'

Ravinder Singh has been charged with weapons offences in Alberta and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence of discharging a firearm in connection with the Ontario cases, but has never been charged in the Swift 1200 AM shootings.

The IRB documents claim representatives of the Ministry of Public Safety and the Crown have discussed staying criminal charges against Singh so he can be removed from Canada.

Jinny Sims is a host at Radio Swift 1200 AM, which was the target of extortion-related attacks last year. Ravinder Singh is suspected of sending a note on behalf of the Bishnoi gang demanding payment. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

But a spokesperson for the Canada Border Services Agency told CBC News the charges against Singh are still outstanding.

Ravinder Singh represented himself at the immigration proceedings, but declined to respond to the allegations against him.

"My father back home is very sick and I want to go as soon as possible. I want to see him before anything bad happens," he told the tribunal at one point.

"I do want to give a statement, but nobody is going to believe on my statement. So, it's okay. I don't want to make any statement."

WATCH | Radio station hit by gunfire: Surrey radio station hit by gunfire amid extortion threats targeting South Asian community | Duration closed caption 2:08

Swift 1200 AM host Jinny Sims says she thinks he should be deported — the sooner the better.

"I used to say, 'No, they should pursue the charges.' [But now] I think if there's a quicker way to get rid of them — get rid of them," says Sims, who has served for the provincial and federal NDP as both a member of B.C.'s Legislative Assembly and an MP.

"This extortion business is destroying our community. It has created such big fear that's it's only when you're going to see these deportations — and I'm not saying just pick up anybody and deport them — but where you've got strong evidence then deport them, and they won't be here recruiting people while they're waiting for a trial."

Known by the alias 'Coach'

Ravinder Singh came to Canada in August 2019 on a study permit.

He later obtained a work permit — which expired last January — for employment at a Surrey-based wall and ceiling company.

Bullet holes are seen in the glass at Radio Swift 1200 AM in May. The station was the subject of an extortion attack allegedly tied to Ravinder Singh, a suspect who faces deportation for organized criminality. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

An Ontario Provincial Police intelligence analyst who testified at Ravinder Singh's admissibility hearing said Singh first came to police attention in fall 2025 after a series of shootings at residences and businesses in Caledon and Brampton, Ont.

"Extortion threats were received by the victim, claiming affiliation to the Bishnoi gang, and there was a demand for finances," the analyst testified.

"Witness statement had provided aliases for involved members. Initially, Mr. Singh was known by the alias 'Coach.' And through investigation, his true identity was determined."

According to the IRB transcripts, police began to make those connections after RCMP arrested Ravinder Singh in Red Deer in November — when he met Jagdeep Singh, who was then a suspect in shootings targeting a tire shop owner in Parkland, about 75 km west of Edmonton.

The attackers shot up a home where seven people were present, later sending a video of the incidents and demanding $2 million.

Ravinder Singh allegedly showed up to meet Jagdeep Singh in a Dodge Challenger, where police found a gun linked to seven extortion-related shootings and a phone that tied him to many more.

'Locations and instructions'

Police examined Ravinder Singh's phone, which is how they discovered that his alleged accomplices knew him by the nickname "Coach."

Investigators allegedly found messages sent to Jagdeep Singh with information about the targets of the Alberta shootings.

Iqbal Singh Bhagria, left, and Ravinder Singh are charged in connection with extortion-related incidents in Caledon and Brampton last fall. Singh is also a suspect in a shooting at Radio Swift 1200 AM. (Peel Regional Police)

And they found WhatsApp messages sent to Iqbal Singh Bhagria, the suspect charged in connection with the extortion shootings in Caledon and Brampton.

"This shows Mr. Ravinder sending locations and instructions that align with the shooting events that occurred," a lawyer for the Ministry of Public Safety claimed.

"And it's also noted that these are the same locations and instructions that were found in Iqbal Bhagria's phone when he was also arrested."

Armed with that evidence, authorities in Edmonton arrested Ravinder Singh a second time in February for immigration and traffic safety warrants.

He was driving a grey Toyota Camry when police picked him up — a vehicle allegedly linked, through distinctive damage and CCTV footage, to a series of Surrey extortion cases which took place in the fall of 2025.

The vehicle was also identified as a suspect vehicle in the Swift 1200 AM shooting.

Gang called 'Hood 420'

Ravinder Singh's admissibility hearing included testimony from RCMP Const. Mohamed El Krich, the primary investigator for the Alberta extortion shootings — which also saw Molotov cocktails thrown at a business.

El Krich said the victim in that case received messages citing Bishnoi gang member Goldy Dhillon and threatening, "Pay us or your family is going to find you in a body bag," or, "If we don't find you today, we'll find you tomorrow."

Lawrence Bishnoi, seen here on the right in 2023, has been behind bars in India since 2015, but authorities say he has built a global terror network. A police witness at Ravinder Singh's immigration proceedings said he believed Singh's Hood 420 gang was linked to Bishnoi. (Rahul Singh/ANI/Reuters)

The RCMP officer said Ravinder Singh's phone contained the "extortion script" sent to Swift 1200 AM Radio, as well as evidence of him searching the addresses of extortion victims and directions for shooters "such as where to stand or where to change the vehicle licence plates."

El Krich also drew the connection between Ravinder Singh and the group known as Hood 420.

"There is content in his phone, indicating that he was a member of this group, including photos of ammunition that was laid out to spell Hood 420, as well as photos of an event where bottle service was an option and they had the group name advertised on the bottle service delivery," El Krich said.

Although associated with marijuana in Canada, the number 420 has a particular meaning in Indian criminal subculture — a reference to Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code which concerns "cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property."

A lawyer for the Ministry of Public Safety asked El Krich if Hood 420 is affiliated with Lawrence Bishnoi, the imprisoned gang leader who authorities say has built a global network from an Indian jail cell.

"Considering that the extortion demands claim affiliation to these criminal organisations, I think that it's very likely there is a connection," El Krich replied.

'What's the point?'

Ravinder Singh has been in immigration detention since February.

RCMP in Alberta have since announced charges against Ravinder Singh and Jagdeep Singh in connection with the Parkland shootings, and B.C.'s provincial Extortion Task Force announced charges against Jagdeep Singh and two others for shootings in Surrey.

And in May, Peel Police's Extortion Task Force included Ravinder Singh and Iqbal Singh Bhagria's names in a roundup of 17 individuals accused of " a [co-ordinated] campaign of intimidation, threats, and escalating violence used to extort local businesses."

A spokesperson for the Peel Police told CBC News the charges remain pending before the courts.

"However, our investigations remain active," Peel Police said in a statement.

"And we anticipate making additional arrests and laying further charges in the near future."

Sims, a host at Swift 1200 AM, points to a bullet hole in the radio studio in May after the extortion-linked attack the previous fall. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

Swift 1200 AM host Sims says that, while recent reports of extortion cases appear to have slowed down, the South Asian community is still very afraid.

She called on police and the CBSA to provide more information.

"You want the victims to keep doing all this stuff, give you everything they do, but then there is silence for weeks and months," she said.

"They need to get updates, and they need to know that you're doing something. Otherwise people are not going to give you names. They're going to say 'What's the point? Nothing happens.'"

World.title: What no one told me about the land that would become my home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is the experience of Ashish Barua, who lives in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.

My daughter came home from summer camp with a piece of art — six little flowers, dot-painted in red and yellow. She set it on the dining table like she'd been waiting all day to show us.

"It's Métis beadwork. Do you know there's a story behind it?" she asked, clearly proud of herself.

I was curious. She told me Métis hunters used to bead their gloves in patterns unique to their own family. During a hunt, a man might drop his glove beside an animal he'd killed as a gauntlet to prove it was his. Later, his family would spot the pattern and know it was theirs.

I wasn't sure she had it right. I looked it up that night, half expecting she'd mixed up some detail.

She hadn't.

When Barua's daughter brought home artwork and told him more about Indigenous history, he was struck by how little he had learned on this topic as a newcomer to Canada. (Submitted by Ashish Barua)

My 10-year-old taught me that. I'd lived in Saskatchewan for a couple years after moving to Canada in 2024 — Saskatoon first, then Regina, now Prince Albert. But I'd never once heard this.

I was proud she'd learned about Indigenous history at school and at camp. But it also bothered me a little. Why hadn't anyone taught this history to us, the adults?

Before that evening, my knowledge of Indigenous Peoples in Canada was sparse, and not always kind. I'd absorbed local stereotypes the way you do when you're new somewhere — a comment here, a headline there, a passing remark nobody bothered to explain.

I never sat down and decided to believe any descriptions of Indigenous people in particular. Those viewpoints just settled in, quietly, the way secondhand furniture ends up in a house nobody remembers buying. I think a lot of newcomers arrive carrying some version of this reality. Nobody hands it to you on purpose. It just comes with the move.

Barua has lived in Canada for a couple of years, but only began learning more about Indigenous history since moving to Prince Albert, Sask. (Lisa Risom/CBC)

Various settlement services we used had covered the basics of making a move: getting a health card, a lease, a driver's licence and teaching how to survive a winter that hits faster and harder than anything I'd ever known. But nobody mentioned I'd moved onto treaty land.

Nobody said this year marks 150 years since Treaty 6 was signed. Nobody told me Prince Albert is Métis homeland too, with its own history running under the one I could see.

So I looked into that history myself, signing up for a course called Advancing Reconciliation that was offered through the First Nations University of Canada.

I expected something dry, but it wasn't. I learned about the treaties, what the Crown promised, and what still hasn't been delivered to Indigenous Peoples. I learned how much of what I thought I knew about Indigenous people was wrong or missing context.

I come from Bangladesh, a country that was under British rule for nearly 200 years, and then under Pakistan's rule for around 24 years. I'd read that history my whole life without ever once piecing it together. My country had faced colonization, just as Indigenous People did, but I'd never actually connected those two things before.

None of this was ever hidden. This history was all just sitting there. What was missing wasn't the information. It was someone putting it in front of me early on and saying, "This matters. You should know it."

My daughter went to a powwow this year through her school. I didn't go. At the time, it barely registered, just another school thing, another event. I couldn't have told you why it mattered.

Barua and his daughter check out a sculpture called Passage Home, which was made to commemorate the signing of Treaty 6 in 1876. (Submitted by Ashish Barua)

But a few weeks ago, I stood in front of Passage Home, the new bronze sculpture down by the Saskatchewan river in Prince Albert. It's shaped like a travois, the kind once pulled by dogs and horses across the plains, and it's meant to symbolize carrying home the Indigenous children who never made it back from residential schools. The city unveiled it in August to mark the 150th anniversary of Treaty 6.

A year ago, I might have walked past it.

Now I stood there longer than I meant to. Inside the sculpture, there are small shoes, standing in for the children who never made it home. I thought about a glove dropped beside a fallen animal, so a family could find their way to it. I thought about a course I'd almost skipped, a powwow I didn't go to.

Standing there, it struck me plainly. You can't really make a home somewhere until you understand the history behind it. And no one was going to hand me that understanding; I had to go find it myself.

I hope the next person who moves to Canada to learn that sooner than I did.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared.

ShinyHunters c laimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI last Tuesday — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — and gave the law enforcement agency one week to rescind an ⁠unflattering statement about the group.

With the deadline approaching, a ShinyHunters representative sent CBC News a statement Monday saying they were never planning to release the sensitive data, adding that the media and the public have "made many false assumptions and wild speculations."

The group has been linked to dozens of cyberattacks targeting large companies and institutions. ShinyHunters typically demand ransom payments in exchange for not releasing sensitive data, but they have been adamant that was not their intention in this case.

Campaign to 'combat disinformation'

ShinyHunters denied asking the FBI for a ransom, but acknowledged "past operations" could leave them open to misinterpretation.

"The reason why we have stated multiple times that this is not extortion is because since the very beginning we had made our decision that we would never publish this data. We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to," the statement said in part.

The group told CBC News that their actions against the FBI were part of a campaign to "combat disinformation" about their tactics.

"If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would've never been this widespread. We'd have been ignored and disregarded. However, now everyone knows what the issue is and what we are doing."

ShinyHunters took issue with an FBI report from May that said, among other things, the group is known to threaten family members of its targets and threaten to release embarrassing or compromising images of its victims.

ShinyHunters denied ever using those tactics and released a statement following last Tuesday's data breach giving the FBI one week to remove or "correct" the report.

The group shared a 5,000-line spreadsheet of breached FBI data with some journalists, which it said represented only a small piece of its claimed two- to three-terabyte trove.

The sample included names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for what it claimed were thousands of FBI employees.

When CBC News asked ShinyHunters on Monday whether they have taken any steps to ensure the shared data isn't leaked by other sources, the representative said they "cannot guarantee" what will happen to those samples, "because that is out of our control and certain journalists violated our trust."

WATCH | ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for a Canvas hack in May: There's a data breach at Canadian schools. What do we know? | Duration closed caption 7:18 Canvas, a program used by postsecondary schools across Canada, has been hit by hackers. A group called ShinyHunters is claiming responsibility — and asking for a ransom. Emsisoft threat intelligence analyst Luke Connolly lays out what we know.

'Can't trust them,' researcher says

Ian Lin, an ethical hacker and head of research and development at Toronto-based cybersecurity company Packetlabs, says that's concerning.

He says he's seen "a number of researchers" claiming online to have obtained the data, in addition to journalists.

"There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," Lin told CBC News.

The hack, which one former FBI operative called a "foreign intelligence service goldmine," has raised concerns about the safety of the agency's employees.

The New York Times reported Monday that the FBI sent out a staff memo acknowledging employees had personal information stolen in a cybersecurity incident, and instructing them to remain vigilant at home and at work and report any unsolicited contacts or threats.

Lin says he does not have high hopes ShinyHunters will keep their word, saying it's common for criminal hacking groups to renege on their promises or to use the same set of data as leverage multiple times.

"Why they did this, I think was for attention. But you still can't trust them to keep safe your data. Because now this is leverage over the law enforcement and FBI. And at any moment they could choose to use this data for their own additional purposes," he said.

"The FBI and law enforcement should all still remain vigilant. There should be massive lessons learned from the FBI side."
