World.title: President Fernández Wants Private Jets Landing in Quepos
World.content:
President Laura Fernández said yesterday that her government wants private jets landing in Quepos, announcing that a tender is already underway for a ₡2.1 billion (about $4.5 million) airfield project on the Central Pacific coast. Fernández made the announcement in Londres de Quepos at the opening of a new bridge over the Naranjo River, the first stop on a three-day tour of Puntarenas province. She said she was certain the investment would lift tourism in the area enormously.

The president told residents she had not come to offer empty promises, adding that the project was already out to bid and paid for with public funds. She presented it as a way to bring better jobs to the canton so young people would not have to move to San José to build a future.

Public Works and Transport Minister Efraín Zeledón laid out the scope. According to the minister, the ₡2.1 billion covers a new apron for private aviation at the existing La Managua aerodrome, with space for up to nine aircraft and one helicopter. A contract for a new passenger terminal would follow, Zeledón said, and total planned investment at the aerodrome would exceed ₡5 billion (nearly $11 million). A new terminal, improved access and an apron for La Managua have appeared in government budget planning for several years.

La Managua is the small airstrip that serves Quepos and Manuel Antonio, one of the busiest beach destinations, and today handles mostly light aircraft on domestic routes. Travelers heading to the area otherwise rely on the main highway to the Central Pacific or on short domestic flights from San José.

The push for private aviation comes as higher-end investment reaches the area, including a luxury resort and residences project next to Manuel Antonio National Park. The Naranjo River bridge that served as the backdrop for the announcement is a 95-meter (312-foot) modular structure that cost ₡466.5 million (about $1 million). It replaces an old suspension bridge that had to be closed to vehicles because of the risk of accidents.

That closure forced families in communities such as Lourdes and Villa Nueva to travel longer distances to reach medical services, schools and jobs. Zeledón said the new crossing will benefit more than 35,000 people in the area. Quepos Mayor Patricia Bolaños Murillo said the bridge serves not only Londres and Naranjito but also connects the canton with Dota and Tarrazú.

Zeledón said the bridge is one of 35 road and bridge projects in the region under PROERI, the government’s emergency program to rebuild infrastructure to a more resilient standard, with more than $70 million committed in the area. He also announced four-year road maintenance contracts for corridors along the Pacific.

Fernández announced a further ₡520 million (about $1.1 million) for work on the Savegre River bridge, which she said had reached the end of its useful life. She also told local fishers that a dredge would arrive in November to clear the Quepos estuary and the fishing channels they depend on. The government is studying an expansion of the offshore areas where Pacific fishers may work as El Niño weighs on their catches, she said.

The stop carried personal meaning for the president, who was born in Puntarenas. Londres is her husband’s hometown, and the municipality named him a favorite son of Quepos during the ceremony. The Puntarenas tour runs through Wednesday and includes a Cabinet session. No date has been announced for awarding the airfield contract or starting construction.

World.title: Keylor Navas Returns as Bryan Ruiz Names First Costa Rica Squad
World.content:
Keylor Navas is back with Costa Rica’s national team as interim coach Bryan Ruiz recalled the veteran goalkeeper on Monday night in his first squad list, bringing experience into a team that has lost both of its Concacaf Nations League matches and now risks relegation from the competition’s top tier.

Ruiz, who replaced the fired Fernando Batista yesterday, also called up Puebla defender Juan Pablo Vargas and Alajuelense midfielders Celso Borges and Roan Wilson. The Costa Rican Football Federation released the list late Monday, after Navas had arrived in the country to join the squad.

Three players named by Batista were left out. Saprissa’s Sebastián Padilla and Mathías Elizondo and Cartaginés midfielder Gianmauro Morera do not appear on the new list, which replaces the squad Batista announced before his dismissal. The changes come with almost no time to prepare. Costa Rica visits Nicaragua on Thursday, Oct. 1, at 8 p.m. at the National Stadium in Managua, then hosts Haiti on Sunday, Oct. 4, at 6 p.m. at Ricardo Saprissa Stadium in Tibás.

La Sele opened the group stage with a 4-3 home loss to Curaçao after leading 3-0 at halftime, then fell 2-0 to Haiti in Kingston, Jamaica. Those results left Costa Rica without a point, level with Nicaragua, which lost 6-1 to Curaçao on Sunday. Curaçao, Haiti and the Dominican Republic each have six points after two rounds. The bottom two teams in each of League A’s two groups drop to League B, which turns Thursday’s match in Managua into a direct meeting between the two teams now sitting in the relegation places.

Navas, 39, is Costa Rica’s most decorated player, a three-time Champions League winner with Real Madrid who still plays at a high level in Mexico. He helped Pumas reach the Liga MX final in May, and his return gives Ruiz an experienced presence behind a defense that conceded six goals in the first two matches.

Borges and Wilson bring a different kind of familiarity. Both play for Alajuelense, where Ruiz has coached the under-20 team and briefly took charge of the senior side. Wílmer López and Edson Soto will serve as his assistants. The full group, including the new additions, trains together for the first time on Tuesday. Ruiz held his first session with the team on Monday, a recovery workout following the loss in Jamaica.

Nicaragua will be without its leading attacker, Jaime Moreno, who is suspended after picking up a second yellow card of the competition against Curaçao. The Nicaraguan federation has also launched a ticket giveaway promotion to fill the stadium in Managua. The stakes extend beyond this window, because Concacaf ties direct qualification for the 2027 Gold Cup to Nations League results.

Costa Rica has not won in eight matches, and its last victory came against Nicaragua in World Cup qualifying on Oct. 13, 2025. Ruiz’s first test comes Thursday night against the last team La Sele beat.

World.title: Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska’s Comeback Gains Momentum in São Paulo
World.content:
Nadia Podoroska’s return to professional tennis has moved well beyond simply testing whether her body could handle competition again. Six months after returning from a 14-month injury layoff, the 29-year-old Argentine reached the first WTA Tour final of her career at the São Paulo Open, a result that lifted her 117 places in the rankings and provided the clearest sign yet that the former Roland Garros semifinalist is again becoming a factor on the women’s tour.

Podoroska entered the WTA 250 event ranked No. 317 and unseeded, but worked her way through the draw before producing the biggest result of her week in the semifinals. She defeated former world No. 2 Paula Badosa 6-3, 6-4, ending an 0-4 career record in WTA Tour semifinals and becoming the first Argentine woman to reach a tour-level singles final since Paula Ormaechea in Bogotá in 2013.

The title ultimately went to Spain’s Kaitlin Quevedo. After Podoroska took the opening set, the 20-year-old Spaniard rallied for a 4-6, 6-4, 6-2 victory in two hours and eight minutes to claim her first WTA title. The final was played Monday, after rain prevented its completion on Sunday. For Podoroska, however, reaching the final may have carried greater significance than the result itself.

She climbed from No. 317 to No. 200 following São Paulo, continuing a remarkable ranking recovery for a player who began the season outside the Top 1,000 and returned to competition without a ranking after more than a year away. Podoroska had not played for 440 days when she returned earlier this year. Her absence began with a hip problem and was complicated by a shoulder injury, leaving her uncertain whether she would play professionally again. During her recovery, she acknowledged that she had seriously considered retirement.

Her comeback began quietly in Argentina before gathering momentum in Europe. In April, Podoroska returned to the rankings after winning an ITF W15 tournament in Madrid, where she came through qualifying and played eight matches during the week. She followed that with a W35 title in San Gregorio in June.

The results became increasingly significant as the summer progressed. At the U.S. Open, Podoroska used a protected ranking to enter the main draw and defeated Switzerland’s Simona Waltert in the first round. It was her first Grand Slam main-draw victory since the 2024 Australian Open and another important step in a comeback that initially centered more on staying healthy than chasing rankings.

São Paulo changed the scale of the conversation. Podoroska was no longer collecting matches at lower-level tournaments. She was beating established WTA players and playing for a tour-level championship.

That carries particular weight because of where she has been before. Podoroska produced one of the biggest breakthroughs in Argentine tennis in recent years when she came through qualifying to reach the 2020 Roland Garros semifinals, defeating then-world No. 5 Elina Svitolina along the way. She eventually reached a career-high ranking of No. 36 in July 2021.

Injuries repeatedly interrupted the seasons that followed, including another lengthy absence after that French Open run. Now the ranking is moving quickly in the other direction. Podoroska started 2026 around No. 1,200, climbed to No. 574 by the end of June and reached No. 317 shortly before São Paulo. Her run to the final pushed her back to No. 200.

A return to the Top 100 remains a considerable climb, but it is no longer a distant target. More importantly, Podoroska has demonstrated that she can again compete with players much higher in the rankings. After spending much of the past two years fighting simply to stay on the court, São Paulo offered something different: evidence that the Argentine’s comeback may be turning into a genuine second chapter of her career.

World.title: Costa Rica Turns to Bryan Ruiz After Firing Fernando Batista
World.content:
Former Costa Rica captain Bryan Ruiz will take temporary charge of the national team after the Costa Rican Football Federation fired Argentine coach Fernando Batista following a disastrous start to the Concacaf Nations League. The federation announced today that Batista and his coaching staff had been removed and that Ruiz would lead La Sele for its two remaining Nations League group matches. Costa Rica travels to Managua to face Nicaragua on Thursday, October 1, before returning home to play Haiti at Ricardo Saprissa Stadium on Sunday, October 4.

The move comes after Costa Rica lost its opening two matches of the competition, falling 4-3 at home to Curaçao on Thursday and then losing 2-0 to Haiti in Kingston, Jamaica, on Sunday. Those defeats ended Batista’s short and unsuccessful spell in charge. He coached Costa Rica in six matches without recording a victory, finishing with one draw and five losses. The team scored four goals and conceded 19 during that stretch.

Batista had been brought in earlier this year as Costa Rica attempted to rebuild following its failure to qualify for the 2026 World Cup. But the results never arrived, and the back-to-back Nations League defeats ultimately convinced federation officials to make another coaching change.

Ruiz, one of the best-known players in Costa Rican soccer history, now steps into the job with only a few days to prepare for Nicaragua. The former national team captain played a central role in Costa Rica’s historic run to the quarterfinals of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, scoring the winning goal against Italy and another against Greece in the Round of 16.

His coaching experience remains limited, although he recently got an early taste of managing at the senior level with Liga Deportiva Alajuelense. Ruiz took temporary control of the club following the departure of Ismael Rescalvo and won both matches he coached before returning to his previous role with Alajuelense’s under-20 team.

The federation has made clear that Ruiz’s appointment with the national team is also temporary. He will oversee the matches against Nicaragua and Haiti before officials begin the process of choosing a permanent coach for the road toward the 2030 World Cup.The immediate challenge is stopping one of Costa Rica’s worst runs in recent memory.

La Sele has now gone 350 days without a victory. Its last win came against Nicaragua on October 13, 2025, during World Cup qualifying. Since then, Costa Rica has gone eight consecutive matches without winning, a stretch that has included qualifiers, friendlies and Nations League games.

That makes Thursday’s match particularly significant. Ruiz’s first game in charge will come against the same opponent Costa Rica defeated the last time it celebrated a victory. Kickoff against Nicaragua is scheduled for 8 p.m. Costa Rica time at the National Stadium in Managua. Ruiz will then make his home coaching debut three days later when La Sele faces Haiti at 6 p.m. at Ricardo Saprissa Stadium.

World.title: Briceño tells UN Belize stands with Cuba, calls for end to US blockade
World.content:
Briceño tells UN Belize stands with Cuba, calls for end to US blockade

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño has renewed Belize’s call for the United States economic blockade against Cuba to be lifted, saying the restrictions continue to place severe pressure on the Cuban economy.

Briceño made the remarks during Belize’s address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The Prime Minister said Belize stands with Cuba and argued that the longstanding economic restrictions, compounded by limits affecting fuel supplies, have worsened conditions on the island.

Briceño described the situation as unnecessary and unjustified.

He also repeated Belize’s call for Cuba to be removed from the United States list of State Sponsors of Terrorism.

The issue remains highly contested internationally. Cuba and a number of governments argue that the US measures have harmed access to financing, fuel, trade and essential goods, while US policy has historically cited national security, foreign policy and human rights concerns in maintaining sanctions.

The United Nations General Assembly has repeatedly debated the economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba, with many member states calling for its removal.

Briceño used his UN appearance to reaffirm Belize’s longstanding diplomatic support for Cuba at a time when the island continues to face serious economic and energy challenges.

World.title: Communities step up to protect the Belize River
World.content:
Communities step up to protect the Belize River

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Friends for Conservation and Development (FCD) is working with communities along the Belize River to help keep watch over its health.

This weekend, FCD met with community leaders and representatives from Santa Familia, Spanish Lookout, Esperanza, Ontario, Roaring Creek and More Tomorrow.

The meeting focused on ways residents can take a more proactive role in monitoring the health and condition of the river.

The effort is part of the GEF6 project, Integrated Management of Production Landscapes to Deliver Multiple Global Environmental Benefits.

World.title: Three ranger recruits pass Chiquibul field test
World.content:
Three ranger recruits pass Chiquibul field test

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Three ranger recruits have successfully completed their field test in the Chiquibul National Park.

Friends for Conservation and Development (FCD) says the recruits were tested on patrolling, navigation, jungle survival, casualty evacuation, and jungle health and hygiene.

FCD congratulated the three and says they are expected to join the Ranger Unit in the coming weeks.

World.title: Panton questions timing of First Lady’s Guatemala visit
World.content:
Panton questions timing of First Lady’s Guatemala visit

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Opposition Leader Tracy Panton is questioning the timing of First Lady Rossana Briceño’s recent official visit to Guatemala.

In a statement titled “PM Briceño unhinged!?!”, Panton said Belizeans listened with grave concern as Prime Minister John Briceño responded sharply to a reporter’s question about the trip.

Panton said the visit deserves scrutiny given Belize’s recent statements at the UN General Assembly on rising tensions with Guatemala, and as the country prepares for oral arguments at the International Court of Justice.

She stressed that the question is not an attack on Mrs. Briceño, who serves as Belize’s Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children. Panton praised her advocacy, especially for children with special needs.

“The question is about the timing of this visit,” Panton wrote.

She said Belizeans are entitled to know what the visit involved, why it happened now and what message it was meant to send.

World.title: Rising cost of living on Cabinet agenda, PM confirms
World.content:
Rising cost of living on Cabinet agenda, PM confirms

By Zoila Palma: Following comments made recently by Deputy Prime Minister Cordel Hyde in which he said “We can’t be living one way and the people another” and called for government officials, including Cabinet members, ministers and area representatives to assess their own allowances.

Prime Minister John Briceno has responded saying that cabinet will address cost of living during its meeting.

“The PUP is always a party of renewal and soul-searching. As I mentioned in the State of the Nation, how much work we have done for the people of this country, how much work have we done in trying to address the issues of the cost of living, because it’s something that we understand and that we discuss every single day. And he is in Cabinet, and he has supported all of these initiatives that we’ve done, and I can understand where he comes from,” PM Briceno said.

“Cordel represents among the poorest constituencies in the area, one of the areas where we have a lot of social problems, so I could understand him saying that. And so when we get into Cabinet, we are going to discuss it and see what more we can do, what else can be done, how can we continue renewing and innovating and energizing the party. But one thing that does not change: we are a party that is based on social justice. The minute we lose that, then we cannot be a member of the PUP,” the Prime Minister added.

World.title: Will Julius Espat stay as Police Minister? PM Briceño says Cabinet will hear first
World.content:
Will Julius Espat stay as Police Minister? PM Briceño says Cabinet will hear first

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño told reporters on Monday that when he makes his decision on who will be given the substantive police portfolio, Cabinet will hear it first.

No timeline. No name. No hints.

That leaves Espat, who currently holds the portfolio, waiting like everyone else.

The police ministry is one of the most demanding jobs in Government. It carries responsibility for public safety, crime fighting and the Belize Police Department. Whoever holds it will be under constant pressure to deliver results.

The question comes at a busy time for the Briceño administration. The Government is dealing with heightened tensions with Guatemala and preparing for the next stage of the territorial dispute at the International Court of Justice.

Until then, the speculation will continue. Will Espat be confirmed in the post, or will someone else step in?

Belizeans will have to wait for Cabinet to meet before getting an answer.

World.title: Development Finance Corporation celebrates 63 years of supporting Belizeans
World.content:
Development Finance Corporation celebrates 63 years of supporting Belizeans

By Zoila Palma: The Development Finance Corporation (DFC) celebrated its 63rd anniversary on September 27, reflecting on more than six decades of supporting the ambitions and aspirations of Belizeans across the country.

The institution marked the milestone by recognizing the employees, clients, partners, and communities that have contributed to its journey and continued role in national development.

DFC noted that its history has been shaped by employees who have dedicated decades of service and clients who have trusted the institution to help them pursue their goals.

The corporation expressed gratitude for the relationships built over the years and reaffirmed its commitment to serving Belizeans and contributing to a stronger, more prosperous future for generations to come.

The institution’s mission is to provide innovative development financial solutions that contribute to the resilient and equitable growth of Belize. Its vision is to become a leading development finance institution supported by modern digital infrastructure, strategic alliances, empowered team members, and a commitment to exceeding clients’ expectations.

DFC also highlighted the core values that guide its operations, including integrity, respect, client focus, and corporate social responsibility.

World.title: Marconi Leal Jr. celebrates dad’s cancer remission after stage 4 diagnosis
World.content:
Marconi Leal Jr. celebrates dad’s cancer remission after stage 4 diagnosis

By Zoila Palma: Minister of State in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Marconi Leal Jr., is celebrating his father, former Belize Rural North Area Representative Marconi Leal Sr., as a cancer survivor after he was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer two years ago.

In an emotional Independence Day tribute, Leal Jr. reflected on his father’s diagnosis, treatment and recovery, describing his continued presence as a blessing to their family.

Leal Jr. recalled that two years ago, while preparing for the Independence Day parade, his father was too weak to march following cancer treatments. He said the family had been devastated when doctors confirmed that Leal Sr. had stage 4 prostate cancer that had spread to the bones throughout his body. “I’ll never forget two years ago when we waited for the parade to start. Before it even started he realized he could not march because he didn’t have the energy to do it after his Cancer treatments,” Leal Jr. shared.

The Minister of State said the diagnosis came as a shock, particularly after a second medical opinion reportedly gave his father a life expectancy of no more than two years.

However, Leal Sr. refused to accept that prediction. Recalling his father’s response after being told about the prognosis, Leal Jr. said, “NEVER! ‘I feel good and I’m fine, Unu could want believe they simple doctors who just wants to make money.’” Looking back, Leal Jr. said the family now recognizes his father’s determination as an important part of a journey that has seen him continue living well beyond that initial prognosis.

Leal Jr. explained that his father underwent treatment and radiation, with the family learning over time how the treatments were helping to manage the disease.

Six months later, they received encouraging news about the response to treatment.

Today, Leal Sr. is in remission and remains active, with his son describing his recovery as remarkable given the extent of the cancer documented in medical tests and imaging. “Through all this he wanted to live. Now, he’s in remission, alive and kicking out and about every single day, proof that faith, courage, and science can share the same stage,” he said.

As the family celebrated Belize’s 2026 Independence festivities together, Leal Jr. expressed gratitude for the opportunity to stand beside his father and reflect on the values he instilled in him.

World.title: ‘We are not breaking ranks’
World.content:
TWO defence lawyers representing murder accused Andre Ruddock appeared in court on Monday as his trial continued, despite colleagues maintaining a pledge to withdraw legal services from all criminal matters islandwide in pursuit of amendments to the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022.

But according to attorney Anthony Williams, he and fellow counsel Venice Brown did not break ranks with their colleagues. Instead they had a duty to their client which had to be fulfilled.

“We want to make it very clear that we are not breaking ranks with our colleagues. Myself and Miss Brown are 150 per cent in support of our colleagues. However, there is a difference — the Jamaica Bar Association knows about it and they also sanctioned it. The difference is that when you are in a part-heard matter you can’t just go and strike like that. You have to seek the permission of your client in writing,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

“If you don’t seek the permission of your client in writing, then you can be deemed to have neglected your client and you can be sanctioned as well. Also, the court can proceed with the matter and the judge can possibly cite you for contempt of court,” Williams explained.

He added that in the absence of defence attorneys a judge may decide to proceed in a part-heard matter because lawyers are expected to be present. He said that if they don’t turn up, they do so at their own peril.

“The situation is different when you are in a part-heard matter, and the lawyer, whoever he or she is, cannot just abandon their client just like that; they have to seek the client’s permission. And in this particular case our client said, ‘Run with it.’ There are many other lawyers who are in the same position, but we have not abandoned our colleagues,” Williams stressed.

In addition to Williams and Brown, a number of attorneys showed up for their clients on Monday at the Home Circuit Court for various reasons, including that some were not in agreement with the protest action.

Essentially, the defence lawyers are arguing that the Act removes discretionary powers from judges, as it mandates a 15-year minimum sentence for an illegal gun possession conviction.

Williams’ client, Ruddock, is being tried in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner in what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual at Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion St James. Ruddock allegedly cut Gardner’s throat on the instruction of his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Smith died in a car crash in St Catherine a few days later while being transported to Kingston to be charged with the incident.

On Monday the fourth witness in the case, a police sergeant based in St James, returned to complete his testimony which he started last week.

He described the scene at the church as “evil, fluid and chaotic”.

“People were moving from one direction to the next. One body was seen close to the pool area,” the witness recalled.

He explained that members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) made their way through barbed wires to gain access to the compound of the church where three people, including Gardner and two male members of the church, lay dead.

One of the men was allegedly killed by Smith, while the police were said to have shot dead the other man who had rushed toward them with a knife. Based on the sustained gunfire and the sacrificial-type activities that were taking place at the church, the security forces had to call for adequate back-up, which included support from the military.

“The soldiers got to the barbed wire. I saw them climbing over and onto the church premises. On reaching the premises I shouted out to them. Police, accompanied by army personnel, proceeded towards a person who was kneeling behind the column at the entrance gate. I observed them accosting this person. They arrested him and carried out a search of him. The police and soldiers then forced open the big entrance gate,” the witness said.

“When they got there, the man was still in the kneeling position with white cloth over his head. He stood up and the officers searched him. When he stood up, from where I was standing [on the roof] I couldn’t see his face. I could only see the height of the person who was about 5 feet two or three inches tall. At that time there were a lot of police personnel and soldiers around this man. They took him on[to] the roadway and I couldn’t see what took place from there,” the witness said, without being able to say who the man was.

World.title: Stitchie: A legacy that connected dancehall, gospel
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie at the 2019 Sterling Gospel Music Awards

Lieutenant Stitchie’s voice may have fallen silent, but the influence of the veteran deejay — who commanded respect in both secular dancehall and gospel music spheres — is expected to continue reverberating across generations.

The veteran artiste, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at Kingston Public Hospital on Monday morning, one day shy of his 61st birthday.

The news comes less than 24 hours after his wife, Sophia Laing, confirmed that the entertainer had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment.

His passing closes a remarkable chapter in Jamaican music — one that began in dancehall and found a path to gospel.

For distinguished cultural analyst, Professor Donna Hope, Lieutenant Stitchie’s ability to remain loved across musical boundaries was rooted not only in his talent, but also in his personality that endeared him to audiences.

“Stitchie was loved because a lot of his songs were humorous. They were fun and they made people happy,” Hope said. She pointed to his enduring early hit Wear Yu Size, noting that the song was “digestible”, catchy and non-combative — qualities that helped establish his connection with listeners.

“Stitchie had an excellent career in dancehall and that followed him into gospel,” Hope continued. “I saw Mr Vegas made a post and I’m sure several others will as the news spreads because a lot of the artistes he would have came up with in that era were still close to him even though they were doing different genres.”

Entertainers and government officials took to social media to pay tribute to the deejay. Among them Prime Minister Andrew Holness, Tarrus Riley and Chevelle Franklyn (who also transitioned from dancehall to gospel).

Professor Hope shared that Stitchie’s significance extended beyond his music.

“Having a relationship with secular artistes was something Stitchie did well because he understood that it was important to minister to the sheep that ought to be brought into the fold,” she said. “This loss will be felt across genres and eras. He is a part of the industry in a way few artistes were, and so he will never be forgotten.”

Basillia Barnaby-Cuff, founder and director of Sterling Gospel Music Awards, agreed.

“I think Stitchie set a beautiful example of how you can remain an influence with people even when you’re in a different season of your life,” she said. “He was able to bridge the gap between the secular and gospel. He was still able to be on stage with secular artistes, singing gospel without compromising his walk with Christ.”

For Barnaby-Cuff, that was the essence of Stitchie’s ministry — not simply preaching to people already inside the church, but allowing his life and testimony to reach those outside it.

“It is about allowing your life to minister to those you wish will come over to Christianity,” she said.

The Sterling Gospel Music Awards family shared a particularly close connection with the artiste in his later years. A few years ago, Stitchie was honoured at the awards with the KFC Big Deal Award, an occasion Barnaby-Cuff now views with gratitude.

“I am just so happy we were able to give him his flowers while he was alive,” she said. “The gospel fraternity and we here at the Sterling Gospel Music Awards are really saddened by this news.”

Even as his health deteriorated, the organisation continued to support him, raising funds towards his care in the hope that his condition would improve.

“As the body of Christ, we are so grateful that he used the latter part of his years in ministry, and that he brought so many other persons to Christ,” she said. “He truly lived a full life and, as children of God, we don’t mourn as if we don’t have hope, and so that hope is something we hold on to and that one day we will see him again in the great resurrection.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside artistes including Papa San and Wickerman. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yu Size, followed by songs such as Natty Dread, as his distinctive delivery and ability to connect with audiences propelled him beyond Jamaica. In 1988, he secured a recording deal with Atlantic Records, marking another significant milestone in a career that was increasingly taking him onto the international stage.

But it was his decision to walk away from secular music and embrace Christianity in 1997 that would ultimately redefine his legacy.

In 2014 he published his autobiography and among his accolades was honoured with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer in 2021 for his contribution to music.

World.title: Debutants Tru-Juice remaining calm despite table-topping JPL start
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC striker Daniel Roberts celebrates after scoring the winning goal in the club’s 1-0 victory over Molynes United in the Jamaica Premier League at Stadium East on Sunday. (Photo: JPL)

DESPITE Tru-Juice FC’s strong start to their debut Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, Assistant Coach Craig Richards says it’s too early to be thinking about the play-offs.

The newly promoted club lead the JPL stadings on seven points after a 1-0 win over Molynes United at Stadium East on Sunday. Striker Daniel Roberts’s 62nd-minute strike was enough as Tru-Juice stay unbeaten after their first three games. They also join Montego Bay United and Waterhouse as the only two clubs who have yet to concede.

Richards says he was pleased with the team’s execution, after nearly a week of preparation.

“We knew that it was going to be a tough-fought game. We know how the Molynes team plays and we’ve been training all week to nullify them — and we also worked on ways to hurt them and it paid dividends,” he said.

“When we play against certain teams, we really assess them and train accordingly, so I’m very pleased. There are parts of the game that I’m disappointed with but there are aspects that I’m very pleased [about], and that’s football. I’m pleased we got three points on the board, and we look forward to the next game.”

Tru-Juice have attracted several top players to join their inaugural season, including Reggae Boyz Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving, and Tafari Chambers.

The Linstead based-club caught the eyes of many during their opening game when they thrashed reigning Caribbean Cup champions Mount Pleasant FA 4-0 and held last season’s semi-finalists, Montego Bay United, to a goalless draw.

Although starting on a positive note, Richards says they’re not placing too much pressure on themselves.

“Our objective is to play quality football and maximise on the points and [see] wherever that leads us,” he said. “Our aim is to compete. And competing can lead us to good places but as it relates to [the] objective [of] top six or whatever, if that should come then we are very welcoming for that but for now we’re taking it three games at a time.

“This is our first season. There are quite a number of teams that have been competing in this competition for some time so they have some experience. While we have experienced players, the club itself is in its first season so we continue to set different objectives at different points of the season, and we’ll see where that leads us.”

Mount Pleasant Head Coach Theodore Whitmore was pleased his team got off the mark after their 2-0 win over Dunbeholden at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex.

After losing their first two games of the season, goals from Trayvone Reid and Nicholas Nelson ensured the St Ann-based club picked up all three points.

“It doesn’t feel like three, it feels like six points,” Whitmore said. “I think we would have met our objective when we got two goals this afternoon; we didn’t concede, we kept a clean sheet, so I think it’s something that we can build on.

“When you look at the table and see Mount Peasant at the foot, nobody expects that. It wasn’t pleasing even for the fans that travel with us every Sunday, so it’s very pleasing [to beat Dunbeholden]. We look forward to the next one; and it gives us now a momentum going into the next game and into the semi-final of the Caribbean Cup.”

World.title: ALL THE KING’S MEN
World.content:
Hunain Shah (second right) of Jamaica Kingsmen celebrates with teammates (from left) Keemo Paul, Andre Russell, and Vitel Lawes after getting the wicket of Roston Chase during their Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League T20 match with St Lucia Kings in Gros Islet, St Lucia, on Friday, August 21. (PHOTO: CPLT20)

JAMAICA Kingsmen Head of Operations Atishai Mansingh says a strong collective effort will be needed to continue cricket’s revival on the island.

The Kingsmen finished runners-up of the recently concluded Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL), after losing to the Antigua and Barbuda Falcons in the final in Barbados.

It was a remarkable run for the Jamaican franchise in their first season as the Kingsmen, having been inactive for the 2024 and 2025 seasons after former owner Kris Persaud sold the franchise and moved on to the now-champions Falcons.

This season also saw the return of CPL to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019, with four games hosted in Kingston.

While pleased with the franchise’s start, Mansingh says he’s focused on helping to grow the sport locally.

“CPL coming back is not going to solve all of the issues that we have in Jamaica cricket,” he said. “It’s a spark, and what we do with that spark is what will determine whether this moment becomes a temporary celebration or the beginning of a genuine revival — and the revival is going to start from the top down.

“We want to encourage all of public and corporate Jamaica to see the highest-paying sport for what it is. The fact is, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park this year, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park next year, but we have to work towards filling Sabina Park in the years coming, because if this park is seen as a football park, as an entertainment park, for the history that it holds, every single one of us are failing. Filling Sabina Park is not about the Kingsmen putting on social media s and giving away tickets. It’s about the teamwork [and] the support which is needed to to build these cricket structures in Jamaica.”

Mansingh says cricket’s development locally cannot be driven solely by finances but must also be fuelled by passion for the sport.

“Players cannot rebuild it alone. The Government and sponsors, though we always request them, also cannot build it alone. Clubs, schools, families, businesses and supporters must all play a part,” he said.

“If we don’t put the love into the sport, who’s going to? [People] say, ‘Who’s going to fix cricket?’ ‘CPL come, they have money, they’re going to fix it’, ‘This person have money so they’re going to fix it’. Money is not going to fix this; it’s the love that we all possess for the sport that’s going to bring the happiness back to the sport.”

Mansingh says more emphasis needs to be placed on women’s cricket as well, with the debut of the Jamaica Empress team in the Women’s CPL providing a good starting point.

“Cricket is not just about a man with a ball and a man with a bat,” he said. “The women are equally important for this sport’s growth. The Kingsmen launched the first-ever Jamaica women’s CPL franchise, the Jamaica Empress. It has given an opportunity to women to see the sport as a way of employment. A sport that was always seen as a gentleman’s sport has now been seen as just simply a sport.

“That is very crucial, because when the likes of Hayley Matthews, Stafanie Taylor, Chinelle Henry are able to go to tournaments across the world and earn US$250,000 [$38 million] for a six-week tournament, that is eye-opening to state that this sport is not just going to fill the pockets of men any more but it’s going to create structures and systems for young girls to say, ‘I want to be like them when I’m older.’ ”

World.title: Profound sorrow
World.content:
A police vehicle seen on the campus of Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after the death of a fourth-form student. Photo: Joseph wellington

DEEP sorrow and grief shrouded Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after a fourth-form student collapsed in class and died.

“I don’t think we’ve ever had such a situation; meaning, it’s typical for us to have students fall ill, we take them for medical attention, and we see them back in school. It’s the first that we’re having an experience where a student has been taken for medical attention and will not be back with us,” Principal Dwight Pennycooke told journalists at the school in the Corporate Area.

The principal said he was unable to give a detailed account of the school’s initial reaction to the incident, as, after receiving the call from the school nurse informing him of the situation, he had been at Medical Associates Hospital where the student was rushed.

However, he shared that his students were compassionate and empathetic and he expected that the school would be in a period of mourning for quite some time.

“I know over the next few days it’s going to be a difficult one for his peers, his teachers, and for us the administration. We’ve never had to walk through something like this, but we will, through the grace of God, and the help of the support, walk through this and ensure that we provide the necessary support to his peers as well,” said Pennycooke.

He added that, in his absence, vice-principals had been ensuring that the school remained settled, while an early dismissal gave students and staff time to “decompress and to process” what had happened.

He further noted that he could not speak to the specifics surrounding the medical emergency, but recalled seeing the school nurse’s urgent response after receiving her call.

“I saw her running. She’s heavily pregnant, and you see her running, and so I think you would appreciate that she had the sense that this is an emergency, and so she dealt with whatever the call was… in that moment. So that is all I’m aware of,” he said.

Pennycooke reiterated that the school would continue to provide necessary support to those in mourning, noting that the Ministry of Education responded to the incident, and that counsellors were immediately deployed.

“Our young men are quite sensitive, and when it comes down to empathy and compassion, I know I’m going to have to support them quite a bit over the next couple of days… We had a counselling team here earlier. We had our women’s girls’ school counsellors come over. Now we have persons from the Ministry of Education, and no doubt we will have them again for the next couple of days,” he said.

The principal’s update followed a statement released by Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management, which detailed that the student was rushed to hospital where he was later pronounced dead after he collapsed at school.

The board expressed profound sorrow for the loss of the student and further extended its condolence to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers, and all whose lives he touched.

The board also said that affected peers and staff were being provided with emotional support and asked that the privacy of the student’s family and the school community be respected at this time.

“We also urge the public to refrain from speculation or the circulation of unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing. The Wolmer’s family stands together in grief and will continue to support the student’s loved ones in the days ahead,” the board said.

World.title: Wolmer’s Boys student dies after collapsing during class
World.content:
Wolmer's Boys School Gate file photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — A fourth-form Wolmer’s Boys High School student has died following a medical emergency at the school on Monday, the school has confirmed.

In a statement, the Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management indicated that the student collapsed during class and was rushed to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

The board expressed profound sorrow at the passing of the young man, describing it as a deeply painful loss for his family and for the entire Wolmer’s community.

“The Joint Board extends its heartfelt condolences to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers and all whose lives he touched,” the statement read.

The school said it is providing support to affected students and members of staff and urged the public to refrain from circulating unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing.

World.title: Lt Stitchie, dancehall icon who found new calling in gospel, dies at 60
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie (Photo via Instagram)

Veteran deejay Lieutenant Stitchie has died.

Observer Online understands that the entertainer, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at hospital on Monday, just one day before he would have celebrated his 61st birthday.

The tragic news comes less than 24 hours after the entertainer’s wife, Sophia Laing confirmed that he had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment at the Kingston Public Hospital.

READ: Lt Stitchie hospitalised with ‘low blood count’

The pioneering dancehall entertainer whose career spanned the formative years of the genre before he made a transition to gospel music, had been ailing for some time. His health issued stemmed largely from a debilitating stroke in the first week of September 2024.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside figures including Papa San, Wickerman and Major Worries. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yuh Size, followed by Natty Dread, before his career expanded internationally with a recording deal with Atlantic Records in 1988.

But perhaps the most defining chapter of Stitchie’s life came when he left secular dancehall behind and devoted himself to ministry after becoming a born-again Christian in 1997. He subsequently built a thriving career in gospel reggae as his transition did little to diminish the respect he commanded within the wider entertainment fraternity.

His death is expected to reverberate across both communities, with artistes who shared stages, sound systems and recording studios with him likely to reflect on the contribution of a man who managed to reinvent himself without losing his place in Jamaican music history.

World.title: Burnham pledges to scrap pension triple lock from 2030
World.content:
Any changes would come after the next election, which will need to be held in 2029 at the latest.

“This change will generate significant savings, which we will use to build up our National Care Service,” Burnham said.

“Some may not realise it, but older people with nothing more than the state pension or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today. Under my plan, this will no longer happen.”

The Labour Party estimated in a note following Burnham's speech that the changes would save £15 billion per year by the end of the 2030s, rising to £50 billion a year by 2050.

The triple lock is divisive and has been called “unsustainable” by economists as it costs the Treasury around £16 billion a year and is set to rise further as inflation and earnings increase.

However, Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said that Burnham’s changes won’t fund his social care plans.

“It is great news that Andy Burnham has neutered the worst element of the triple lock,” he said. “Better reforms were available, but this one is a big improvement. It will not, however, be the answer to funding universal social care.”

World.title: Budget : comment Matignon compte durcir l’accès des étrangers aux APL et allocations familiales
World.content:
D’après la mesure, les ressortissants étrangers de pays tiers (soit hors Union européenne, espace économique européen et Suisse), devront justifier d’un an de résidence régulière dans l’Hexagone avant de pouvoir bénéficier de certaines prestations familiales.

Aujourd’hui, les étrangers en situation régulière peuvent bénéficier des prestations familiales, sans durée minimale de résidence, même si des délais existent déjà pour certaines aides comme le RSA (5 ans) ou l’allocation de solidarité aux personnes âgées (10 ans).

En plus des allocations familiales, l’article concocté par la direction de la Sécurité sociale et soumis au Conseil d’Etat prévoit que les prestations versées par la CAF telles que l’allocation de soutien familial (ASF), l’allocation de rentrée scolaire (ARS), la prestation d’accueil du jeune enfant (Paje) ou encore le complément familial soient soumises au délai de carence.

Trois prestations sont en revanche exemptées : l’allocation d’éducation de l’enfant handicapé (AEEH), l’allocation journalière de présence parentale (AJPP), destinée notamment aux parents d’un enfant gravement malade ou handicapé, et l’allocation forfaitaire versée en cas de décès d’un enfant.

En outre, le délai s’appliquera également aux aides au logement, comme les APL et les allocations de logement familiale et de logement social.

Le précédent de la loi immigration

Pour rédiger la mesure, le gouvernement s’est appuyé sur les observations du Conseil constitutionnel de janvier 2024 qui, au moment de la loi immigration portée par Gérald Darmanin, avait jugé qu’une mesure similaire avec un délai de cinq ans de résidence était disproportionnée.

World.title: Le Pen faces fallout after Bardella accused of antisemitic remarks
World.content:
“The system will do anything — including the most disgusting things — to try to hinder this momentum,” Le Pen said Tuesday, sitting next to Bardella as they addressed reporters in the National Assembly, France’s lower house of parliament.

“We sense the early signs of total war, attempts at destabilizing the presidential campaign,” Bardella said.

Yet the allegations themselves are rattling Le Pen’s campaign given her years-long effort to distance her party from its antisemitic past. The National Rally’s predecessor, the National Front, was founded by Nazi collaborators and Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie, who was repeatedly convicted of hate speech. Le Pen kicked her father out of the party in 2015 for repeating his claim that the Holocaust was a “detail” of history.

The fallout of this latest scandal could be particularly damaging given how Le Pen jumpstarted Bardella’s career and put him at the forefront of a detoxification effort.

Too young to have been involved with the party’s old guard, Bardella was supposed to be a fresh face that could help the party make inroads in parts of the electorate where the Le Pen name carried too much baggage — notably with older voters and in the Jewish community.

Since taking the reins of the National Rally in 2021, Bardella has sold the party as a defender of France’s Jewish population and pointed to his full-throated support of Israel as proof. The 31-year-old traveled to Israel in 2025 after receiving an invite from the Israeli Minister for Diaspora Affairs Amichai Chikli.

World.title: UK must avoid US-style climate debate, minister says
World.content:
Katie White speaks at the POLITICO Pub during the Labour Conference in Liverpool, England, Sept. 29, 2026. | Baldo Sciacca for POLITICO

The U.S. has been “undermined” by climate rows, Katie White argued.

LIVERPOOL, England — The U.K. should not follow the U.S. into a “binary” debate on climate policy, a government minister warned Tuesday.

The government will try to “build bridges” on energy policy where it finds common ground with Donald Trump's climate-skeptical White House, Climate Minister Katie White said, speaking at the POLITICO Pub at the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, while trying to avoid the risks of a polarized debate at home.

“America has stalled,” White argued, because of a debate on climate she characterized as “a binary, right-and-wrong, this is the right way, this is the wrong way, and the left is pro climate and the right hasn't been.”

World.title: Scottish Labour leader says UK rejoining EU ‘not a realistic prospect’
World.content:
But Marra said that while he’d support a U.K. effort to rejoin should Europe find itself in a “different place” in the future, he admitted it may not be a “realistic prospect” for a generation or more.

“Politics in Europe, I think, is really unstable at the moment. It’s facing many of the same challenges that we are in the U.K. in terms of the global economic instability, challenges in the Middle East, and migrant crises across parts of Europe have really destabilized politics.”

Marra, who took over as leader after Labour suffered a humiliating defeat in May’s Scottish Parliament election, instead urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to be “pragmatic” about forging closer links with the bloc.

“What we do need is a closer relationship because we know the economic cost that’s resulted from Brexit. I want to see us doing that on a case-by-case basis,” he said. “Some of the things we’ve done around Erasmus and so on, I think that is a key thing.”

His comments come amid growing debate among senior Labour ministers about the next steps in the U.K.’s relationship with Brussels at the party’s annual gathering in Liverpool.

In a major intervention ahead of the conference, former Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair said there should be a plan to rejoin a “reformed EU” in the next decade.

Andy Burnham has not yet ruled out including conditions for a fresh membership bid in his party’s next election manifesto, but is expected to expand on his approach when he speaks to the Labour faithful later today.

World.title: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig vows to put ‘grown-up shoes’ on when hosting Donald Trump
World.content:
She added: “But there’s a serious point, isn’t it? If you are saying that you want to be a globally competitive city that has a growing economy and delivers for your residents, then you’ve also got to put your grown-up shoes on.

“And when people come to town, you’ve got to make sure that you’re hosting world leaders in a way that reflects the U.K. in a professional and serious way.”

‘Cool, calm heads’

Craig, who grew up in Northern Ireland, was pressed on Trump’s incendiary recent call for Irish reunification. She urged caution on the issue — but declined to say if she would give her message to the U.S president directly at the G20.

“I don’t think the mayor of Greater Manchester’s got that democratic mandate to tell the president of the U.S. what her thoughts and feelings are about the place that she grew up,” Craig said. But she stressed that the Good Friday Agreement “gives peace and let communities begin to thrive.” And she called for “cool, calm heads” to avoid stoking fresh tensions.

Craig met Mamdani in the U.S. earlier this month at a meeting of the Urban20, which brings together mayors from G20 countries. She told POLITICO that she spent time in New York handing out coffee machines to people moving into new affordable apartment blocks.

“The serious work that we’re doing there is that the challenges are the same in most major cities across the world around affordability,” Craig said. “There is a great role that progressive mayors around the world can play in helping shift the tone in national politics to show what can happen when you actually get stuff done.”

World.title: Alan Milburn rejects tax cut for youth jobs
World.content:
Milburn — who published a report in May warning the number of young people not in work or education could hit 1.25 million by the early 2030s without urgent action — is currently drawing up recommendations for ministers to address the crisis.

“In six months time, this is going to feel much more like a manifesto for change,” he said.

The former health secretary — who was chair of the Social Mobility Commission between 2012 and 2017 — also warned that young people from working class backgrounds face greater barriers to opportunity today.

Reflecting on his own journey from growing up on a council estate to sitting around the Cabinet table, Milburn said he has reached the “pretty depressing conclusion” that it seems “less likely rather than more likely” to happen today.

“It is one of the reasons why we’ve got to deal with this challenge,” he said. “Life shouldn’t have to rely on luck; it should rely on opportunity.”

World.title: Global economic impact of Iran war ‘unbearable,’ Qatar warns as talks continue
World.content:
The Iran war has put an “unbearable” strain on the global economy, Qatar warned on Tuesday, as it said meetings aimed at reaching a deal were continuing and Doha resumed its role as a mediator between Washington and Tehran.

 

“How long can the international economy withstand the results of what is happening in our region?” Foreign ministry spokesperson Dr Majed Al Ansari said at a press briefing in Doha.

Asked about the prospects for an agreement, Al Ansari said, “In any agreement, there are obstacles. Our role is to overcome the difficulties and try to bridge the gap between the two sides, and that is what is happening now.”

He said meetings had taken place in recent days, while Qatar passed messages between the parties. He would not say how far the negotiations had progressed.

Al Ansari said another escalation would bring more hardship to the region. Qatar was still pressing for a peaceful resolution despite being hit by missiles from Iran, he said.

The Gulf states, Iraq and Jordan had not chosen to take part in the war between Iran and the US, Al Ansari said. They had no separate conflict with Tehran to settle, he argued.

“This is an aggression, an unwarranted aggression against our countries,” he said, adding that Tehran needed to make clear that it would not attack neighbours caught up in a war they had not joined.

Despite the attacks, Qatar remained in contact with Iran as it tried to mediate an end to the war. Al Ansari said a lasting settlement would also require regional security arrangements based on coexistence and non-aggression.

For now, Doha was trying to bring the parties closer to an agreement and reopen Hormuz to free navigation, he said.

Dr Al Ansari said the Gulf exported far more than oil and gas to the world, including urea and ammonia, important to agriculture and fertiliser production, as well as helium, petrochemicals and aluminium.

He pointed to effects on crop yields in vulnerable countries and increased coal burning in places that had been cutting back. The strain could grow worse as winter approaches, he warned.

The war which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for Gulf exports.

Qatar has repeatedly stated it wanted full freedom of navigation restored as part of any peace deal between Washington and Tehran.

World.title: Eiffel Tower director announces departure after row over sidelining of female staff
World.content:
The Iron Lady will soon have a new director. Weakened since female staff were sidelined during a visit by a Hindu religious group in early September, the chief executive of the Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE), Patrick Branco Ruivo, announced on Tuesday 29 September that he will leave his post at the end of the year.

 

His position, at the head of SETE since 2018, had been severely undermined after female employees were excluded during a visit in early September by members of the ultra‑conservative Hindu movement Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha.

The decision to keep women working at the monument away from the visitors sparked a strike by Eiffel Tower staff and led to the closure, on 7 September, of the capital’s most iconic landmark for the entire day. "Some [female employees] were asked to leave their posts and to withdraw to other rooms", workers said in a statement.

Two investigations have since been carried out, at the initiative of the mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire. The internal inquiry "brought to light a series of malfunctions and shortcomings in the organisation of protocol visits", which "resulted in the exclusion of female staff on the day of the visit, an unacceptable situation", the Eiffel Tower operating company said in a statement released on Tuesday.

Among the most visited sites in Paris, the Eiffel Tower has 402 employees, welcomes 6.7 million visitors a year and generates a turnover of 156 million euros. Responsible for managing the monument, SETE is a local public entity owned 99% by the City of Paris and 1% by the Greater Paris Metropolis.

World.title: IEA could consider more oil reserve releases as Europe faces tough winter
World.content:
The IEA has hinted that releasing further strategic oil reserves could be an option to ease supply shortages.

 

Speaking at a meeting of EU energy ministers in Dublin, International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said that the agency has released 400 million barrels of crude oil from its strategic reserves since March and that one-third of that has yet to “come to the markets”.

The released stocks are equivalent to "20% of the overall stocks", Birol said, adding that "80% is still in our pocket. If there is a need and if our member countries do agree with it, we are ready to act in order to address current and future market challenges_."_

He also added that currently, "it is not the number one agenda for the IEA".

His comments came as EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen talked on Tuesday about the extra costs Europe has been facing since the start of the war in Iran. He said that European Union countries have spent more than €100 billion extra on energy imports since the outbreak of the war in Iran. Despite that additional spending, they have received “not one extra molecule of gas or oil”.

The disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has tightened global oil and diesel supplies. The waterway carried about a fifth of the world’s traded oil before the war, and Europe relies heavily on imported diesel.

Jørgensen called for faster investment in electricity and power infrastructure to reduce the bloc’s reliance on imported fossil fuels.

After cutting its reliance on Russian energy following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU became more dependent on energy imports from the US, particularly for diesel.

“Europe is one of the most exposed regions — if not the most exposed one — when it comes to diesel because Europe imports a huge amount of diesel and we are entering the harsh season, the winter season,” said Birol.

The US supplied around half of the EU’s diesel imports in August.

Europe’s diesel supply has been squeezed since EU sanctions on Russian oil products took effect in 2023. Disruption to Middle Eastern supplies has since increased demand for US diesel shipments.

Now, as Europe approaches winter with diesel supplies already tight, the US is considering export restrictions. Euronews previously reported that the European Commission called a possible US export ban a “bad idea” that could hurt both economies.

Fuel prices are already high. The EU’s average diesel price reached a record €2.23 per litre last week. As Euronews reported, diesel cost €2.40 per litre in France and €2.56 in Denmark on Tuesday last week.

What could a US diesel export ban cost Europe?

According to Oxford Economics, a full US ban could raise European wholesale diesel prices by 40% to 50%. Analysts in a recent report calculate that some of that increase could reach consumers, adding €0.50 to €0.60 per litre, including VAT, and a few tenths of a percentage point to inflation.

Those are estimates for a full ban, not a forecast for the narrower restrictions that US officials have also discussed. Oxford Economics says the scope, duration and possible exemptions remain unclear.

Finding replacement diesel would take time. Oxford Economics points to constraints on supplies from the Middle East and says shipments from Asian refiners would take longer to reach Europe. It also expects that Europe could draw on emergency reserves if US restrictions drove diesel prices higher, potentially limiting the increase.

Even US refiners oppose a possible diesel export ban

US trade groups have warned President Donald Trump that an export ban could backfire. In a 23 September letter, the Business Roundtable, the American Petroleum Institute and more than two dozen other groups argued that refiners might have to cut production if they could not export surplus diesel. That would also reduce their output of petrol and jet fuel.

Energy data firm Kpler says US refineries operated at more than 95% of capacity for much of the summer, reaching around 98% in the final week of August. That leaves little room to raise output. Keeping exported diesel in the US could initially lower prices on the Gulf Coast, Kpler says, but storage and transport constraints would make it difficult to spread that relief across the country. Lower refining margins could eventually lead producers to cut output.

Oxford Economics estimates that a full ban could lower US diesel prices by roughly 30% within weeks. But it, too, warns that storage problems and reduced refinery runs could push up petrol and jet fuel prices, offsetting some of the benefit for US consumers.

Ireland’s energy minister, Darragh O’Brien, said a US ban was “unlikely” because it would damage economies on both sides of the Atlantic, but urged the EU to prepare. “We have to be guarded. We can’t be complacent,” he said.

World.title: Azerbaijan Tourism Board CEO: Baku-Brussels flights on the horizon for 2027
World.content:
Azerbaijan is set to boost connectivity for European travellers, with four weekly direct flights between Brussels and Baku.

 

Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026, Florian Sengstschmid, Chief Executive Officer of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, said that Azerbaijan Airlines will be operating flights between Brussels and Baku from 8 May 2027.

Sengstschmid added that the Azerbaijani capital has transformed over the past decade to become a regional hub, highlighting that Baku Heydar Aliyev International Airport is ranked five stars on Skytrax's regional rankings. The national carrier was also named the best regional airline in Central Asia by Skytrax this year.

While he said the four-weekly routes will improve connectivity, Sengstschmid hopes visitors will use Baku as a gateway to explore the country further afield.

“It's really to travel beyond Baku – to travel along the Silk Road, through the side valleys, ancient heritage villages,” he said, while also highlighting the country’s UNESCO World Heritage Sites, settlements, cities on the greater Caucasus Mountains and the Khan’s palace.

Another hidden gem he spoke about was Sim in southern Azerbaijan. Sengstschmid described the village as "a fairy-tale with moss", replete with wooden buildings, waterfalls, and various fauna and flora.

“It feels a bit like you're in the jungle, but in the middle you're basically in Azerbaijan,” he said. “And this describes the diversity you can experience once you really go out of the city – dive into the country and meet the wonderful, lovely people.”

He also pointed to the country's diversity with various climate zones, which offers travellers experiences in semi-desert landscapes to mountain peaks that exceed 4,000 metres high above sea level all in one destination.

In 2025, tourism to the country generated 7 billion Azerbaijani Manat (€3.5 billion), which accounted for 5.4% of the country’s GDP. Azerbaijan has garnered visitors by hosting major events such as Formula 1, and previously Eurovision and COP29.

When asked to sum the country in three words, he replied with “real, warm and uplifting”. For Sengstschmid, Azerbaijan “continues to reveal many new sights and this is what it still does to me, although living there for many, many years and calling it my home”.
