World.title: Spanish government unveils new measures aimed at easing housing crisis
World.content:
The Spanish government on Tuesday approved two new decrees aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis.

 

Measures included in the decrees range from stronger protection against evictions and limits on speculative purchases to tax incentives, as well as new rules for renting and zero-interest financing to help people buy their first home.

The move comes at a time of growing public pressure over soaring housing costs and mounting difficulties for people looking both to rent and buy.

Spain's Minister for Housing and Urban Agenda, Isabel Rodríguez, has described housing as "the main problem facing Spaniards" and presented the measures as a broad response to a crisis she sees as particularly "complex."

The agreement is split into two separate decrees.

The first contains most of the measures and is focused on four main areas: protecting tenants from evictions, curbing speculation, tackling abuses in the rental market and making homes more affordable.

The second is aimed at giving tenants more stability and security in their rental contracts.

The approval came after tense negotiations within Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's coalition government.

The cabinet meeting started more than an hour late because of disagreements from Sumar, the junior coalition partner, over concessions being offered to Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party whose support could be crucial when Congress votes to ratify the measures.

"It has been a very difficult and complex text", Rodríguez said after the meeting, whilst also thanking those involved in drawing it up.

The government is now looking to fast-track the measures through parliament and has asked Congress to hold an extraordinary session this Friday.

"We are going to try to ensure this text sees the light as soon as possible," Rodríguez added, describing the law as "ambitious" and insisting there was "a broad social consensus in our country around these measures to ease the housing crisis."

Four pillars of the main package

The first and broader decree is built around four main areas.

The first aims to strengthen protection against evictions.

"We do not want any more cases like Maricarmen's," Rodríguez said, referencing the case of an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her home in Madrid this month.

The government plans to extend the so-called "social shield" until 2030, with the aim of bolstering protection for vulnerable people at risk of losing their home.

"Let's put our foot down on speculation," the minister added as she presented the second set of measures.

The government intends to curb speculative purchases of housing and identify companies engaged in such operations to stop them from "trading in an essential good."

The government also wants to act on acquisitions made by so-called vulture funds and to use the tax system to steer investment towards affordable housing rather than speculative deals.

The third pillar focuses on fraud in the rental market, particularly the use of short-term and room-by-room contracts to sidestep rules governing residential lets.

Rodríguez also pointed to illegal tourist apartments, which she said should be shut down by regional authorities. The government is also proposing a new 10% VAT tax on tourist apartments.

Tax breaks and zero-interest financing

The fourth pillar is aimed at improving affordability and access to housing.

Among the measures announced are tax breaks for landlords, which the government says could allow some families to save the equivalent of one month's rent.

The government is hoping to complement regulatory measures with tax incentives and to make it easier for people to move from renting to home ownership for those who, despite having sufficient income, struggle to build up enough savings.

For such cases, Rodríguez announced "Tu Casa," a new zero-interest financing scheme designed to help people purchase their first home.

The government also wants to boost the construction of affordable housing and has unveiled a cut in VAT to 4% for protected and publicly developed housing.

Second decree focuses on rental stability

Alongside this broad package of measures, the Council of Ministers has approved a second decree of urgent measures to strengthen the stability of tenancy contracts.

Rodríguez explained that this second measure addresses "a very specific aspect" of the rental housing crisis. She argued that the government has long been trying to amend the current model to provide greater security for people living in rented accommodation.

"We want to provide that stability so people can live in rented housing with peace of mind," Rodríguez said.

Housing protests continue

People gather during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen to demand stronger laws to protect renters at Puerta del Sol in Madrid, Spain. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The government has been facing growing pressure from a housing protest movement.

The Tenants' Union is among the organisations behind an encampment set up in Madrid's Puerta del Sol, as well as demonstrations held in other Spanish cities.

The groups have decided that they would keep the encampment in place regardless of the cabinet's decision, meaning the approval of the two decrees does not mean the protests are coming to an end.

Regional authorities have given the central government's delegation 48 hours to dismantle the site and warned that they would take the matter to court if it were not removed.

World.title: Middle East oil exports rise as LNG traffic through Hormuz picks up
World.content:
Middle East crude oil exports rose in September to their highest monthly level since the Iran war began seven months ago.

 

Preliminary data from Kpler put regional exports at 16.3 million barrels a day. That was still around 3.2 million barrels a day below the 19.5 million recorded in February.

Saudi Arabia accounted for much of the increase, more than doubling its exports from 2.45 million barrels a day in August to around 5.4 million in September.

Flows through the Strait of Hormuz were projected to reach about 9.7 million barrels a day as Saudi Arabia sent additional crude from its Gulf terminals after attacks damaged its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. The regional total also includes oil shipped from ports outside the strait.

Several Qatar-linked LNG tankers also crossed Hormuz this month after no visible crossings were recorded in August.

Normal exports have not resumed, however, and QatarEnergy has extended delivery suspensions for some customers in Europe and Asia.

Edison said it had received a new notice from QatarEnergy extending force majeure until early December. Another six LNG cargoes due at Italy’s Adriatic LNG terminal will not be delivered.

That brings the number of missed cargoes since April to 35. Edison has replaced 23 of them, mainly with gas from the United States.

Edison’s 25-year contract with QatarEnergy supplies 6.4 billion cubic metres of gas a year, equal to around 10% of Italy’s total consumption.

Some customers in Pakistan and Bangladesh have also been told that delivery suspensions will continue through November.

Force majeure allows a company to suspend its contractual obligations when events outside its control prevent it from fulfilling them.

The disruption began after joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February in the opening salvo of the ongoing war, which has sharply reduced traffic through Hormuz, while both the US and Iran targeted commercial ships in and around the strait.

US President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen Hormuz and end the fighting within seven days. The proposal had been passed to Washington through Qatari mediators, who are continuing to push for talks.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said no infrastructure in the region would be safe unless Iran’s security was guaranteed, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

“In a region where Iran cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either,” he said.

Which LNG tankers crossed Hormuz?

Ship-tracking data from Kpler and LSEG showed GasLog Skagen off Sri Lanka on Sunday carrying LNG from Qatar’s Ras Laffan terminal. It had last been tracked inside the Gulf on 20 September.

Al Ghashamiya delivered a Qatari cargo to India last week, while Shandong Redwood carried LNG to Pakistan. Al Daayen emerged from Hormuz with a shipment bound for China.

An empty Qatar-linked tanker, Al Mafyar, was also tracked entering the strait on 22 September.

The total number of crossings is unclear because some ships turn off their tracking systems as they pass through Hormuz, making them harder to locate.

Qatar exported only 18 LNG cargoes during the first six months of the war, compared with 509 in the same period a year earlier, according to data provider ICIS.

Every LNG tanker leaving Qatar must pass through Hormuz because the country has no alternative export route.

Qatar’s Energy Minister Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said last week that building a pipeline around the strait would make no economic sense. Such a route would require a new plant outside Qatar to turn piped gas into LNG before it could be loaded onto tankers.

Attacks on Ras Laffan damaged two LNG production units, cutting Qatar’s production capacity by around 17%. Al-Kaabi said repairs would take about three years, but the country’s 12 undamaged units could return to normal operations within weeks once ships could pass through Hormuz safely and regularly.

World.title: Houthi attacks put Turkey’s new Saudi defence pact to the test
World.content:
Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia are putting Turkey's new defence pact with the kingdom to its first major test – forcing Ankara to weigh support for its ally against the risk of being drawn deeper into the conflict.

Advertising

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on 7 August, committing themselves to the principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.

The three countries' military chiefs met in the Saudi capital on Friday, a day after the Iran-backed Houthis launched their latest barrage of missiles targeting Riyadh and Saudi Aramco oil facilities in Yanbu.

In recent weeks, Saudi Arabia has reported intercepting numerous Houthi drone and ballistic missile attacks from neighbouring Yemen.

The military chiefs discussed intelligence sharing, military coordination and integrating their capabilities, Saudi and Pakistani statements said. Turkey's defence ministry did not comment on the meeting.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Saudi expectations

Turkey has so far stopped short of committing itself to military action.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this month that Ankara was looking into providing what he called “technical support”, without elaborating on what that could involve.

Saudi Arabia could look to Turkey for air defence systems, counter-drone technology, radars and maritime security, given the expertise and capabilities of the Turkish military and defence industry, said Amed Khuzaie of the Washington-based think tank N7 Foundation.

“The Mecca Agreement pact will prove its vitality and importance only if it's deemed to be functional,” Khuzaie told RFI.

The Riyadh meeting followed talks in New York on Thursday involving the Saudi and Turkish foreign ministers and Pakistan's deputy prime minister and foreign minister on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

Turkish media citing foreign ministry sources said the meeting focused on ongoing “technical negotiations”.

But providing support to Saudi Arabia could expose Turkey to retaliation from the Houthis.

“By God, if Turkey and Pakistan become involved, we will strike them with an iron fist,” Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis, said in an Iraqi television interview.

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Risk of retaliation

The warning should be taken seriously given the Houthis' military presence around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical waterway linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, explained Amed Nagi, a Yemen expert at the International Crisis Group.

“[The Houthis] targeted US and UK shipping in the Red Sea,” Nagi said. “They could do the same beyond [that] to the Gulf of Aden, because we know Turkey is very active in the Horn of Africa.

"So I think these are the areas that the Houthis will think about if there is any sort of retaliation against Turkey.”

In 2024, the Houthis attacked US military and commercial shipping in the Red Sea, damaging the Gibraltar Eagle bulk carrier with a cruise missile and sinking the British-linked cargo ship MV Rubymar.

Saudi Arabia could also look to Israel for support if its new partners do not provide what it needs, Khuzaie said.

“Who has better intelligence in the region than the Israelis today?” he said. “Diversifying resources, if one fails you, you have another side that could assist.”

The risks for Ankara go beyond possible Houthi retaliation. Turkey must also manage its relationship with Iran, which backs the Yemeni group.

“It is not in the interest of Turkey to have a direct confrontation with any actor in the region, and the Houthis have become a proxy of Iran; Turkey doesn't want a confrontation with Iran directly," said Bilgehan Alagoz, an international relations professor at Istanbul's Marmara University.

"Turkey is trying to solve the issue from a diplomatic point of view.”

In a joint statement last week, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt said that dialogue and diplomacy were the only sustainable way to resolve the region's conflicts, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself under international law.

Fidan met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in New York on Friday.

Fidan later said they discussed Iran's negotiations with the United States and conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but that diplomatic efforts had yet to produce a breakthrough.

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Iran balancing act

The diplomatic efforts come as Turkey's relationship with Iran faces other strains.

Turkey-based international relations analyst Soli Ozel said Ankara has for decades walked a “fine line” between rivalry and cooperation with Tehran while balancing its relationships with Iran and Western allies, particularly the United States.

Turkey's banking regulator recently revoked the operating licence of Iran's Bank Mellat branch in Istanbul, although the official notice did not say the move was intended to enforce US sanctions.

The US Treasury also said Ankara had agreed after talks with Washington to stop flights by Iran's Mahan Air as part of efforts to comply with US measures against Tehran. Three Turkish airlines also suspended flights to Iran.

Turkish authorities have also repeatedly accused Iran of hostile operations inside the country, including assassinations and abductions of Iranian dissidents.

In January, security forces arrested six people suspected of spying for Iran and gathering information about the Incirlik air base, which is used by US forces.

Becoming involved in the conflict against the Houthis could upset Ankara's already delicate relationship with Tehran, Ozel told RFI.

“The Iranians who actually have a lot of [intelligence] capabilities in Turkey, we’ve seen that before, then you find yourself in a hot or cold war,” he said.

World.title: TV journalist is crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom
World.content:
Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has ascended to the throne after King Oyo died at the age of 34 due to a cancer battle. He previously worked for Ugandan broadcaster UBC as a TV anchor and editor.

A TV journalist on Tuesday was crowned king of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom.

What do we know so far?

Edward Rukidi Kiganangoma has ascended to the thrown after his predecessor, King Oyo Kyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, died unexpectedly last month.

King Oyo was only 34 and had lost his cancer battle while receiving treatment in the US. Oyo had became king at only three years of age.

Oyo's death sparked a succession battle in Uganda, with Oyo's mother pushing for the late king's undisclosed son to be the next monarch.

King Oyo was laid to rest earlier this month after a nine-day period of mourning [FILE: September 10, 2026] Image: Michael Muhati/REUTERS

However, the royal Babito clan chose Kiganangoma, now Nyabongo I, as the heir to the throne out of a group of eligible princes.

Kiganangoma took part in a coronation ceremony in the remote town of Fort Portal in western Uganda to ascend to the throne.

Coronation rituals included a mock battle and animal sacrifices. The ceremony in Fort Portal was televised and attended by thousands of people.

Kiganangoma, who is 56 years old, had worked as a journalist and editor for Ugandan public broadcaster UBC.

Tooro's new king vows to 'protect our culture, our traditions and customs'

"We have a big task to protect our culture, our traditions and customs and good conduct among our people," the new king said in his maiden speech. He had also told the New Vision newspaper: "My family never let me treat royal descent as an entitlement."

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni was present for the coronation ceremony of the new king.

While expressing sadness over King Oyo's passing, Museveni also said he congratulates "his Highness Nyabongo. I have been watching him on the news and he is a good newsreader. I am sure he will do a good job."

Uganda is a constitutional republic with a president voted in democratically.

However, the country's four major precolonial kingdoms still hold cultural influence over the East African nation, despite not wielding any political power. The kings are involved in maintaining social order and safeguarding the heritage of their respective kingdoms.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Satirist launches site naming Cornell students accused in gang-rape lawsuit
World.content:
Writer Toby Morton is using a new website to amplify allegations in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit involving seven Cornell students. The reopening of the case is causing an outcry on social media.

Toby Morton, who wrote several episodes of the animated comedy series "South Park," launched a website seeking accountability in connection with an alleged 2024 sexual assault case involving seven Cornell University fraternity members. The site names seven men accused of sexually assaulting a 20-year-old woman who was allegedly unconscious after being given drugs and alcohol at a Cornell fraternity house and collects personal data and photos of the members involved.

"I've received messages reminding me I'm not a journalist, I'm 'just a satirist,'" Morton wrote in a September 27 Instagram post regarding the creation of his website TheCornell7.org. "This is true, but it makes me more dangerous," he added, saying he has "nobody to tell me I've gone too far."

The case has recently drawn a surge in public attention after the accuser, identified as Jane Doe to protect her identity, filed a lawsuit in mid-September. Her complaint alleges that she was brutally sexually assaulted in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity while unconscious after being pressured to take ketamine, smoke marijuana and drink alcohol at the fraternity house on Cornell's campus in Ithaca, New York. The university, she said in the lawsuit, failed to protect her. Cornell conducted an internal investigation after the incident, but no one was charged.

The reopening of the case has caused renewed attention on social media Image: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

Since the lawsuit was filed on September 16, the case has generated widespread commentary on social media. Some have criticized Cornell and the district attorney's office, while others have questioned the allegations.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who handled the original case, said his office has reopened it and plans to present evidence to a grand jury amid public questions about why no criminal charges were initially filed.

Van Houten said in a statement that his office is considering bringing criminal charges related to the incident, though the allegations in the civil complaint are "dramatically different" from the woman's statement to police two years ago — in her statement to authorities, she did not allege she was drugged without her knowledge or that she did not consent to engage in sexual acts.

Justice sought

Cornell's Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus after the alleged incident in 2024. The accuser also dropped out of Cornell University, according to her attorney.

One of the most chilling allegations of the lawsuit is that a message was sent to a Chi Phi Snapchat group at about 1:42 a.m., inviting members to the room to abuse Doe, who was heavily under the influence of drugs and alcohol. The lawsuit alleges that more men then entered the room and that the assault continued for several hours until Doe lost consciousness.

"There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn't. I've never seen anything like it," an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, told CBS. Giuffra pointed out that two of the seven accused fraternity members were expelled, while the others received lesser disciplinary measures. "Not one of these guys was arrested," Giuffra told the network.

Actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as 'horrific' on social media Image: Cover Images/picture alliance

Politicians and actors speak out

Many people, from US politicians to Hollywood actors, have spoken out about the case in recent days. US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, condemned what she described as a "culture of rape" protected by elite institutions. "When I read what happened at Cornell, those men posted in a group chat. That means it was normal to them. That means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture, and what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore," she said Sunday at a forum near Cornell's campus.

British actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as "horrific" on social media and expressed her support for the student involved. Pugh, who is also currently on a promotional tour for her upcoming Netflix series "East of Eden," wrote a lengthy statement on Instagram, saying that "Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world. You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won't be harmed in return."

"Those who protect and impose light sentences on men who rape and destroy lives should be punished and closely scrutinized. Why are you protecting someone so fiercely?" she wrote.

American actor Josh Gad, best known as the voice of Olaf in Disney's"Frozen" films, also commented on the Cornell case, criticizing what he described as insufficient disciplinary consequences for the students accused of sexual assault. In an Instagram post, Gad said sexual violence should not be treated as a mistake or addressed with limited disciplinary action by a university, arguing that the alleged conduct had "destroyed a life” and calling for greater accountability.



Edited by Joshua Lang.

World.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
World.content:
The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.

At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.

Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.

"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.

"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

Malick Diouf believes Africa as an Olympic host is the logical next step Image: DW

With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.

Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.

"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."

Senegal an attractive option for many reasons

The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.

"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.

Senegal gears up for Youth Olympic Games To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.

"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

The Youth Olympics in Dakar might well be the last summer edition of the youth games, adding even more importance to the first ones in Africa Image: Nicolas Remene/Le Pictorium/IMAGO

A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.

"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."

From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference
World.content:
Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about difficult dilemmas.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, only in the role for a few months after replacing Keir Starmer, has told the Labour Party conference in his native Liverpool that his government wants to restore hope and end "politics as usual."

But the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade is trying to balance a series of evidently conflicting fiscal goals: bolstering economic growth, reducing cost-of-living pressures, safeguarding pensions and making care costs more affordable, upgrading creaking infrastructure and significantly boosting military spending.

That's all while battling a populist challenge from Reform UK and Restore Britain on the right and the Green Party on the left. This led Labour to severe local and regional election defeats in May and ultimately spelt his predecessor Starmer's demise.

Housing Secretary and party members' favorite Angela Rayner was among the speakers warming up the audience on Tuesday ahead of Burnham Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire/PA Images/picture alliance

What did Burnham say in his conference speech?

Burnham, a Liverpool lad who was mayor of Manchester prior to moving to take up Britain's top political job, repeated his most common mantra since coming to power, namely that "more of the same" will not solve the various issues facing the UK.

"We can't carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards," Burnham said. "More of the same isn't good enough and isn't going to get us where we need to be."

The conference's banner headline "hope again" was not incompatible with a more honest conversation, Burnham said.

"Hope comes from honesty ... and saying the things politicians usually avoid," he said.

He cited Labour's post-war government under Clement Atlee, famed for achievements like setting up Britain's National Health Service, as an example of his party's past credentials, having "built the peace" in the public interest. He said that since the 1980s and the Conservative-dominated Margaret Thatcher era of his youth, this direction was lost.

"I will say it straight, Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialization, deregulation, privatization, austerity, Brexit, and what has it given us? A country run for vested interests, not in the public interest — with power held in too few hands, and too many places left to drift," Burnham said.

Burnham told the audience he would take on "the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long," including social care, high levels of youth unemployment, and greater public control of once-nationalized core interests like energy, water and housing.

"The British right talk about 'taking back control," Burnham said, evoking the slogan of the 2016 Brexit campaign. "Never forget that they are the ones who gave it away in the first place!"

Major UK broadcasters are also on site in Liverpool for Labour's conference week, hoping for face time with the prime minsiter and other leaders Image: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

Why is Burnham, and Britain, in such a tricky bind?

Burnham said on coming to power that he wanted his premiership to be a "circuit-breaker for Britain" after years of rising prices and anemic growth.

He hit the ground with a handful of new policies like a cap on bus fares, temporarily removing value added tax from electricity bills amid the Iran war, and announcing a bid to stamp out rough sleeping.

But critics say his more grand stated strategy lacks detail and could prove economically unfeasible.

Burnham is constrained by a series of factors, including Labour's 2024 election campaign pledges under Starmer's leadership, Britain's strained public finances, and the suddenly risk-averse debt markets that have started heaping pressure on most developed economies of late.

Borrowing costs for his UK government, as it eyes a series of new banner spending plans, hit a 10-year-high on the morning of Burnham's speech.

Pledges for a 'National Care System' and commission on electoral reform

In a sign of this lacking spending wiggle room, Burnham has already pushed back his stated aim to formulate reform plans for Britain's social care system.

He said on Tuesday that a "National Care System" would be put forward in time for the next election, currently scheduled for 2029. He said it would be a change "as significant" to the UK as the foundation of the state-funded National Health Service, and also essential to ensure the wider NHS' survival.

He said the plan would be "fully funded, and not by borrowing."

Burnham said that he did not expect such reforms to be easy, and acknowledged "I may pay a political price," but he said they were necessary steps and the kind of leadership he'd promised the party when seeking to replace Starmer this summer.



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood addressed the conference on Monday, with the anti-migration Reform UK probably the biggest electoral threat to Labour — if not necessarily the party Labour voters are migrating Image: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

These challenging economic realities coincide with Labour facing multi-pronged political threats. They hail from right-wing populist parties like the anti-immigration Reform UK, from left-wing populists claiming to hold an economic magic wand like the Green Party, and from nationalist parties in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland advocating independence from the UK.

Burnham also issued appeal to rival political parties late in his speech, saying he would seek as much cross-party consensus as possible for his plans.

He also announced that he would set up a "new national commission on electoral reform," inviting all other parties to contribute to its work.

He said Labour would stand in 2029's election on a platform of reforming the UK voting system so that "every person's vote counts," as party members had advocated in repeated conference votes in past years.

For decades, successive Labour and Conservative governments would not touch Britain's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post voting system, because they were major beneficiaries of it.

What do people say about Burnham's message?

The sense in Liverpool is that Burnham is getting through with his message. Paul James is a taxi driver and union member from Manchester, who says that he has met Burnham while he was Manchester's mayor and that he trusts him: "He never says he can do something unless he can do it." He wants the new prime minister to focus on building council houses, as Burnham is promising once more in his speech he would do.

Pollster Luke Tryl summarizes what Burnham does well: "People think he gets them," he understands their concerns.

Stephen Kinsella from the pressure goup Patriotic Millionnaires hopes that Burnham will focus on wealth taxes. And while there is no concrete plan for higher taxes for richer people, it is clear that Burnham's ambitious plans, like "fixing the broken social care" system, will require extra funds.

"He communicates a sense of optimism, a sense that we can do things as a country," he added.

Kinsella also hopes that Burnham will edge Britain closer to Europe — a sentiment that was echoed at some of the fringe meetings.

Ann Webster, a headteacher from Leicester, is talking passionately about conversations she has had with her Brexit-voting community at home: "People are not stupid, they have noticed that they are poorer after Brexit."

And indeed, Burnham acknowledged in his speech that "Brexit has not given us control — Brexit has done more harm than good."

He promised to build consensus around a new relationship with Europe, without going into details.

World.title: North Korea has recently completed two road bridges easing transport to strategic allies Russia and China
World.content:
Two recently opened bridges are expected to ease trade and transport between North Korea and its powerful neighbors. The new connections come as Pyongyang builds strategic ties with China and Russia.

A long-delayed bridge linking North Korea and China could finally open in early October, more than a decade after its completion, as Pyongyang simultaneously expands transport links with Russia.

South Korean news outlets have reported that the New Yalu River Bridge, connecting China's northeastern city of Dandong with the trade hub of Sinuiju in northwestern North Korea, could formally open by October 6, which marks the 77th anniversary of North Korea-China diplomatic relations.

Analysis published by the 38 North think tank showed significant progress on customs, immigration and warehouse facilities on the North Korean side, where construction had remained largely unfinished for years.

The cable-stayed New Yalu River Bridge is located about 15 kilometers (9 miles) downstream toward the Yellow Sea from the older crossings connecting central Dandong and Sinuiju.

The four-lane road bridge stretches over 3,000 meters across the river, with a network of approach roads connecting it to the surrounding areas.

It was intended to ease pressure on the aging Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which carries both road and rail traffic and remains one of the most important routes between North Korea and China, Pyongyang's top trading partner.

Improving links to both Russia and China

The expected opening of the improved link with China comes after a road bridge crossing the Tumen River located across the peninsula was opened on September 7 connecting North Korea's Rason region with Khasan in Russia's Primorsky region.

Until then, the two countries' narrow land border had been connected by rail but not by road.

"North Korea allowed the Chinese bridge to sit unused for more than a decade, but North Korea hurried more than Russia did," Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW.

That difference, he argues, provides clues to Pyongyang's strategy, which appears to be deliberately managing the pace of its improving relations with Russia and China to avoid returning to excessive dependence on Beijing.

"If it depends too much on China as it did in the past, North Korea's autonomy could be undermined," Han said, adding that Pyongyang is seeking to take advantage of good ties with both China and Russia while preserving its independence.

The former Unification Ministry official added that Russia has an interest in expanding transport routes through North Korea toward the Pacific, including through the port of Rajin, while Pyongyang could benefit from increased trade, tourism and opportunities to send workers to Russia.

He added that Russia needs North Korean labor, arguing that North Korean workers are more diligent than their Russian counterparts.

China, meanwhile, has its own reasons to ensure that North Korea does not become excessively reliant on Russia, the former official said.

"From China's perspective, it needs to keep North Korea from leaning too far toward Russia," Han said.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have grown since 2023, when North Korea began providing weapons and troops for the Ukraine war. As the Russia-North Korea strategic relationship has deepened, China has been taking steps to reassert itself as the North's primary partner.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said the bridges have added geopolitical implications.

"Pyongyang could now use its deepening ties with China and Russia, along with Trump's interest in engaging Kim, to strengthen its diplomatic leverage and take a more assertive approach toward South Korea," Ahn told DW.

North Korea slowly reopens

Pyongyang virtually sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, sharply reducing trade and restricting even the entry of foreign diplomats.

Cross-border freight trains between Dandong and Sinuiju resumed in 2022. Passenger trains followed on March 12 this year, restoring rail travel between North Korea and China for the first time in six years.

Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ahn described the prospective bridge opening as historically significant.

"The New Yalu River Bridge is effectively the first modern bridge between North Korea and China," Ahn said.

Plans for a new bridge date to 2009, when then-Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and North Korean officialsagreed on the project to relieve the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, built in 1943.

Construction on the new bridge began in 2011, largely financed by Beijing, and the bridge itself was essentially completed in 2014. The opening was complicated by delays on building a customs center on the North Korean side.

Ahn added the opening could be interpreted as a signal that Pyongyang intends to move toward greater economic openness, even if that process proceeds slowly.

Yalu River Bridge to bolster China trade

A former senior South Korean Unification Ministry official, who requested anonymity, told DW that renewed trade could also benefit China's northeastern provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang.

Before sanctions and the pandemic disrupted commerce, businesses in the region imported North Korean goods, including seafood, while Chinese products flowed in the opposite direction.

"Both sides need this," the former official said.

North Korea needs Chinese goods and opportunities to earn foreign currency, while parts of northeastern China can benefit from renewed cross-border commerce, he added.

The official said the long delay also reflected Pyongyang's previous reluctance to build customs, logistics and other infrastructure required on its side.

The bridge itself was completed several years ago, but its opening has been delayed Image: Yomiuri Shimbun/AP Photo/picture alliance

"The fact that it is opening now means North Korea has built customs, clearance facilities and logistics warehouses," he said. "From that perspective, North Korea needs it more. It now needs goods coming in from China."

Former South Korean intelligence official Han expects the new crossing to accelerate trade recovery toward pre-pandemic trade levels.

"The opening of the Yalu River bridge will further stimulate trade between North Korea and China," Han told DW.

North Korea particularly needs imports for construction and industrial production, including factory components, he said.

But Han cautioned against expecting an uncontrolled trade boom.

He pointed to Pyongyang's increasingly centralized trade system, under which the state has tightened control over imports instead of allowing individual factories and enterprises to conduct commerce more independently.

A shortage of foreign currency could provide another constraint, Han said, pointing to the sharp rise in the unofficial exchange rate for the US dollar inside North Korea.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Women and children displaced by Nepal's floods say safe housing, privacy and stability remain out of reach as they try to rebuild their lives
World.content:
Families living in temporary shelters in northern Nepal say safety and privacy remain out of reach as concerns about trafficking and abuse mount.

One month after deadly flash floods in Nepal swept away Karishma Tamang's community in Rasuwa District, the pregnant 26-year-old is still struggling to find a safe place to call home.

Karishma, who is expecting her second child, has been moving from place to place with her 4-year-old daughter since the devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border at the end of August.

"Initially, we were kept in a covered hall at Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District," she told DW, adding that hundreds of people shared the same shelter for days.

"Now we have shifted to a small makeshift family tent at the nearby Barahachaur area. Still, we can't sleep during rainy nights as it leaks when it rains." Her brother and his two children remain missing after the flood.

Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

There is no proper toilet, although a small makeshift latrine has been set up near the tents, Karishma said.

Children and pregnant women like Karishma need privacy and safety, but such facilities remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas.

"It would be great to have a stable place to stay, where I could cook my own meals, feel safe and have some comfort," she said.

Safety concerns in temporary shelters

The August 26 flood, triggered by a glacier collapse along the Nepal-China border, killed about 1,450 people and left more than 5,500 missing. Reconstruction costs are estimated to be $4.8 billion (€4.2 billion).

At least seven people, including girls, women and local volunteers at temporary shelters and camps, spoke to DW. Although none reported experiencing sexual harassment or abuse, their accounts point to widespread concerns about safety and vulnerability in the aftermath of the floods.

Sabita Tamang, who lost her 5-year-old daughter, nephew and niece in the floods, is also staying in a makeshift tent in Barahachaur. The 24-year-old said she has to travel beyond the nearest tap to bathe and collect water.

Privacy and safety remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas Image: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

"We feel uncomfortable taking a bath in an open space among strangers and unknown locals," she told DW. "Many children have seen their family members, friends and neighbors caught in the floods," she said, raising concerns about the impact on their mental health and education.

Risk of trafficking and abuse

Save the Children Nepal has warned that protection measures for children and their families must be strengthened across flood-affected areas amid concerns about trafficking, violence, exploitation and child marriage.

Many families have moved into rented rooms. Yet hundreds are being housed in temporary shelters and makeshift tents in Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

Save the Children Nepal raised concerns about privacy and safety for girls and women because unfamiliar people have unrestricted access to shared spaces.

Ayush Joshi, director for advocacy, campaigns, communications and media at Save the Children Nepal, told DW that the organization's report was based on qualitative assessments involving affected people, including women and children, as well as volunteers deployed in flood-hit areas.

The disaster has affected more than 80,000 people. Thousands who lost everything are living in emergency shelters Image: Pedro Pardo/AFP

"Many temporary shelters are built without planning. Camps on the outskirts of towns have inadequate lighting at night and lack separate washrooms and private spaces," Joshi told DW, noting that there is unrestricted access for unfamiliar people.

"Such situations naturally increase the risk of insecurity, potential harassment and exploitation, especially for young girls and children."

According to Joshi, in the aftermath of the disaster, many people became separated from their families, while some children lost their lives and older siblings had to become caregivers for younger siblings.

"In such circumstances, cases of school dropouts and child marriage could increase," he added, referring to Save the Children's field assessment . "We have seen many children facing mental health issues, like becoming angry, frightened and crying loudly. There is a need for socio-emotional healing."

What does the government say?

The Nepali government has also assessed the risks of trafficking and potential child abuse and has collaborated with organizations such as Save the Children, the police and local authorities to strengthen protection measures at displacement sites.

After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chakra Bahadur Budha, spokesperson at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, said the government had increased monitoring and surveillance and was raising awareness about gender-based violence and trafficking.

"We have mobilized and kept all relevant stakeholders on high alert to check at points of entry and exit, so as to protect affected people from being trafficked or abused," he told DW.

Authorities took back at least 78 children from two Buddhist monasteries in Kathmandu and placed them in temporary camps. Budha explained that the monasteries had rescued and supported the children, offering long-term shelter, education and employment, but the government discourages such arrangements outside established procedures.

"We have strictly discouraged religious or charitable organizations from keeping children without following legal procedures," Budha told DW. "Adoption has also been discouraged for now, but children can be placed with close relatives, such as uncles and aunts, for their protection after verification of their relationship."

The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said at least 541 children have either lost their parents or become separated from their families.

Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centers in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction
World.content:
Spain's cabinet ministers said they have consensus on new measures to curb the housing crisis in the country after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen last week from her apartment sparked protests.

Spain's coalition government on Tuesday said it has agreed new measures to tackle the country's housing crisis after the forceful removal of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment in Madrid last week, sparked nationwide solidarity protests.

Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said the housing legislation includes a ban on evictions until 2030, tighter rules for short-term rentals and a two-year extension for existing leases.

"It's ‌time ​to intervene in the speculative housing market and ​begin to rebalance the scales between ⁠citizens ​and vulture funds," ​Garcia, who belongs ​to the ‌leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, ​wrote ⁠in a post on ⁠X.

Legislation still needs to pass through parliament

The Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.

But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.

Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.

Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.

A case that triggered mass protests in Spain

Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.

Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.

Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.

Thousands demonstrate against evictions and the housing crisis in Spain Image: Richard Zubelzu/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Demonstrators set up camps at Puerta del Sol square Image: David Canales/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Protesters were angry that Maricarmen was removed from the apartment she lived in since 1956 Image: Bruno Thevenin/Middle East Images/picture alliance

According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.

The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.

Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.

She is a wheelchair user too.

People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.

More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.

Maricarmen to return home because of 'social mobilization,' lawyer says

Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."

"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.

"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

World.title: Albania: As corruption cases multiply, experts question whether the anti-corruption drive is addressing the causes or just the symptoms.
World.content:
From a former president to the ex-intelligence chief, Albania is prosecuting senior officials at a rate once thought impossible. But do more prosecutions mean less corruption or simply better enforcement?

On September 22, the head of Albania's State Intelligence Service, Vlora Hyseni, was in Baku, Azerbaijan, attending an international conference of intelligence service chiefs. Back in Tirana, the Special Court had ordered her house arrest over two suspected criminal offences: supporting the perpetrator of a crime and disclosure of investigative secrecy.

The investigation into Hyseni emerged from a wider corruption case involving the National Agency for Information Society (AKSHI), the agency responsible for much of Albania's digital public infrastructure.

Prosecutors suspect that she used information available to her as intelligence chief to help a person wanted in that investigation.

Hyseni turned herself in to the Albanian authorities later that day and remains under house arrest as the investigation continues. She has since been dismissed as head of the intelligence service.

Rise in criminal proceedings and investigations

Hyseni's case is the latest in a series of criminal proceedings that have reached unusually high into Albania's political and state establishment.

Political scientist Afrim Krasniqi says that after the 2016 reform, Albania's new justice institutions were expected to 'focus on high-level corruption and "VIP" cases' Image: Afrim Krasniqi/Privatarchiv

A former president has spent almost two years in detention, a former prime minister is on trial, the mayor of Tirana has been behind bars since early 2025, two former deputy prime ministers under Prime Minister Edi Rama have also faced criminal proceedings, and investigations have been launched into senior officials in agencies controlling large areas of public spending and state infrastructure.

These are all separate cases, but they all involve alleged abuse of public power.

How did Albania get here?

For years, the problem was completely the opposite: High-level corruption in Albania was widely associated with impunity.

This is why bringing senior political figures accused of wrongdoing before the courts became one of the central expectations of the justice reform launched in 2016.

"The expectation was that the new justice institutions would focus on high-level corruption and 'VIP' cases," says Afrim Krasniqi, a political scientist and executive director of the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. "There were individuals who stood above the law, and impunity was pronounced," he told DW.

Dorian Matlija says that Albania is 'becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it' Image: Kristi Çavo

The reform fundamentally reshaped Albania's justice system and created new institutions to investigate corruption and organized crime, including the Special Anti-Corruption Structure, SPAK.

But the change was not immediate. Building the new institutions took years, and older cases were often more difficult to investigate.

For Dorian Matlija, a lawyer and executive director of Albanian civil society organization Res Publica, the number of senior officials now facing criminal proceedings does not necessarily mean that corruption is more widespread today than it was in the past.

"What has changed significantly is the institutional reaction," Matlija told DW. "Today, SPAK is a specialized structure with greater independence, stronger capacities and international support, as well as the willingness to undertake investigations that have broken the myth of the untouchability of senior officials."

The other side of accountability

But bringing senior officials before the courts is only one measure of whether institutions are working.

Albania applied for EU membership in 2009 and was granted candidate status in June 2014. Pictured here: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen (both center) Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

By the time a corruption case reaches prosecutors, the alleged abuse has already taken place. For Matlija, this is where Albania's progress is far less clear.

"We are becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it," he said.

Matlija points to the institutions and mechanisms that are supposed to act before a case becomes criminal: administrative controls, audits, conflict-of-interest rules and asset declarations. In his assessment, these have often proved ineffective.

The European Commission's 2025 report on Albania reaches a similar conclusion. It said that SPAK has made "tangible progress towards a solid track record in the fight against corruption." At the same time, the report says that corruption remains widespread and that "the institutional framework for prevention of corruption continued to have a limited impact."

The impact on citizens

The problem is also visible in citizens' encounters with public officials.

In a 2023 survey by the anti-corruption and good governance coalition SELDI (Southeast Europe Leadership for Development and Integrity) , 52% of respondents in Albania said they had experienced corruption pressure from public officials, while 40% reported having paid a bribe.

Krasniqi sees the problem in broader political terms. Albania has been governed by Rama's Socialist Party since 2013, and the party currently holds an outright majority in parliament. He argues that this prolonged political dominance has weakened the checks and balances that should constrain the executive.

"We have a deformed system," he said. "The head of the executive controls the executive, parliament and institutions."

He argues that this concentration of power has been accompanied by informal networks of influence, with people outside state institutions able to shape political decisions, legislation and the use of public assets.

Rama has repeatedly maintained that criminal responsibility is individual when investigations have reached senior officials. Responding to the Hyseni case, he returned to the same position.

"When a senior official has opened an account with justice, the case of the former intelligence chief is an individual matter between her and the justice system," Rama said.

What does this mean for Albania's EU accession hopes?

In May, the EU confirmed that the country had met the interim benchmarks for the "fundamentals" cluster, which includes the rule of law, and moved into a phase focused on implementation and lasting results.

Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index shows Albania improving from 33 points in 2012 to 39 in 2025 but still ranking below all EU member states.

For Matlija, Albania's efforts to advance EU integration helped create the conditions that allowed institutions such as SPAK to become stronger and more independent.

"The EU no longer demands only the adoption of laws and reforms, but also concrete and sustainable results. This creates constant pressure for justice institutions to be genuinely effective and independent of political power," he said.

For Krasniqi, this is also where the meaning of European integration lies. Membership, he argues, should not be judged only by Albania's progress through the formal accession process, but by whether the country itself changes.

"The essence should be for Albania, Albanian society and Albanian institutions to change and improve, so that we become worthy of integration," he said. For him, that change should also be felt by citizens through greater social security, prosperity and independence, rather than being just a series of formal achievements.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
