World.title: Poland offers to host facility producing Patriot missiles for Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the factory could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security. The news was revealed by deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who also confirmed that Poland would seek to establish a Patriot servicing and production facility even if it does not host Ukraine’s. Poland wants to host Patriot production Poland has proposed that the US and Ukraine launch joint production of Patriot missiles. Warsaw is citing security concerns and is proposing to host the facility in Poland instead of Ukraine: “If such a factory is planned to be built in… pic.twitter.com/syCkNt0o0V — Belsat in English (@Belsat_Eng) September 27, 2026 Patriot missile systems have been a key part of Ukraine’s defence against Russian aerial attacks. However, Kyiv has suffered from a shortage of missiles used in the system, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to appeal to allies to transfer their interceptors as well as to allow Ukraine to produce them itself. US President Donald Trump initially told Zelensky at a meeting in July that “we are gonna give you a licence to make Patriots”. However, he then backtracked on that offer later the same month. But, following weeks of uncertainty, on Friday last week Zelensky claimed that Trump had personally told him he had made a “final decision” to approve a licence for Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles. Washington has not confirmed that development. Asked about the issue on Saturday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told broadcaster TVN, “let’s see if it happens”. However, she added that, “we proposed that, if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in the so-called safe territory”. Poland is already the primary hub for military equipment, goods and people being transported in and out of its eastern neighbour. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that, regardless of where the plant serving Ukraine is located, Poland would also still seek to establish a facility for servicing and, eventually, production of Patriots. “What my interlocutors in Washington confirmed is that, even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, it does not change our efforts and does not rule out consent for Poland,” she said. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka was in Washington last week for talks with US officials. In May this year, another deputy defence minister, Cezary Tomczyk, told TVN that Poland had “received preliminary approval from the US State Department to produce missiles for Patriot systems”. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 In 2018, as part of its Wisła air defence programme, Poland signed a $4.75bn contract to purchase Patriot launchers and missiles from the US. In October 2023, the first Patriot systems procured from the US were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport. In December 2025, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries. Poland also has an agreement to domestically produce launchers for Patriot systems through cooperation between Polish state-owned defence contractor Huta Stalowa Wola SA and US defence giant Raytheon. Poland has announced a $1.2bn deal that will see a Polish state-owned defence firm manufacture 48 launchers for Patriot missile systems domestically in cooperation with US defence giant Raytheon https://t.co/PQOjKvhqYM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2024 The issue of Ukraine’s need for more Patriot missiles caused domestic political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition reacted angrily to reports that the government had handed over some interceptors to Ukraine. In July, the government confirmed that it had done so. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that only five missiles had been transferred to Ukraine. In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the Iran war had depleted America’s stockpile of Patriot missiles to 800 interceptors from roughly 2,300 before the war began. Last week, Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, confirmed that his country has also proposed that it could manufacture interceptors and perhaps even entire Patriot systems. World.title: “Don’t blame Ukrainian nation,” says Polish priest injured in deadly knife attack
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One of the priests injured in a knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland last week – which left one of his colleagues dead and another fighting for his life in hospital – has delivered a homily calling for people to forgive the attacker and not to blame Ukrainians as a whole for his actions. “I ask you not to repay evil with evil, but with love, support, understanding and care,” said a visibly injured Father Adrian Mantykiewicz. “I ask you to respect and support each other as two brotherly nations.” 🙏 Poruszające słowa ks. Adriana po ataku nożownika w Opactwie w Jarosławiu. W swojej pierwszej homilii po napaści duchowny mówił o przebaczeniu, miłości do bliźniego i odpowiadaniu dobrem nawet na doznaną krzywdę. pic.twitter.com/zGEGvC5meB — Goniec.pl (@GoniecPL) September 28, 2026 On Thursday last week, a 31-year-old Ukrainian man, who can be named only as Ihor H. under Polish privacy law, entered the grounds of the Benedictine abbey in the town of Jarosław. Using a knife he took from a kitchen, he attacked five people before he was stopped. One priest, Stanisław Zbojnowicz, died from his injuries shortly afterwards. Another, Marek Pieńkowski, is still being treated in hospital. Ihor H. was arrested at the scene and, on Saturday, a court approved a request from prosecutors for him to be placed in detention for three months. For now, he is being held in a psychiatric facility, with prosecutors saying that he “displayed symptoms of mental illness”. President @Zelensky has condemned an "evil" knife attack by a Ukrainian man at a Catholic abbey in Poland today, which left a priest dead and others injured Polish Prime Minister @donaldtusk says the perpetrator will face the “full severity of Polish law” https://t.co/SIonlR4JpJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Saturday, in a church that is part of the Benedictine abbey complex, Mantykiewicz celebrated the Eucharist for Zbojnowicz. With bruising under his left eye and bandages on his head and hand, he delivered a homily in which he addressed the attack, its victims, and the perpetrator. “I am a disciple of my master, a disciple of my lord, and Christ teaches me love,” he said. “And from this place, as a disciple of Jesus Christ, I wish to say very clearly in my name, in the name of Father Marek, and in the name of Father Stanisław, that we forgive.” “I ask you to pray for our tormentor,” he continued. “He needs this prayer most of all. Because no matter what happened, we must overcome the evil that occurred here in our abbey with goodness, love, and forgiveness.” Mantykiewicz also appealed for people not to blame Ukrainians more broadly for the incident. There have been fears that the attack could prompt a backlash against Ukrainians, Poland’s largest immigrant group, who have already been experiencing a growing number of hate crimes this year. “I also want to ask you not to blame the nation from which the perpetrator came,” said the priest. “The evil was committed by a specific person…responsible for their own actions. It was not done by other people. It was one person, one person alone.” “Let us be disciples of Christ. Disciples who help others with love, care, respect, help and kindness,” he continued. “It does not matter who they are, what nation they come from, what religion they are, or what colour their skin is; they are human beings…and we must not deprive anyone of their dignity.” On Friday, the head of the Polish Catholic church’s council for migrants and refugees, Bishop Krzysztof Zadarko, gave a press conference at which he condemned the “outpouring of aggression and artificially stoked hatred towards Ukrainians that this event [in Jarosław] has fuelled”. “The church can only appeal to the consciences, primarily of Catholics and Christians, but also of all people, that this is not the right response; it is downright reprehensible, and incompatible with the Gospel,” he added, quoted by broadcaster RMF. “We are dealing with a tremendous tragedy, but shifting the blame of one person onto an entire society, ethnic group, or nationality is wrong,” he added. Agresja i niechęć do kogokolwiek jest nie do pogodzenia z wiarą chrześcijańską – mówił przewodniczący Rady KEP ds. Migrantów i Uchodźców bp Krzysztof Zadarko podczas konferencji prasowej przed 112. Światowym Dniem Migranta i Uchodźcy.https://t.co/M46RXggVTR pic.twitter.com/uZWodfR7sG — EpiskopatNews (@EpiskopatNews) September 25, 2026 Thursday’s attack caused widespread shock and mourning in Poland, and also prompted condolences from Ukraine, including President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said that “we are shocked by this evil”. On Saturday, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told broadcaster TVN that he had spoken with Ihor M.’s mother and was able to provide more information about him. He confirmed that the man had left Ukraine in 2022 and lived in Germany. Bodnar, however, said that media reports claiming Ihor M. had served in the Ukrainian military were false. Regarding the motive, Bodnar said that it appears Ihor M. “had some kind of mental illness”. He pledged that the Ukrainian authorities would cooperate and were “working on all the information we can provide to the Polish side”. World.title: Russia condemns Polish city’s “barbaric” removal of Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the removal of a monument in the Polish city of Rzeszów expressing “gratitude” to the Soviet Red Army. It called the move “barbaric” and “sacrilegious”. The monument – part of which will be moved to a nearby Soviet cemetery and another to a museum – has been the subject of a long-running legal and political battle, amid wider debate in Poland about “decommunising” public spaces, especially in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 23 września 2026 r. w Rzeszowie (województwo podkarpackie), decyzją władz polskich i z naruszeniem dokumentów rosyjsko-polskich dotyczących ochrony obiektów dziedzictwa memorialnego, rozpoczęto proces demontażu pomnika wdzięczności żołnierzom… pic.twitter.com/HYuNeLG5dy — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) September 24, 2026 The Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army, standing 8.5 metres tall and weighing 6.6 tons, was erected in Rzeszów, southeastern Poland, shortly after the end of World War Two, when the Soviets had pushed Nazi Germany out of Poland and then installed their own communist government. It is located on Ghetto Victims Square, a public space also created after the war on the grounds of the city’s former Jewish cemetery, which had been destroyed by the German occupiers in 1942. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state historical body, notes that the monument was erected just a few metres from where two Polish anti-communist resistance fighters who had been members of the wartime Home Army (AK) had been publicly hanged by the communists. The monument’s plinth featured bas-relief sculptures depicting Red Army Generals Ivan Konev and Karol Świerczewski, soldiers, and industrial and agricultural workers carrying a hammer and sickle. At the top of the 8.5-metre column was a statue of a woman and child. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. That triggered a legal battle over the monument in Rzeszów. The government-appointed provincial governor and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body, moved to have it dismantled, arguing that the monument glorified communism. But city hall – led by left-wing mayor Tadeusz Ferenc, who had been a member of the communist party before 1989 – challenged the decision. It argued that the monument did not promote communism and noted that its name, referring to gratitude to the Red Army, was not an official one. In 2019, the provincial administrative court sided with the city and overturned the decision to remove the monument. However, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 prompted many Polish municipalities that had not removed Soviet-era monuments to begin doing so. In April 2022, Rzeszów’s current mayor, Konrad Fijołek, announced that his city’s monument would be taken from its current location and placed in a Soviet soldiers’ cemetery elsewhere in the city. “In principle, I am not in favour of dismantling or demolishing monuments, as they are a testament to history,” said the mayor. “But in light of the current wartime reality, this monument should not remain in its current location. But we are not barbarians; we will not demolish the monument, but relocate it.” However, the IPN opposed the idea of relocating the monument and refused to cover the costs of doing so. It wanted it to be eliminated entirely. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 As a result, the city is paying 156,000 zloty (€35,700) for the monument to be taken away, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. The bas-reliefs will go to the Soviet cemetery while the statue of mother and child will go to the city’s Museum of Technology and the Military. Work to remove the monument began this week and is expected to last until November. Once the above-ground section has been removed, a special conservation committee, including a representative of Poland’s Rabbinical Commission for Cemeteries, will determine how to proceed with the monument’s foundation. The beginning of the removal work prompted anger from Moscow, with the Russian embassy in Warsaw issuing a statement that called it a “sacrilegious step”. It demanded “the immediate cessation of work” and restoration of the monument to its previous state. “With regret, we must state once again: the barbaric policy of the Polish authorities, consisting of destroying everything that serves as evidence of the invaluable feat of the soldiers and officers of the Red Army in liberating Poland from Nazi occupation, is being continued at an ever faster pace,” they continued. Russia regards the Soviet Union’s driving Nazi Germany out of Central and Eastern Europe at the end of World War Two as a “liberation”. However, many in the region reject that term, given that it involved bringing their countries under brutal Soviet domination instead. In its statement, the Russian embassy also claimed that the actions in Rzeszów are a “violation of Russian-Polish documents concerning the protection of memorial heritage sites”. Moscow regularly claims that Poland’s removal of Soviet memorials violates a 1994 agreement between the two countries on respect for graves and other places of memory. It did so in August this year, when protesting the demolition of a monument in the town of Pyrzyce. However, Poland points out that the agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Rzeszów is also home to one of the famous – or infamous, depending on one’s perspective – communist-era monuments in Poland, the 38-metre-tall Monument to the Revolutionary Struggle. It has become a landmark of the city. In 2017, the IPN recommended that it be removed under the “decommunisation” law. The owners of the land upon which it sits also wanted to demolish it. However, mayors Ferenc and Fijołek sought to protect the monument, and their efforts succeeded last year, when it was added to Poland’s list of protected monuments, preventing it from being destroyed. World.title: Polish president “doesn’t like” Trump inviting Putin to G20 but will still attend summit
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish President Karol Nawrocki “does not like” the fact that the Trump administration has invited Vladimir Putin to this year’s G20 summit in the United States, says his chief foreign policy aide. However, Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, still plans to attend the event – which Poland has been invited to as a guest rather than a full G20 member – in order to represent Polish interests and push for full membership of the group. 🔴 "Nie podoba nam się to". Nawrocki ma problem po decyzji Trumpa Prezydent Karol Nawrocki weźmie udział w grudniowym szczycie G20 w Miami, na który zaproszono również Władimira Putina. Szef Biura Polityki Międzynarodowej Kancelarii Prezydenta Marcin Przydacz przyznał na antenie… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 26, 2026 The G20, a major intergovernmental forum, holds an annual summit whose location rotates among members. This year’s event will take place in December at a golf resort in Miami owned by Trump. On Wednesday this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Trump has invited Putin to attend the summit, saying that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage…with other world leaders” and “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept”. “If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens,” added Rubio. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.” Marco Rubio on Russia: We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with Trump, but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he will accept. pic.twitter.com/e0GSz7Y8gm — Clash Report (@clashreport) September 23, 2026 Last December, Rubio also announced Poland’s invitation to the summit as a guest, saying that it would be “assuming its rightful place in the G20”. In May this year, the US also “expressed its strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member”. Poland will be represented by Nawrocki, who is a vocal critic of Putin and Russia, and is himself on a Russian wanted list for his work leading efforts to demolish Soviet-era monuments in Poland. In an interview on Sunday with news website Wirtualna Polska, the head of Nawrocki’s international policy office, Marcin Przydacz, was asked if the US was right to invite Putin. “We don’t like it,” he replied. “But we were invited to the G20 summit as guests, and it’s not our role to tell the participants who should be part of it,” he added, noting that Russia is a founding member of the G20. However, “if it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums.” Nevertheless, “President [Nawrocki] is going to Miami and doesn’t intend to change his plans at this stage”, confirmed Przydacz. “Poland will be at the G20 summit because it’s in our interest…This isn’t the only format in which we sit with countries we disagree with.” However, he also added that, “if the Russian leader actually intends to come, and is not just invited, we will discuss this with our European and Euro-Atlantic allies”. Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially due to the COVID-19 pandemic and later amid the fallout from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against him. The US is not a member of the ICC, so the arrest warrant does not apply on its territory. Przydacz told Wirtualna Polska that Putin “should be held accountable for his crimes”. Asked if Nawrocki would shake hands with the Russian president at the G20, Przydacz said that he “doesn’t think any interactions will occur”. The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026 He also emphasised that Poland’s invitation to the summit was a “major success, demonstrating our growing role”. He said that Nawrocki would use the event to push its ambition to become a full member of the group. He added that it would also seek to “bring a Central European perspective” to the event, representing the entire region, which has so far been excluded from the G20. Earlier this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that, in his opinion, the US should make Putin’s invitation to the G20 conditional upon Russia implementing a ceasefire in Ukraine, reported news website Interia. However, he noted that, when a G20 meeting of finance ministers took place in the US earlier this year, Poland had attended alongside Russia. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support to its eastern neighbour. Poland has also been one of the primary targets of Russia’s hybrid actions against European countries, including airspace violations, acts of sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation. World.title: Czech Study Finds Supporting Homeless People Can Save Public Money
World.content:
A Czech experiment in which homeless people received CZK 100,000 with no conditions attached suggests that early financial support can reduce some of the costs associated with homelessness.

The project, known as New Leaf, was carried out by the Czech organization Neposeda in cooperation with researchers from Charles University.



The findings indicate that the state spends an average of about CZK 200,000 a year on each person experiencing homelessness, with healthcare, social services and police work accounting for a significant share of the total.

The researchers concluded that leaving people without support can ultimately be more expensive for public finances than providing targeted assistance.

How the New Leaf experiment worked

The project ran from summer 2024 until the end of 2025 and was inspired by a similar initiative in Canada.

Researchers focused on people who had been living on the streets for no more than two and a half years. The aim was to examine whether intervention at an earlier stage of homelessness could prevent longer-term problems.

Participants were divided into several groups. Forty people received CZK 100,000 without restrictions on how the money could be used. Another 20 were offered the support of a personal social worker instead, while 40 people formed a control group and received no additional assistance.

The study initially involved 100 people. One participant died from a serious illness shortly after the project began, leaving 99 participants in the final research sample.

The researchers tracked participants’ use of public services and their contact with state authorities, including emergency medical services, hospitals, outpatient healthcare, social services and police.

Healthcare accounts for the largest share

The study estimates that the state spends around CZK 200,000 annually on each homeless person.

Healthcare represented almost 43% of the estimated expenditure. Low-threshold services, which provide basic support and a safe place for people experiencing homelessness, accounted for around a quarter of the total.

Police work represented another 9%, or more than 18,000 crowns per person each year.

The wider cost to public finances

Data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs recorded 11,641 homeless people in the Czech Republic in the previous year.

Based on the estimated annual cost per person, direct public expenditure associated with homelessness amounts to roughly 2.33 billion crowns a year.

World.title: Smartwings Cuts Prague Flights as Winter Schedule Shrinks
World.content:
Smartwings is reducing its winter flight schedule from Prague, with several routes being cancelled, frequencies cut and new connections postponed until spring 2027.

The biggest changes will affect Spain, a popular choice for Czech travelers looking for warmer weather during the autumn and winter months.

The airline will suspend flights between Prague and Valencia from November 2 until the beginning of March.

Flights to several other Spanish destinations will also be reduced. Smartwings will cut its Málaga service from two flights a day to one, while Barcelona will move from daily flights to four to six services a week.

Flights to Mallorca will be reduced from four per week to two. The Prague–Madrid route will continue, but flights will operate on an irregular schedule.

Smartwings is also suspending flights from Prague to Nice until early March.

New Prague routes pushed back

Several routes that were expected to launch this year will now have to wait until spring 2027.

The postponed connections include new services to Venice and Bergen, Norway. Smartwings has also delayed the return of flights to Brussels and Bucharest.

Both Brussels and Bucharest were suspended in the spring, with Smartwings originally planning to restore the routes in October.

Eurowings also reduces Prague services

Eurowings is making changes to its Prague schedule as well. The German carrier has cancelled its planned winter flights to Madeira, Portugal.

The route had been scheduled to return for the winter season, but Eurowings will instead offer tickets to Madeira through a partnership with Smartwings, which continues to operate flights to the Portuguese island.

Eurowings will also suspend its Prague–Stockholm service for most of January.

Higher fuel costs affect airline schedules

The changes come as airlines face higher operating costs linked to fuel prices.

According to Eurocontrol, the European organization responsible for coordinating air traffic management, jet fuel prices in Europe more than doubled between the beginning of the year and mid-September.

Airlines around the world have been adjusting schedules as fuel costs fluctuate amid the conflict in the Middle East. Route cancellations and reduced frequencies are among the measures carriers are using to adapt to changing market conditions.

World.title: Home Baking Returns to Czech Kitchens as Flour Sales Rise
World.content:
Home baking is gaining momentum in the Czech Republic, with online supermarket Rohlik.cz reporting a sharp increase in demand for baking ingredients this year.

Flour has been at the center of the trend. Sales of organic flour have risen by almost 72 percent compared with the previous year, while conventional flour sales increased by around 23 percent.



The change has also affected the balance of sales. Organic flour previously accounted for about 19 percent of flour purchases at Rohlik.cz. That figure has now climbed to almost 25 percent.

The figures suggest that customers are not simply buying more flour but are also paying greater attention to the type and quality of the ingredients they use.

Rohlik.cz CEO Miroslava Vopatová says baking continues to play a role in family life, particularly as an activity shared across generations. The supermarket has responded by offering products at different price points, from private-label options to organic and farm-produced ingredients.

Yeast sales tell a different story

The increase in demand for flour has not been mirrored by yeast.

Sales of yeast have been gradually falling since the surge in home baking during the coronavirus pandemic. One shift remains noticeable, however: shoppers are increasingly choosing fresh yeast rather than dried yeast.

Home baking in the Czech Republic is also strongly seasonal. Christmas remains the busiest period of the year, while a smaller increase usually occurs in March and April. Demand drops during the summer months.

For experienced bakers, the quality of the final product often depends on relatively simple details. Yeast dough needs enough time and warmth to rise properly, while rushing the process can affect the result.

The preparation of the filling matters as well. Curd cheese should be drained thoroughly before being added to a cake or pastry, reducing the risk of excess moisture making the dough soggy. Fruit fillings should also be sufficiently thick rather than watery.

These practical details can make a noticeable difference, particularly in traditional Czech pastries whose recipes are often passed down through families.

World.title: New Flights from Prague to Asia Boost Competition on Airfares
World.content:
Travelers flying from Prague this autumn have more options as airlines add capacity and new direct connections, particularly to Asia.

At the same time, increased competition is putting pressure on carriers to keep fares under control, according to data from Czech booking portal Letuška.cz.



The biggest changes are visible on long-haul routes. New services from Prague are making destinations in Asia more accessible, while airlines already serving the Czech market are responding with promotional fares.

“Thanks to high competition and new capacity from Prague, the autumn flight market offers very favorable travel conditions,” said Josef Trejbal, commercial director of Letuška.cz. He said the arrival of new Asian connections has helped revive demand for long-haul travel and encouraged established airlines to introduce more competitive offers.

Direct flights strengthen Prague’s links with Asia

Asia is once again attracting greater interest from Czech travelers. One factor is the growing number of direct or more convenient connections from Prague, which can reduce the need for lengthy transfers through major Middle Eastern hubs.

STARLUX Airlines, for example, is offering flights from Prague to Taipei from around CZK 21,000. The direct service provides an alternative to itineraries involving a stopover and can save travelers both time and, depending on the itinerary, money.

Another new option will be available from October 10, when flights to Hanoi are scheduled to begin on the Prague–Almaty–Hanoi route. Tickets listed through Letuška.cz start at around CZK 18,000.

The expansion comes as airlines compete more aggressively for passengers on long-haul routes departing from Prague.

Caribbean and Latin America see strong growth

Europe remains the most popular region for Czech travelers, but demand for long-haul destinations is also changing. According to Letuška.cz, Latin America and the Caribbean have recorded the sharpest year-on-year increases, with demand growing by hundreds of percent in some cases.

The Caribbean in particular has benefited from rising interest among travelers looking beyond Europe. Latin American destinations have also seen a significant increase in bookings compared with the same period last year.

The stronger demand is coinciding with changes in the competitive landscape. New routes from Prague are challenging airlines that have traditionally carried passengers to Asia and Australia through Middle Eastern hubs.

Major Gulf carriers including Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad are responding with promotional fares, adding further pressure to ticket prices.

World.title: Five Free Things to Do in Prague This October
World.content:
Prague will offer a range of free cultural events in October, from exhibitions and science films to family entertainment and hands-on craft workshops.

Several major institutions will also open their doors to the public on October 28, Czech Independence Day.



Here are five events where the main program is free, followed by a guide to some of the places that can be visited without charge on the October 28 public holiday.

Free admission at the National Gallery

October 3–4 and October 28, 10:00 AM–6:00 PM

The National Gallery Prague will offer free access to selected exhibitions on two occasions in October.

On October 3 and 4, visitors can see 1956–1989: Architecture for Everyone at the Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác) without paying an entrance fee. The offer forms part of Architecture Day, this year’s festival built around the theme “I Dwell, Therefore I Am.”

The Architecture Day program will also include free tours and workshops at several National Gallery sites, including the Trade Fair Palace, the Convent of St. Agnes of Bohemia and Schwarzenberg Palace. Some activities require advance registration.

Another opportunity comes on October 28, when the National Gallery will waive admission to its eight permanent exhibitions. The program includes medieval and Old Master collections as well as exhibitions covering the First Republic, the period from 1939 to 2021 and Asian art.

The free admission applies to the specified permanent collections and does not cover all temporary exhibitions. The gallery is also preparing additional activities for the public holiday.

Midnight Circus brings family entertainment to Prague 8

October 3, 10:00 AM–7:00 PM and October 4, 10:00 AM–12:00 PM – DDM Prague 8 – Spirála, Přemyšlenská 15

The Spirála Children and Youth Center in Kobylisy will become a temporary circus venue during the first weekend of October.

Midnight Circus will feature clowns, fortune tellers, a storyteller and a House of Horrors, alongside other attractions aimed at families. Visitors can also enter a themed bathhouse.

The daytime program is free and does not require advance registration. Instead of paying directly for individual attractions, visitors receive “Principálky” at the entrance, a special circus currency that can also be earned through activities during the event.

An evening show on Saturday will feature a UV light performance followed by a fire show. Unlike the daytime program, this performance requires a ticket costing CZK 50, payable in cash at the venue. It is not recommended for children younger than five.

Try traditional crafts at the New Town Hall

October 13–14, 8:00 AM–4:00 PM – New Town Hall, Karlovo náměstí 1/23, Prague 2

The New Town Hall will host the 13th edition of Crafts Live (Řemesla živě), an event designed to introduce visitors to traditional and practical trades and the schools where they can be studied.

Visitors will have the opportunity to try different crafts for themselves and speak directly with representatives of vocational schools about their courses and study programs.

Admission to the event is free, although some individual workshops may charge a fee.

Science documentaries come to Suchdol

October 19–22 – Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, Suchdol

The Prague Science Film Fest returns with a program of international science documentaries, including several Czech premieres.

The films explore subjects ranging from the way the human brain can mislead us to the role of fungi and the behavior of otters. Among the scheduled titles are How the Brain Tricks Us, My Otter Diary and The Kingdom of Fungi.

Film screenings will be accompanied by discussions with scientists, filmmakers and other experts, giving visitors an opportunity to explore the topics beyond the films themselves.

The festival will also include an outdoor screening of the Oscar-nominated documentary Fire of Love, an exhibition focused on antelope conservation in Africa and a filmmaking workshop.

Admission is free, and this year’s program does not require registration.

Where to go for free on October 28

October 28 is a public holiday in Czechia, marking the establishment of the independent Czechoslovak state in 1918. Several important Prague buildings traditionally open to visitors on the day.

Straka Academy

The seat of the Czech government will open its meeting rooms, press rooms and garden to the public. The exact visiting hours had not yet been announced at the time of publication.

Wallenstein Palace and Kolowrat Palace

The Czech Senate will open both buildings from 7:30 AM to 5:00 PM. Visitors will be able to see, among other areas, the Senate meeting hall.

Thun Palace

The Chamber of Deputies will open Thun Palace on Sněmovní Street from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM. Tours start at the main entrance at Sněmovní 4.

Municipal House

The representative rooms on the first floor, including Smetana Hall and the Mayor’s Hall, will be accessible free of charge from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. Guided commentary in Smetana Hall will be available every 15 minutes.

World.title: Czech Women Win Billie Jean King Cup Again After Eight Years
World.content:
Czech Republic eased past Ukraine to win the Billie Jean King Cup for the 12th time.

This year’s Wimbledon finalists Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova breezed past their opponents to secure a 2-0 victory and deny the Ukrainians a first title in the competition.



Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon, comfortably beat Anhelina Kalinina 6-2 6-3 in the opening singles match before Noskova’s 6-3 ⁠7-6 (7-5) win over world number seven Elina Svitolina ‌secured the title.

It is the Czechs’ first win at the event since 2018, making them the second-most successful nation in its history after the United States, who have 18 titles.

In her first year as Czechia captain, Barbora Strycova has made history.

Former Grand Slam doubles champion Strycova is just the fourth woman to win the Billie Jean King Cup as both a player and a captain. Strycova joins a Hall of Fame cast of Margaret Court, Chrissie Evert and Billie Jean King in achieving that feat.

CZECHIA'S NEW ALL-STARS ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS 🇨🇿🏆#BJKCup pic.twitter.com/W8B2WucxI0 — Billie Jean King Cup (@BJKCup) September 27, 2026

She’s also the first player in event history to win the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title as a player and the Billie Jean King Cup title as a player and a captain. Strycova won the Billie Jean King Cup juniors title alongside Petra Cetkovska and Lucie Safarova in 2001.

The Czechs also knocked out Great Britain in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen, China, which led GB captain Anne Keothavong to describe them as “the strongest team here”.

World.title: Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
World.content:
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.

The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.



The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.

Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.

The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.

Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.

This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.

Rollout will depend on local regulations

The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.

Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.

For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.

Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.

Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.

Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
World.content:
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).

The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.



Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.

One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.

Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.

“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”

Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.

The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.

The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

World.title: Budapest police apologise after journalist receives insulting, misogynistic internal email
World.content:
The Budapest Police Headquarters has apologised to an HVG journalist after an internal email describing her as a “screaming blue stocking” was apparently sent to her by mistake.

Journalist had requested interview on street harassment

HVG journalist Noémi Martini first contacted the communications department of the Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) in early September to request an interview with Budapest police chief Colonel Norbert Tamás Baricska about street harassment in the capital.

The request was initially turned down. Martini subsequently began collecting accounts from people who had experienced harassment on the streets through an anonymous questionnaire.

According to HVG, more than 300 stories were submitted within a few weeks, 93% of them from women. Most described sexual harassment on Budapest streets or on public transport.

The journalist then contacted the police again, asking whether another representative could discuss the issue, as the responses appeared to point to a broader problem.

BRFK spokesperson Soma Csécsi subsequently called Martini and asked her to send specific questions so that a suitable police representative could be found. The National Police Headquarters (ORFK) later responded in writing, but only answered some of the questions.

Martini then asked why she could not put her questions directly to a police representative and, if written answers were the only option, why only some of her questions had been addressed.

Internal email apparently sent to journalist

According to HVG, an email was sent to Martini a few hours later that appears to have been intended for police staff rather than the journalist herself.

The message began with “Dear Attila!” and included three police employees among the recipients. Discussing Martini’s interview request, it reportedly said that, according to Soma, “a screaming blue stocking” would not be given an interview by the Budapest police chief.

The term “blue stocking” is a derogatory expression traditionally used for a woman portrayed as overly intellectual or opinionated.

BRFK launches internal investigation

In a statement published on Tuesday, BRFK acknowledged the incident and apologised for the tone of the internal correspondence.

The police said the language used was “unacceptable” and did not reflect its communication standards or the ethical requirements associated with them. It stressed that respectful and factual communication is expected when dealing with journalists, members of the public and colleagues alike.

BRFK also addressed the underlying issue raised by the journalist, stating that street harassment of women is a real problem. It said both reported and unreported cases must be taken seriously and that all legally available means should be used to prevent such incidents.

“We apologise to the journalist, everyone affected and the public,” the police said, adding that an internal investigation would be launched into the incident.

The statement did not identify the employee or employees responsible for the wording of the email.

World.title: Fidesz: ‘Ukrainian mafia’ operatives have infiltrated Hungarian state institutions
World.content:
The Fidesz party claims that the “Ukrainian mafia” is paying dozens of people in Hungary who have already infiltrated state institutions. The opposition party also said that people allegedly “paid by Ukrainians” and making false accusations would eventually face legal consequences.

Fidesz made the claims in a statement sent to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Tuesday, accusing the “Ukrainian mafia” of transferring huge amounts of money through Hungary without restraint.

According to the party, Hungarian authorities put an end to this activity under the previous “national government”, and therefore deserve recognition rather than accusations. Fidesz added that the authorities would receive this recognition once the party “restores the rule of law in Hungary”.

USD 40 million and EUR 35 million in cash, plus gold, seized

According to the MTI report, officers from the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) and the Counter-Terrorism Centre (TEK) seized two vehicles on the M0 motorway on 5 March on suspicion of money laundering.

The vehicles, owned by Ukraine’s Oschadbank, were reportedly transporting USD 40 million and EUR 35 million in cash, as well as 9 kilograms of gold, from Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank to Ukraine.

The seven-member, unarmed crew was questioned the following day and subsequently expelled from Hungary. They later filed complaints alleging inhumane treatment and violations of their rights.

Former prosecutor says ‘gold convoy’ case was politically created

Pál Fürcht, former head of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office for Investigations, also commented on the case on Tuesday in an open letter published on the Facebook page of authorised lawyer Lóránt Horváth.

Fürcht wrote that experienced prosecutors at the Budapest Investigative Prosecutor’s Office concluded in May, based on the evidence collected up to that point, that the so-called “gold convoy case” was a case created for political reasons.

According to Fürcht, the investigation at the time indicated that then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán himself had instructed the intelligence services on 3 March to arrest the Ukrainian cash couriers on 5 March. (Read more details HERE.)

He claimed that, while carrying out the task allegedly set by politicians, the intelligence service consulted a department head at the Office of the Prosecutor General on 4 March, as well as the Prosecutor General himself.

Fürcht said that on 5 March, the intelligence service’s criminal complaint reached the investigative authorities within a record four to five hours, instead of the three-day period provided by law. He said this happened with the involvement of the Prosecutor General, the deputy Prosecutor General and another senior prosecutor.

The complaint reportedly came with an instruction from the prosecution service that an investigation had to be launched.

According to Fürcht, even this process was almost too slow, as the operation against the alleged gold convoy was already well underway.

He argued that if the leadership of the Office of the Prosecutor General had sent the instruction to launch the investigation even half a day later, the Ukrainian cash couriers would already have safely returned home and the task allegedly set by the prime minister could not have been carried out.

The Fidesz statement and Fürcht’s open letter offer different interpretations of the background to the case. The claims made public so far do not in themselves establish that “Ukrainian mafia” operatives had infiltrated Hungarian state institutions, or that the people referred to by Fidesz had made false accusations.

World.title: Exclusive interview: “The ‘N’ still stands for non-governmental, doesn’t it?” – Máté Hajba on EU-funded lobbying
World.content:
Máté Hajba is the director of Hungary’s Free Market Foundation, which has published a new report examining what it calls “circular lobbying” in Brussels: public institutions funding NGOs that, among their activities, seek to influence the policies of those same institutions. The report examines nine organisations, identifies roughly €12.8 million in annual public funding, and says around 96.8% of the public funding it identified came from the European Commission. Daily News Hungary spoke with Hajba about whether Brussels has created an echo chamber financed by European taxpayers.

Daily News Hungary: Let’s put this crudely. Brussels gives NGOs taxpayers’ money, some of those NGOs lobby Brussels, and Brussels then hears supposedly independent civil society demanding policies it helped finance. Is that really the system?

Máté Hajba: Put that way, it does sound exceptionally efficient, doesn’t it? You provide the money, help finance the advocacy, receive the advocacy, and then point to civil society as evidence of public demand for the policy. As a Hungarian, I saw how self-servingly such a practice worked in my country under the Orbán regime, which the EU so often and rightly criticised.

Of course, reality in the EU is more complicated, and we should not pretend that every euro in an EU grant is paying somebody to knock on an MEP’s door. Lobbying is legal, advocacy is legitimate, and EU funding does not automatically make an organisation a puppet of the European Commission.

But that is precisely why transparency matters. If these relationships are entirely proper, there should be no problem showing taxpayers exactly where the money goes and what activities it supports. “Trust us, it’s civil society” is not really a substitute for a receipt. This lack of transparency erodes trust in public institutions and NGOs, at a time of global turmoil when justly earned trust is most needed.

Daily News Hungary: You found roughly €12.8 million in annual public funding among just nine organisations, with about 96.8% of the public funding you identified coming from the European Commission. At what point does “independent civil society” start sounding like a rather creative accounting term?

Máté Hajba: The “N” in NGO still stands for “non-governmental,” as far as I am aware. That does not mean an NGO stops being independent the moment it receives a public grant. Plenty of organisations receive government or EU funding for perfectly legitimate work.

But when a public institution becomes a significant financial supporter of organisations that are simultaneously trying to influence public policy, taxpayers are entitled to ask whether the relationship is transparent enough. It is basic due diligence the EU owes to its taxpayers.

And there is a very simple way to test whether people genuinely believe the principle they are defending: reverse the politics. Imagine the Commission giving millions to organisations lobbying against climate regulation, against further tobacco restrictions, or for dramatically tighter migration rules. Would everyone who currently sees no problem suddenly become fascinated by the details of EU grant agreements?

If your standard of transparency changes depending on whether you like the cause, then you do not have a transparency standard. You have a favourite team.

Daily News Hungary: Brussels spends quite a lot of time telling member states how to manage public money. Are you essentially saying the EU should try some of its own medicine?

Máté Hajba: I would phrase it more politely, but since you have already phrased it for me: yes, consistency would be refreshing.

The European Union is right to demand transparency when public money is spent. The European Court of Auditors has itself identified shortcomings in the transparency of EU funding to NGOs. So the answer is not to abolish NGOs, ban lobbying, or silence organisations whose politics somebody dislikes. The answer is almost embarrassingly boring: publish the information properly.

Create one genuinely searchable system where a taxpayer can see how much public money an organisation receives, who provided it, under which program, what it was supposed to finance, and which advocacy activities are connected to that funding.

Then let everyone lobby. Environmentalists, businesses, trade unions, health campaigners, free-market organisations, everyone. Democracy is supposed to contain competing voices.

But when taxpayers are paying for some of those voices, taxpayers should be allowed to see the bill. If everything is above board, putting the receipt on the table should be the least controversial idea in Brussels.

World.title: Russian-linked forensic technology reached Hungarian police, US case reveals
World.content:
A company selling powerful digital forensic tools to law-enforcement agencies across Europe — including the Hungarian police — has been accused by US authorities of concealing its Russian ownership and the fact that its software was developed in Russia. The case has raised fresh questions over Russian surveillance software in Europe and the security of technologies used to access highly sensitive digital evidence.

As The Hungary Insider reported based on a POLITICO investigation, Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics worked with EU-backed projects and supplied technology to law-enforcement agencies across several European countries.

The company develops digital forensic software designed to extract, preserve and analyse information from electronic devices such as smartphones and computers. Such tools can be used by investigators to recover messages, photographs, location information and other data relevant to criminal investigations.

US prosecutors now allege, however, that Oxygen Forensics concealed significant aspects of who actually controlled the company and where its technology was developed.

Hungarian police bought Oxygen Forensics technology

Hungary is directly connected to the case.

According to a Hungarian government procurement document cited by POLITICO, Hungarian police signed an IT contract with Oxygen Forensics in December 2024 worth HUF 10.14 million (approximately EUR 26,000). The contract ran until December 2025.

The Hungarian example is significant because Oxygen’s technology is not an ordinary office software package. Digital forensic systems are specifically designed to work with information extracted from computers and mobile devices during investigations.

POLITICO reported that Oxygen products have also been used or recognised by law-enforcement authorities elsewhere in Europe, including Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland.

The company’s presence extended to EU-backed initiatives as well. Public records reviewed by POLITICO show that Oxygen was involved with two projects aimed at improving the handling and analysis of electronic evidence in criminal investigations.

The European Commission told the publication that Oxygen was not a member of the project consortia and therefore did not receive Commission funding through them.

If you missed it: Hungarian intelligence services undergo sweeping reorganisation after Orbán era

Why Russian surveillance software in Europe raises security concerns

For foreign readers, the significance of the case lies largely in what digital forensic software is capable of doing.

Unlike conventional business applications, forensic tools can operate close to some of the most sensitive information handled by police and investigative authorities. Their purpose is precisely to extract and analyse data from devices, potentially including communications, photographs, documents and other evidence.

This means that the identity of a supplier’s owners, the location of its developers and control over its software-development environment can become important security considerations.

The US Department of Justice alleges that Oxygen Forensics presented itself to American government customers as an independent US-based company, while five Russian nationals actually owned and controlled it through a Cyprus-based holding company. Prosecutors also allege that the software was developed by a team working in Russia.

The same five people also owned a Russian company which, according to the US authorities, sold versions of the technology to customers reportedly including Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), Investigative Committee and Interior Ministry.

These allegations are particularly sensitive in Europe following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which fundamentally changed the EU’s security relationship with Moscow.

No allegation that the software contained malicious code

There is an important distinction in the case. The US criminal complaint does not allege that Oxygen’s software contained malicious code or that it was used to gain unauthorised access to customers’ computer systems or data, the US Department of Justice explicitly stated.

In other words, the current case should not be interpreted as evidence that Russian authorities obtained information from Hungarian police systems or from other European customers through Oxygen software.

The allegations instead concern the company’s ownership, control, development arrangements and representations made to government customers.

US authorities have charged Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber and Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Reiber was arrested in Idaho, while Davydov was detained at London’s Heathrow Airport, with the United States seeking his extradition. Both defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

A wider European supply-chain question

The affair nevertheless highlights a broader challenge for European governments: understanding who ultimately controls the technology used inside sensitive public institutions.

This is particularly important for Russian surveillance software in Europe, as software supply chains can involve developers, owners, cloud infrastructure and corporate structures spread across several jurisdictions.

For Hungary, the procurement identified by POLITICO now provides a concrete domestic dimension to what might otherwise appear to be a distant US criminal case.

The key unanswered questions include what exact systems Hungarian police used, what information those systems could access, and whether Hungarian authorities carried out any subsequent security review after concerns emerged about Oxygen Forensics’ Russian connections.

For now, the publicly known allegations do not establish that Hungarian data were compromised. They do, however, put the Hungarian procurement into a much wider debate over how European law-enforcement agencies vet the companies entrusted with technology designed to handle some of their most sensitive digital evidence.

What’s next? Only one year left to use Russian gas: will the Hungarian economy truly grind to a halt without it?

World.title: 5-year high in Hungary: New-build homes flood the market as prices show signs of cooling
World.content:
The supply of new-build homes for sale in Hungary has reached a five-year high, with buyers currently able to choose from around 10,700 advertised flats and houses across the country, according to fresh data from property website ingatlan.com.

At the same time, price growth is slowing in the cheaper segment of the new-build market. The cheapest 10% of newly built flats nationwide can now be bought for up to HUF 59 million, just HUF 1 million more than a year ago.

New-build prices vary sharply across Hungary

The cheapest 10% of new-build properties cost up to HUF 71 million in Budapest, HUF 48 million in county capitals and other major cities, and HUF 41 million in smaller towns and villages.

There are significant differences between individual cities. Among new-build flats, Zalaegerszeg currently has the lowest prices, with the cheapest 10% of the market available for less than HUF 34 million. The equivalent threshold is HUF 46 million in Győr, while it stands at HUF 47 million in both Veszprém and Szombathely.

For new-build houses, Nyíregyháza has the lowest threshold among the cities highlighted by ingatlan.com, at HUF 69 million. The figure is HUF 77 million in Kecskemét and HUF 87 million in Székesfehérvár.

Within Budapest, the lowest entry price is currently found in District XIX, where the cheapest 10% of new-build properties are priced from HUF 50 million. The threshold rises to HUF 62 million in Districts X and XVIII and HUF 64 million in District VIII.

If you missed it: Green light for 280 new Budapest homes as huge development acquires permits

Affordability becoming increasingly important

László Balogh, chief economic expert at ingatlan.com, said affordability is becoming an increasingly important factor in the competitiveness of new-build properties. While new homes have continued to become more expensive compared with last year, the slower increase in the cheaper segment could give buyers more room to choose from the growing supply.

Balogh also said the future of Hungary’s preferential 5% VAT rate on new homes is becoming an increasingly important issue for both buyers and developers. The reduced rate is currently due to expire at the end of the year.

According to the expert, raising the rate to the standard 27% VAT would not appear realistic at current property prices. He therefore expects the preferential VAT rate for buyers of new-build residential properties could remain in place after 2026, potentially continuing into 2027. This is an expert expectation rather than a confirmed government decision.

World.title: Budapest is taking on a bigger role at one of the world’s biggest banks
World.content:
Budapest has become one of Morgan Stanley’s important international technology and analytics centres over the past two decades, with nearly 3,000 employees, according to Dániel Mayer, head of the investment bank’s Budapest office.

Speaking to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI), Mayer said the Budapest office began in 2006 as a mathematical modelling centre and has steadily expanded in importance. It is now the company’s second-largest centre of its kind globally, after India.

Nearly 3,000 employees across multiple fields

Around half of Morgan Stanley’s Budapest employees work in technology, while the office also has significant teams in finance, risk management, analytics and data management. Other functions represented in Budapest include legal, compliance and internal audit. The city is also home to several of the company’s global functions, including sustainable finance and corporate marketing.

Mayer highlighted the continuous increase in the responsibilities entrusted to the Budapest centre as the most important change over the past two decades. In a growing number of areas, global professional decisions are now made in Budapest, rather than teams there simply preparing work or providing support.

The increase in headcount has affected every division. The technology organisation is the largest, with nearly 1,500 employees. Morgan Stanley’s risk management operation began in Budapest in 2008 with just 10 people and now employs several hundred specialists.

One financial team also started with only five employees and has since grown to more than 60 people, now overseeing a global function.

Budapest becomes a global centre of expertise

Budapest has become one of the intellectual centres of Morgan Stanley’s global network, Mayer said. Among the city’s advantages are its exceptional talent pool and strong university system, as well as its time zone, which allows teams to support the Asian, European and US markets.

The knowledge and trust built up over two decades are also important assets, he added. “Global systems are developed and operated from Budapest, and world-class professional decisions are linked to the city,” Mayer said.

Photo: depositphotos.com

Morgan Stanley expands use of generative AI

Artificial intelligence and automation are also transforming the work carried out in finance, technology and risk management. Mayer said Morgan Stanley was an early adopter of generative AI and was among the first companies to deploy generative AI solutions in live operations in its wealth management business.

Budapest-based teams played a central role in developing these tools, while the company’s automation centre of expertise is also based in the city.

Morgan Stanley has now moved from experimentation to company-wide implementation. Some 98% of its employees have access to at least one generative AI tool, while the company is also specifically testing so-called agentic automation.

At the same time, Mayer stressed that the company sees AI as a way of complementing human work rather than replacing it. AI can take over repetitive tasks and provide colleagues with data and analysis more quickly, freeing up their time to serve clients, address strategic questions and, ultimately, make decisions that remain in human hands.

He also believes that the growing use of AI-generated code will increase the need for highly skilled programmers who can review it, making talented developers even more valuable. “This also creates new opportunities, for example for data scientists and technology specialists, and we are continuously training our employees so they can make the most of these opportunities,” Mayer said.

Have you heard? Scandal erupts around Morgan Stanley’s Budapest analyst operation

Focus on the next generation of talent

According to Mayer, the key to Budapest’s competitiveness lies in developing the next generation of talent and encouraging continuous learning. This is why Morgan Stanley has invested in university partnerships for two decades, from education initiatives to internship programmes. The company also continuously trains its employees to use the latest technologies.

Particular attention is being paid to preparing the next generation. Mayer cited the Smartiz training programme, run jointly with the Association of Hungarian Women in Science (NaTE) for secondary-school girls. The programme aims to encourage more young women to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

Mayer said he expects Budapest’s importance within Morgan Stanley’s international organisation to continue growing, primarily as the centre takes on more responsibilities and the tasks assigned to it become increasingly complex.

World.title: PM Magyar: Two former ministers in the hands of authorities
World.content:
Miklós Seszták and Balázs Hankó were detained on Monday after parliament suspended their immunity, in a dramatic escalation of ongoing investigations involving former government officials.

Two former Hungarian ministers were in custody by Monday evening after parliament lifted their immunity in separate criminal investigations, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said.

Magyar described Monday as the first major day of what he called the “Purification” operation (Tisztítótűz), accusing his political opponents of engaging in what he called an “unworthy game of hide-and-seek”. His comments came after former ministers Seszták Miklós and Hankó Balázs were both taken into custody.

The Hungarian Parliament voted in a special session on Monday to suspend the immunity of Seszták, a Christian Democrat (KDNP) MP, and Hankó, a Fidesz MP and former minister of culture and innovation. It also suspended Magyar’s immunity in a separate case.

Seszták detained after going to prosecutors

Seszták voluntarily went to the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office in Budapest on Monday morning, shortly after parliament suspended his immunity. He was subsequently detained, according to his lawyer and multiple Hungarian media reports.

The Prosecutor’s Office had requested the suspension of his immunity over suspected acceptance of an official bribe. The investigation is linked to allegations involving corruption, although Seszták has denied wrongdoing.

Hankó taken into custody in Budapest

Hankó remained in Parliament for much of the day, saying he was prepared to cooperate with the investigation and that he had nothing to hide.

He was eventually summoned to the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) building on Huszti út in Budapest after 8 PM. Hír TV reported that he gave a statement there before being detained. According to his lawyer, Hankó was then taken to Kecskemét, where his formal questioning as a suspect would take place.

The investigation concerns suspected mismanagement of funds connected to the National Cultural Fund (NKA). Prosecutors previously said investigators were examining decisions involving more than 1,000 funding applications worth over HUF 17 billion.

Miklós Seszták, Péter Magyar and Balázs Hankó.

Hankó has rejected the allegations and described the proceedings as politically motivated. Fidesz parliamentary group leader János Bóka likewise called the case a political proceeding and alleged that the political right was being targeted.

Magyar, meanwhile, said that by the end of Monday “two former ministers are in the hands of the authorities”. The investigations are continuing, and the detention of the two politicians does not in itself establish criminal liability.

World.title: Tremors of 1956 in the Soviet bloc: How far did Hungary’s revolution reach into the USSR?
World.content:
On December 4, 1956, Anton Bachkai (Bacskai in Hungarian) walked into his church in the village of Mala Kopania (Kiskopány), sprinkled it with holy water, and began the liturgy. For the first time in seven years, he praised the Pope. In 1949, the Soviet regime had forced this Greek Catholic priest into Russian Orthodoxy. Now he told his flock the story of the Apostle Peter. “Peter turned against Christ’s church, but then repented,” Bachkai said later. “Peter was pardoned by God, and so will I be.” A rival Orthodox priest complained that parishioners knew the reason: the uprising in Hungary. God may have pardoned Bachkai. The KGB did not. Early in 1957, it arrested him for “worshiping the Vatican and the imperialist West.”

Author: Dr. Johanna C. Granville (more about her below)

Seventy years ago this October, the Hungarian revolution sent tremors across the Soviet bloc. Just across the border, in Soviet Ukraine, officials warned loudly of Hungarian “contagion.” The KGB hunted priests, students, and teenagers. But how dangerous were the Hungarians of Transcarpathia to Soviet power? The files of the KGB, still kept in the archive of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in Uzhhorod, show what that fear looked like, how little stood behind it, and where the regime’s real fear lay.

The night of November 3 to 4

Late on November 3, 1956, Károly Lusztig was finishing his newspaper for Sunday when the telephone rang. Officials summoned the Hungarian editor to Uzhhorod. Over a secret line, a deep voice dictated János Kádár’s first proclamation as head of the new Soviet-backed government, and Lusztig translated it. “My legs started to tremble,” he later wrote. “‘This means blood’ flickered through my mind.” Yet this Hungarian communist of Jewish heritage, who had lost his whole family in the war, also called it one of the most exciting nights of his life. Months later, Tibor Barzsó felt no such thrill. Forced to translate for the Soviet army, he “could hardly wait to get rid of the uniform.” The regime needed Transcarpathian Hungarians even as it distrusted them, and their loyalties split.

On November 4, Soviet tanks rumbled through Hungarian villages in western Ukraine toward the border. In Koson (Mezőkaszony), István Ormos said he heard Hungarian music drifting across from Barabás, then cries for help. In July 1957, Prokopy Savchuk, head of the KGB in Transcarpathia, admitted that children in Solotvyno (Aknaszlatina) had spread leaflets. Adults feared war. Between October 16 and November 10, citizens in the region withdrew 4,491,000 rubles from their bank accounts and deposited only 50,000. Hungarian teenagers wrote leaflets of their own. The historian György Dupka recorded their memories in interviews, and the files of the KGB add details from their interrogations. Many compared the deportation of young insurgents from Hungary into Soviet prisons to the malenky robot of 1944. None of this amounted to an organized movement.

Older Hungarians remembered other systems, and in the regime’s eyes that memory made them dangerous. In 1958, the forester József Kivári praised the goods and the efficient accounting methods of prewar Czechoslovakia and Hungary to his colleagues. He served four years in a camp in Mordovia as a result. Dr. M. V. Somogyi, chief surgeon at the hospital in Berehove, told a closed meeting of the party on October 22, 1956, that the Soviet party had become “Menshevist.” He lost his post. Neither man had done more than speak. The regime punished words, not deeds.
