World.title: Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019070/Weaving History: China’s ‘Wig Capital’ Fights to Keep Its Crown
World.content:
The hair business in Xuchang, in China’s central Henan province, has been growing since the 16th century. Starting from opera props, the city is now the “Wig Capital of the World.”

Roughly 60% of wigs on the global market come from Xuchang. According to the local commerce bureau, the industry’s total import-export value hit 11.56 billion yuan ($1.72 billion) in the first half of 2026, up by nearly 11% year on year.

The core of this pillar industry, Jian’an District, is home to 311 foreign trade enterprises shipping hair products — and business is booming. Yet life behind the sales figures isn’t so rosy.

Although cross-border e-commerce platforms have helped companies reach new markets, including North America and Europe, businesses here say the commissions they charge are making it difficult to turn a profit.

The industry is also facing a potential serious labor crisis, with high-than-average salaries failing to attract more talent, especially younger workers.

Long and short of it

According to local historical archives, people in Xuchang began collecting human hair as early as the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), using it to make theatrical props and fake beards.

It wasn’t until 1900, when Bai Xihe from the city’s Quandian Village collaborated with a German merchant to establish a hair trading depot, that a wider industry began to emerge. Soon, villagers were fanning out nationwide to find supplies, with the raw materials pooled in Jian’an.

By the 1930s, Xuchang had dozens of workshops making processed hair, or dangfa, which was shipped through ports in Qingdao in the eastern Shandong province and Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, to overseas markets including Japan and the Philippines.

Dangfa is a semi-finished product made from human hair that has been washed, straightened, sorted, and tied into bundles. It’s a key upstream raw material for wigs.

Many rural families opened small home-based operations, forming the embryo of a cottage industry. The men would travel around the nation collecting hair, while the women stayed home to sort and knot wigs strand by strand, an essential craft that takes at least six months to master.

“An industrial ecosystem doesn’t come together overnight,” says Tian Liangjun, vice president of the Xuchang Hair Products Association, established in 2004. “Our industry has more than a century of accumulated history. The raw materials, the talent, the technology, the market intelligence are all here — and so are the supporting accessories, equipment, printing, and packaging.”

By the time China began to open its economy in the late 1970s and early ’80s, Xuchang possessed the raw materials and manufacturing capacity, but companies from South Korea had control of the network channels to overseas markets. They purchased hair and semi-finished goods from Xuchang and sold finished products to beauty supply stores in the United States. Chinese enterprises were consigned to contract processing, with limited profits and little market leverage.

“In the past, more than 80% of the U.S. hair-product market was controlled by South Korean companies. They had us by the throat,” Tian says. “We depended on them, so when South Korean agents came to Xuchang to inspect the goods, they acted like they were above us. Some of us even had to bring them bowls of water to wash their hands at the end of their inspection.”

However, things changed in 1990, when entrepreneur Zheng Youquan founded the Xuchang Hair Products General Factory, which saw local businesses advance to producing finished wigs.

Zheng was born in 1954 in the city’s Xiaogong Village and learned wig-making as a child before entering the hair processing trade in the ’80s.

When he opened his own factory, he faced a major challenge: the three-head sewing machine, a core piece of equipment, wasn’t made in China and no foreign manufacturers would sell him one. So he enlisted the help of a retired factory worker from Qingdao who could draw the machine’s inner workings from memory, which a team of local engineers then used to build it.

Using this technology, Zheng’s plant produced Xuchang’s first wigs for foreign buyers, branded Qicai Xiufa, meaning “colorful tresses.” Three years later, he established Rebecca Hair, a Sino-U.S. joint venture with Sina International Corp., and entered the North American market. In 2003, Rebecca became the first hair-product enterprise listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

Tian believes Zheng helped catapult the local industry to a new level, transforming the city from a trading hub for raw materials into a major production base for finished goods.

Cutting out the middleman

The emergence of cross-border e-commerce in the mid-2010s was another game changer. Global platforms such as AliExpress and Amazon enabled Xuchang manufacturers to bypass the middleman and deal directly with overseas consumers, as well as create their own brands.

UNice, which specializes in hair products for Black and Latino women, began trading on multiple platforms in 2014 and set up its own sales website about four years later. “We decided to create our own brand and registered trademarks in China, the European Union, and the United States,” says Wang Qi, who works for the brand. “With third-party platforms, you need to play by their rules, and there are all sorts of uncertainties. Building our own site reduced our dependence on platforms and put operations in our own hands. More importantly, we have full control over product quality.”

Some Xuchang companies have also opened warehouses overseas to gain a better understanding of the destination market and to cut costs with cheaper bulk freight.

“In 2025, the cumulative additional tariffs the U.S. imposed on Chinese hair products reached 145% at one point, and the tariff costs on small parcels below the $800 tax-free threshold rose sharply,” recalls Bo Luwen, who runs a wig business in Jian’an. “Surrounding factories shut down because they couldn’t ship anything.” His company had a stockpile in U.S. warehouses, so it was shielded from the market shock.

He adds that warehouses do more than provide cover in emergencies; they also improve the customer experience. A consignment shipped from China to North America can bob on the ocean for weeks before reaching the buyer, whereas goods sent from within the continent can arrive the next day.

OQ Hair, an online brand offering 100% human hair products, released a glueless wig in 2023 that promises to cut application time from 30 minutes to a few seconds. Thanks in part to a short promotional video that garnered 3 million views, the company recorded sales of more than 10 million yuan within six months.

“The rise of cross-border e-commerce completely broke the South Korean monopoly over distribution channels,” Tian says. “We went from contract manufacturing to making our own brands — from passive to active. This was when our industry truly came into its own.”

Split ends

Yet the hard work is far from over. Although cross-border e-commerce platforms led to a breakthrough in distribution, “they bred new problems, too, including relatively high commissions and ever-shifting rules,” Tian explains. “Sellers also can’t autonomously decide what to sell or how to price it.”

The commissions charged by Amazon, AliExpress, and Temu run from 5% to 20%, he says. “This is squeezing our companies’ already-thin margins. It’s hard for sellers on those platforms to make money.”

Another concern is the worsening talent shortage. Many steps in industrial wig-making still require manual labor, and anecdotal evidence suggests that fewer people are willing to work in Xuchang’s factories, especially younger generations. Some businesses are even offering to pay front-line employees 8,000 yuan a month, well above average, yet still struggle to fill vacancies.

A hand-sewn wig takes a skilled worker about a week to complete, and machines cannot fully replace hand-knotting. As older craftspeople are aging out, some skill-intensive tasks are now being outsourced overseas.

Against this backdrop, many companies see only one way forward: abandon the low-end price war in favor of premium, branded products. Leading enterprises are also investing in research and development, hoping to move toward fully automated production.

On the retail side, there’s also Xuchang Hair Expo City, a specialized wig trading and commercial market near the city’s railway station and long-distance bus terminal.

“Xuchang may be the wig capital, but for years, visitors couldn’t find a single place to actually buy one here,” says Tian, who has run the market since it was founded in 2022. ‘There were plenty of manufacturers, but none of them served walk-in customers. The industry had no storefront you could see and touch.”

Inside, shelves are stacked with everything from synthetic wigs selling for a few dozen yuan to hand-knotted wig caps made from 100% real human hair priced at more than 10,000 yuan.

“We want buyers worldwide to know that when it comes to buying a wig, Xuchang is all they need,” Tian says. The market’s annual sales volume, including via e-commerce channels, is now about 200 million yuan, with most customers coming from other regions of China. However, he adds that the number of foreign buyers is increasing.

Whatever happens, Tian believes that genuine quality is the ultimate trump card. “If your goods aren’t good, no one will want them, even if you beg.”

(Due to privacy reasons, Wang Qi and Bo Luwen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Cheng Ting, Kang Jiaxin, Yang Yuan, and Fang Yuejia.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Eunice Ouyang; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Workers style wigs at a factory in Xuchang, Henan province, 2019. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019051/A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.title: A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019051/A Dying Tradition? The Haunting Beauty of China’s ‘Day of the Dead’
World.content:
By 8 p.m. on Aug. 26, the great banyan tree at the center of Boshi Village is already surrounded by offerings. Bowls filled with fresh fruit, roasted meat, and other snacks are stacked rows deep among the tree’s gnarled roots. The air hangs thick with candle and incense smoke.

Locals have laid out the smorgasbord of treats as part of the Shigu festival, a series of rituals predominantly held in southern China each year that is often likened to Mexico’s Day of the Dead.

While it’s far from well-known overseas, Shigu has long been one of China’s most important and vibrant festivals. Like the Day of the Dead, it’s a centuries-old tradition to honor the deceased and draws on a rich mix of religious and folk practices.

But Shigu is also a distinctly local celebration that embodies many unique aspects of Chinese culture — and especially the culture of Chaoshan, the southern coastal region where Boshi Village is located.

Shigu — which literally translates as “feeding the lonely ghosts” — sees communities come together to care for the spirits of the departed: making offerings, chanting Buddhist scripture, and even communicating with the deceased.

It’s unclear when the festival first emerged, but references date back to at least the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279). For a long time, the Shigu festivities in Chaoshan drew bigger crowds than any other event apart from Chinese New Year.

To grasp Shigu’s significance, it’s necessary to understand how it fits into China’s traditional cosmology. According to Confucian and Taoist practices, families have a responsibility to care for the spirits of their departed loved ones, leaving offerings of food, paper money, and even alcohol to ensure they are comfortable in the afterlife.

But many people die with no children to care for their souls, while seafarers and soldiers often perish far from home and their bodies are never returned to their hometowns. If neglected, these spirits become “lonely ghosts” that wander the Earth, spreading woe and harassing the living.

The Shigu festival is designed to prevent this. Taking place in the seventh lunar month of the traditional Chinese calendar — when Yanwang, the king of hell, is said to open the gates of the underworld — communities lay out offerings for these lonely souls, giving the hungry ghosts temporary relief.

In this, Shigu differs from the Day of the Dead, which is more about families honoring their ancestors. China’s Qingming Festival in early April is perhaps a closer equivalent in that sense, though its traditions of tomb-sweeping and quiet family ceremonies are quite different.

Over the centuries, the Shigu festival has become more elaborate. Offerings are now often accompanied by communal rituals that blend Buddhist and local folk traditions. (In many places, the festival is also called “Pudu,” a name that derives from the Buddhist concept of “universal salvation” — or delivering all souls from suffering.)

In Chaoshan, many groups organize “spirit-writing” ceremonies — a practice akin to using a Ouija board to communicate with ghosts, except characters are written in sand. Others organize processions between local temples and offering grounds, led by officials chanting Buddhist scripture.

Local charities, meanwhile, donate everything from medicine to coffins to people in need in mass “merit-making ceremonies.” Most famously, the impoverished are allowed to grab the food laid out for the spirits during a ritual known as the “scramble for the offerings” — though these days the contests tend to be infiltrated by a fair number of tourists.

Today, Shigu is still marked across the Chinese-speaking world, but the celebrations are particularly central to life in Chaoshan — a reflection of the region’s turbulent history.

Chaoshan has long had a large population of hungry ghosts. For centuries, wars and uprisings across the region left countless people without a proper burial. More recently, millions set sail from Chaoshan to seek work overseas, forming large diasporas across Southeast Asia and even further afield.

To care for all these wandering souls, towns and villages across Chaoshan still mark Shigu at the end of every summer. Though the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, known as the Zhongyuan Festival, is widely regarded as the height of the Shigu festival, communities hold their ceremonies on different days throughout the month. No one is sure how and when the dates were selected.

In Nansha, a village near the city of Shantou, the Zhongyuan Festival celebrations are in full swing when Sixth Tone visits in late August. Shopkeepers unable to join the collective village ceremony set up tables outside their businesses to lay out offerings. Other villagers gather at the local temple and ancestral hall to organize the main events.

Elderly residents take charge. Some use loudspeakers to blare out appeals in Chaoshan dialect, calling on villagers to donate money and rice for the Pudu. Others fold triangular paper offerings or prepare baskets of “guye fish rice,” a staple offering used in local rituals.

Inside the temple, a group of women performs a ceremony to honor the wandering spirits — known affectionately as guye, or lonely elders. Donated flour, rice, cooking oil, and fruit are piled in front of the temple for needy villagers to collect.

At the ancestral hall, neat stacks of rice cakes, bread, snacks, and baskets of “guye fish rice” are arranged in a courtyard in front of the main entrance. Lin Qiwei, a local village elder, begins a ceremony to make the offerings at 3 p.m., kneeling and chanting a sacrificial text.

“Orphaned souls with no one to claim you, come here and eat,” Lin calls. “Once you have eaten your fill, return each to your place; do not disturb the living; do not frighten the children.”

After the ceremony comes the much-anticipated “scramble for the offerings,” where locals compete to grab the delicacies. Local beliefs hold that consuming food blessed by the spirits brings good fortune. The ritual also serves as a form of charity, to help villagers who have fallen on hard times.

But the “scramble for the offerings” has become controversial in recent years. As the ritual’s fame has grown — with influencers posting videos of the spectacle on Chinese social media — it has begun to attract large groups of outsiders, who often crowd out those who are truly in need.

Yet, despite its viral popularity, the reality is that today’s Shigu festival is a shadow of its former self. In the early 20th century, practically every household in Chaoshan took part in the festivities and incense burned all month long, according to folk-custom researcher Lin Xuejin.

After 1949, the festivals were suspended for decades, as traditional practices and beliefs were discouraged as “feudal superstitions.” They slowly revived after “reform and opening-up” began in the late 1970s, but mass internal migration and breakneck economic development have also taken their toll.

Today, while villages across Chaoshan still hold Shigu, the monthlong community-wide celebrations have dwindled to one-off collective events on selected days, run almost entirely by older residents. Young people are noticeably scarce in Nansha — except for the gaggle of influencers and creators filming and livestreaming the events.

The Chinese internet’s sudden embrace of Shigu can feel jarring. As Lin chants his appeal to the lonely ghosts before an audience mostly made up of retirees, several drones whir overhead, waiting to capture the excitement of the coming “scramble for the offerings.”

But locals hope the trend can help revive the festival. Several villagers say the influx of content creators has encouraged younger generations to value their local culture more — and pushed older residents to keep organizing the ceremonies despite falling attendance.

Fu Xingcong, a Ph.D. candidate at Beijing’s Minzu University of China studying Shigu practices in Chaoshan, tells Sixth Tone that these external forces have strengthened local cultural identity and given the declining tradition a much-needed boost.

Back in Boshi Village, locals are doing their best to preserve the festival in their own way. Chen, a woman in her 40s, drives up from the nearby city of Chaozhou to pay her respects shortly after 8 p.m.

Watched by her teenage daughter, she carefully inserts incense sticks into her specially prepared bowls of braised goose, cured pork, and soft white rice cakes, arranges them on the ground, and then kowtows while murmuring her wishes.

Chen, who gave only her surname, says she returns to her ancestral village for the Shigu festival every summer. Though she moved to the city many years ago, she still feels it’s important to maintain this link to her old home and pass it on to the next generation.

“This was something I absorbed from childhood,” Chen tells Sixth Tone. “Once you grow up and get married, it becomes your responsibility to perform these rituals.”

Cunxin Charity Hall, Downtown Shantou

Nansha Village, Shantou

This article is co-authored by Wu Huiyuan.

(Header image: At the “scramble for the offerings” in Shantou’s Nansha Village, Guangdong province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019075/17,000 Shipwrecked Relics Given to Chinese Research Centers
World.title: 17,000 Shipwrecked Relics Given to Chinese Research Centers
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019075/17,000 Shipwrecked Relics Given to Chinese Research Centers
World.content:
Over 17,000 artifacts recovered from a more than 700-year-old shipwreck off the coast of eastern China have officially been transferred to several Chinese archaeological institutions.

At a Monday ceremony in Zhangzhou City, in the eastern Fujian province, the artifacts were distributed among the Archaeological Research Center of the National Cultural Heritage Administration, the Fujian Provincial Institute of Archaeology, and the Zhangzhou Museum, among others.

The handover marks the first implementation of nationwide trial guidelines issued in July by the National Cultural Heritage Administration. The directive aims to standardize archaeological relic preservation, research, and display, citing an increasing number of archaeological excavations and findings in the country.

Under the new rules, archaeological teams must transfer recovered artifacts to state-owned museums, libraries, or cultural institutions within six months of submitting excavation reports to the National Cultural Heritage Administration and provincial cultural heritage authorities.

The recently transferred artifacts come from a shipwreck dating back to the late Yuan dynasty (1279–1368). Measuring 17 meters long and 4.5 meters wide, the wreck was discovered in 2014 in the waters between Zhangzhou and the nearby Shengbeiyu islet, where the Maritime Silk Road’s southern and eastern routes intersect. The site lies about 30 meters below the surface and is surrounded by reefs and complex waters, making the area prone to shipwrecks.

More than 20,000 artifacts were recovered from the wreck between 2022 and 2023, including over 17,000 celadon — or green-glazed porcelain — bowls, plates, cups, and incense burners. Other finds include pottery jars, lead weights, and seals.

The relics come from the Longquan kiln in the eastern Zhejiang province, one of the largest ceramic production centers in Chinese history and a major source of porcelain for overseas markets. Spanning 1,700 years and renowned for its distinctive jade-green and light-blue glazes, the kiln’s wares became an important commodity in maritime trade networks, reaching markets around Asia and Europe.

Some of the pieces from the shipwreck, including their inscriptions, are unusually large, offering clues about how Chinese kilns adapted their products for overseas markets, according to historical experts.

The ship’s cargo, along with similar finds in east China, suggests it may have set sail from Zhejiang’s coastal Wenzhou City for southeast Asia as a privately operated trading vessel.

“The excavation of the shipwreck marks an important milestone in China’s underwater archaeology,” Liang Guoqing, who led the excavation team, told local media. “It has also allowed the public to see firsthand the thriving trade in Longquan celadon and the prosperity of the Maritime Silk Road during the late Yuan dynasty.”

Archaeologists at the Archaeological Research Center of the National Cultural Heritage Administration said the wreck is also the first Yuan dynasty ship discovered in China with a fully preserved bilge keel — a structure attached to the bottom of a vessel to reduce roll. The discovery provides rare physical evidence for the study of ancient Chinese shipbuilding and navigation.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Ceramics inside the Yuan Dynasty shipwreck near Zhangzhou, Fujian province. Xinhua)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019064/When Surgery Isn’t Enough for China’s MRKH Patients
World.title: When Surgery Isn’t Enough for China’s MRKH Patients
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019064/When Surgery Isn’t Enough for China’s MRKH Patients
World.content:
Twenty-eight-year-old Ada, a pseudonym, and her boyfriend had reached the point of discussing marriage, but she was keeping a major secret from him: she has MRKH.

MRKH, short for Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome and also known as Müllerian agenesis, is a rare congenital disorder of the female reproductive system, affecting approximately one in 4,500 to 5,000 women. Most patients are born without a uterus and with an absent or underdeveloped vagina. In China, women with the condition have long been derogatorily labeled “stone women.”

Ada knew the condition could complicate her sex life, but she believed that was something she could address before marriage. She researched MRKH on her own and eventually found Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital, in the country’s south, where she planned to undergo vaginal reconstruction surgery.

She told no one but her mother about the procedure. And saw little reason to tell her boyfriend. “After vaginal reconstruction, nothing will really feel any different (for him). I can give him the same thing, so why do I need to spell it out? If I did, it would only affect him psychologically.”

Like many MRKH patients, Ada was drawn to Shenzhen Luohu District People’s Hospital by its reputation. Although it is administratively only a district-level hospital, it has become a leading center for MRKH treatment. More than 20 years ago, doctors there pioneered the “Luohu technique,” a form of laparoscopic peritoneal vaginoplasty in which the vagina is reconstructed using tissue from the patient’s abdominal cavity. Since then, the hospital has performed more than 5,000 operations for various congenital malformations of the lower female reproductive tract, treating more MRKH patients than any other medical institution in China.

Many of these patients endure a long, painful search for medical care before finding their way to Luohu. They typically first seek treatment during adolescence because they have never had a period, or because they experience cyclical abdominal pain without menstrual bleeding. At the hospitals they visit, they may be the first MRKH patient doctors have encountered. Some are examined with multiple people looking on, only to be bluntly told that nothing can be done.

But the medical experience is only one source of pain. Patients must also contend with social and cultural pressures that can profoundly affect how they see themselves. Sighs and self-recrimination from family members can gradually lead patients to internalize the belief that they are not “complete women.” The question of whether to disclose their condition to an intimate partner can be equally fraught, bringing self-doubt and inner conflict, whatever they decide.

Research my team conducted suggests these anxieties also shape seemingly ordinary aspects of daily life. Some people with MRKH avoid public baths, swimming pools, and changing rooms. Even walking down the sanitary pad aisle in a supermarket can make them uncomfortable.

At Luohu District People’s Hospital, patients have a good chance of having their physical condition treated. But successful surgery rarely puts an end to their troubles. Dr. Qin, the clinical lead, told me frankly that surgical success marks only a biological transformation of the body. Patients still face the long process of returning to family life and rebuilding intimate relationships. A major gap exists between successful treatment and this broader recovery process, one doctors cannot fill on their own.

Even within this medically advanced team, some unease remains. Team members worry that outsiders could misunderstand reconstructive procedures involving intimate reproductive organs as dubious or unorthodox. Doctors are therefore often reluctant to talk openly about the procedures, while patients can feel they have been left to navigate their implications alone. The silence on both sides reinforces the problem.

This is precisely where medical social work can play a role.

In the autumn of 2025, after spending three months conducting sociological research with MRKH patients and the medical professionals who treat them, I joined Luohu District People’s Hospital’s Gynecology Department 3 as the supervisor of a team of social workers. We began providing medical social services for MRKH patients, helping them rebuild their sense of identity and dignity while encouraging medical professionals to shift their focus from “treating illness” toward “treating the person.”

After all, surgeons can reconstruct the body, but recovery involves more than the physical: patients must also rebuild their sense of self and return to society with dignity.

From the beginning, I knew we were in largely uncharted territory. China has no standardized assessment tools designed specifically for people with MRKH, nor an established, validated model for providing them with social services. Therefore, we had to develop our approach within the constraints of a working hospital, learning from patients and refining our methods as we went.

Our work gradually took shape in three areas.

First, we tried to bridge the gap between physical and psychological care by taking on emotional needs that clinical treatment could not easily meet.

Negative medical experiences have made many patients highly sensitive about exposing their bodies. Even an ordinary consultation room can easily trigger traumatic memories of being examined while others watched. We worked with the department to train medical staff in gender sensitivity and ethics. With their support and cooperation, we also secured private spaces for one-on-one conversations and made small changes to the rehabilitation area to make it feel less clinical and reduce patients’ discomfort when seeking care.

Our individual work with patients focused in part on helping them separate their physical differences from their sense of self-worth. Social workers encouraged them to question beliefs they had internalized, particularly the idea that “without a uterus, I am not a complete woman,” and to develop a healthier relationship with their bodies.

There are limits to what we can do. Because no locally developed assessment tool exists for MRKH patients, we rely on interviews and clinical observation to track changes in their physical and psychological well-being. Budgetary and institutional constraints also limit how much we can change the care environment.

Second, we sought to break the isolation surrounding MRKH by creating spaces for peer and family support.

We organized small in-person patient-sharing sessions and themed support groups. These included highly practical exercises such as what we call “disclosure rehearsals,” which help patients think through conversations with intimate partners in advance. If a partner asks about the condition, how should the patient respond? What are they comfortable disclosing? What risks might different approaches carry, and how might a partner react?

We also experimented with family interventions. Through family meetings, we tried to help relatives move beyond the entrenched belief that a woman’s value is tied to her ability to reproduce. At the same time, we established an online peer-support community where patients could connect.

But these efforts created challenges of their own. Many patients worried about their identities being exposed, so willingness to participate in person varied considerably. Online, we had to strike a difficult balance between allowing members to support one another and preventing the spread of medical misinformation or the amplification of distress. Some families were also deeply reluctant to discuss MRKH at all and refused to participate in family meetings.

Third, we began looking beyond the immediate clinical setting through modest advocacy efforts.

At this early stage, we were not seeking sweeping policy reform. Instead, we focused on specific problems we encountered in our work. Some patients, for example, struggled to afford surgery. We also encountered language in primary medical settings that objectified women or reduced them to their reproductive functions.

In response, our social workers contacted the She Unbinds Asia Foundation to explore dedicated financial support for people with MRKH, prioritizing patients experiencing financial hardship. But securing such dedicated funding is difficult and inherently uncertain. A stable system of financial support remains out of reach.

Despite these difficulties, I am determined to continue. Supervising this exploratory social work project has made me deeply aware that dignity is not restored through a single intervention. It is rebuilt little by little, through interactions between patients, medical professionals, social workers, and families.

Our efforts have also borne tangible results. Patients are testing different ways to navigate everyday life and gradually learning to live with their condition on their own terms. Social workers, too, are learning through trial and error, continually adjusting and refining their approaches.

The lessons extend beyond MRKH. Every year in China, large numbers of people with rare diseases enter operating rooms and leave the hospital with their physical conditions treated but the wounds to their sense of identity still unhealed. Yet social services for these patients remain severely underdeveloped.

Every obstacle we have encountered in Luohu, and every lesson we have learned, can therefore serve as a signpost for those who follow. Our experience may help not only support people with MRKH, but also develop locally grounded approaches to medical social work for other rare diseases and hidden illnesses in China.

As a university educator, I can also bring what we have learned back into the classroom. It shows students that social work is more than textbook theory. It is the painstaking work of helping people whose experiences place them outside the mainstream rebuild their dignity within the very real constraints of the world around them.

With contributions from Yang Feixu and Ni Sihan.

Translator: Gabriel Kwan.

World.title: Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019073/Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.content:
A Beijing court ordered a hospital to resume embryo-transfer treatment for a widow seeking to use two frozen embryos she and her husband created before his death.

On Sept. 22, Beijing’s Chaoyang District People’s Court disclosed details of the case while releasing its annual white paper on medical disputes. The court said it had ruled in favor of the woman, surnamed Zhang, who would be responsible for the related costs. It found that her request did not violate any law, the couple’s agreement, or ethical principles.

Zhang and her husband, Li, married in 2016 and later sought fertility treatment after she experienced repeated miscarriages and Li was diagnosed with secondary infertility. In 2019, the couple underwent treatment at a Beijing hospital’s reproductive center, where three embryos were frozen.

Li died of a brainstem hemorrhage in July of that year. Zhang later used one of the embryos and gave birth to a daughter, leaving two embryos remaining.

Years later, Zhang asked to use the two remaining embryos, but the hospital refused. It cited the difficulty of obtaining consent from her late husband, concerns that the request was linked to an inheritance dispute, a contract provision allowing the embryos to be destroyed if either spouse died, and the lack of approval from the hospital’s ethics committee.

Zhang said she was willing to assume all legal, ethical and moral responsibilities arising from the embryo transfer and any resulting childbirth. Zhang’s mother-in-law supported her decision, and Zhang later filed a lawsuit.

China’s regulations on human assisted reproductive technology, issued in the early 2000s, restrict access to such procedures to married couples and exclude single women.

The hospital argued that Zhang no longer met that requirement after her husband’s death, while Zhang argued that the embryos had been created during their marriage and that she should be allowed to proceed.

The Chaoyang court found that Zhang’s request did not violate the law, the couple’s agreement or ethical principles. It said there was no unresolved inheritance dispute, as Li’s estate had already been settled through notarization and a settlement agreement. The court also found that Zhang and Li had formed a clear, shared intention to have children before his death.

The judges said Zhang’s case differed from that of unmarried women seeking assisted reproductive treatment because the embryos had been created during her marriage. Having already helped Zhang complete one successful embryo transfer, the hospital could not later rely on restrictions on treatment for “single women” to deny access to the remaining embryos, the court said.

The court ordered the hospital to resume treatment, with Zhang responsible for related costs. It said Zhang was an independent rights holder under the embryo-transfer service contract. The judges said disputes involving assisted reproductive technology should balance legal limits, ethical considerations, family consensus and contractual obligations.

The court included the case in its annual white paper on medical disputes, describing it as an example of new legal questions arising from advances in assisted reproductive technology.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: E+/VCG)

World.title: Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019063/Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.content:
Chinese scientists have identified a pathway connecting the spleen to the brain that may in part explain why women are more susceptible than men to cognitive decline as they age.

The study, published Sept. 18 in the peer-reviewed journal Neuron, was led by Ma Huan, vice dean of the School of Brain Science and Brain Medicine at Zhejiang University, in eastern China.

Existing literature shows that although women live on average longer than men, they are more susceptible to cognitive impairment from midlife onwards. Scientists have lacked a clear biological explanation for this phenomenon, attributing it until now primarily to estrogen.

The new research, however, has found that the spleen may influence brain aging through a pathway involving a gene on the X chromosome, which becomes more active in women as they age.

Using gene-expression data from 11 major organs in a preexisting database, the team found that beginning around age 40, signs of cellular senescence — when cells stop dividing and begin to malfunction — rose sharply in women’s brains and spleens, exceeding levels observed in men of the same age. A similar pattern was confirmed in naturally aging mice and in donor human brain tissue.

The researchers’ findings raise a key question: Is cognitive decline in part the result of the body sending a signal to the brain telling it to age?

In searching for that signal, the researchers identified miR-10a-5p, a microRNA — a type of gene expression regulator — whose levels rose in the spleens and brains of middle-aged female mice but not in their male counterparts.

The team then looked for proteins that regulate miR-10a-5p and discovered that RBMX, a protein encoded by a gene on the X chromosome, binds to, stabilizes, and allows the microRNA to accumulate. This process only occurred in female mice, as females carry two X chromosomes.

Next, the researchers injected mice with a compound to block miR-10a-5p, finding this lowered its levels in their brains, as did removing their spleens — indicating that the organ is a major source of the microRNA. Because the compound used does not efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier, the results imply that muting it elsewhere in the body may be enough to alter levels in the brain.

Once inside neurons in the brain, miR-10a-5p suppresses a protein called γCaMKII linked to calcium regulation within mitochondria — structures within the cell that generate its energy. When levels of this protein fall — which occurs during middle age in females — calcium signaling weakens and energy output declines, pushing neurons toward senescence. Restoring the protein in mice with reduced γCaMKII reversed these changes.

“We’ve tended to treat cognitive aging as something confined to the brain,” Qu Jing, the first author of the study, told Sixth Tone. “This work suggests the brain isn’t an isolated organ, and age-related changes in peripheral tissue may start shaping its condition much earlier than we assumed.”

The findings also suggest that because some of the brain’s miR-10a-5p originates elsewhere in the body, testing for it in patients’ blood could help assess brain-aging risk long before cognitive symptoms appear. Second, because reducing miR-10a-5p levels in the body affects the brain, it may be possible to protect against cognitive decline without developing a drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

“One important message from this work is that midlife isn’t just a stage where you wait for aging to happen, but a possible critical window for maintaining long-term brain health,” Qu said, adding that because the study points to a connection between the immune system and the brain, sustaining a well-functioning immune system may matter for cognitive health too.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Amana/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.title: In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.content:
SHANGHAI – At the Sept. 19 Shanghai premiere of her feature debut, “Shanghai Daughter,” Shen Zhongmin carried a rubber seed from the forests of the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, nearly 3,000 kilometers away in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, where her late father had worked.

“The seed fell from the canopy and struck me as I retraced his life there,” Shen, 41, tells Sixth Tone.

Her father was among the millions of urban Chinese youths “sent down” to work in rural areas under the Down to the Countryside Movement, a campaign that ran from the mid-1950s through the late 1970s. He spent a decade on a state-run rubber farm near China’s border with Myanmar but rarely spoke to his daughter about those years.

Shen, who works professionally as Agnis Shen, first traveled to Xishuangbanna in 2011, the year after her father died. A former culture editor at the Shanghai-based magazine The Bund and the author of “The Traveler’s Desire,” a collection of short fiction. She returned to the region repeatedly, retracing her father’s life and meeting people from his generation.

Nearly a decade after her first trip, those encounters and widespread coverage of a herd of wild Asian elephants wandering north from Xishuangbanna helped inspire the idea for a film. The herd’s journey drew attention to the rubber plantations that had transformed parts of the region’s rainforest habitat.

Blending fiction with documentary methods, “Shanghai Daughter” follows Ming, a fictional Shanghai woman played by Liang Cuishan, as she seeks out her father’s former acquaintances in Xishuangbanna.

She encounters workers’ dormitories facing demolition and a landscape where mining and modern agriculture are replacing former rubber plantations. She also meets rubber tappers, village doctors, ethnic Dai villagers, and ecological researchers, all of whom appear as themselves and recount their own experiences.

“The film asks how we deal with memory,” Shen says. “When you want to understand something from the past but cannot find reliable firsthand records, how do you search for the answers?”

“Shanghai Daughter” had its world premiere in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival in February and was later selected for the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the Malaysia International Film Festival.

Seven months later, the film’s Shanghai premiere drew at least a dozen former sent-down youths from the city, all now in their 70s. They traveled about an hour by subway to attend.

At the theater, they shared old photographs from their years in Xishuangbanna, including images taken with Shen’s father, Shen Wanxiong, and posed for a group photo with the director.

Among them was Shen Weilong, 73, a former rubber tapper who had worked alongside Shen Wanxiong and describes him as his best friend. Looking at one of the photographs, he jokes, “This one doesn’t show just how handsome he was. If you want to know what he looked like, just look at his daughter.”

As he speaks about his generation, tears well in his eyes. “Our generation is rarely talked about, and now our time is running out,” he says.

Sixth Tone spoke with Shen Zhongmin the following day as she continued a multi-city promotional tour. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Not a single scene in “Shanghai Daughter” was shot in Shanghai. Why did you choose the title, and what does it mean to you?

Shen: “Shanghai daughters” was originally a local term. Villagers near the farms used it for daughters left behind by sent-down youths. Over time, the label seemed to replace each woman’s real name.

Because of my father’s history, I am also, in a sense, a “Shanghai daughter,” and so I went there too. In Xishuangbanna, the phrase took on a double meaning for me. It suggested a kind of twin existence, like looking in a mirror. We seemed to have completely different yet intersecting destinies, one born in Shanghai and the other 3,000 kilometers away in Xishuangbanna.

To me, “daughter” carries something different from either “woman” or “boy.” One of the first Dai expressions my father taught me was “long yin,” meaning “girl.” The image of a girl carries a particular gentleness that can help heal or ease the deep wounds and heaviness behind this subject. The emotional connection extends beyond father and daughter to one girl and another, and one daughter and another.

I did not want to remain trapped within a particular historical wound or view that period only through criticism. I hoped to create something relevant to the present and oriented toward the future, an expression of repair, renewed empathy, and hope.

Sixth Tone: By telling the story from a daughter’s perspective, the film approaches the sent-down youth movement through one family. How does that perspective differ from other portrayals of the movement?

Shen: This is a deeply personal and highly artistic undertaking. It emphasizes experiencing and observing our surroundings and sensory world anew.

While writing the screenplay, I did extensive research. I gathered oral histories, consulted historical archives, and reconnected with researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who study rainforest restoration. But I wanted to hold back those “concrete” materials for as long as possible and put perception first. Thoughts and opinions can easily create divisions, and once expressed, they have their limits. Perception, however, can be shared and remains more open.

Later, an academically minded journalist asked whether this might be related to ecofeminism. I thought the observation was perceptive. It points toward a perspective that moves beyond anthropocentrism and rejects a structure in which “I am the center, and everyone else is the other.”

Sixth Tone: Rubber trees, dragon fruit, and other elements of the landscape recur throughout the film. How did you use them to connect personal memory with the region’s history?

Shen: During my fieldwork in Xishuangbanna, I often walked around whenever I had time. I gradually came to see the landscape itself as a theater. All the legends and stories I had heard, with their intense dramatic and emotional tension, lay silently buried in a small hill in the village.

Generations have cultivated different crops there, from rice and corn to bananas and, more recently, dragon fruit. A small patch of primary forest protected by the Dai people remains on the hillside. Beneath the present landscape lie my father’s old dormitory and the former rubber plantation.

People disappear faster than memories, but stories spanning more than half a century survive in the land’s subtle traces. When you look at the plants and the land and listen to their voices, it feels as if they are telling you stories, though not in a language humans can hear.

I brought the rubber seed to the screening because, to me, it represents a transformation of cause and effect. More than half a century ago, people had little choice but to clear primary rainforest and plant rubber trees to meet the needs of national development. We now understand that this harmed local biodiversity.

A Chinese Academy of Sciences team is rehabilitating degraded rubber groves. Its goal is not to return them to primary rainforest, which would be scientifically unsound, but to rebalance relationships among species. The researchers are restoring poor-quality groves left by haphazard planting and tapping and introducing species that can bridge rubber plantations and native tropical rainforest. By giving the rubber trees a range of “good neighbors,” they can gradually restore the ecosystem’s layers.

To me, they are taking the “effect” of an earlier decision and planting within it a new, positive “cause,” one that may bear better fruit in the future. The relationship between seed and fruit becomes a metaphor for the transformation of cause and effect. I find that deeply inspiring.

Making the film also took me to Malaysia, where I saw some of the country’s earliest rubber trees. Without that initial transplantation, rubber would not have been planted on such a large scale in Xishuangbanna, and many of these stories would not exist.

Sixth Tone: Why did you blend fiction and documentary methods rather than make a conventional documentary centered on your own search?

Shen: I have always felt that the boundary between reality and fiction is unclear, much like the line between dreams and waking life. Historical narratives also have a dreamlike quality for me, something I have explored in my fiction.

If I had relied on documentary methods alone to examine the sent-down youth movement or my relationship with my father, the film would have felt too narrow.

I drew on my own experience to present subjects I have long cared about in a more contemporary, open form. If I had appeared as myself and made a pure documentary, the film would have become too narrow, confined by the standards of historical fact and leaving viewers less room to project themselves into it and experience it openly.

Sixth Tone: How did you approach your father’s past and his former co-workers while making the film? How did they respond after the premiere?

Shen: My father rarely spoke about the decade he spent in Xishuangbanna. People of his generation generally do not talk about those experiences.

You could sense a deep wound behind the way an older audience member spoke yesterday. At times, his questions seemed to judge other people, but they ultimately revealed his own views and emotions.

I didn’t even know my father had tapped rubber. He had never told me what work he did there. Only when I first walked into the plantation did I understand that these were rubber trees and that his generation had planted and tapped them.

At first, I avoided contacting my father’s former co-workers. I knew they would be eager to help and provide a great deal of firsthand material. But the film began with the particular relationship between my father and me. He had told me very little and died before I could learn more, so I went there to search for and reconstruct that missing part of his life.

I also did not want to disturb them for what was, after all, a small personal project. Revisiting those experiences can be extremely painful, especially for some of them.

Since yesterday’s premiere, I have spent all morning replying to their messages. Today, they are gathering for a reunion lunch to discuss the film.

One of my father’s former co-workers wrote: “Thank you to the screenwriter, creative team, and director for bringing a fitting close to our 50 years as sent-down youths.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A still from “Shanghai Daughter.” Courtesy of Shen)
