World.title: OpenAI hack sparks crackdown on weak government websites
World.content:
The OpenAI Medicare breach has prompted an urgent bolstering of government cyber systems to ensure resistance against AI threats.

New details have also been revealed about OpenAI's notification to the government, sent months after its agent went rogue and gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics portal administered by Services Australia.

Following the incident all government departments and agencies have been required to take stock of how their systems may be exposed to risks posed by AI and other emerging technologies.

On Wednesday Home Affairs issued a directive advising departments to target older software and technology.

OpenAI to face inquiry Australia is looking to impose a dual notification requirement under tougher new standards enforced after OpenAI's breach of a Medicare website.

Systems of Government Significance will be prioritised and a review is due by the end of the year.

Less vital systems will be assessed by the end of March next year.

Acting Home Affairs Minister Richard Marles stressed the importance of constantly reviewing the systems in a rapidly changing environment.

"AI is changing the environment in which we operate at extraordinary speed. Government systems need to keep up," he said in a statement.

"We can't wait for an old system to fail before replacing it. We need to identify vulnerabilities and deal with them before they can be exploited."

Richard Marles says government systems need to "keep up" with the risks posed by emerging technology. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The breach has sharpened Labor's plans to impose reporting requirements on artificial intelligence companies.

Australia is set to introduce legislation for national standards to put "guardrails on AI", which would include mandatory standards for data centres, before the end of the year.

A rapid review into the OpenAI breach is due to conclude within weeks and the findings are expected to inform the national standards.

New details about OpenAI government disclosure

OpenAI has faced scrutiny over the two-month delay in informing the government about the Services Australia breach, as well the nature of the disclosure.

The website targeted was a legacy system that has since been shut down, with the data moved to a more secure address.

A copy of the letter obtained by ABC reveals the framing to the government, which was notified of "security vulnerability identified" during a review of the agent's activity.

"An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password," the notification said.

"It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server."

OpenAI has since admitted the agent took actions the company "did not intend" during the incident.

On Tuesday the ChatGPT maker apologised for the breach, which was carried out by an internal-only model that did not have the safeguards used in publicly available products.

In a blog post on OpenAI's website, the company said it intended to "rebuild trust with the Australian people".

"We are sorry and working to do better in the future," the post said.

"This is a new kind of cyber incident which represents an emerging global challenge."

World.title: Estonia slams Russian 'sabotage' after arson attack on defence company
World.content:
EU and NATO leaders are rallying in support of Estonia and Ukraine after the Baltic country accused Russia of "sabotage" in an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer, a claim the Kremlin immediately rejected.

The revelations have outraged Estonia's government, with the country's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, accusing Moscow of aiming to "intimidate us and [weaken] our support for Ukraine.

"We can conclude with certainty that the arson attack … was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation," he said on X.

Mr Tsahkna said an investigation into the August 15 arson attack against the defence company Milrem Robotics, which makes ground drones used in Ukraine, determined that Moscow was responsible.

The Kremlin was quick to deny Estonia's allegation of involvement. (AP: Dmitri Lovetsky)

The findings caused immediate condemnation from Estonia's military allies.

"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against NATO allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine," NATO chief Mark Rutte said.

" But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine. "

Kremlin denies involvement

The Kremlin swiftly dismissed Estonia's accusation as "baseless" and with "absolutely no relation to reality".

"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow in response to an AFP question.

Russia has Germans rethinking Nazi-era protections European intelligence officials say Russia is behind hundreds of hybrid attacks on the continent this year, and that Western allies are too complacent in the face of Moscow's increasing aggression.

Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Along with its neighbours, Latvia and Lithuania, the country has ramped up defence investment and remains a staunch ally of Kyiv.

The European Union said it stood with Estonia calling the arson attack "reckless", and would not be put off supporting Ukraine.

"Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen," European Commission spokesman Christian Wigand said.

French President Emmanuel Macron also called the arson attack a "dangerous escalation" by Russia, and another in a "multiplication of these hostile acts".

"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Mr Macron said on X.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics added that "more support for Ukraine … will be needed and must be provided".

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson called the attribution of the attack "extremely serious" and "directed against Europe as a whole".

AFP

World.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas leader in Gaza
World.content:
An Israeli air-strike killed the head of Hamas' armed wing in north Gaza, officials on both sides said, with the militant group describing him as a leader of the October 7, 2023 attack that precipitated war in the Palestinian enclave.

Izz al-Din Al-Beik, the head of Hamas' armed wing in the northern Gaza Strip, was among three killed in Israeli-strikes on Tuesday.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said the Israeli military targeted Al-Beik, who they accused of planning attacks and recruiting militants.

Medics said the Israeli strike hit an apartment building in Gaza City's Nasr neighbourhood around dawn.

A second person died from wounds after the attack, health officials said.

Later on Tuesday, an Israeli air-strike near a medical clinic in Jabalia refugee camp killed one person, taking the day's death toll to at least three, medics said.

The military said it had targeted a militant in the area.

Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of an October ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks.

Hundreds gather for mass funerals in Gaza

Also on Tuesday, Palestinians in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza buried the remains of 41 people killed by Israeli fire nearly three years ago.

Their bodies were recently recovered from ruins.

Hundreds of relatives and friends gathered in an open space to pay respect as the remains were placed in white shrouds decorated by Palestinian flags.

"There are mixed feelings between relief, sadness, and pain. But thank God, the fire in my heart has eased a little, because my husband now has a grave that my orphaned children and I can visit,” said Areej Farajallah, who lost her husband in the October 31, 2023 strike.

Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 bodies remain buried in wreckage. A Palestinian recovery team that combed wreckage in Gaza City last month said it found the remains of 112 people from the same clan.

“With minimal equipment, their remains were recovered after hours of work, retrieving what was left of bones, some skulls, and hair with which it is extremely difficult for us to identify them," said Rami Al-Ayedi, of Gaza's Civil Defence Service.

Mourners attend a mass funeral for 41 Palestinians whose bodies were recovered from the rubble of a residential building hit in an Israeli strike on October 31, 2023, according to the Civil Defence, in Nuseirat refugee camp in the central Gaza Strip, September 29, 2026. (Mahmoud Issa via Reuters)

The Israeli military says it has killed at least 20 Hamas figures this month, including some it identified as senior commanders or people who took part in the October 7, 2023 attacks or held Israeli hostages.

Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuilding its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza deal.

A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year called for the eventual reconstruction of the territory, but little progress has been made amid a failure to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's health officials. The Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed.

Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel's assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.

Reuters

World.title: Pay, rosters and future jobs at heart of WA's latest coal strike
World.content:
More than 100 mine workers have been joined by Collie residents in a push for higher wages ahead of the WA government's planned shutdown of coal-fired power generation in the state.

The workers from Chinese-owned Premier Coal, the main supplier to the state-owned Muja and Collie power plants, began a two-hour work stoppage at 4pm on Tuesday.

The state government has promised to shutter both power stations, located 200km south of Perth at the heart of the state's largest electricity grid, by 2030, despite doubts over replacement generation.

The Mining and Energy Union said workers were opposed to proposed roster changes, some of which, it said, could result in staff losing about $30,000 a year in penalty rates.

The union says the offer from Premier Coal could leave workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

MEU district secretary Greg Busson estimated average annual salary sat at about $150,000 a year, with more than 90 per cent of the mine's workforce unionised.

While Premier had offered a twelve per cent increase spread over four years, Mr Busson said the union wanted any increase front-loaded.

Premier Coal operates one of WA's two remaining coal mines, both of which are located in Collie. (ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia)

"Depending on which roster the company choose to move to, it could mean up to $30,000 a year reduction in people's wages," Mr Busson said.

" They need to maximise their income for the last bit of the working coal mine. "

Workers now work 12-hour shifts on a four-days on, four-days off, four-nights on, four-nights off rotation.

Mr Busson said two of the proposed rosters would effectively end night shifts and associated penalties.

"The worst [roster] is 8.5 hours all-day shift, Monday to Friday, because they lose all their penalties for weekends and night shift," he said.

A Premier Coal spokesperson said the company was committed to reaching a fair agreement.

"Premier Coal has participated in good faith negotiations throughout the enterprise bargaining process," the spokesperson said.

"Our focus remains on the safety of our workforce and the continuation of safe and efficient operations."

A Premier Coal spokesperson says the company intends to continue negotiating in good faith. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

Anxious about other work in Collie

Mr Busson said $150,000 a year might seem a generous salary, but the work was often dangerous and the pay was less than that taken home by coal workers in other states.

He said workers were also anxious about finding other opportunities in the town as mining operations wound down.

Collie has been the heart of coal mining and power generation in WA for more than a century. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

Mr Busson said that was despite the state government spending more than $700 million on a transition fund to help the town survive the end of coal.

"As hard as the government is trying, we haven't got any new industries in Collie yet," he said.

" Some of these people have to make hard decisions about moving their families away, which is not what anyone wants. "

A state government spokesperson said a number of industries in the Collie Basin were being supported and pointed to the creation of 500 jobs during the construction of Synergy's big battery.

Workers have stepped up calls for clarity around WA's transition away from coal-fired power. (ABC News: Nic Perpitch)

"The Cook Labor Government is committed to Collie's Just Transition, with more than $700 million allocated to support the community and workers," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"This includes $3.2 million to support Premier Coal's workers, including contractors, affected by the company's recent shutdown.

"Together with the recently released Plan for the Collie Basin, which outlines how former coal mining and power generation sites can be repurposed for future industry, the government is continuing to invest … to secure more local jobs and economic opportunities for Collie well beyond 2030."

World.title: 'Remarkable lives': Slain police officers honoured in Canberra
World.content:
Police officers who died in the line of duty have been honoured at an emotional service in Canberra for National Police Remembrance Day.

New touchstones displaying the names of four officers were added to the National Police Memorial in advance of the ceremony on Tuesday afternoon.

They include slain Victoria Police Detective Leading Senior Constable Neal Thompson and Senior Constable Vadim de Waart-Hottart, who were gunned down by Dezi Freeman at Porepunkah in the state's northeast in August 2025.

Victoria Police Detective Leading Senior Constable Neal Thompson was one of two officers fatally shot by Dezi Freeman in Porepunkah in 2025. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the ceremony, said the officers were killed in "despicable circumstances" while carrying out their duties.

Western Australia Detective Senior Constable Maxine Bembridge, who died in May after a crash on her way to work, and retired New South Wales Sergeant Mark Bransgrove, who died from cancer attributed to his service, have also been remembered.

"These few stories tell only a tiny part of four remarkable lives," Ms Mostyn said.

Officers marched from AFP headquarters to the National Police Memorial on the edge of Lake Burley Griffin. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

A solemn procession of about 300 officers on foot, horseback, and motorbikes made the pilgrimage from the Australian Federal Police headquarters to the memorial.

Tearful family members laid wreaths at the national monument at the edge of Lake Burley Griffin.

Acting AFP Commissioner Ian McCartney said it was a day of mourning and a chance to pay tribute to "the selfless and the brave".

Family members of officers killed in the line of duty attended the National Police Remembrance Day service. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"I can see that there are loved ones and colleagues here who were not here last year, and we know what that means," he said.

" We will share the burden of grief with you, and importantly, we will share the incredible and inspiring lives of those who will live forever as heroes in our country. "

There were also tributes for Sydney Constable Mia Lay, who was killed in a police car crash last week.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn paid tribute to New South Wales Constable Mia Lay, who died in a police car crash last week. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"Mia was 20 years old, a tender young age, and had only served with the New South Wales Police Force for 16 months," Ms Mostyn said.

" Her parents and partner have spoken about how much she loved being a police officer. "

Acting Commissioner McCartney said her death was "heartbreaking" and cast a long shadow over the proceedings.

"It is another example of the arbitrary cruelty of service when our members are taken from us too young and too soon," he said.

In the 20 years since the National Police Memorial was unveiled, 117 names have been added. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Constable Lay's name is expected to be formally added to the National Police Memorial next year.

This year marks two decades since the monument was unveiled in Canberra.

Since then, the number of names inscribed has grown from to 719 to 836.

World.title: Crossland to miss NRL GF with four-game ban for Cleary tackle
World.content:
Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland has been suspended for four games by the NRL judiciary for the tackle that left Penrith's Nathan Cleary with a broken leg.

Crossland pleaded guilty to the dangerous contact charge on Tuesday before fronting the judiciary to learn his fate.

He will now miss this Sunday's NRL grand final.

The ban would also rule him out of New Zealand's three World Cup pool games.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop tackle on Cleary in the 36th minute of Newcastle's preliminary final win over the Panthers.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle.

Crossland was represented by barrister James McLeod, who made the case for his client to receive a two or three-week ban.

Crossland cited his career record, telling the judiciary he had never before been sent off. He admitted he got the execution of the tackle wrong but insisted "wasn't trying to hurt anyone".

Phoenix Crossland said he made a remorseful call to Nathan Cleary after the incident. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Arguing for a four-game suspension, the NRL said Crossland's tackle failed to exercise a proper duty of care and, while accidental, did not show enough caution towards Cleary.

Crossland told the judiciary was deeply remorseful for Cleary's injury and had reached out to the Panthers star.

"I called him yesterday. It was obviously a tough phone call," Crossland said.

"I reached out to his dad [Panthers coach Ivan Cleary] as well.

"Nathan was great, he said not to worry about and he understood it was an accident.

"He was such a gentlemen, he told me to stop saying sorry.

"He's my favourite player in the game by a mile. He's the best player in the game and I look up to him."

Phoenix Crossland was sent off in the 36th minute of the preliminary final for the tackle. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Crossland described the incident and fallout as a low point in his life. In his submissions, McLeod produced abusive Instagram messages that had been directed towards Crossland in the past 48 hours.

"It's killing me, it's been the worst couple of days of my life," Crossland said.

"It's meant to be the best week of my life and it's been far from it."

The verdict sets up a scenario where 19-year-old Knight Diesel Hagan could make his NRL debut in a grand final.

It would be the first time such a debut has taken place in 90 years. Eddie Lockhart was the last to do it in 1936, for Balmain.

Harrison Graham will almost certainly shift to a starting role for Newcastle in the grand final, while other options for the Knights include Thomas Cant and Jermaine McEwen.

World.title: Coward punch sentence an 'absolute load of rubbish', victim's parents say
World.content:
A teenager who coward-punched an 18-year-old man outside a nightclub on Hindley Street, leaving him with a traumatic brain injury, has avoided a custodial sentence.

The 17-year-old, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was sentenced in Adelaide Youth Court today after previously pleading guilty to two counts of basic assault causing harm over the February 14 attack.

His victim, 18-year-old Beau Brownbill, has since been diagnosed with a permanent traumatic brain injury.

Magistrate Luke Davis handed the 17-year-old six months' detention but suspended the sentence upon the teenager entering a bond to be of good behaviour for two years.

Outside court Mr Brownbill's father said the sentence was "an absolute load of rubbish".

"My son sits with a jail sentence in his head for the rest of his life and that guy's now free to walk, as free as a bird, [it] is an absolute load of rubbish," Tony Brownbill said.

"He needs to reflect about what happens to you when you do something wrong.

" He's got his life back. Beau's got no life for the rest of his life. "

CCTV footage of Beau Brownbill and the assailant on Hindley Street. (Supplied)

Mr Brownbill's mother said the family was "deeply disappointed and devastated" by the outcome.

"It feels like a secondary blow to our family," Megan Brownbill said.

"We family believe that if you commit a violent life altering attack you should face "full accountability".

Ms Brownbill said that the family had asked the prosecution to appeal the sentence, and that they had been "actively liaising" with the Pat Cronin Foundation and the Sammy D Foundation "to advocate for systematic change, educate the next generation and put an end to senseless violence".

"We'll work along these incredible foundations to do everything we can do to make a difference," she said.

During the sentencing hearing, the prosecutor said Beau Brownbill had "almost fully recovered" from a brain injury he sustained in a sporting accident at the time of the attack.

The Youth Court heard Beau Brownbill had been diagnosed with a permanent traumatic brain injury as a result of the punch. (ABC News: Michael Clements)

Magistrate Davis said the offending was "pointless and avoidable".

"The actual blows occurred in a matter of seconds [and had] profound lifelong consequences," he told the court.

Magistrate Davis said he accepted that there was "an element of self-defence", but described 17-year-old's reaction as "completely unwarranted".

He also said the offender "ran off in a cowardly fashion".

Outside court Beau Brownbill said that he still had the "motivation to go out to the gym, see my friends [and] do what I want".

"Yeah, we haven't had the best outcome, but I want to keep on living my life how I want it to be," he said.

World.title: 32kg of cocaine held in Fiji court's evidence room replaced with flour
World.content:
More than $10 million worth of cocaine stored at a Fiji court as evidence in a long-running drug-trafficking trial has been replaced with flour, in yet another apparent example of internal corruption that has plagued Fiji's authorities.

The ABC has confirmed 32 kilograms of cocaine stored at the Suva High Court for the long-running trial of Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman had been replaced and is now effectively missing, with police investigating the incident.

Earlier this month, local media organisation Fiji Village reported that 7kg of cocaine involved in the trial was missing, and on Tuesday afternoon reported that the rest of the cocaine had been replaced with flour.

It means 39kg of cocaine from the trial is now unaccounted for.

Depending on the purity of the cocaine involved, its street value could be worth as high as $15 million.

Cocaine bricks wash up on Fiji beach Twenty-seven bricks of cocaine have washed up around Fiji's remote Komo Island in recent weeks. Residents are worried about what the find will bring.

Fiji Police issued a statement on Tuesday afternoon confirming "forensic tests" of the drugs had come back negative.

"The exhibits were all tampered with, and the investigation is focused on those directly charged with the management of the exhibits at the High Court Registry," the statement said.

"A person of interest allegedly involved in the incident is currently overseas and will be questioned."

Fiji is ground zero in the Pacific's drugs crisis Watch part one of Foreign Correspondent's special investigation.

Aziz Rahman was convicted in 2021 and sentenced to 23 years in prison, but later appealed the sentence and walked free in February 2026.

Fiji's public prosecutor appealed that and won, and the conviction was reinstated with Aziz Rahman returning to jail.

In Fiji, evidence generally remains in the courtroom until the appeal process is complete. It is understood the discrepancies in the cocaine were discovered by authorities when they went to destroy the evidence this month.

Fiji has become ground zero in the Pacific's struggle with transnational drug trafficking, with an ABC investigation earlier this year uncovering Australian connections in the transportation of drugs through the country.

The latest incident comes after Fiji's prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, last year disbanded the country's narcotics bureau in the wake of 27 officers being taken to court for drug-related offences over the previous three years.

Fiji police seize alleged $780m cocaine haul — but 'narco sub' is still missing Fijian chiefs reported suspicious activity along their stretch of coastline to law enforcement agencies — which then swooped on an alleged $780 million drug operation.

It is unclear who was responsible for the management of the missing cocaine; however, the country's Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions has indicated the "storing and securing of drugs" was a police matter.

Fiji Police Assistant Commissioner Mesake Waqa told the ABC earlier this year that the force was "not a corrupt institution".

"Corruption is something that has challenged us for quite some time," he told ABC's Foreign Correspondent program.

"We have officers who have crossed the line, and we have been transparent about it; in every case that is reported to us, we will investigate it."

World.title: Queensland Ballet posts another multimillion-dollar loss
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArts Queensland Ballet posts another multimillion-dollar loss Nick Dent September 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Ballet posted a net operating loss of $5.24 million after a near 30 per cent slump in annual box office revenue. But the multimillion-dollar hit to the bottom line in 2025 was a significant improvement on the $9.5 million loss the previous year, which prompted the company to cut 29 staff, including eight dancers. Total income rose 13 per cent on the prior year to $24.9 million, according to its 2025 annual report. Queensland Ballet posted a $5.24 million loss for the 2025 calendar year. David Kelly Queensland Ballet chair Brett Clark OAM said the result represented encouraging progress in a challenging environment, but long-term sustainability would “require continued cost discipline across the organisation”.



“While there is considerably more work ahead, we now have a stronger foundation, greater clarity and a clear path toward building a financially resilient, artistically ambitious Queensland Ballet,” he said. QB’s total box office for 2025 was more than $5.1 million from 50,098 tickets sold, down from more than $7.6 million in 2024. Staged annually, The Nutcracker is consistently the company’s most successful production. David Kelly As always, the company’s standout performer was its annual staging of The Nutcracker, which sold 19,782 tickets and generated $2.5 million in revenue. Other popular performances included Romeo & Juliet and Dangerous Liaisons.



The company’s annual Giving Day exceeded its $2 million target, raising more than $2.22 million for the Academy of Queensland Ballet. For 2025, Queensland Ballet received $3.7 million in funding from the state government through Arts Queensland, with the Department of Education and Queensland Health supplying another $1.3 million. A further $1.9 million came from the Department of Housing and Public Works for the cafe and restaurant fitout at the ballet’s West End headquarters, the Thomas Dixon Centre. However, Queensland Ballet only received $873,440 in annual investment from Creative Australia for 2025 under the National Performing Arts Partnership Framework. By contrast, The Australian Ballet received more than $7 million in federal funding. The annual investment under the framework is locked in until 2028.





“We must be ambitious about creating new work, but also intelligent about how it is created, where it premieres, and the audiences it can reach,” Queensland Ballet artistic director Ivan Gil-Ortega said. World.title: The king of dinner theatre does lunch
World.content:
The latest brushes with fame (C8) involve air travel. Here’s Mark Berg of Caringbah South: “While having lunch in 1994 with friends in a Bondi Beach hotel, an elderly American gentleman wearing loafers, accompanied by an aged but glamorous lady, stood at the top of the stairs and called to me in an American accent, ‘Young man, can you please help me down these stairs?’, which I did. They were Hollywood stars Van Johnson and Kathryn Grayson. His feet were swollen after the long flight, and he was struggling to walk. They were deeply grateful for the assistance.”

On a flight from Delhi to Kashmir I sat next to Ben Kingsley not long after Gandhi was released,” claims Joe Veness of Ingleburn. “On arrival our luggage was mislaid so Ben and I searched the terminal together. I carried a camera but was too polite to use it. Nobody believed me when I told them I’d been to India and met Ben Kingsley.”

Recent talk of the Jumbo jet reminds me of when I worked for a government department and my phone extension was 747,” says Natasha Lee of Alexandria. “After a few work trips on 747s one of my work colleagues suggested my nickname should be ‘Jumbo’. I was not impressed.”

“As a young teacher in the 1970s, fresh from city life, not only did I encounter bogong moths (C8) in the wonderful country town of Tumut, but also observed that the high school magazine was called Bogong,″ recalls Lyn Langtry of East Ryde.

Marie and Tim Slack-Smith’s anniversary cruise (C8), reminded Colin Campbell of Coogee of the time “years ago, when my wife and I were planning a European holiday and were trying to decide whether to finish up in Prague or Berlin. That weekend the DS cryptic crossword included ‘Put Berlin off the plan’. Didn’t have to tell us twice!”

World.title: Queues at 9am, full by 11.30am: Housing crunch challenges rough-sleeping plan
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHomelessness Queues at 9am, full by 11.30am: Housing crunch challenges rough-sleeping plan Cara Waters September 29, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Homelessness services warn that they are stretched beyond capacity and the state government’s $27.8 million assertive outreach program to reduce rough sleeping will further increase demand. Under a new statewide expansion of the “by-name” program, which already operates in inner Melbourne, teams of homelessness workers will be sent onto streets around Victoria to profile homeless people, build trust, prioritise those in the greatest need, and connect them to housing and other support services. The total number of people sleeping rough is unknown as some do not seek help. Eddie Jim However, homelessness services warn crisis accommodation centres are regularly full before lunchtime, and that homeless people end up being placed in unsafe accommodation. The City of Melbourne has been operating a by-name homelessness list since 2019 – rather than waiting for people to access services – but homelessness continues to grow in the CBD, with 140 people on the list.



Council to Homeless Persons chief executive Deborah Di Natale backed the state government’s push for assertive outreach as a vital lifeline for people sleeping rough, but she said it would probably cost $31 million to deliver and did not go far enough. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Eye contact and a coffee: The $28m plan to drastically cut rough sleeping “Homelessness is increasing across Victoria, and we know that the single biggest investment that is going to make a difference to ending homelessness in Victoria is to make a commitment to build more social housing,” she said. Council to Homeless Persons data shows 10,673 people sleeping rough sought support from specialist homelessness services in Victoria last year, a 25 per cent increase in five years. The actual number of rough sleepers in the state is unknown because many of them do not seek support. These are the people who are targeted with assertive outreach.



“If you have a look at people who are working on the frontline now, they have got a queue from 9am, by about 11 or 11.30 am every single housing option is exhausted, and they are then dealing with a queue of people that they can’t provide any crisis accommodation for,” Di Natale said. One young woman working on the frontline told her: “I have to make a decision about this woman who has come to me. Do I put her in this really unsafe, dodgy rooming house that I know is totally inappropriate? Or do I say, continue sleeping rough, knowing that when you are sleeping rough you are likely to be the victim of crime?” Melbourne City Mission chief executive Paul Wappett also backed assertive outreach as a positive start but similarly said more support services were needed, particularly for young people. “We’re going to increase the demand by doing these assertive outreach programs, and it’s important that we identify who needs these services and give our best opportunities to try and provide all the support that we need to,” he said. “But it will highlight just how much more housing we need for people who find themselves in homelessness.” Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio backs assertive outreach, and will outline his approach to tackling homelessness at next month’s Melbourne Assembly public forum.



Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece said the level of homelessness was less than its peak in 2019, when there were 500 homeless people in the CBD, but that the council’s by-name list – which proactively identifies every rough sleeper, tracks their progress, and aligns housing supply with individual needs – was not enough on its own. Lord Mayor Nick Reece says more housing is needed to tackle the homelessness problem. Penny Stephens “Homelessness, rough sleeping, is one of the most complex societal problems that we face, and it’s so multifaceted,” Reece said. “One component of it is the crisis in the mental health system manifests itself in people with acute mental health issues presenting on the streets.” The council has increased its Melbourne outreach team to seven workers, including trained mental health officers to deal with people with acute mental health issues. It has also opened the Make Room homelessness service, which houses 50 people. “Make Room has made a big difference in Melbourne,” Reece said. “But the truth is, we could use another two Make Rooms in the City of Melbourne.”



Related Article City life ‘I made a mistake’: Charities still waiting for Reece’s promised $9 million for the homeless Reece said that in a typical month, the council’s support team interacted 400 times with people experiencing homelessness, and service users made 5500 visits to the council’s safe-space program in August. “Across the board we need more services, more beds and more homes,” he said. “Obviously, when you’re assertively reaching out and helping someone on the street and giving them a pathway, they need somewhere to go. “That means that we need that injection of funds in emergency accommodation, temporary accommodation, and long-term accommodation as well.” Reece attracted criticism this year after failing to deliver on his promise of $6 million in homelessness funding to the Salvation Army and a further $3.2 million to Melbourne City Mission.



“The City of Melbourne’s putting more money into food relief than ever before, and Vincent Care, who are now delivering on that contract, are delivering more warm meals, hot breakfast to people than ever before,” he said. World.title: ‘Worst couple of days of my life’: Crossland cops four-match ban for Cleary tackle
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Worst couple of days of my life’: Crossland cops four-match ban for Cleary tackle Chris Barrett September 29, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A remorseful Phoenix Crossland has described the fallout to a tackle that broke the leg of Nathan Cleary as “the worst couple of days of my life” as he was suspended for Sunday’s grand final. The Newcastle hooker was banned for four matches at a judiciary hearing on Tuesday night, stripping him of a place in the Knights’ title decider against the Sydney Roosters and the start of New Zealand’s World Cup campaign. Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland is sent off on Sunday. NRL Photos The 26-year-old joins an unfortunate list of players to have sat out grand finals with suspension, among them Cameron Smith in 2008 with Melbourne, Latrell Mitchell with South Sydney in 2021, Steve Roach with Balmain in 1988 and Arthur Beetson with the Tigers in 1969. Crossland’s destiny was all but sealed from the moment Cleary’s left leg was twisted in a hip-drop tackle during the first half of Sunday’s preliminary final and he was sent off.



The Panthers halfback suffered a compound fracture of his ankle and faces months of recovery after undergoing surgery. “It’s been the worst couple of days of my life,” Crossland said. “He’s my favourite player by a mile so to be the reason he’s in hospital … it’s killing me.” Loading Having been referred directly to the judiciary without a charge or grading, the only question to be answered was how many games Crossland would be suspended for. He took full responsibility for a tackle gone wrong as he was trying to save a try and revealed he had phoned Cleary’s father and Penrith coach Ivan Cleary to apologise on Monday, as well as the champion No.7 himself.



“I had to apologise first and foremost to make sure he’s doing all right,” said Crossland, who became emotional when asked about the prospect of missing a grand final. “It’s a horrific incident and he’s our best player. I reached out to his dad as well. I apologised to him. It ruined a great game and left a sour taste in everyone’s mind.” Nathan Cleary posted a statement from his hospital bed supporting Crossland. Instagram Crossland, who was the awarded the Danny Buderus medal as the Knights’ best and fairest player for the season, has been the subject of online abuse since being given his marching orders on Sunday which Cleary has condemned. In his absence, Harrison Graham is set to be promoted to start at dummy half against the Roosters, but teenage hooker Diesel Hagan was also named in the Knights’ extended grand final squad for what could be a remarkable entry to the NRL.



Related Article NRL grand final ‘Clearly knocked out’: Top neurologist questions Watson’s fitness for grand final If Hagan plays on Sunday he would be the first player to make his debut in a grand final since Eddie Lockhart for Balmain against the Roosters in 1936. He is no relation to Michael Hagan, Newcastle’s coach when they last won a premiership in 2001. Michael Hagan and former Newcastle grand final winner Mark Hughes provided character references for Crossland to judiciary panel members Ryan James, Paul Simpkin and chairman Geoff Bellew, who were shown 12 angles of the offending tackle. During an 80-minute hearing, Knights lawyer James McLeod had proposed a two- to three-game sanction but the panel imposed the four-match ban suggested by NRL counsel Patrick Knowles SC after deliberating for 17 minutes. A gracious Crossland said he would turn his attention immediately to supporting his teammates.



“I want to thank everybody inside for a fair hearing,” he said. “I apologise to Nathan and the Panthers and more importantly the game and the fans. “It’s a terrible start to the most important week of the year due to myself. As soon as I walk out of this building my focus goes to the Newcastle Knights winning this grand final [and] helping Harrison Graham prepare as best as he can and get a win on Sunday.” Crossland’s suspension will be completed during the pool stage of the World Cup if New Zealand notifies the International Rugby League that he would have been selected. World.title: Poultry fanciers’ show dreams fail to hatch after bird flu scare
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Royal Show Poultry fanciers’ show dreams fail to hatch after bird flu scare Carolyn Webb September 29, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As an elder statesman of poultry-fancying, Alf Woods is mentoring someone in the craft, and you could say his protege is a chick off the old block. Woods, who has been a poultry competitor for almost 90 years, is cock-a-hoop that his 10-year-old great-grandson, Blair, is egg-cited by the hobby. Chookas for next year’s show: Alf Woods, 98, and his great-grandson, Blair, 10, at the family chicken coops in Greenvale. Jason South “It’s a passing of the baton to a younger person, and I think it’s great,” Woods said. Blair’s first competitions this year including winning best junior at the Pekin Bantam Club of Victoria’s annual show at Ballarat, and Woods said Blair had been ready “to take on the big boys” at his first Melbourne Royal Show.



But those dreams have shattered like a broken egg. Photo: Matt Golding In August, organisers announced that the show’s poultry competitions and exhibitions were cancelled for 2026 due to the surge of H5N1 bird flu cases around Australia. Fanciers were dismayed, but agreed the move was necessary to protect birds from the deadly virus. Blair had tended, and registered to compete, with his five Pekin bantams – gifts from his “Pa”, Alf.



Woods, who first competed with chooks at then-named Royal Melbourne Show in 1939, aged 11, was himself aiming to bring 19 entries, including Old English Game fowl, to the 2026 show at the Melbourne Showgrounds. In his element: Alf Woods pictured in 2008 with an Old English Game fowl at the-then Royal Melbourne Show, now Melbourne Royal Show. Craig Abraham Woods, who turns 99 on October 26, said he felt terrible he couldn’t attend, but he understands. “If one bird at the royal [show] got the disease, they could kill every bird in the royal.” At home in Greenvale in Melbourne’s outer north, Woods keeps his birds in covered pens that protect them from possible infection from wild birds.



Woods, has missed only a few Melbourne Royal shows in his life, including the shows cancelled during World War II and the COVID-19 pandemic. “It’s a great experience,” he said. “I don’t mind if I win or don’t win a prize. I talk to my old friends and the new friends coming along. I just love talking to people.” Michael Holmes, of Wangaratta, the head of the show’s poultry committee and a competitor for 45 years, said “a lot of people are disappointed” and it was “an empty feeling” not competing. Michael Holmes pictured at his Wangaratta property with his prize brown leghorn rooster. Jason Robins But he said cancelling poultry was the right move for our biosecurity and “hopefully, we’ll get going again next year”.



Tony Milton, from Healesville, said he was disappointed not to be bringing his Rhode Island reds and Sebright breeds to be judged against the Australian standard. But he said it was “better to err on the side of caution”. Related Article Lunch with Why this science writer will hole up on a farm in WA if bird flu strain mutates According to the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA), there have been no detections of H5N1 bird flu in poultry in Australia. Among non-poultry birds, 220 positive cases of the flu have been detected in 32 local government areas in Victoria, across 21 different species.



A poultry housing requirement for flocks of 50 or more birds is in place in Victoria for coastal and southern municipalities to help reduce contact with wild birds. The Victorian government recommends poultry owners outside the specified areas also prevent contact between birds and poultry with wild birds, in combination with other biosecurity measures. World.title: ‘Ultimate superbug’: New form of antibiotic resistance uncovered
World.content:
Exclusive NationalScience ‘Ultimate superbug’: New form of antibiotic resistance uncovered Angus Dalton September 29, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. You’re reading an excerpt – sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox. In the brutal arms race between drugs and bugs, serendipity has often been on humanity’s side. In 1928, Alexander Fleming left a petri dish unsealed and later found it overgrown with a green fuzz that had partly killed his culture of Staphylococcus aureus. He’d discovered penicillin. Clostridioides difficile commonly causes severe gut infections in hospitals. Scientists have uncovered a new way it’s evolving to outfox drugs. Nathan Perri That was the opening salvo in what would become an evolutionary battle between medical researchers and their pathogenic microbial enemies that have rapidly evolved to outfox antibiotics and kill more than 1.2 million people each year through drug-resistant infections.



But recently, an unexpected discovery by scientists at Monash University has unveiled both a new weapon against bacteria and an unexpected defence. “Bacteria are evolving in ways that we’re not anticipating – it’s creating another level of superbug,” says Professor Dena Lyras, director of the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute, who focuses on a hospital-haunting bug that can unleash deadly diarrhoea. Clostridioides difficile under the microscope. Wikimedia Hidden yet horrid Nearly a century after Fleming’s accidental discovery, bacterial researchers found themselves once again flummoxed in the lab.



Lyras and her colleagues were trying to grow Clostridioides difficile, a bacterium that commonly infects the gut after antibiotic treatment in humans. “Every hospital has a problem with C. difficile. And it’s sort of a bit hidden. But we have elderly patients who become very sick and die of it,” Lyras says. The researchers’ lab-raised bacterium grew fine, but it couldn’t make spores, which in this species is key to reproduction and infection. The researchers were stumped. “Gosh, they’re tough, I tell you … You irradiate them for 200 hours and they still aren’t 100 per cent dead.” Professor Dena Lyras on “ultimate superbug” spores They investigated the batch and discovered the liquid medium they were growing the bacteria in contained a type of substance called a cephamycin.



They had inadvertently discovered a spore-busting antibiotic – that cephamycins could help treat C. difficile and other spore-forming nasties such as anthrax. “A lot of spores are made in the patient as they’re infected. We discovered a group of antibiotics that actually stopped sporulation in its tracks,” Lyras says. “It was fantastic.” In it for the long game: Professor Lyras in her lab in 2009. Luis Enrique Ascui It wasn’t long, of course, before the bacteria fired back. “In about 10 per cent of the strains that we examined, this sporulation-blocking strategy didn’t work. We wondered why it wasn’t working – and that’s where we discovered this subset of strains that have this new resistance gene.”



Like an ‘armoured truck’: The new discovery Some bacteria have a “normal” form – where they grow, eat, reproduce and, in C. difficile’s case, gleefully infect people’s colons – and a “spore” form. These spores are extremely hard to kill. “Spores are the survival version of the cell,” Lyras says. “They’ve got their DNA packed in the middle, and then they’ve got layers of stuff around them like an armoured truck, tightly packed without that much water. So it’s just really tough.” What Lyras and her colleagues have now reported in Nature Communications is an antibiotic resistance gene arising in the spore form of bacteria – not the normal form – for the first time. “We hadn’t anticipated that; it’s not been described before, and it’s making that cell type tougher, stronger, more likely to survive in the environment. That’s going to have repercussions in a hospital where you can’t kill these spores off,” Lyras says.



“Gosh, they’re tough, I tell you. You’ve got to have like half an hour of contact with bleach to kill them. You irradiate them for 200 hours and they still aren’t 100 per cent dead.” Related Article Exclusive

Science Slowly strangled: Cancer institute to close as research centres buckle under funding crisis In the resistant bacteria, a new gene codes for a protein that can continue making spores, even when hit by antibiotics. The spores can survive hospital-grade disinfectants and hot laundry temperatures. Because they’re already Terminator-tough, spores taking on a drug-resistant gene create the “ultimate superbug”, like a seed that can lie dormant in soil for years before sprouting, Lyras says.



The spores can persist for as long as two years in hospitals. Off the back of the findings, Lyras asks: “Do we need to rethink our strategies that we’re using to clean the hospitals, to clean the beds, to clean the surfaces, to clean the sheets, to clean the toilets and the sinks?” CSIRO’s predicted global impact of antimicrobial resistance by 2050 Deaths from infections that were previously treatable with antibiotics will exceed 10 million

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) will result in up to 7.5% global decrease in livestock production

A decline in global GDP of between 3.8-5%

An increase in 28.3 million people in extreme poverty

Global real exports shrinking by 1.1%

Global healthcare costs increase from $300 billion to >$1 trillion per year. Dragon blood and doom The new discovery underscores the urgency of finding new ways to kill infectious bacteria.



Some scientists are looking at the antimicrobial elixir that is honey and bug-killing compounds found in Komodo dragon blood, while others have used AI to uncover more than 12,000 antibiotic compounds in ancient microbes called Archaea. Copper is also of interest because the metal ions punch holes in microbial membranes. One recently published 10-year study estimated the installation of copper-infused resin on counter tops, sinks, tray tables and bedside rails in a Texan hospital had prevented 78 C. difficile infections. Some scientists, including microbiologist Dr Kenya Fernandes, have turned to natural solutions like honey to address the critical global health crisis of antimicrobial resistance. Janie Barrett Another promising approach is engineering viruses called bacteriophages to attack and kill superbugs. The problem is that much of the blue-sky research that uncovers new antibiotic molecules is underfunded. Converting one of these compounds into a useful drug is then enormously expensive and time-intensive.



There’s also little incentive for big pharmaceutical companies to bring new antibiotics to market. Antibiotics might be used just once and even then, the mantra is to not overuse them lest you contribute to the antibiotic resistance problem. New drugs are also often quickly out-evolved. A range of new antibiotic approaches are under investigation, yet reliant on dwindling funding. Janie Barrett That’s why antibiotics are the “opposite of a profitable blockbuster drug”, according to Professor Mark Blaskovich at the Institute for Molecular Bioscience, University of Queensland. Experts have urged the government to set up a “Netflix” style agreement that would see regulator payments pour into pharmaceutical companies, like a subscription, in return for access to a stream of new antibiotics.

World.title: Queensland Ballet posts another multimillion-dollar loss
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArts Queensland Ballet posts another multimillion-dollar loss Nick Dent September 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Ballet posted a net operating loss of $5.24 million after a near 30 per cent slump in annual box office revenue. But the multimillion-dollar hit to the bottom line in 2025 was a significant improvement on the $9.5 million loss the previous year, which prompted the company to cut 29 staff, including eight dancers. Total income rose 13 per cent on the prior year to $24.9 million, according to its 2025 annual report. Queensland Ballet posted a $5.24 million loss for the 2025 calendar year. David Kelly Queensland Ballet chair Brett Clark OAM said the result represented encouraging progress in a challenging environment, but long-term sustainability would “require continued cost discipline across the organisation”.



“While there is considerably more work ahead, we now have a stronger foundation, greater clarity and a clear path toward building a financially resilient, artistically ambitious Queensland Ballet,” he said. QB’s total box office for 2025 was more than $5.1 million from 50,098 tickets sold, down from more than $7.6 million in 2024. Staged annually, The Nutcracker is consistently the company’s most successful production. David Kelly As always, the company’s standout performer was its annual staging of The Nutcracker, which sold 19,782 tickets and generated $2.5 million in revenue. Other popular performances included Romeo & Juliet and Dangerous Liaisons.



The company’s annual Giving Day exceeded its $2 million target, raising more than $2.22 million for the Academy of Queensland Ballet. For 2025, Queensland Ballet received $3.7 million in funding from the state government through Arts Queensland, with the Department of Education and Queensland Health supplying another $1.3 million. A further $1.9 million came from the Department of Housing and Public Works for the cafe and restaurant fitout at the ballet’s West End headquarters, the Thomas Dixon Centre. However, Queensland Ballet only received $873,440 in annual investment from Creative Australia for 2025 under the National Performing Arts Partnership Framework. By contrast, The Australian Ballet received more than $7 million in federal funding. The annual investment under the framework is locked in until 2028.





“We must be ambitious about creating new work, but also intelligent about how it is created, where it premieres, and the audiences it can reach,” Queensland Ballet artistic director Ivan Gil-Ortega said. World.title: The king of dinner theatre does lunch
World.content:
The latest brushes with fame (C8) involve air travel. Here’s Mark Berg of Caringbah South: “While having lunch in 1994 with friends in a Bondi Beach hotel, an elderly American gentleman wearing loafers, accompanied by an aged but glamorous lady, stood at the top of the stairs and called to me in an American accent, ‘Young man, can you please help me down these stairs?’, which I did. They were Hollywood stars Van Johnson and Kathryn Grayson. His feet were swollen after the long flight, and he was struggling to walk. They were deeply grateful for the assistance.”

On a flight from Delhi to Kashmir I sat next to Ben Kingsley not long after Gandhi was released,” claims Joe Veness of Ingleburn. “On arrival our luggage was mislaid so Ben and I searched the terminal together. I carried a camera but was too polite to use it. Nobody believed me when I told them I’d been to India and met Ben Kingsley.”

Recent talk of the Jumbo jet reminds me of when I worked for a government department and my phone extension was 747,” says Natasha Lee of Alexandria. “After a few work trips on 747s one of my work colleagues suggested my nickname should be ‘Jumbo’. I was not impressed.”

“As a young teacher in the 1970s, fresh from city life, not only did I encounter bogong moths (C8) in the wonderful country town of Tumut, but also observed that the high school magazine was called Bogong,″ recalls Lyn Langtry of East Ryde.

Marie and Tim Slack-Smith’s anniversary cruise (C8), reminded Colin Campbell of Coogee of the time “years ago, when my wife and I were planning a European holiday and were trying to decide whether to finish up in Prague or Berlin. That weekend the DS cryptic crossword included ‘Put Berlin off the plan’. Didn’t have to tell us twice!”

World.title: Homeowners bear cost of Trump’s behaviour
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Homeowners bear cost of Trump’s behaviour September 29, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. COST OF LIVING Nicholas Kristof highlights the damage being done to international accord by the US administration, and the continued worthy work of the United Nations (″⁣The UN is terrible – but right now, we need it desperately″⁣, 28/9).

It was shocking to see President Trump last week make an address full of dire threats of annihilation of Iran at the UN General Assembly, which should be a forum for promoting peace. The actions of the Trump administration in its second term have had a disastrous effect on the wellbeing of so many countries. These include the closure of USAID, withdrawal from the World Health Organisation, and not providing the support Ukraine needs to protect its cities from aerial attack.

The US’s totally ill-considered war with Iran has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with the consequent rise in oil prices feeding inflation around the world. The import tariffs introduced by Trump – against all economic wisdom – are also fuelling inflationary pressures and slowing world trade.

The US’s huge and ballooning budget deficit and public debt is driving up interest rates internationally as investors demand better returns for holding government bonds.

These are the main factors making management of the Australian economy by the Reserve Bank and the government very difficult, and other nations face similar dilemmas. It has become more important than ever for democracies around the world to coordinate their actions in the areas of economic management, international aid and strategic policies, to counteract the harmful effects of the misguided actions of the Trump administration.

Andrew Trembath, Blackburn Economic system aids, protects the super rich

According to the Australian Financial Review, the fortunes of Australia’s wealthiest 200 people, rose by $39 billion collectively, to $707 billion during the last financial year. However, it will once again be the country’s mortgage holders and renters, many of whom are seriously struggling, who will be penalised by the RBA and by default, charged with the job of bringing inflation under control.

Australia has now morphed into an economic system that facilitates and encourages the concentration of extraordinary wealth.

Craig Jory, Albury, NSW



RBA causes mortgagee misery

What is the point of the Reserve Bank? One of its main functions seems to be to cause misery to mortgage holders. Its attitude to current and potential unemployed people is atrocious. It doesn’t show any compassion or consider them as individual human beings who hate being unemployed and are desperately looking for work.

Lorraine Bates, Balwyn What cuts would Taylor and Wilson make?

The Liberal Party claims that the government’s so-called spending addiction is largely responsible for the Reserve Bank’s four interest rate increases this year. However, neither Angus Taylor nor Tim Wilson have outlined what government spending they want to see reduced.

That makes their criticism an empty argument.

Garry Meller, Bentleigh Vary GST rate to control inflation

Varying interest rates seems to be the only tool the Reserve Bank uses to control inflation. This means the burden of economic management falls entirely on those with mortgages or other debts, while providing a windfall for lenders.

Surely, the burden should be borne by us all through increasing or decreasing tax rates. The goods and services tax, which we all pay, could be adjusted, perhaps every six months, so the cost of cooling or stimulating the economy is born more equally.

Harley Powell, Elsternwick THE FORUM Barnaby’s choice

Barnaby Joyce is advocating that the Albanese government reverses its decision to restrict the period backpackers can spend in Australia. For him, the change is a blow to the agricultural sector’s ability to recruit workers. (“Labor pushes to boost Pacific workers as Joyce says some Australians ‘bung lazy‴⁣⁣, 29/8.

Oddly however, he is also on the record as saying that you have to pay a competitive wage to attract the right sort of worker – the “if you pay peanuts you get monkeys” argument. So, given that the hourly rate for apple pickers, for example, is said to equate to around 4 cents per piece, maybe the industry could look at paying pickers more.

That needn’t come out of farmers’ pockets – Joyce could justifiably point to the supermarkets, who are making significant profits, and pressure them to accept a slightly lower margin.

One Nation has a catch phrase: “take back Australia”. Pauline Hanson has said she aims to “drain the billabong”.

Some people might say that, if Joyce is on board with those goals, then advocating to retain what John Howard introduced is a bit gutless.

Alun Breward, Malvern East



Hanson on hate speech

It is not surprising that Labor, the teals and Jewish community leaders are calling for tougher hate speech laws (″⁣Hanson and Spender seek tougher hate speech laws″⁣, 29/9), but Hanson?

Talk about the ‘pot calling the kettle black’.

Hanson has never shied away from using hate speech. In February, she said on Sky News, ″⁣You say, ‘There’s good Muslims out there’. How can you tell me there are good Muslims?″⁣, as one example.

Let’s hope any tougher laws catch Hanson in her bigoted speech.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn AI is made by humans

The AI component of an “agent” is a language model, no different from ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini – text goes in, and text comes out. With “agentic AI” the input text includes a problem to be solved, or a goal to be achieved. The model outputs the next step to be taken towards the desired result. This output may include lists of programs or commands to be executed to gather further information that the model needs to progress the task. Having no ability to execute any commands itself, the text-generator relies on a conventional controlling program to execute the commands and feed back the results.

Humans trained the models with insufficient constraints on the commands they could request to be executed. Humans wrote the programs that blindly executed the commands without for consequences.

It is clear where responsibility for their actions lies. We already have laws to address human irresponsibility and negligence. We should use them.

Mark Summerfield, Northcote Hope for the best

With Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s abusive exploitation of the United Nations pulpit fresh in our minds, Nicholas Kristof does us a great favour with his spirited defence of the organisation (″⁣The UN is terrible – but, right now, we need it desperately″⁣, 28/9).

In one telling sentence he reminds us ″⁣that millions more children would die every year if it weren’t for UNICEF, the World Food Program, the UN Refugee Agency and the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs″⁣.

He could also have named UNRWA, the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees.

Whether the malign recalcitrance of the United States, Russia and China on the Security Council can be overcome by a new ″⁣charismatic, outspoken leader″⁣ remains to be seen. The hope seems forlorn, but hope we must.

Tom Knowles, Parkville Invasive AI

Ever since the introduction of rabbits into Australia we have been subject to the ravages of invasive species. Rabbits, trout, carp, deer, fire ants, you name it. Now we have Artificial Intelligence, another form of invasive species.

At present, no one has been able to curb its malign presence. What we need is something of the order of the dung beetle, introduced to clean up after cattle, and which dairy farmers will tell you has succeeded beautifully.

Now that AI is let loose on the world, and those responsible inform us that it has escaped, can we expect its creators to enable AI to do what cane toads were originally expected to do.

Oh wait, what was the problem in the first place?

John Whelen, Box Hill Sth Virtually unassisted

This experience is becoming far too familiar. I had an item I wanted to buy, so I did as we’ve been trained to do and checked the company’s website. No luck. So I thought I’d ring them. The virtual assistant could not understand my single word request, so I spelt it out. I was then put through to ″⁣the team″⁣, but the call went unanswered. I tried three times. There was no offer to leave a message, just to call back. The company’s time is important. Mine’s not.

Jan Lacey, North Melbourne



Public school effort

As I spun around my enjoyable copy of Good Weekend last Sunday, it was with dismay I realised that the happy, caring and engaged learners smiling out at me were all from private schools.

As a product of regional public schools, I now teach in them. Each day I see very similar faces turning up and putting their best foot forward, accessing all the same strategies (granted, probably not the pilot training) in a sector without anywhere close to the financial advantages offered within private school communities.

Any chance that one day we can see an  run for the opportunities, ingenuity, and absolute effort put into our public schools?

Because the other 95 per cent of us ideally need to feel good about what we can afford to buy as well.

Andrew Porter, Bright Child-free spaces

What goes for dogs also goes for children. I have lost count of the times I’ve been in my local pub/cafe where parents let their children run riot, screaming, yelling, climbing. Can we please ban children from them.

Laurens Meyer, Richmond Letters to editor mystery

Your correspondent (Letters, ″⁣Lift your game, people″⁣, 29/9) suggests that letters to the editor lack originality and hence calls for more letters which contain some new ideas.

It is likely that many truly original ideas are contained in letters received by the editor but readers do not discover them because they were not printed. They might have been judged to be too offensive, inaccurate or downright wacky to appear.

However, this quality control is sometimes hard to fathom.

As someone who has written many (literally thousands written, hundreds printed) letters to the editor in more than 50 years, I am often surprised by which letters appear and which do not.

In the latter case, after momentary disappointment I might mutter, ″⁣But that was a good one. It was so original.″⁣

Rod Wise, Surrey Hill Try this idea for size

Re Letters, (“Lift your game, people”, 29/9). Whilst not a new idea, downsizing AFL teams to sixteen rather than eighteen players plus interchange as evidenced in historic VFA games, would help overcome many challenges associated with congested play.

Russell Harrison, Sandringham It’s complicated

Balderdash to your correspondent (29/9). Letter writers to The Age cover a wide and complex range of themes, old and new.

Footy, dogs, grief, learning and bikies are some of mine. Myra Fisher of East Brighton stretches even wider!

Glenda Johnston, Queenscliff



Wharfie Time genius

I’ve been a basketball court announcer/DJ, and something like Wharfie Time is a gift from the gods. I really feel for whoever pressed go, and sad that we’ll probably never hear it again.

It’s a tough gig to get right, to find that balance between letting the game do the talking and getting the fans involved. And I always had the Ted Lasso “Oi Wanker” fans telling me I played too much music. Or the wrong music. Or at the wrong time.

Wharfie Time was genius. Totally original, reflecting the soul and origins of the club, stirring, anthemic, dramatic, someone really nailed it thinking that up. And the fans loved it. It’s just so hard, and I’ve been there, knowing when to throw the switch.

Think of it this way: if they hadn’t played it, Freo most likely still would have lost and every fan, YouTuber, pundit, podcaster and player would have been empurpled demanding to know why the didn’t play it.

″⁣No Wharfie Time Costs Freo the Final” screams the West Australian! “We were waiting but it never came” players say.

Everywhere else, especially basketball, if you banned Walk of Life by Dire Straits, We Are The Champions by Queen, almost every AC/DC song and that god awful Sweet Caroline, the unimaginative dills playing the music would be all out of ideas.

It’s a shame when something truly clever and original gets the blame for a loss. But, being able to play that in a grand final at a neutral venue, well now, that’s a whole other question.

Mark Chandler, Brisbane Time’s up

I think we have seen the end of Wharfie Time, except that it will probably enter the vernacular as a synonym for a premature celebration.

Peter Neuhold, Elsternwick AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Trump

Peter Hartcher, writing of the US -China meeting, summed up Trump perfectly describing him as ″⁣like an over-excited adolescent″⁣(“Groveller-in-chief spurs Xi threat”, 29/9). This is exactly how Trump behaves on every issue!

Kay Moulton, Surrey Hills



Taiwan academic Chen Fangyu refers to “the Chinese communists’ enormous propaganda resources and their continuous attempts ... to brainwash the US public” (29/9). It seems like they’ve already succeeded with Trump.

Mind you, there isn’t much there to wash.

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills If Trump is bent on renaming a possibly liberated Hormuz Strait after himself, it will always be known as Trump’s Truth Bypass.

Jenifer Nicholls, Windsor “Trump offered to sell arms to China, US ambassador says” (29/9). ″⁣Pig Iron Trump″⁣?

Glenn Wood, Bardon, Qld One Nation

Pauline Hanson wants a crackdown on hate speech. Has she listened to herself?

Jane Cheong, Aspendale Gardens I’m in the market for a second-hand light plane. Can anyone point me in the right direction? Some craft spirits and beers would certainly sweeten the deal.

Mick Hussey, Beaconsfield



AFL

The greedy AFL placed financial gain ahead of fan enjoyment by granting Seven exclusive live coverage of the grand final. Millions of fans used to ad-free coverage during play on streaming services had to endure annoying adverts following every goal.

Phil Lipshut, Elsternwick Loved the pre-grand final extravaganza ... who was that fabulous woman on the stage with William Barton?

Raeleene Gregory, Ballarat East Finally

With the outrageous impact on the Yemeni people, I look forward to seeing weekend demonstrations against the Houthi rebels.

Irene Zalstein, East Doncaster The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Queues at 9am, full by 11.30am: Housing crunch challenges rough-sleeping plan
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHomelessness Queues at 9am, full by 11.30am: Housing crunch challenges rough-sleeping plan Cara Waters September 29, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Homelessness services warn that they are stretched beyond capacity and the state government’s $27.8 million assertive outreach program to reduce rough sleeping will further increase demand. Under a new statewide expansion of the “by-name” program, which already operates in inner Melbourne, teams of homelessness workers will be sent onto streets around Victoria to profile homeless people, build trust, prioritise those in the greatest need, and connect them to housing and other support services. The total number of people sleeping rough is unknown as some do not seek help. Eddie Jim However, homelessness services warn crisis accommodation centres are regularly full before lunchtime, and that homeless people end up being placed in unsafe accommodation. The City of Melbourne has been operating a by-name homelessness list since 2019 – rather than waiting for people to access services – but homelessness continues to grow in the CBD, with 140 people on the list.



Council to Homeless Persons chief executive Deborah Di Natale backed the state government’s push for assertive outreach as a vital lifeline for people sleeping rough, but she said it would probably cost $31 million to deliver and did not go far enough. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Eye contact and a coffee: The $28m plan to drastically cut rough sleeping “Homelessness is increasing across Victoria, and we know that the single biggest investment that is going to make a difference to ending homelessness in Victoria is to make a commitment to build more social housing,” she said. Council to Homeless Persons data shows 10,673 people sleeping rough sought support from specialist homelessness services in Victoria last year, a 25 per cent increase in five years. The actual number of rough sleepers in the state is unknown because many of them do not seek support. These are the people who are targeted with assertive outreach.



“If you have a look at people who are working on the frontline now, they have got a queue from 9am, by about 11 or 11.30 am every single housing option is exhausted, and they are then dealing with a queue of people that they can’t provide any crisis accommodation for,” Di Natale said. One young woman working on the frontline told her: “I have to make a decision about this woman who has come to me. Do I put her in this really unsafe, dodgy rooming house that I know is totally inappropriate? Or do I say, continue sleeping rough, knowing that when you are sleeping rough you are likely to be the victim of crime?” Melbourne City Mission chief executive Paul Wappett also backed assertive outreach as a positive start but similarly said more support services were needed, particularly for young people. “We’re going to increase the demand by doing these assertive outreach programs, and it’s important that we identify who needs these services and give our best opportunities to try and provide all the support that we need to,” he said. “But it will highlight just how much more housing we need for people who find themselves in homelessness.” Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio backs assertive outreach, and will outline his approach to tackling homelessness at next month’s Melbourne Assembly public forum.



Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece said the level of homelessness was less than its peak in 2019, when there were 500 homeless people in the CBD, but that the council’s by-name list – which proactively identifies every rough sleeper, tracks their progress, and aligns housing supply with individual needs – was not enough on its own. Lord Mayor Nick Reece says more housing is needed to tackle the homelessness problem. Penny Stephens “Homelessness, rough sleeping, is one of the most complex societal problems that we face, and it’s so multifaceted,” Reece said. “One component of it is the crisis in the mental health system manifests itself in people with acute mental health issues presenting on the streets.” The council has increased its Melbourne outreach team to seven workers, including trained mental health officers to deal with people with acute mental health issues. It has also opened the Make Room homelessness service, which houses 50 people. “Make Room has made a big difference in Melbourne,” Reece said. “But the truth is, we could use another two Make Rooms in the City of Melbourne.”



Related Article City life ‘I made a mistake’: Charities still waiting for Reece’s promised $9 million for the homeless Reece said that in a typical month, the council’s support team interacted 400 times with people experiencing homelessness, and service users made 5500 visits to the council’s safe-space program in August. “Across the board we need more services, more beds and more homes,” he said. “Obviously, when you’re assertively reaching out and helping someone on the street and giving them a pathway, they need somewhere to go. “That means that we need that injection of funds in emergency accommodation, temporary accommodation, and long-term accommodation as well.” Reece attracted criticism this year after failing to deliver on his promise of $6 million in homelessness funding to the Salvation Army and a further $3.2 million to Melbourne City Mission.



“The City of Melbourne’s putting more money into food relief than ever before, and Vincent Care, who are now delivering on that contract, are delivering more warm meals, hot breakfast to people than ever before,” he said.
